# Overview



This page is your architectural entry point into **IDPConformerGenerator** (IDPCG). It answers four questions a first-time contributor or user needs before writing any code: *what problem does this software solve*, *how is the repository organized*, *what is the end-to-end workflow*, and *where should you read next*. Each section is grounded in the actual source files, so every claim here can be traced back to code.

Sources: [index.rst](docs/index.rst#L1-L31)

## What Is IDPConformerGenerator?

IDPConformerGenerator is a flexible, modular platform for generating **ensembles of disordered protein states**. It builds conformers by sampling backbone torsion angles of relevant sequence fragments extracted from real protein structures in the RCSB Protein Data Bank. In plain terms: intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) have no single fixed 3D shape — they exist as a *population* of shapes — and this tool generates that population computationally, with user-defined control over secondary-structure populations (including populations matched to NMR chemical shift data). The resulting conformer pools are intended as input for further experimental-data-fitting approaches such as re-weighting or sub-setting algorithms.

The current release is **v0.10.1**, and the project is backed by three peer-reviewed/pre-print publications spanning three capability pillars, summarized below.

| Pillar | What it does | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| **IDPCG core** (`idpconfgen build`) | Generates large, diverse conformer pools of full-length disordered proteins by fragment-based torsion sampling | J. Phys. Chem. A 2022, DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpca.2c03726 |
| **LDRS** (`idpconfgen ldrs`) | Local Disordered Region Sampling — models disordered/missing segments attached to folded domains, including multi-chain complexes | Bioinformatics 2023, DOI: 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad739 |
| **AlphaFlex** (v0.8.X+, `alphaflex/`) | Proteome-scale ensembles of disordered regions derived from AlphaFold2 human proteome predictions (AFX-IDPCG protocol) | bioRxiv 2025, DOI: 10.1101/2025.11.24.690279 |

Sources: [README.rst](README.rst#L26-L36), [README.rst](README.rst#L70-L91), [README.rst](README.rst#L95-L97), [\_\_init\_\_.py](src/idpconfgen/__init__.py#L1-L3), [alphaflex/README.rst](alphaflex/README.rst#L1-L4)

## Repository at a Glance

The repository follows a conventional scientific-Python layout with a `src/`-based package, a curated examples library, and an extensive test suite. Here is the top-level structure, annotated by function:

```
IDPConformerGenerator/
├── README.rst                  # Project description & citations
├── pyproject.toml / setup.py   # Packaging; builds the idpcpp C++ extension
├── requirements.txt / .yml     # Dependency pins (pip / conda)
├── tox.ini                     # Test automation matrix
├── src/idpconfgen/             # THE PACKAGE
│   ├── cli.py                  # Subcommand dispatcher (21 subcommands)
│   ├── cli_*.py                # One module per CLI subcommand
│   ├── components/             # Pluggable strategies (bgeo, sidechains, k-mer probs)
│   ├── core/                   # Build definitions, exceptions, chemistry constants
│   ├── libs/                   # 20+ focused libraries (geometry, parsing, I/O, …)
│   ├── cpp/idpcpp.cpp          # pybind11 performance extension
│   └── conformer_generator.py  # Sequence k-mer search engine (see tip below)
├── example/                    # 6 reproducible research walkthroughs
├── tests/                      # ~30 pytest modules + fixture data
├── docs/                       # Sphinx docs incl. per-subcommand UML diagrams
├── alphaflex/                  # AlphaFlex proteome-scale protocol (v0.8.X+)
└── alphas/                     # Helper scripts + Rosetta-style residue params
```

To obtain the source, clone the repository or download the ZIP archive directly, as illustrated in the official first-steps guide:

![Downloading IDPConformerGenerator source](https://github.com/julie-forman-kay-lab/IDPConformerGenerator/blob/main/docs/assets/download.png?raw=true)

Three directories deserve special attention for a newcomer: `example/` contains fully reproducible scenarios (from a 100-PDB smoke test to multi-chain complexes) that double as living documentation; `tests/data/` ships curated fixture files (DSSP outputs, mmCIF samples, torsion JSONs) you can reuse in your own experiments; and `docs/UMLs/` contains UML class diagrams for nearly every major subcommand, rendered from PlantUML sources.

Sources: [first_steps.rst](docs/first_steps.rst#L12-L27), [setup.py](setup.py#L15-L28), [example/small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L1-L10), [alphaflex/README.rst](alphaflex/README.rst#L1-L10)

## The Two-Phase Workflow

Everything IDPCG does reduces to **two conceptual phases**, a distinction the maintainers themselves highlight as the key mental model for users. Phase 1 compiles a reusable *torsion-angle database* from experimental structures; Phase 2 samples that database to synthesize new conformers for your sequence of interest.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph P1["Phase 1 — Structural Database (build once, reuse forever)"]
        direction LR
        A["pdbdl<br/>download PDB/mmCIF<br/>from RCSB"] --> B["sscalc<br/>run DSSP for<br/>secondary structure"] --> C["torsions<br/>extract backbone<br/>φ/ψ angles"]
    end
    DB[("idpconfgen_database.json<br/>torsion-angle database")]
    subgraph P2["Phase 2 — Conformer Generation (run per target)"]
        direction LR
        D["build<br/>full IDP ensembles"] --> E[("PDB<br/>ensemble")]
        F["ldrs<br/>IDR loops on<br/>folded domains"] --> E
    end
    C --> DB
    DB --> D
    DB --> F
```

The canonical command chain (from the bundled smoke-test example) makes the pipeline concrete:

| Command | Phase | Purpose | Key output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `idpconfgen pdbdl cull100 -u -n -d pdbs.tar` | 1 | Downloads PDB files listed in a culled PISCES list, keeping only needed chains | `pdbs.tar` |
| `idpconfgen sscalc pdbs.tar -rd -n` | 1 | Runs DSSP to assign secondary structure per residue | `sscalc.json` + `sscalc_splitted.tar` |
| `idpconfgen torsions sscalc_splitted.tar -sc sscalc.json -o idpconfgen_database.json -n` | 1 | Extracts backbone torsion angles into a human-readable JSON database | `idpconfgen_database.json` |
| `idpconfgen build -db idpconfgen_database.json -seq EGAAGAASS -nc 10 --dloop-off --dany -n` | 2 | Assembles 10 full-length conformers for the given sequence | PDB files in working folder |

The `-n` flag controls parallelism across every command — appending it alone uses all available CPU threads except one, because all IDPCG operations distribute over multiple cores. Notice the asymmetry between phases: the database is built **once** and can be shared across projects and colleagues, while conformer generation is cheap and repeated per target sequence. Secondary-structure content is controlled at build time: `--dhelix`/`--dstrand` extend sampling beyond the default loop fragments, and the `-csss` flag accepts per-residue secondary-structure probabilities derived from NMR chemical shifts (processed via the `csssconv` subcommand from CheSPI/δ2D outputs).

Sources: [first_steps.rst](docs/first_steps.rst#L48-L58), [small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L28-L64), [small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L77-L105), [usage.rst](docs/usage.rst#L20-L27)

## Architecture Overview

Internally, IDPCG is a **subcommand-dispatch architecture**: a single `idpconfgen` executable routes to 21 independently-designed CLI modules, which in turn orchestrate a layered stack of strategy components, algorithm libraries, and a compiled C++ kernel. The single entry point is `python -m idpconfgen` (or the installed console script), which calls `maincli()` in `cli.py`.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    U["User terminal<br/>idpconfgen …"] --> D["cli.py<br/>argparse subcommand dispatcher"]
    D --> P["Primary pipeline<br/>pdbdl · sscalc · torsions · torsionsJ · build · ldrs"]
    D --> S["Secondary utilities<br/>bgeodb · fetch · csssconv · validate · stats · …"]
    P --> CMP["components/<br/>bgeo_strategies (4) · sidechain_packing (2) · xmer_probs"]
    S --> CMP
    CMP --> LIB["libs/<br/>libbuild · libcalc · libfilter · libmulticore · libcif · …"]
    P --> LIB
    LIB --> CPP["idpcpp<br/>pybind11 C++ extension"]
    P -.->|"invokes"| EXT["External third-party tools<br/>DSSP · MCSCE · Int2Cart (GPU, optional)"]
```

The dispatcher separates subcommands into two tiers: **primary routines** that constitute the main database-creation and building pipeline (`pdbdl`, `sscalc`, `torsions`, `torsionsJ`, `build`, `ldrs`), and **secondary routines** that provide auxiliary database tooling and analysis (`bgeo`, `bgeodb`, `fetch`, `ssext`, `fastaext`, `validate`, `dssppii`, `makecsss`, `csssconv`, `sethpc`, `merge`, `stats`, `search`, `resre`). Beneath the CLI tier, `libs/` provides focused single-responsibility libraries — `libcalc` for quaternion-based coordinate math, `libbuild` for assembly bookkeeping, `libfilter`/`libvalidate` for clash checking — while `components/` implements swappable strategy plugins selected through CLI flags. Performance-critical code is delegated to `idpcpp`, a pybind11 C++ extension compiled during installation. Two external scientific programs complement the stack: **DSSP** (required for secondary-structure calculation) and **MCSCE** (sidechain packing), with **Int2Cart** as an optional GPU accelerator for covalent bond geometry.

> [!TIP]
> **Naming trap:** despite its name, `conformer_generator.py` does *not* contain the main conformer-building engine — it hosts the `ProteinSearch` class, a recursive k-mer sequence pattern matcher that backs the `idpconfgen search` subcommand. The actual building engine lives in `cli_build.py` (~1,900 lines) orchestrating `libs/libbuild.py` and `libs/libcalc.py`. Keep this in mind when grepping the codebase.

Sources: [\_\_main\_\_.py](src/idpconfgen/\_\_main\_\_.py#L1-L16), [cli.py](src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L93-L115), [cli.py](src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L26-L56), [first_steps.rst](docs/first_steps.rst#L35-L37), [setup.py](setup.py#L15-L28), [conformer_generator.py](src/idpconfgen/conformer_generator.py#L8-L13)

The project also maintains formal UML class diagrams for each major subcommand; the overall pipeline diagram is reproduced below:

![IDPConfGen pipeline UML](https://github.com/julie-forman-kay-lab/IDPConformerGenerator/blob/main/docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pipeline.svg?raw=true)

Sources: [UMLs/](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pipeline.svg#L1)

## Key Concepts for Newcomers

Before diving into the deep-dive pages, four concepts recur throughout the codebase and documentation. Understanding them now will make every later page easier:

| Concept | Plain-language meaning | Where it lives | Deep-dive page |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Torsion-angle database** | A JSON dictionary mapping sequence fragments to the φ/ψ backbone angles observed in experimental structures — the "raw material" for building | `cli_torsions.py` → output of Phase 1 | [Building Pipeline](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble) |
| **K-mer torsion probabilities** | Probability statistics over sequence windows of varying length (monomer → pentamer) used to bias which fragments get sampled | `components/xmer_probs.py` | [K-mer Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling) |
| **Bond-geometry strategies** | Four pluggable schemes for assigning bond lengths/angles during assembly | `components/bgeo_strategies/` | [Bond Geometry](8-bond-geometry-strategies) |
| **Sidechain packing** | Algorithms that attach amino-acid side chains onto the built backbone | `components/sidechain_packing/` | [Sidechain Packing](11-sidechain-packing-methods) |

The bond-geometry strategy choice deserves a brief comparison, since it is the most user-visible build parameter (`--bgeo-strategy` flag):

| Strategy | Behavior | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| `sampling` (default) | Samples bond geometries to overcome the diversity limits of fixed geometry | none |
| `fixed` | Uses average per-residue bond geometries from a Dunbrack PISCES database | none |
| `exact` | Uses exact bond/bend angles and lengths for each residue of the sampled fragment | database rebuilt via `bgeodb` |
| `int2cart` | GPU-assisted coordinate reconstruction from internal coordinates | Int2Cart installed + CUDA GPU |

Sources: [usage.rst](docs/usage.rst#L46-L60), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L30-L38), [first_steps.rst](docs/first_steps.rst#L35-L37)

## Quality & Testing Infrastructure

The project maintains a substantial verification layer: roughly 30 pytest modules in `tests/` covering everything from low-level parsers (`test_libcif.py`, `test_libpdb.py`) through numeric kernels (`test_libcalc.py`, `test_libenergyij.py`) to end-to-end CLI behavior (`test_cli_build.py`, `test_cli_ldrs.py`). Continuous integration runs the suite on every push (see the test-status badge), and `tox.ini` defines the automation matrix used for reproducible test environments. All fixtures live under `tests/data/`, so test behavior is deterministic and offline-friendly.

Sources: [tests/](tests/tcommons.py#L1), [README.rst](README.rst#L6-L13), [tox.ini](tox.ini#L1)

# Quick Start



IDPConformerGenerator (IDPCG) is a flexible, modular platform for generating ensembles of disordered protein states by sampling backbone torsion angles of sequence fragments extracted from the RCSB Protein Data Bank [README.rst](README.rst#L15-L27). This page compresses the entire journey from an empty terminal to your first conformer ensemble into three verified steps: **install**, **understand the two-phase workflow**, and **run the minimal working example**. Everything documented here is drawn directly from the repository's own onboarding materials and source code — no speculative commands.

By the end of this page you will have: an installed `idpconfgen` command (v0.10.1) [src/idpconfgen/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/__init__.py#L69-L70), a working torsion-angle database, and 10 conformational structures of a test peptide on disk. Deeper installation variants (HPC clusters, third-party accelerators) and a full tutorial live in their dedicated catalog pages, linked at the end.

Sources: [README.rst](README.rst#L15-L37), [src/idpconfgen/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/__init__.py#L69-L70)

## The Big Picture: One Gateway Command, Two Core Activities

Every interaction with the software flows through a single entry point: the `idpconfgen` command. Internally it is a dispatcher that exposes sub-clients (sub-commands), each registered in the CLI parser — six form the main database-creation pipeline (`pdbdl`, `sscalc`, `torsions`, `torsionsJ`, `build`, `ldrs`), with a further fourteen utility routines (e.g., `csssconv`, `fetch`, `validate`, `stats`) available as secondary sub-commands [src/idpconfgen/cli.py](src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L54-L105). Conceptually, all of this reduces to **two activities** the official first-steps guide asks you to keep in mind:

1. **Create your structural database** — fully customizable, reusable across projects, and shareable with colleagues.
2. **Generate conformers** — via `idpconfgen build` for full IDP conformers, or `idpconfgen ldrs` for disordered regions inside folded domains [docs/first_steps.rst](docs/first_steps.rst#L38-L68).

The following diagram maps how the sub-commands chain together to serve these two activities — each arrow is a real file artifact passed from one command to the next:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["PISCES culled list<br/>(cull100 / culled list)"] -->|"PDB IDs"| B["idpconfgen pdbdl"]
    B -->|"pdbs.tar"| C["idpconfgen sscalc<br/>(requires DSSP)"]
    C -->|"sscalc.json +<br/>sscalc_splitted.tar"| D["idpconfgen torsions"]
    D -->|"idpconfgen_database.json<br/>(torsion-angle DB)"| E["idpconfgen build"]
    D -->|same DB| F["idpconfgen ldrs<br/>(IDR in folded domains)"]
    E -->|".pdb conformers<br/>(× nc)"| G(("Ensemble"))
    F --> G
    H["CSSS probabilities<br/>(csssconv / makecsss)"] -.->|"optional<br/>-csss flag"| E
```

**Key insight**: the database phase is a one-time investment per project — once `idpconfgen_database.json` exists, the build phase can be re-run endlessly against it with different sequences and sampling strategies. The `build` command reads this human-readable JSON database and assembles conformers by sampling torsion angles from fragments relevant to your target sequence [example/small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L62-L76).

Sources: [src/idpconfgen/cli.py](src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L54-L105), [docs/first_steps.rst](docs/first_steps.rst#L38-L68), [example/small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L62-L76)

## Step 1 — Express Installation (≈10 minutes)

IDPConformerGenerator is pure Python (Python ≥3.8, <3.12) and has been verified on Ubuntu 18.04/20.04 LTS, WSL 2.0, and the Graham cluster (Digital Research Alliance of Canada) [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L10-L16), [requirements.yml](requirements.yml#L1-L14). Clone the repository, then run the express installer — three commands, executed **sequentially**, waiting for each to finish:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/julie-forman-kay-lab/IDPConformerGenerator
cd IDPConformerGenerator
./install_miniconda3.sh
source activate.sh
./install_deps.sh
```

Each script has one precise responsibility:

| Script | Action | Verified implementation |
|---|---|---|
| `install_miniconda3.sh` | Downloads and installs Miniconda3 (py39) into a local `miniconda3/` folder inside the repo | [install_miniconda3.sh](install_miniconda3.sh#L1-L10) |
| `activate.sh` | Sources `miniconda3/bin/activate` to enable the conda environment | [activate.sh](activate.sh#L1-L4) |
| `install_deps.sh` | `conda env update --file requirements.yml`, then `python setup.py develop --no-deps` to register the package | [install_deps.sh](install_deps.sh#L1-L7) |

The express route takes ~10 minutes because it installs the package manager itself plus all dependencies; skilled conda users can instead build an environment directly from `requirements.yml` in 2–4 minutes [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L33-L51). Deletion is equally simple: remove the `IDPConformerGenerator` directory and everything goes with it.

> [!TIP]
> The environment does **not** persist across terminal sessions. Every new terminal window requires re-activation before the `idpconfgen` command exists: `cd path/to/IDPConformerGenerator && source activate.sh`. This is the single most common first-run failure.

Sources: [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L33-L72), [install_miniconda3.sh](install_miniconda3.sh#L1-L10), [install_deps.sh](install_deps.sh#L1-L7), [activate.sh](activate.sh#L1-L4), [requirements.yml](requirements.yml#L1-L14)

## Step 2 — Verify the Command Gateway

With the environment active, confirm the entry point responds. Running `idpconfgen -h` prints the dispatcher's help, which enumerates every registered sub-command; running bare `idpconfgen` also prints help because the parser short-circuits when fewer than two arguments are given [src/idpconfgen/cli.py](src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L117-L147). Every sub-command additionally supports its own `-h`, e.g. `idpconfgen build -h`, which is the canonical way to discover fine-tuning parameters [example/small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L47-L48).

A side effect worth knowing for support requests: any invocation writes an `idpconfgen.version` file to the current directory recording the exact version in use [src/idpconfgen/cli.py](src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L141-L144).

Sources: [src/idpconfgen/cli.py](src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L117-L147), [example/small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L47-L48)

## Step 3 — Your First Conformer Ensemble (the 4-Command Pipeline)

The repository ships a deliberately minimal integration test: the **small peptide example**, which builds a demo database from just 100 PDB entries and produces 10 conformers of the sequence `EGAAGAASS`. It exists specifically "to test the installation" — the resulting database is for verification, not science [example/small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L1-L12). Navigate to `example/small_peptide/` and run the four commands in order:

```bash
cd example/small_peptide
idpconfgen pdbdl cull100 -u -n -d pdbs.tar
idpconfgen sscalc pdbs.tar -rd -n
idpconfgen torsions sscalc_splitted.tar -sc sscalc.json -o idpconfgen_database.json -n
idpconfgen build -db idpconfgen_database.json -seq EGAAGAASS -nc 10 --dloop-off --dany -n
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S0["Start: example/small_peptide/"] --> S1["1. pdbdl cull100<br/>downloads 100 PDBs → pdbs.tar"]
    S1 --> S2["2. sscalc pdbs.tar -rd<br/>assigns DSSP secondary structure<br/>→ sscalc.json + sscalc_splitted.tar"]
    S2 --> S3["3. torsions ... -o idpconfgen_database.json<br/>extracts (φ, ψ, ω) torsion angles"]
    S3 --> S4["4. build -db ... -seq EGAAGAASS -nc 10<br/>samples torsions → 10 .pdb conformers"]
    S4 --> D(("Done: 10 conformers<br/>in working folder"))
```

Each command consumes the previous command's artifact and produces the next one's input — the pipeline is a strict file-mediated chain:

| # | Command | Input | Output | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `idpconfgen pdbdl cull100 -u -n -d pdbs.tar` | PISCES-format culled list (only the first column — PDB ID + chain — is read) | `pdbs.tar` with pre-filtered PDB files | Downloads structures from RCSB, stripping unnecessary chains/residues [example/small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L17-L52) |
| 2 | `idpconfgen sscalc pdbs.tar -rd -n` | `pdbs.tar` | `sscalc.json` (sequence↔SS map) + `sscalc_splitted.tar` (chains split into continuous segments) | Secondary-structure assignment via installed DSSP [example/small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L54-L61) |
| 3 | `idpconfgen torsions sscalc_splitted.tar -sc sscalc.json -o idpconfgen_database.json -n` | split tar + SS map | `idpconfgen_database.json` — the **torsion-angle database** | The one file `build` ultimately needs; human-readable JSON [example/small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L63-L69) |
| 4 | `idpconfgen build -db idpconfgen_database.json -seq EGAAGAASS -nc 10 --dloop-off --dany -n` | database + target sequence | 10 `.pdb` conformer files | Generates the ensemble; `-nc` controls the count (default 1) [example/small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L72-L81), [src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L243-L249) |

Three flags deserve explanation before you run them. The `-n`/`--ncores` flag is shared by all commands: bare `-n` uses **all CPU cores except one**, while `-n 4` pins exactly four [src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L522-L537). The `--dany` flag samples the database purely by sequence identity, and requires `--dloop-off` because loop-search is active by default; conversely `--dhelix`/`--dstrand` extend sampling to helices and strands (they require the `-rd` flag you already passed to `sscalc`) [src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L380-L415). The `-seq` flag accepts either an inline one-letter sequence or a FASTA file path [src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L417-L428).

> [!TIP]
> DSSP is only needed for step 2 — i.e., only when building a database *from scratch*. If you download the team's pre-built database JSON (based on a ~27k-chain PISCES culled list, linked from the installation docs), you can skip installation of DSSP entirely and jump straight to `build` [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L196-L210).

Sources: [example/small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L17-L106), [src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L380-L537), [src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L243-L249), [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L196-L210)

## Optional First Experiment — Probabilistic Secondary-Structure Sampling

The same example folder includes a second, optional `build` variant demonstrating Custom Secondary Structure Sampling (CSSS): the CheSPI/δ2D prediction file `probs8_ex.txt` is converted to a probability JSON, then passed to `build` via `-csss` [example/small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L84-L100):

```bash
idpconfgen csssconv -p8 probs8_ex.txt -o csss_ex.json
idpconfgen build -db idpconfgen_database.json -seq EGAAGAASS -nc 10 -csss csss_ex.json --dloop-off -n
```

The `-csss` flag requires `--dloop-off` and replaces the `--dhelix/--dstrand/--dany` selection with per-residue probabilities (L/H/E) from the JSON produced by `csssconv` [src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L297-L305). This is your first taste of the sampling-strategy layer that later pages unpack in depth — for reproducibility in either mode, note that `-rs` sets a random seed (default 0) [src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L596-L604).

Sources: [example/small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L84-L100), [src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L297-L305), [src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L596-L604)

## Troubleshooting Quick Reference

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `idpconfgen: command not found` in a new terminal | Environment not activated | `cd` to repo root and `source activate.sh` [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L64-L72) |
| `sscalc` fails with DSSP missing | Third-party dependency absent | Install DSSP (v2, v3, or v4 supported; check `mkdssp --version`) or use the pre-built database JSON [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L196-L210) |
| Sidechain packing unavailable | MCSCE not installed (it is optional) | Follow the MCSCE install steps, then use `-scm mcsce` in `build` [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L213-L245) |
| Want better covalent bond geometry | Int2Cart not installed (needs CUDA GPU) | Install Int2Cart on top of the `idpconfgen` environment [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L247-L273) |
| Sampling only loop-like fragments | Loop search is on by default | Toggle with `--dloop-off`, `--dhelix`, `--dstrand`, or `--dany` per the flag compatibility rules [src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L380-L415) |

Sources: [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L64-L273), [src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L380-L415)

## Where to Go Next

You have now completed the install-and-verify loop. The recommended reading progression through this catalog:

- **[Installation & Environment Setup](3-installation-and-environment-setup)** — cluster installations (Graham/DRAC), manual conda environments, and full third-party software setup (MCSCE, Int2Cart, CheSPI, δ2D, SPyCi-PDB, X-EISDv2) before scaling beyond the toy example.
- **[Tutorial: First Conformer Ensemble](4-tutorial-first-conformer-ensemble)** — a guided, parameter-by-parameter walkthrough of the same pipeline you just ran.
- **[Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview)** — how the CLI dispatcher, component plugin pattern, and multiprocessing layer fit together under the hood.
- **[Research Examples Library](23-research-examples-library)** — five production-grade case studies (`cnot7`, `drksh3`, `slc26a9`, complexes, peptides) showing how real projects scale the 4-command pipeline.

For reference while exploring: the complete sub-command catalog is `pdbdl`, `sscalc`, `torsions`, `torsionsJ`, `build`, `ldrs` (main pipeline) plus `bgeo`, `bgeodb`, `fastaext`, `fetch`, `ssext`, `validate`, `dssppii`, `makecsss`, `csssconv`, `sethpc`, `merge`, `stats`, `search`, `resre` (utilities) [src/idpconfgen/cli.py](src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L56-L105).


# Installation & Environment Setup



IDPConformerGenerator (IDPCG) is a scientific Python suite, which means its installation has two layers: a **Python runtime environment** (Conda) and the **package itself** (an editable install that also compiles a small C++ extension). This page covers everything needed to go from a fresh machine to a working `idpconfgen` terminal command — the express installation path, the dependency matrix, the build step internals, environment activation, updating, HPC alternatives, and the optional third-party tools that extend the core. Usage of the tool itself is deliberately out of scope here; once installed, continue to the [Tutorial: First Conformer Ensemble](4-tutorial-first-conformer-ensemble).

Sources: [README.rst](README.rst#L48-L51), [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L1-L6)

## The Installation Stack at a Glance

The express installation is not a single `pip install` — it is a three-stage pipeline that bootstraps a **local, project-private Conda distribution** inside the repository folder. This design keeps IDPCG fully isolated from your system Python: everything lives under `IDPConformerGenerator/miniconda3/`, and uninstalling is simply deleting the repository directory. The pipeline end state is a Conda environment named `idpconfgen`, an editable copy of the Python package, a compiled `idpcpp` extension module, and a console command named `idpconfgen`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["install_miniconda3.sh"] --> B["./miniconda3/<br/>local Miniconda3-py39 distribution"]
    B --> C["activate.sh<br/>source miniconda3/bin/activate"]
    C --> D["install_deps.sh"]
    D --> E["conda env update<br/>--file requirements.yml"]
    D --> F["python setup.py develop --no-deps"]
    E --> G["idpconfgen Conda environment<br/>Python 3.8–3.11 · numpy · numba<br/>scipy · matplotlib · pybind11 · tox"]
    F --> H["editable idpconfgen package"]
    F --> I["idpcpp<br/>C++/pybind11 extension"]
    H --> J["terminal command:<br/>idpconfgen"]
    I --> J
```

The complete installation stack decomposes into four layers:

| Layer | Artifact | Produced by | Beginner explanation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package manager | `./miniconda3/` directory | `install_miniconda3.sh` | A private copy of Conda, so the project never touches your system Python |
| Python environment | Conda env `idpconfgen` | `install_deps.sh` (first step) | An isolated sandbox holding Python 3.8–3.11 and all pinned scientific libraries |
| Application package | `idpconfgen` (editable) | `install_deps.sh` (second step) | The source code in `src/` is linked into the environment rather than copied, so code edits are live |
| Native extension | `idpcpp` module | build step inside `setup.py` | A compiled C++ speed-up module bridged into Python via pybind11 |

Sources: [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L44-L57), [install_miniconda3.sh](install_miniconda3.sh#L1-L10), [install_deps.sh](install_deps.sh#L1-L7)

The installation-relevant files are concentrated at the repository root, making the setup easy to audit. The following tree is your map for everything this page discusses:

```
IDPConformerGenerator/
├── install_miniconda3.sh   # Stage 1: bootstrap local Conda
├── activate.sh             # Activation helper for every new terminal
├── install_deps.sh         # Stage 2+3: env creation + package build
├── requirements.yml        # Conda environment definition (source of truth)
├── requirements.txt        # pip mirror of the same pins
├── pyproject.toml          # Build-system declaration (pybind11)
├── setup.py                # Package metadata + idpcpp extension compilation
├── devtools/
│   ├── requirements.txt    # CI/testing tooling (coverage, coveralls)
│   └── docs_requirements.txt  # Sphinx documentation toolchain
├── tox.ini                 # Task automation: test, lint, docs, build
└── src/
    └── idpconfgen/
        ├── cli.py          # Entry point target: idpconfgen.cli:maincli
        └── cpp/
            └── idpcpp.cpp  # Source of the compiled idpcpp extension
```

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L4), [setup.py](setup.py#L17-L26)

## Platform Support & Prerequisites

The maintainers state that IDPCG uses only Python-based APIs and therefore runs anywhere Python runs, provided third-party requirements are met. Concretely verified test targets are Ubuntu 18.04 LTS, Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, Windows via WSL 2.0, and the Graham cluster of the Digital Research Alliance of Canada (DRAC) — which makes Linux the path of least resistance for beginners.

| Platform | Status | Recommended route |
|---|---|---|
| Ubuntu 18.04 / 20.04 LTS | Explicitly tested | Express scripts (three commands) |
| Windows | Via WSL 2.0 | Express scripts inside WSL |
| DRAC Graham cluster (HPC) | Explicitly tested | `virtualenv` route (no Conda in home folder) |
| Any OS with Python | Expected to work | Manual `conda env create -f requirements.yml` |

Beyond `git`, two prerequisites matter. The stage-1 script downloads Miniconda with `wget`, so `wget` must exist; and the build stage compiles a C++ extension through pybind11, so a working C++ toolchain is required for the compile to succeed.

Sources: [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L3-L14), [install_miniconda3.sh](install_miniconda3.sh#L5-L6), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L4)

## Express Installation: The Three-Command Path

After cloning the official repository (`git clone https://github.com/julie-forman-kay-lab/IDPConformerGenerator`) and entering the folder, the entire setup reduces to three commands executed **in sequence, each fully finished before the next**. The maintainers document the expected cost: creating the environment from `requirements.yml` alone takes 2–4 minutes, while the express path takes roughly 10 minutes because it also fetches and installs the Miniconda manager itself. If you downloaded the ZIP instead of cloning, skip the `git clone` step as noted in the first-steps guide.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start(["git clone the repository"]) --> Step0["cd IDPConformerGenerator"]
    Step0 --> S1["1. ./install_miniconda3.sh<br/>download + silent-install Miniconda3 into ./miniconda3"]
    S1 --> S2["2. source activate.sh<br/>activate the freshly installed local Conda"]
    S2 --> S3["3. ./install_deps.sh<br/>conda env update + editable build of idpconfgen"]
    S3 --> V["Verify: idpconfgen -h prints the subcommand list"]
    V --> Done(["Done — source activate.sh in every new terminal session"])
```

![download](https://github.com/julie-forman-kay-lab/IDPConformerGenerator/blob/main/docs/assets/download.png?raw=true)

Each script is a few lines and worth reading before running — transparency is a feature here:

| Script | Content | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `install_miniconda3.sh` | `wget` the `Miniconda3-py39_24.3.0-0-Linux-x86_64.sh` installer into `miniconda3/`, then `bash ... -b -u -p miniconda3` for a silent, self-contained install, then deletes the installer | A private Conda distribution, entirely inside the repo folder |
| `activate.sh` | `source miniconda3/bin/activate` | Puts the local Conda on your `PATH` for the current shell |
| `install_deps.sh` | `conda env update --file requirements.yml` followed by `python setup.py develop --no-deps` | Builds the `idpconfgen` Conda environment, then installs the package in editable mode with its native extension |

Sources: [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L21-L57), [docs/first_steps.rst](docs/first_steps.rst#L17-L19), [install_miniconda3.sh](install_miniconda3.sh#L1-L10), [install_deps.sh](install_deps.sh#L1-L7)

> [!TIP]
> The `--no-deps` flag in `python setup.py develop --no-deps` is deliberate, not an omission. Inspecting `setup.py` shows `install_requires` is an empty list: the Conda environment created from `requirements.yml` is the single authority on dependency versions. Letting pip resolve dependencies too would create two competing version resolvers and could silently violate the carefully pinned scientific stack (e.g., the `numpy<2` ceiling).

> [!TIP]
> Notice the exact filename in `install_miniconda3.sh`: `Miniconda3-py39_24.3.0-0-Linux-x86_64.sh`. The express one-command path is **Linux x86_64-specific**. On macOS or other architectures, bypass the express scripts and create the environment manually with `conda env create -f requirements.yml`, which is the route the maintainers recommend for users "skilled managing custom Python environments".

## The Dependency Matrix: requirements.yml vs requirements.txt

The project ships two dependency manifests that describe the **same scientific stack** for two different package managers. `requirements.yml` is the authoritative Conda definition consumed by `install_deps.sh`; `requirements.txt` is the pip-formatted mirror used by flows such as tox test environments and cluster installs. Beginners only need to know one rule: `requirements.yml` drives the express install; `requirements.txt` is what tooling like `tox -e test` consumes.

| Dependency | Pin | Role in IDPCG |
|---|---|---|
| python | `>=3.8, <3.12` | Runtime floor and ceiling |
| numpy | `>=1.22.4, <2` | Numeric foundation for geometry/torsion math |
| numba | `>=0.53.0, <1` | JIT compilation of performance-critical kernels |
| pybind11 | `>=2.9.2, <2.13.6` | Python↔C++ bridge for the `idpcpp` extension |
| scipy | `>=1.8.1, <2` | Scientific algorithms |
| matplotlib | `>=3.5.2, <4` | Plotting output |
| setuptools | `>=70.0.0, <80` | Build backend |
| pip | latest | Wheel/package installation |
| tox | `=4` | Task automation (tests, lint, docs, builds) |

The pinning style reveals deliberate defensive engineering: upper bounds guard against breaking major releases (`numpy<2` is the classic example — NumPy 2.0 broke ABI compatibility across the scientific ecosystem), while the pybind11 window `>=2.9.2, <2.13.6` brackets the range compatible with the extension build. `requirements.txt` repeats the same constraints minus the `python` and `pip` entries, which pip does not manage.

Sources: [requirements.yml](requirements.yml#L1-L14), [requirements.txt](requirements.txt#L1-L8), [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L32-L42)

## Under the Hood: What `setup.py develop --no-deps` Builds

The build step performs two distinct jobs, and understanding them demystifies most install errors. First, it registers the package in **editable/develop mode**: combined with the `src` layout (`package_dir={'': 'src'}`), the installed `idpconfgen` points at the repository source, so any code change is immediately reflected without reinstalling. Second — and this is the non-obvious part — it compiles a **pybind11 C++ extension** named `idpcpp` from the single translation unit `src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp`, declared via `Pybind11Extension` and wired through a custom `build_ext` command class.

Key metadata from `setup.py`:

| Field | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` / `version` | `idpconfgen` / `0.10.1` | Package identity; matches the version in the README |
| `packages` / `package_dir` | `find_packages('src')` / `{'': 'src'}` | Source lives under `src/`, not the repo root |
| `python_requires` | `>=3.8, <4` | Broader than the Conda pin — Conda is stricter |
| `install_requires` | *(empty)* | Dependencies deliberately delegated to Conda |
| `entry_points` | `idpconfgen = idpconfgen.cli:maincli` | This line creates the terminal command |
| `ext_modules` | `idpcpp` from `src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp` | The compiled C++ speed-up module |

The build system itself is declared in `pyproject.toml` as `setuptools` + `wheel` + `pybind11~=2.6.1`, which is why the conda environment pre-installs pybind11 before `install_deps.sh` ever runs.

Sources: [setup.py](setup.py#L14-L30), [setup.py](setup.py#L51-L100), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L4), [CONTRIBUTING.rst](CONTRIBUTING.rst#L48-L56)

## Activating the Environment in Daily Use

Installation is not activation — **every new terminal window starts outside the environment**, and the maintainers call this out in bold in their docs. To work with IDPCG, navigate to the repository root and run:

```bash
cd path/to/my/IDPConformerGenerator
source activate.sh
```

Because the environment is a standard Conda environment, the equivalent — and slightly more explicit — invocation is `conda activate idpconfgen`, which the first-steps guide also demonstrates. Verification is immediate: a working install puts the `idpconfgen` command on your `PATH`, and running it displays the suite of subcommands (sub-clients) the first-steps page describes — some tasks are single commands, others chain several.

Sources: [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L59-L64), [activate.sh](activate.sh#L1-L4), [docs/first_steps.rst](docs/first_steps.rst#L25-L32)

## Updating an Existing Installation

The update procedure embraces the "everything inside one folder" philosophy by **destroying and rebuilding the entire Conda installation**: remove `miniconda3/`, pull the latest source, and re-run the same three express commands. Because your environment is fully local and disposable, this is safe — but it has a documented side effect you must plan for.

```bash
rm -rf miniconda3
git pull
./install_miniconda3.sh
source activate.sh
./install_deps.sh
```

The reinstall wipes anything that was layered **on top of** the `idpconfgen` environment. The docs explicitly list the casualties: MCSCE, Int2Cart, SPyCi-PDB, and X-EISDv2 must be reinstalled into the fresh environment after an update — keep their install recipes handy (see the optional integrations section below).

Sources: [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L66-L87)

## HPC Route: DRAC Graham Cluster via virtualenv

Shared HPC systems often forbid Conda installations in home directories, so the docs provide a fully specified alternative for the Graham cluster using Python's built-in `virtualenv`. The flow diverges from the express path in its first half and reconverges on the same final build command:

| Step | Command | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Load system modules | `module load scipy-stack dssp boost` | Supplies scientific stack, DSSP, and Boost |
| Create environment | `virtualenv --no-download idpcgenv` then `source idpcgenv/bin/activate` | `--no-download` uses only cluster-local wheels |
| Prime dependencies | `pip install --no-index --upgrade pip`, `pip install numba --no-index`, `pip install pybind11 --no-index`, `pip install tox` | `--no-index` searches DRAC's mirror first, web as fallback |
| Clone & install | `git clone ...`, `cd IDPConformerGenerator`, `python setup.py develop --no-deps` | Identical editable build as local |
| Reactivate per session | `cd`, `source idpcgenv/bin/activate` | On every future login |

Note that on this route you install `numba` and `pybind11` **before** the package, because with `--no-deps` pip never resolves them for you — the environment must already contain everything `setup.py` needs at build time.

Sources: [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L89-L130)

## Optional Third-Party Software: Extending the Environment

The core install is deliberately lean; heavier capabilities are opt-in add-ons installed **on top of** the `idpconfgen` environment (the docs even recommend that SPyCi-PDB and X-EISDv2 live inside it, since they depend on IDPConfGen themselves). None are mandatory — install only what your workflow needs:

| Tool | What it adds | Unlocked command/flag | Install route |
|---|---|---|---|
| DSSP (v2, v3, or v4) | Secondary-structure assignment | `idpconfgen sscalc` when compiling a database from scratch | `sudo apt install dssp` on Ubuntu 22.04+ (installs v4); check with `mkdssp --version` |
| MCSCE | Monte-Carlo sidechain packing on generated backbones | `idpconfgen build -scm mcsce` (adds a dedicated parameter group) | Clone `THGLab/MCSCE`; `pip install tensorflow tqdm pathos`; `python setup.py develop --no-deps` inside it, then reinstall IDPCG on top |
| Int2Cart | On-the-fly bond-geometry optimization | Automatic during `build` | Requires a CUDA-compatible GPU; install `sidechainnet` then `int2cart` via `pip install -e`; cluster needs `module load cuda` |
| CheSPI | Chemical-shift secondary-structure (CSSS) conversion | `idpconfgen csssconv` | External per its repository instructions |
| δ2D | Alternative CS-based secondary-structure prediction | `idpconfgen csssconv` | External per its repository instructions |
| SPyCi-PDB | Experimental data back-calculators | Ensemble validation workflow | `pip install pandas natsort`, clone into the parent directory, `python setup.py develop --no-deps` |
| X-EISDv2 | Reweighting/scoring protocol | `xeisd` CLI | Same pattern: `pip install pandas natsort`, clone, editable install |

Two time-savers documented by the maintainers: if you use a pre-prepared database JSON (a Dunbrack PISCES-based database is linked from the installation page), **you do not need DSSP at all**; and if both SPyCi-PDB and X-EISDv2 are wanted, the `pandas`/`natsort` pip installs are done only once for both. For DSSP version 4, note that `idpconfgen sscalc` normalizes PPII assignment across versions by default (`--native-ppii` keeps v4's own PPII calls) — relevant only when generating databases.

Sources: [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L132-L153), [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L162-L190), [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L210-L231), [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L247-L257), [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L259-L307)

## Developer Environment & Task Automation

If you intend to contribute rather than just use, the setup differs only in the first step: fork the repository, clone **your fork**, add the upstream remote, and then create the environment explicitly with `conda env create -f requirements.yml` followed by the same editable install. The `develop` mode plus the `src` layout guarantee you always execute the code you are editing — a property the contributing guide names explicitly as the point of the configuration.

Task automation runs through **tox**, pinned to v4 in `requirements.yml` and self-contained in `tox.ini`. Each environment isolates one concern:

| Tox env | Purpose | Notable configuration |
|---|---|---|
| `test` | pytest + coverage + hypothesis | Sets `TOXTESTING=1`, which **skips C++ compilation** — no compiler needed to run tests |
| `lint` | flake8 + isort checks | numpy docstring convention, 80-char lines |
| `docs` | Builds the Sphinx documentation | Uses `devtools/docs_requirements.txt` (sphinx 5.x, sphinx-argparse, rtd-theme) |
| `build` | sdist/wheel packaging + twine checks + version bump dry-runs | Uses `devtools/clean_dist_check.py` |
| `pr` | Verifies a changelog entry exists | Runs `devtools/check_changelog.py` |
| `radon` / `safety` | Complexity metrics / CVE checks | Optional quality gates |

The `TOXTESTING` mechanism is visible directly in `setup.py`: the extension is only declared when the environment is *not* a tox test run (`TOX_ENV_NAME` absent, or `TOXTESTING` present), and `tox.ini` sets `TOXTESTING=1` in its test env. This is why contributing is possible on compiler-less machines. For building the docs yourself: `tox -e docs` emits HTML into `dist/docs` from the Sphinx sources in `docs/`, whose toolchain (`sphinx>=5,<6`, `sphinx-argparse==0.3.1`, `sphinx-rtd-theme>=1.0.0`) is declared in `devtools/docs_requirements.txt`.

Sources: [CONTRIBUTING.rst](CONTRIBUTING.rst#L41-L86), [tox.ini](tox.ini#L16-L31), [setup.py](setup.py#L14-L30), [devtools/docs_requirements.txt](devtools/docs_requirements.txt#L1-L7), [devtools/requirements.txt](devtools/requirements.txt#L1-L6)

## Troubleshooting Quick Reference

Most installation friction maps onto a small set of recurring causes:

| Symptom | Root cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `idpconfgen: command not found` in a new terminal | Environment not activated (every shell starts de-activated) | `source activate.sh` from the repo root, or `conda activate idpconfgen` |
| `ImportError: TensorBoard logging requires TensorBoard version 1.15 or above` when testing Int2Cart's `BackboneBuilder` import | TensorBoard version conflict from the Int2Cart stack | Verify via `python -c "from modelling.models.builder import BackboneBuilder"`, then `pip install tensorboard==1.15.0` |
| MCSCE / Int2Cart / SPyCi-PDB / X-EISDv2 vanish after updating | The documented update procedure deletes the entire `miniconda3/` tree | Re-run each add-on's installation after `install_deps.sh` |
| Build step fails while compiling `idpcpp` | No C++ toolchain available (pybind11 compiles native code at install time) | Install a compiler toolchain (e.g., `build-essential` on Debian/Ubuntu), then re-run `./install_deps.sh` |
| Wrong Python or pip being used after manual setup | System Python shadowing the Conda env | Confirm `which python` points into `miniconda3/envs/idpconfgen` (or `idpcgenv` on DRAC) |

Sources: [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L59-L64), [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L233-L245), [docs/installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L85-L87), [setup.py](setup.py#L19-L26)

## Where to Go Next

With the environment installed and `idpconfgen` responding on your command line, the natural progression through this documentation is: [Tutorial: First Conformer Ensemble](4-tutorial-first-conformer-ensemble) to produce your first output, then [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview) for the mental model of how the suite is organized. Follow-ups matched to the optional components you installed: [Sidechain Packing Methods](11-sidechain-packing-methods) explains what MCSCE does once `-scm mcsce` is enabled, [NMR Chemical Shift Matching](10-nmr-chemical-shift-matching) covers the CheSPI/δ2D CSSS territory, and [Testing Strategy & Fixtures](22-testing-strategy-and-fixtures) deepens the tox-based developer workflow introduced above.


# Tutorial: First Conformer Ensemble



This tutorial walks you, step by step, from an empty working directory to your first ensemble of intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) conformers using IDPConformerGenerator (IDPCG). You will compile a small torsion-angle database from a culled list of 100 PDB structures and then sample 10 conformers of a 9-residue peptide — the canonical "small peptide" exercise bundled in the repository's `example/small_peptide/` folder. Every command shown here is verified against the repository source and bundled examples, so you can reproduce it exactly on your machine. Before starting, complete [Installation & Environment Setup](3-installation-and-environment-setup); this tutorial assumes the `idpconfgen` conda environment is active.

Sources: [README.rst](/example/small_peptide/README.rst#L1-L14), [first_steps.rst](/docs/first_steps.rst#L30-L38)

## Prerequisites & Environment Check

IDPCG runs entirely through the command line: after activating your environment (`conda activate idpconfgen`), the single `idpconfgen` command unlocks all sub-clients, and every sub-client has its own `-h` help flag. Two external dependencies matter for this tutorial: **DSSP** (required by the `sscalc` step) and optionally **MCSCE** (for the recommended side-chain packer, covered later). Verify your setup by running `idpconfgen -h` — you should see the routine list, which confirms the entry point in `cli.py` resolved all sub-parsers correctly. The repository even ships a visual guide for downloading the source, reproduced below.

![download](https://github.com/julie-forman-kay-lab/IDPConformerGenerator/blob/main/docs/assets/download.png?raw=true)

Sources: [first_steps.rst](/docs/first_steps.rst#L25-L38), [usage.rst](/docs/usage.rst#L4-L23), [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L80-L117)

## The Two-Phase Mental Model

All IDPCG workflows separate into **Step 1: create a structural database** and **Step 2: generate conformers**. The database phase downloads experimental PDB structures, annotates their secondary structure, and extracts backbone torsion angles (ω, φ, ψ) into a single human-readable JSON file — `idpconfgen_database.json`. The building phase then recombines these observed torsion fragments to synthesize new conformers for *your* target sequence. Crucially, the database is fully reusable and shareable across projects: you build it once, then sample from it as many times as you like. For a scientific-grade database, the maintainers recommend a PISCES culled list with `pc80` identity and 0.0–2.0 Å resolution (≈24,857 chains); this tutorial uses the bundled 100-structure `cull100` file so it finishes in minutes.

Sources: [first_steps.rst](/docs/first_steps.rst#L49-L67), [README.rst](/example/small_peptide/README.rst#L100-L105)

The full data flow looks like this — three commands build the database, one command samples conformers:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["cull100<br/>(PISCES culled PDB-ID list)"] -->|"idpconfgen pdbdl<br/>-d pdbs.tar -u"| B["pdbs.tar<br/>(filtered PDB structures)"]
    B -->|"idpconfgen sscalc<br/>-rd"| C["sscalc.json<br/>+ sscalc_splitted.tar"]
    C -->|"idpconfgen torsions<br/>-sc sscalc.json<br/>-o idpconfgen_database.json"| D["idpconfgen_database.json<br/>(torsion-angle database)"]
    D -->|"idpconfgen build<br/>-seq ... -nc 10"| E["conf_X.pdb<br/>(conformer ensemble)"]
    D -.->|optional| F["csssconv → csss_ex.json"]
    F -.->|"build -csss csss_ex.json"| E
```

Sources: [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L50-L78), [usage.rst](/docs/usage.rst#L24-L29)

## Step 1 — Download Structures with `pdbdl`

Create a working directory, copy the `example/small_peptide/cull100` list into it, and run the downloader. The `cull100` file emulates the PISCES format: **only the first column is read** (PDB-ID + chain identifier, e.g. `12E8H` = PDB `12E8`, chain `H`), and no header lines are allowed. Supported ID formats are `XXXX`, `XXXXY`, or `XXXX_Y`; if no chain is given, every chain is saved separately. The `-d pdbs.tar` flag directs output into a tarball, `-u` performs the *actual* download (without it, only a dry-run comparison occurs), and `-n` engages multiprocessing (bare `-n` uses all CPU threads except one).

```bash
idpconfgen pdbdl cull100 -u -n -d pdbs.tar
```

The resulting `pdbs.tar` contains *parsed and filtered* structures: solvent/ligands removed, only amino-acid elements kept, `altLoc 'A' or ' '` only, first model only for multi-MODEL files, and chains renumbered — exactly the information IDPCG needs, nothing more.

```bash
mkdir my_first_ensemble && cd my_first_ensemble
cp <repo>/example/small_peptide/cull100 .
idpconfgen pdbdl cull100 -u -n -d pdbs.tar
```

| Flag | Meaning | Why it matters here |
|---|---|---|
| `cull100` | Positional: PDB-ID list file | Only column 1 is parsed; no headers |
| `-u` | Perform the real download | Omit it and nothing downloads |
| `-n` | Use all cores minus one | Speeds up ~100 parallel downloads |
| `-d pdbs.tar` | Destination (folder or TAR) | TAR keeps the workspace tidy |

Sources: [README.rst](/example/small_peptide/README.rst#L11-L42), [cli_pdbdownloader.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_pdbdownloader.py#L10-L40)

## Step 2 — Annotate Secondary Structure with `sscalc`

Next, run DSSP over the tarball to identify each residue's secondary structure. IDPCG supports DSSP v2, v3, and v4 (invoked via `-cmd`, defaulting to the `mkdssp` executable), and upgrades assignments to DSSP-PPII polyproline-II conventions. The `-rd` flag **reduces** DSSP codes to the coarse IDP-relevant alphabet (loop/helix/strand grouping) — keep it for a simplified database. This step produces two artifacts: `sscalc.json` (sequence ↔ secondary-structure identity dictionary) and `sscalc_splitted.tar` (PDB chains split into continuous segments), the input for the next step.

```bash
idpconfgen sscalc pdbs.tar -rd -n
```

> [!TIP]
> Because IDPCG is modular, `sscalc` merely wraps a parser around whatever DSSP executable you point at with `-cmd /path/to/dssp`. If your DSSP lives in a non-standard location or is named differently (e.g., `dssp` instead of `mkdssp`), pass it explicitly: `idpconfgen sscalc pdbs.tar -rd -n -cmd dssp`.

Sources: [README.rst](/example/small_peptide/README.rst#L44-L58), [cli_sscalc.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_sscalc.py#L1-L15), [cli_sscalc.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_sscalc.py#L59-L92)

## Step 3 — Extract Torsions into the Database with `torsions`

Now extract the ω/φ/ψ backbone torsion angles from the split structures and merge them with the sequence/SS metadata. The protocol per structure is strict: it reads only backbone N, CA, C atoms, computes the three torsions, and **fails any structure** where N/CA/C counts mismatch, consecutive atoms exceed 2.1 Å apart, or the file is otherwise inconsistent — broken entries are logged and skipped rather than silently corrupting the database. The `-sc sscalc.json` source flag folds the secondary-structure dictionary in, and `-o idpconfgen_database.json` writes the final database. Angles are saved in radians by default (add `-deg` for degrees).

```bash
idpconfgen torsions sscalc_splitted.tar -sc sscalc.json -o idpconfgen_database.json -n
```

Open the resulting JSON in any editor — it is deliberately human-readable, with keys per source chain and `OMEGA`/`PHI`/`PSI` lists as values. **This single file is all the build step consumes**; the intermediate `pdbs.tar`, `sscalc.json`, and `sscalc_splitted.tar` are safe to delete afterward.

Sources: [cli_torsions.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_torsions.py#L1-L35), [README.rst](/example/small_peptide/README.rst#L60-L67)

## Step 4 — Build Your First Ensemble with `build`

The moment of truth: synthesize conformers for the tutorial peptide `EGAAGAASS`. The builder samples torsion fragments matching the target sequence from the database, assembles backbone coordinates via internal-coordinate (quaternion) math, packs side chains, and rejects candidates exceeding energy thresholds. The minimal command below requests 10 conformers (`-nc 10`) using *loop-only* sampling with amino-acid substitutions allowed (`--dany`), with FASPR side chains by default:

```bash
idpconfgen build -db idpconfgen_database.json -seq EGAAGAASS -nc 10 --dloop-off --dany -n
```

After some time, 10 PDB conformers appear in your working folder alongside `energies.log` (per-conformer energy values) and a hidden `.idpconfgen_build` log. Sampling modes are **mutually exclusive** — `build` raises a `ValueError` if you combine them, and errors out if you give none:

| Sampling flag | Samples from… | Constraint |
|---|---|---|
| *(default)* `--dloop` | Loop regions only | Enabled unless `--dloop-off` |
| `--dhelix` / `--dstrand` | Adds α-helices / β-strands | Requires `--dloop-off` |
| `--dany` | Any secondary structure | Exclusive with the above |
| `--duser` | User-defined SS regexes | Exclusive with the above |
| `-csss file.json` | Probabilistic custom SS | Requires `--dloop-off` |

| Build parameter | Flag | Default | Role in this tutorial |
|---|---|---|---|
| Database | `-db` | required | The JSON from Step 3 |
| Sequence | `-seq` | required | `EGAAGAASS` or a `.fasta` file |
| Conformer count | `-nc` | 1 | `-nc 10` for a small ensemble |
| Backbone energy threshold | `-etbb` | 100 kJ | Fragment rejection cutoff |
| Side-chain energy threshold | `-etss` | 250 kJ | Post-packing rejection cutoff |
| Side-chain method | `-scm` | FASPR | `-scm mcsce` if MCSCE installed |
| Skip side chains | `-dsd` | off | Backbone-only output |
| Output folder | `-of` | cwd | Organize ensemble files |
| Random seed | `--random-seed` | 0 | Reproducibility |
| Cores | `-n` | 1 | Parallel conformer workers |

Sources: [README.rst](/example/small_peptide/README.rst#L69-L80), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L238-L247), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L286-L368), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L470-L483)

## Step 5 (Optional) — Chemical-Shift-Guided Sampling with CSSS

If you have NMR chemical shifts processed by **CheSPI** or **δ2D**, convert their output into a standardized probability file and sample conformers biased toward those propensities. The `csssconv` sub-client reads a CheSPI `probs8_*.txt` (`-p8`) or δ2D `.txt` (`-d2D`) file and groups predicted structures into the L/H/E alphabet — probabilistically weighting loop (L), helix (H), and strand (E) per residue. To build with the resulting JSON, pass `-csss csss_ex.json` together with `--dloop-off` (custom sampling and the standard flags cannot coexist). Note the symmetrical design: if you prefer the *full* DSSP code set without L/H/E grouping, build the database *without* `-rd` and call `csssconv` with `--full`.

```bash
# Standardize CheSPI output
idpconfgen csssconv -p8 probs8_ex.txt -o csss_ex.json

# Build a probability-biased ensemble
idpconfgen build -db idpconfgen_database.json -seq EGAAGAASS -nc 10 -csss csss_ex.json --dloop-off -n
```

**Before/after — what changes in the build command:**

| Aspect | Unbiased build (Step 4) | CSSS-guided build (Step 5) |
|---|---|---|
| Sampling source | Database SS categories | Per-residue L/H/E probabilities |
| Required flags | `--dloop-off --dany` | `--dloop-off -csss csss_ex.json` |
| Database preparation | `sscalc … -rd` | Same (`-rd`) for grouped codes |
| Extra input file | None | `csss_ex.json` from `csssconv` |

Sources: [README.rst](/example/small_peptide/README.rst#L82-L98), [cli_csssconv.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L12-L56), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L293-L303)

## Verifying Results & Troubleshooting

Success looks like: ten `conf_*.pdb` files in your directory, an `energies.log` listing each conformer's final energy, and the closing `finished properly` message that `maincli()` emits after every sub-client completes. Remember that IDPCG is **deterministic** — the random seed defines the sampling progression, so identical commands reproduce identical ensembles. The table below maps the failures beginners hit most often to their root causes and fixes:

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `pdbdl` downloads nothing | Missing `-u` flag | Re-run with `-u` (dry-run is default) |
| `sscalc` fails immediately | DSSP not installed / not on PATH | Install DSSP; pass `-cmd /path/to/dssp` |
| `torsions` skips many chains | Broken structures (>2.1 Å gaps) | Expected behavior; check `.rpr_on_crash` logs |
| `build`: "Give at least one sampling option" | All SS flags off | Add e.g. `--dany` or remove `--dloop-off` |
| `build`: sampling options conflict | Mixing `--dany` with `-csss`/`--dhelix` | They are mutually exclusive; pick one |
| MCSCE errors or hangs | Memory pressure / long trials | Try `-dsd` backbone-only, then run `mcsce` separately |
| Slow performance | Single core | Append `-n` (uses all cores minus one) |

For the MCSCE fallback path, generate backbones with `-dsd`, then pack side chains externally: `mkdir ./ens_mcsce && mcsce ./bb_folder 100 -w -o ./ens_mcsce -s -m simple -l mcsce_log` — a two-stage pattern the drkN SH3 example documents for exactly this situation.

Sources: [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L125-L143), [drksh3_example/README.rst](/example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L49-L104), [cli_torsions.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_torsions.py#L14-L22), [README.rst](/example/small_peptide/README.rst#L100-L105)

## From Toy Example to Real Research

You have now executed the *entire* IDPCG pipeline end-to-end. The same four commands scale directly to research: swap `cull100` for a full PISCES list (e.g. `cullpdb_pc90_res2.0_R0.25_d201015_chains24003`), point `-seq` at your protein's FASTA file, and raise `-nc` to 100 or more — as demonstrated with the unfolded drkN SH3 domain, where MCSCE side chains (`-scm mcsce`) are recommended for production ensembles. When you're ready to understand *why* fragments combine the way they do, continue with the Deep Dive track below.

> [!TIP]
> For sequences longer than 300 residues, the builder switches to a fragment-wise "long" mode (enable explicitly with `--long`, or force it above 100 AA with `--force-long`). You can even hand-tune fragment boundaries with `--long-ranges 1-150,151-300,` — note the trailing comma requirement.

Sources: [drksh3_example/README.rst](/example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L1-L58), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L249-L282)

**Suggested reading progression:**

- Review environment pitfalls in [Installation & Environment Setup](3-installation-and-environment-setup)
- See how the engine you just used works internally: [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble)
- Understand the fragment-sampling mathematics behind `build`: [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling)
- Reproduce full research case studies: [Research Examples Library](23-research-examples-library)
- Master every flag and sub-client: [CLI Subcommand System](17-cli-subcommand-system)

# Architecture Overview



IDPConformerGenerator is a modular scientific CLI application that generates conformer ensembles for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) by combining observed backbone torsion angles from experimental structures with probabilistic sampling. This page maps the system's layered architecture, the plugin registries that make its algorithms interchangeable, its concurrency model, and the supporting infrastructure — giving intermediate developers a reliable mental model before diving into the building engine itself. All claims below are verified against the source tree; no behavior is inferred beyond what the code documents.

![Pipeline UML](https://github.com/julie-forman-kay-lab/IDPConformerGenerator/blob/main/docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pipeline.svg?raw=true)

The diagram above is the project's own UML rendering of the high-level pipeline, maintained in PlantUML source under [docs/UMLs](/docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pipeline.svg). Additional per-subcommand diagrams (`idpconfgen_fetch`, `idpconfgen_sscalc`, `idpconfgen_pdbdl`, and others) live in the same directory and are catalogued on the [UML Design Diagrams](25-uml-design-diagrams) page.

Sources: [idpconfgen_pipeline.svg](/docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pipeline.svg), [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L1-L14)

## Design Philosophy and Repository Layout

The project follows a strict **src-layout** packaging convention: all importable code lives under `src/idpconfgen/`, with tests, examples, and documentation as first-class siblings at the repository root. Packaging is handled by setuptools with a **pybind11** build hook that compiles the `idpcpp` C++ extension from a single translation unit, `src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp` — and notably, the extension build is bypassed when running under tox (`TOX_ENV_NAME` detection), keeping the test environment pure-Python.

Sources: [setup.py](/setup.py#L52-L64), [setup.py](/setup.py#L14-L30)

| Directory | Role | Key Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `src/idpconfgen/` | Application package | `cli.py` dispatcher, 20+ `cli_*.py` subcommands, `conformer_generator.py` |
| `src/idpconfgen/libs/` | Domain & infrastructure libraries | 20 `lib*.py` modules (structure, math, I/O, multiprocessing) |
| `src/idpconfgen/core/` | Static domain definitions | `definitions.py`, `build_definitions.py`, `exceptions.py`, sidechain templates |
| `src/idpconfgen/components/` | Pluggable algorithm strategies | `bgeo_strategies/`, `sidechain_packing/`, `xmer_probs/` |
| `src/idpconfgen/cpp/` | C++ acceleration | `idpcpp.cpp` (pybind11), FASPR license |
| `alphas/l-caa/` | Per-residue geometry parameters | `ALA.params` … `VAL.params` (20 amino acids) |
| `tests/` | Test suite | ~30 `test_*.py` files mirroring library modules, fixture data in `tests/data/` |

Sources: [setup.py](/setup.py#L1-L10), [definitions.py](/src/idpconfgen/core/definitions.py#L1-L9)

The package ships as version 0.10.1, targets Python ≥3.8, and is GPL-licensed research software under the Julie Forman-Kay Lab. The single console-script entry point is declared as `idpconfgen = idpconfgen.cli:maincli`, with a parallel `python -m idpconfgen` path provided by `__main__.py` that delegates to the same function.

Sources: [setup.py](/setup.py#L52-L76), [setup.py](/setup.py#L93-L100), [__main__.py](/src/idpconfgen/__main__.py#L10-L16)

## The Layered Package Architecture

The codebase separates concerns into four horizontal layers with strictly downward dependencies: a thin **entry/dispatch layer**, a wide **CLI module layer**, a **component layer** of swappable algorithm strategies, and a **library layer** of reusable domain primitives. Understanding this stratification is the prerequisite for reading the diagram below: arrows indicate "calls into", and every `cli_*.py` module may draw from both the component registries and the library layer, but never upward.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    U["User shell: idpconfgen subcommand"] --> EP["cli.py :: maincli — argparse dispatcher"]
    EP --> CM["cli_* modules — one per subcommand<br/>pdbdl / sscalc / torsions / build / ldrs / ..."]
    CM --> CP["components/ — strategy registries<br/>bgeo_strategies · sidechain_packing · xmer_probs"]
    CM --> LB["libs/ — domain libraries<br/>libbuild · libcalc · libstructure · libparse ..."]
    CP --> LB
    LB --> CORE["core/ — static definitions & exceptions"]
    LB --> PERF["Performance kernels — idpcpp (pybind11) + numba njit"]
```

The library inventory is best evidenced by `cli_build.py` itself, whose import block enumerates the collaborating primitives: `libbuild` (conformer masks, energy-function preparation), `libcalc` (torsion angles, quaternion coordinate construction, numba-compiled kernels), `libfilter` (`aligndb` fragment alignment), `libparse` (sequence chunking with `njit` variants), `libio` (JSON/database readers), `libpdb`/`libstructure` (PDB atom-line formatting, array round-tripping), and `libhigherlevel` (reduction utilities).

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L63-L104), [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L18-L44)

A naming clarification worth anchoring early: despite its name, `conformer_generator.py` is **not** the conformer-building engine. It contains `ProteinSearch`, a recursive sequence-pattern matcher with mismatch tolerance, supporting the `search` subcommand's fragment lookup against a sequence database. The actual builder lives in the `build` subcommand (`cli_build.py`) backed by `libbuild`/`libcalc`.

Sources: [conformer_generator.py](/src/idpconfgen/conformer_generator.py#L1-L27), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1-L10)

## Entry Points and the CLI Dispatch Contract

The dispatcher implements a **module-as-subcommand** pattern. Each `cli_*.py` module is a self-contained argparse unit, and the top-level `cli.py` merely registers them — first the "main DB creation pipeline" routines (`pdbdl`, `sscalc`, `torsions`, `torsionsJ`, `build`, `ldrs`), then secondary utilities (`bgeo`, `fetch`, `ssext`, `validate`, and more). Dispatch is deliberately dynamic: after parsing, `maincli` invokes `cmd.func(**vars(cmd))`, where `func` was bound to the chosen module's `main` at registration time.

Sources: [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L50-L78), [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L80-L117), [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L125-L143)

The following sequence shows the dispatch path for a representative build invocation (`idpconfgen build -db torsions.json -seq ...`); the prerequisite is knowing that `add_subparser` sets `func=module.main` as a parser default at startup, so the runtime hop is a single dictionary-backed lookup.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant M as maincli (cli.py)
    participant A as Namespace (argparse)
    participant F as main (cli_build.py)
    U->>M: idpconfgen build -db torsions.json -seq MMMM...
    M->>A: load_args() parses subcommand
    A-->>M: Namespace with func=cli_build.main
    M->>F: cmd.func(**vars(cmd))
    F->>F: populate globals, init logger, Pool workers
    F-->>U: conformer PDBs + log stream
```

The registration contract is a five-attribute protocol every CLI module must satisfy, documented verbatim in `libcli.add_subparser`:

| Attribute | Kind | Role in the Contract |
|---|---|---|
| `_name` | `str` | Subcommand keyword (`build`, `sscalc`, …) |
| `_usage` | `str` | Usage line shown by the parser |
| `_help` | `str` | One-line help in the subcommand list |
| `ap` | `ArgumentParser` | The module's own argument definitions, merged via `parents=[module.ap]` |
| `main` | callable | Entry logic, receives all parsed options as keyword arguments |

Sources: [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L240-L267), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1930-L1932)

> [!TIP]
> Argument-type coercion is centralized in reusable `argparse.Action` subclasses in `libcli.py` (`FolderOrTar`, `CSV2Tuple`, `ReadDictionary`, `ListOfPositiveInts`). When adding a subcommand, compose these Actions instead of re-validating inside `main()` — the parser then rejects malformed input before any computation starts.

Sources: [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L31-L120)

## Strategy Registries: Pluggable Algorithm Components

Two families of algorithms are exposed as **strategy registries** — plain dictionaries mapping option strings to initializer functions — so the build workflow can swap implementations without touching its control flow. The sidechain-packing package documents this intent explicitly: every strategy must output the same types and share a compatible input API, returning an array mask plus coordinates compatible with that mask.

Sources: [sidechain_packing/__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L1-L17)

| Registry | Options | Default | Selection Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bond geometry (`--bgeo-strategy`) | `fixed`, `sampling`, `exact`, `int2cart` | `sampling` | `argparse` `choices` + `CheckBgeoInstallation` guard |
| Sidechain packing (`-scm/--sidechainmethod`) | `faspr`, `mcsce` | `faspr` | `choices=_spm` over the methods dict |

The `int2cart` entry demonstrates a graceful degradation pattern: a custom `argparse.Action` checks `has_int2cart` at parse time and raises a parser error pointing to the installation docs if the optional dependency is absent — failures surface before any worker processes spawn.

Sources: [sidechain_packing/__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L25-L44), [bgeo_strategies/__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py#L15-L24), [bgeo_strategies/__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py#L56-L67)

The uniform sidechain API is enforced at the call site in the builder: after backbone completion, `build_sidechains(template_coords)` is invoked identically for both strategies, and only the returned `(mask, coords)` pair is written into `all_atom_coords` — the builder has no knowledge of which packer ran.

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1695-L1707), [sidechain_packing/__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L47-L57)

## Domain Core and Data Assets

The `core/` layer holds **static, import-time-constant domain knowledge** free of computation: amino-acid code mappings (`aa3to1`/`aa1to3`, including protonation and phosphorylation variants like `HIE`, `SEP`, `TPO`), bond-geometry key conventions (`Cm1_N_Ca`, `N_Ca_C`, …), and van der Waals radii sets (Tsai 1999, Bondi 1964). Because these are pure data, `definitions.py` explicitly avoids importing the package's `Path` helper to break circular-import chains.

Sources: [definitions.py](/src/idpconfgen/core/definitions.py#L12-L57), [definitions.py](/src/idpconfgen/core/definitions.py#L60-L80), [definitions.py](/src/idpconfgen/core/definitions.py#L1-L9)

Domain assets sit alongside the code as packaged data: per-amino-acid geometry files in `alphas/l-caa/*.params`, Amber/PDB-named sidechain templates under `core/sidechain_templates/`, the ff14SB forcefield XML in `core/data/`, and the Dunbrack 2010 backbone-dependent rotamer binary (`dun2010bbdep.bin`) bundled with the sidechain-packing component. Geometry constants consumed by the builder (C–O and H–N distances, bend-angle constructions, proline/N-terminal hydrogen coordinates) are exposed through `core/build_definitions.py` and imported directly by `cli_build.py`.

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L48-L58), [sidechain_packing/__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L18-L22)

## Concurrency Model and Performance Kernels

The execution infrastructure rests on two decisions visible in the code. First, `libmulticore.pool_function` wraps `Pool.imap_unordered` in a generator, pairing it with a `ProgressWatcher` and granular exception triage — `IndexError` is logged-and-ignored (a known multiprocessing quirk), `IDPConfGenException` is logged as an error, and results stream out lazily rather than materializing in memory.

Sources: [libmulticore.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L55-L94)

Second, the builder exploits **module-level globals** as the inter-process transport: `BGEO_*`, `ANGLES`, `SLICES`, and mask objects are populated once in `main()` before the pool forks, so workers read them at native memory speed with zero serialization overhead. The module comment states this rationale verbatim, and a complementary helper, `consume_iterable_in_list`, exists precisely because generator closures cannot be pickled into pool workers.

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L110-L125), [libmulticore.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L16-L28), [libmulticore.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L98-L100)

> [!TIP]
> The fork-based globals pattern is why `cli_build.py` calls `populate_globals()` in `main()` and why every numeric inner loop leans on locally bound function references (`RC=np.random.choice`, `GSCNJIT=get_seq_chunk_njit`). When extending the builder, keep new per-worker state in module globals — passing it through `Pool` arguments would force pickling of NumPy arrays on every task.

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1841-L1847), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L23-L33)

Compute-heavy kernels are pushed out of the interpreter two ways: the compiled `idpcpp` pybind11 extension built from `cpp/idpcpp.cpp`, and numba `njit`-decorated functions living in the libraries (`rotate_coordinates_Q_njit`, `rrd10_njit`, `get_seq_chunk_njit`). A third optimization tier is algorithmic: the fragment assembly loop implements **backtracking with bounded retries** — after ~30 failed trials it rolls back one fragment via append/pop registers (`bbi0_R`, `COi0_R`, `res_R`), escalating rollbacks progressively, and restarts the whole conformer if the backtrack reaches the chain origin.

Sources: [setup.py](/setup.py#L17-L26), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L74-L101), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1600-L1664)

Accepted conformers pass an energy gate before emission: sidechain coordinates are folded in through the packing mask, `ALL_ATOM_EFUNC` scores the full-atom model, conformers exceeding `energy_threshold_sidechains` are discarded with a log record, and survivors are yielded as `(total_energy, all_atom_coords)` pairs consumed downstream by the multiprocessing pipeline.

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1709-L1727)

## Testing and Documentation Infrastructure

The test suite mirrors the library structure one-to-one — `test_libbuild.py`, `test_libcalc.py`, `test_libccd.py`, `test_multicore.py`, and so on — with shared helpers in `tests/tcommons.py` and a curated fixture corpus under `tests/data/` (DSSP files, mmCIF edge cases, torsion JSONs, tar archives, FASTA files). The CI-relevant subtlety appears back in `setup.py`: extension compilation is skipped under tox unless `TOXTESTING` is set, so pure-Python tests run without a toolchain.

Sources: [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L1-L14), [bgeo_strategies/__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py#L43-L53)
