Documentation is maintained in a Diátaxis-aligned structure under `docs/` (installation, first steps, usage, FAQ, API reference) with PlantUML sources (`*.pu`) and rendered SVGs for each major subcommand — the project treats these diagrams as versioned artifacts rather than afterthoughts. Research recipes live in `example/` (complex multi-chain modeling, custom fragments, AlphaFold-derived workflows), each with its own README.

Sources: [conformer_generator.py](/src/idpconfgen/conformer_generator.py#L1-L5), [libmulticore.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L1-L8)

## Architectural Principles Summary

Three principles recur across every layer and explain most design choices you will encounter: (1) **registries over conditionals** — swappable algorithms are dictionaries of uniform-API functions checked by `argparse.choices`; (2) **statics over computation** — domain facts live as import-time constants in `core/`, keeping hot paths free of lookups; (3) **streaming over materialization** — dispatch, multiprocessing, and conformer generation all pass control through generators/yields, bounding memory regardless of ensemble size.

Sources: [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L90-L117), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L110-L125), [libmulticore.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L76-L94)

**Suggested reading progression**: follow the data through its lifecycle next with [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble), then study the strategy internals in [Bond Geometry Strategies](8-bond-geometry-strategies) and [Sidechain Packing Methods](11-sidechain-packing-methods). The dispatch contract you saw here is expanded in [CLI Subcommand System](17-cli-subcommand-system), the concurrency details in [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture), and the compiled kernels in [C++ Extension & Numba Kernels](13-c-extension-and-numba-kernels).

# Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble



This page documents the complete data pipeline that IDPConformerGenerator uses to transform raw structural data into an ensemble of intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) conformers. The system is architected as two loosely-coupled phases: **Phase 1** compiles an experimental torsion angle database from curated PDB structures, and **Phase 2** consumes that database to stochastically assemble all-atom conformers through fragment-based internal-coordinate building with energy-gated validation. As an advanced developer, you will find here the precise control flow, memory architecture, and validation semantics that govern ensemble production — the algorithmic internals of individual stages (quaternion math, bond strategies, sampling theory) are covered by their dedicated pages in this catalog.

## Architectural Overview: A Two-Phase System

The pipeline's central design decision is the strict separation between *database compilation* (expensive, done once per structural library) and *conformer construction* (cheap per-conformer, repeated thousands of times). The intermediate artifact bridging both phases is a single human-readable JSON file, `idpconfgen_database.json`, which stores backbone torsion angles indexed by sequence context.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph P1["Phase 1: Database Preparation"]
        A["PISCES cull list<br/>(PDBID + chain)"] --> B["idpconfgen pdbdl"]
        B --> C["pdbs.tar<br/>(parsed, trimmed PDBs)"]
        C --> D["idpconfgen sscalc<br/>(DSSP)"]
        D --> E["sscalc.json<br/>+ sscalc_splitted.tar"]
        E --> F["idpconfgen torsions"]
        F --> G[("idpconfgen_database.json")]
        G -.-> H["idpconfgen bgeodb<br/>(optional, exact strategy)"]
    end
    subgraph P2["Phase 2: Ensemble Construction"]
        G --> I["idpconfgen build<br/>-db ... -seq ... -nc N"]
        I --> J["SLICEDICT_XMERS<br/>+ XMERPROBS globals"]
        J --> K["per-core<br/>conformer_generator()"]
        K --> L["energy-gated<br/>backtracking loop"]
        L --> M["*.pdb ensemble<br/>+ energies.log"]
    end
    H --> I
```

The repository ships a dedicated UML diagram of this pipeline, which complements the per-subcommand UMLs (`idpconfgen_pdbdl`, `idpconfgen_sscalc`, `idpconfgen_bbsplit`) in the same folder:

![Building Pipeline UML](https://github.com/julie-forman-kay-lab/IDPConformerGenerator/blob/main/docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pipeline.svg?raw=true)

This decoupling means Phase 2 never touches raw structural files at runtime — the JSON database is the only input required by `build`, which is why the docs state that "the other files are safe to be removed" once the JSON exists.

Sources: [usage.rst](docs/usage.rst#L14-L32), [small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L30-L42)

## Phase 1 — Compiling the Torsion Angle Database

Phase 1 is a four-step reduction chain, each step consuming the previous artifact. The canonical invocation from the bundled small-peptide example is:

```bash
idpconfgen pdbdl cull100 -u -n -d pdbs.tar
idpconfgen sscalc pdbs.tar -rd -n
idpconfgen torsions sscalc_splitted.tar -sc sscalc.json -o idpconfgen_database.json -n
idpconfgen build -db idpconfgen_database.json -seq EGAAGAASS -nc 10 --dloop-off --dany -n
```

The input to `pdbdl` is a culled chain list (typically from the Dunbrack PISCES database), where only the first column — PDBID concatenated with chain ID — is read, and no header lines are permitted. The `sscalc` step requires the external DSSP program and produces two artifacts: `sscalc.json` (sequence-to-secondary-structure mapping) and `sscalc_splitted.tar` (PDB chains split into continuous segments). The `torsions` step merges both into the final torsion database, a regular JSON file.

| Step | CLI Subcommand | Input Artifact | Output Artifact(s) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `pdbdl` | Cull list (PDBID+chain) | `pdbs.tar` | Download and parse PDB/mmCIF, strip unneeded chains/residues |
| 2 | `sscalc` | `pdbs.tar` | `sscalc.json`, `sscalc_splitted.tar` | DSSP secondary-structure assignment and chain splitting |
| 3 | `torsions` | `sscalc_splitted.tar` + `sscalc.json` | `idpconfgen_database.json` | Extract (omega, phi, psi) torsions indexed by sequence context |
| 4 | `bgeodb` *(optional)* | `idpconfgen_database.json` + `sscalc_splitted.tar` | `idpconfgen_extended_database.json` | Extend database with per-residue bond/bend geometry for the `exact` strategy |

The optional `bgeodb` extension exists because the default `sampling` strategy derives bond geometry from a bundled statistical library, whereas `exact` requires fragment-specific bond angles and lengths carried in the extended database. For a treatment of how these four strategies (`sampling`, `fixed`, `exact`, `int2cart`) differ internally, see [Bond Geometry Strategies](8-bond-geometry-strategies); for the CLI mechanics of Phase 1 subcommands, see [CLI Subcommand System](17-cli-subcommand-system).

Sources: [small_peptide/README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L10-L80), [usage.rst](docs/usage.rst#L44-L62)

## Phase 2 — Build Orchestration in `main()`

The `build` subcommand's orchestration lives in `main()` of `cli_build.py`, which performs four orchestration duties before any conformer is built: parameter validation, long-sequence fragmentation, sampling-index preparation, and multiprocess dispatch.

**Mutual exclusion validation** runs first: the sampling-mode arguments `(dloop, dhelix, dstrand)`, `dany`, `duser`, and `custom_sampling` are mutually exclusive — `main()` raises `ValueError` if more than one is truthy, or if none is provided. This gates whether secondary-structure-aware regex filtering is applied to fragment selection.
Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L470-L487)

**Long-sequence handling** engages for sequences exceeding 300 residues (or 100 with `--force-long`). The sequence is split into chunks (default 150 AA, or 50 AA with `--force-long`, or via explicit `--long-ranges 1-113,114-210,211-301,` patterns), with the crucial detail that **two residues of overlap** are prepended to each subsequent fragment to permit stitching. Each fragment then receives its own slice dictionary, probability table, and global state snapshot, stored in `LONG_GLOBALS` for fragment-wise construction via `build_in_fragments`.
Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L497-L535), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L157-L173)

**Sampling index preparation** constructs the lookup structures the builder will query during construction: `prepare_slice_dict` maps fragment sizes and secondary-structure filters onto positions in the `ANGLES` database array; `compress_xmer_to_key` rewrites the user's requested k-mer sizes/probabilities to only those actually observed in the database (`XMERPROBS`); and `get_adjacent_angles` builds the adjacent-fragment accessor used by the `exact` strategy.
Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L747-L774)

**Dispatch** computes the work split — if `nconfs < ncores`, cores collapse to 1; otherwise conformers are divided per core with the remainder built post-pool — then launches a `multiprocessing.Pool` where each worker executes a `partial` of `_build_conformers` wrapped in `report_on_crash` for fault isolation. This is the same consumption pattern documented in [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture).
Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L540-L549), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L786-L812)

> [!TIP]
> A code-archaeology note: the module named `conformer_generator.py` is *not* the build engine — it contains a `ProteinSearch` class for k-mer pattern matching against sequences. The actual conformer-building generator lives inside `cli_build.py`. Do not let the filename misdirect your navigation.

Sources: [conformer_generator.py](src/idpconfgen/conformer_generator.py#L7-L103)

## Global Memory Architecture

`cli_build.py` intentionally trades encapsulation for multiprocessing throughput: module-level globals are populated once in the parent process, then inherited copy-on-write by forked workers, giving "fast reads with non-significant overhead" during conformer production. `populate_globals()` is the single initialization point that materializes all of them.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph INPUTS
        DB[("idpconfgen_database.json")]
        SEQ["input_seq (user FASTA)"]
        FF["forcefields[forcefield]<br/>topology factory"]
    end
    subgraph POP["populate_globals()"]
        DB --> BG["BGEO_full → bgeo_reduce →<br/>BGEO_trimer + BGEO_res"]
        FF --> TOP["topobj = ff(add_OXT=True,<br/>add_Nterminal_H=True)"]
        SEQ --> RP["remap_sequence →<br/>A/G/P template sequence"]
        TOP --> AAL["ALL_ATOM_LABELS / MASKS / EFUNC"]
        RP --> TML["TEMPLATE_LABELS / MASKS / EFUNC"]
    end
    subgraph WORKERS["forked worker processes (read-only)"]
        BG --> Q["conformer_generator loop:<br/>BGEO fallback chain"]
        TML --> Q
        AAL --> SC["sidechain packing +<br/>ALL_ATOM_EFUNC gate"]
    end
```

The dual-representation design is the load-bearing detail: **`ALL_ATOM_*`** globals describe the full-atom target sequence (every sidechain atom labeled), while **`TEMPLATE_*`** globals describe an Ala/Gly/Pro-remapped skeleton upon which the backbone is actually built. Backbone construction runs exclusively against the template (three atom types keep the energy function evaluation cheap), and only after the backbone passes validation are coordinates transferred into the all-atom array and sidechains packed. The forcefield topology is instantiated with `add_OXT=True` and `add_Nterminal_H=True` so that terminal chemistry is present in both representations.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L110-L155), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L818-L899)

## The `conformer_generator` Contract

`conformer_generator()` is a Python **generator** with a strict protocol that consumers must respect. Its first `yield` emits the shared label arrays — `atom_labels`, `res_nums`, `res_labels` — which remain constant for every conformer from that builder instance. Every subsequent `yield` returns a `(energy, coords)` tuple, where `coords` is an `(N, 3)` float64 array aligned by index with the labels.

```python
builder = conformer_generator(input_seq='MGAETTWSCAAA', ...)
atom_labels, res_nums, res_labels = next(builder)  # first yield: labels
energy, coords = next(builder)                     # subsequent: one conformer each
```

The generator accepts an injectable `generative_function` callable, tested at startup with a probe call `generative_function(nres=1, cres=0)` — it must return a `(primer_template, agls)` pair, where `agls` is a flat array of torsion angles in (omega, phi, psi) triplets. This hook is what allows alternative sampling backends to drive the builder without touching its internals. When `generative_function=None`, the builder falls back to the internally populated `SLICEDICT_XMERS`/`ANGLES` globals.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1027-L1150), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1253-L1260), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1241-L1251)

## The Fragment Build Loop

Each conformer materializes through a nested loop structure: an outer infinite loop (one iteration per emitted conformer) containing an inner fragment loop. Before each conformer, all coordinate arrays are reset to `NaN` and a **seed** of three coordinates is installed — two dummy atoms (`dummy_CA_m1`, `dummy_C_m1`) plus the N-terminal nitrogen at the origin — because the first torsion to be placed is an omega, which requires a simulated "residue −1" to rotate around.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["Seed: 2 dummy atoms + N-terminal N<br/>bbi = 1"] --> R{"Sample fragment<br/>nres = randint(1, 6)"}
    R --> T["Draw (omg, phi, psi) triplets<br/>+ trimer context GET_TRIMER_SEQ"]
    T --> G{"bgeo_strategy"}
    G -->|sampling| F["RC( BGEO_full[res][tpair][torpair] )<br/>↓ KeyError → BGEO_trimer<br/>↓ KeyError → BGEO_res"]
    G -->|fixed| FB["Cycle per-residue averages"]
    G -->|exact| FE["Fragment-specific bangs/blens"]
    G -->|int2cart| FI["GPU internal-coordinate lookup"]
    F --> C["make_coord_Q: extend backbone from<br/>(bond_len, bend_angle, torsion)"]
    C --> CO["Carbonyl O + amide H via<br/>make_coord_Q_planar"]
    CO --> SS["Attach A/G/P sidechain templates<br/>place_sidechain_template"]
    SS --> E{"ANY energy > etbb?"}
    E -->|"yes"| B["Backtrack: rollback registers,<br/>NaN-out fragment, escalate 30/5/5"]
    B --> R
    E -->|"no"| D{"backbone_done?"}
    D -->|"no"| R
    D -->|"yes"| P["Pack real sidechains"]
    P --> E2{"ANY energy > etss?"}
    E2 -->|"yes"| X["Discard, continue loop"]
    E2 -->|"no"| Y["yield (energy, coords)"]
```

Within the per-torsion iteration, the builder extracts the trimer sequence context (`GET_TRIMER_SEQ`) and a rounded torsion-pair key (`RRD10`), then resolves bond geometry through the strategy-specific branch. The **sampling strategy's fallback chain** is the pipeline's robustness mechanism: a random choice is drawn first from the maximally specific context (residue + trimer + exact torsion pair in `BGEO_full`), degrading on `KeyError` to trimer-level statistics (`BGEO_trimer`), and finally to bare per-residue distributions (`BGEO_res`). This guarantees building never starves, even for sequences underrepresented in the database. Each resolved geometry then feeds `MAKE_COORD_Q_LOCAL` — the quaternion-based placement of N, Cα, and C atoms from the three preceding backbone atoms — followed by planar placement of the carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogens via `MAKE_COORD_Q_PLANAR`. The mathematics of these placements are the subject of [Coordinate Geometry & Quaternion Math](7-coordinate-geometry-and-quaternion-math), and the statistical construction of the BGEO hierarchy is detailed in [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling).

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1296-L1311), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1344-L1388), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1415-L1484), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1525-L1555)

## The Validation Gauntlet: Energy-Gated Backtracking

IDPConformerGenerator does not reject whole conformers on backbone clashes — it **rewinds**. After each fragment is placed, `TEMPLATE_EFUNC(template_coords)` evaluates the template energy, and if *any* atom exceeds `energy_threshold_backbone` (default 100 kJ, tunable via `-etbb`), the builder performs register-based rollback: the atom-index registers (`bbi0_register`, `COi0_register`, `res_R`) are popped to the previous checkpoint, the offending fragment's coordinates are `NaN`-masked, and building resumes with a fresh fragment draw.

The rollback itself **escalates in depth** to escape pathological regions of conformational space: a fragment is retried up to 30 times before one additional prior fragment is also rolled back (`number_of_trials2`), that level retries 5 times before a third-level rollback (`number_of_trials3`), each likewise retrying 5 times. If rollback unwinds past the seed, the conformer is abandoned entirely and restarted; 500 consecutive start failures (`max_start_attempts`) cancel production with a logged error and the conformer count achieved so far. This is a fragment-granularity alternative to the global energy minimization approaches used elsewhere — see [Energy-Based Clash Filtering](12-energy-based-clash-filtering) for the downstream, conformer-level filter.

| Gate | Scope | Default Threshold | Failure Response | Hard Limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Backbone energy | Per fragment (template) | 100 kJ (`-etbb`) | Rollback with 30/5/5 escalation | 500 start restarts → cancel |
| Sidechain solution | Per conformer | — (solver-dependent) | `None` returned → conformer discarded | None (retry next iteration) |
| Sidechain energy | Per conformer (all-atom) | 250 kJ (`-etss`) | Conformer discarded | None (retry next iteration) |
| Long-mode stitching | Per fragment pair | `max_clash=40`, `tolerance=0.4` | Fragment rebuilt at dead ends | Reported per conformer |

After the backbone passes and `backbone_done` flips, the template's backbone, NH, H-term, and C-terminal coordinates are copied into the all-atom array via boolean masks, real sidechains are packed through the configured `sidechain_packing_methods` entry (default FASPR — see [Sidechain Packing Methods](11-sidechain-packing-methods)), and the full structure is re-evaluated with `ALL_ATOM_EFUNC` against the sidechain threshold. Only conformers surviving every gate are emitted via `yield SUM(total_energy), all_atom_coords`.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1333-L1341), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1596-L1675), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1689-L1727), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1009-L1023), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L328-L349)

## Output Artifacts and Energy Logging

Accepted conformers are serialized as standard-format PDB files named `{conformer_name}_{n}.pdb`, where `n` is drawn from a multiprocessing-safe `Queue` (`CONF_NUMBER`) so filenames remain unique across cores. Energies are written incrementally to `energies.log` (configurable via `-el`) by the `EnergyLogSaver` singleton, which runs only in the parent process and accepts cross-processor calls, flushing one `confname,energy` line per accepted conformer. This log doubles as the input artifact for downstream ensemble reweighting and analysis workflows.

| Artifact | Producer | Format | Consumer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `{name}_{i}.pdb` | `gen_PDB_from_conformer` + worker loop | PDB (ATOM records) | Downstream analysis, `validate` subcommand |
| `energies.log` | `EnergyLogSaver.save` | CSV-like (`name,energy`) | Ensemble reweighting, QC |
| `.idpconfgen_build` logfile | `init_files` | Rotating text log | Debugging, run auditing |

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L371-L395), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L138-L141), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1730-L1759)

## Key Build Parameters Reference

The parameter surface most relevant to pipeline behavior is summarized below; the full per-atom geometry definitions these parameters select are cataloged in [Build Definitions Reference](21-build-definitions-reference).

| Parameter | Default | Effect on Pipeline |
|---|---|---|
| `-nc / --nconfs` | 1 | Total ensemble size; split across cores with remainder handled serially |
| `-nc / -ncores` | 1 | Worker pool width; collapsed to 1 if `nconfs < ncores` |
| `--bgeo-strategy` | `sampling` | Selects the bond-geometry resolution branch in the build loop |
| `-etbb` | 100.0 kJ | Backbone fragment rejection gate; directly controls backtracking frequency |
| `-etss` | 250.0 kJ | Post-packing rejection gate (ignored with `-dsd`) |
| `-dsd / --disable-sidechains` | off | Skips packing and the sidechain energy gate entirely |
| `-csss / --custom-sampling` | None | Per-residue secondary-structure probability distribution (replaces `--d*` flags) |
| `--long` / `--long-ranges` | off | Fragment-wise building for >300 AA; default 150 AA chunks with 2-residue overlap |
| `--seed` | 0 | Seeds `np.random` per worker for reproducible sampling |
| `-ff / --forcefield` | first entry | Selects topology factory for labels, masks, and energy functions |

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L223-L368)

- For the quaternion algebra inside `make_coord_Q` and `make_coord_Q_planar`: [Coordinate Geometry & Quaternion Math](7-coordinate-geometry-and-quaternion-math)
- For the four bond-geometry strategies and their database requirements: [Bond Geometry Strategies](8-bond-geometry-strategies)
- For how `SLICEDICT_XMERS` and the BGEO statistical hierarchy are constructed from PDB data: [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling)

# Coordinate Geometry & Quaternion Math



Every atom IDPConformerGenerator places — backbone extension, carbonyl oxygen, C-terminal carboxyl, docked sidechain template — is the product of one numerical kernel library. This page dissects that library: `libs/libcalc.py`, the module where classical trigonometric placement and unit-quaternion rotation coexist, plus the consumption patterns in `libs/libbuild.py`. You will learn the two placement paradigms, the exact Hamilton-product machinery, the per-kernel input conventions (where silent 2× errors live), and the Numba performance engineering that shapes the API itself. This is the mathematical substrate beneath [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble); here we go one level deeper into first principles.

Sources: [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L1-L15), [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L21-L25)

## Architectural Position: One Module as the Single Source of Numerical Truth

The design is deliberately centralized. `libcalc.py` (966 lines) holds every pure-geometry function — frames, torsions, distances, and all six quaternion kernels — while `libbuild.py` (1215 lines) handles conformational bookkeeping: atom-group masks, fragment-slice dictionaries, and force-field parameter preparation. The dependency edges are unidirectional and thin: `libbuild.py` imports exactly three Numba kernels from `libcalc.py` (`calc_all_vs_all_dists_njit`, `multiply_upper_diagonal_raw_njit`, `sum_upper_diagonal_raw_njit`) for its energy-preparation path, and both modules draw physical constants (bond lengths like `distances_N_CA`, `distances_CA_C`, `distances_C_Np1`; angles like `build_bend_CA_C_OXT`) from `core/build_definitions.py`. Geometry constants never live in the math module — they are injected, keeping `libcalc.py` free of biochemical semantics.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    BD["core/build_definitions.py<br/>bond lengths, bend angles"] --> LC["libs/libcalc.py<br/>frames, quaternions, torsions, distances"]
    LC --> LB["libs/libbuild.py<br/>masks, slice dicts, energy prep"]
    BD --> LB
    LB --> BP["Building pipeline<br/>see Page 6"]
```

This separation has a practical consequence for contributors: any change to rotation semantics is testable in isolation against `tests/test_libcalc.py`, without instantiating a conformer. The heavy Numba decoration strategy also differs between the modules — `libcalc.py` defers all `njit` wrapping to the module tail, a pattern detailed in the final section.

Sources: [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L12-L25), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L8-L11), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L959-L966)

## Two Placement Paradigms: NeRF-Style Frames vs. Quaternion Kernels

`libcalc.py` implements the same geometric operation — "place an atom given three predecessors and internal coordinates" — through two independent mathematical frameworks. The legacy path mirrors Natural Extension Reference Frame (NeRF) logic: `make_coord_from_angles` converts spherical coordinates `(θ, φ, d)` into a local position, `rotation_to_plane` builds a 3×3 orientation matrix from an atomic frame, and `make_coord` composes them: compute local coordinate, rotate into the molecular frame via `np.dot(new_coord, rotation.T)`, then translate by the parent atom.

```python
# the local-coordinate constructor, libcalc.py L167-L171
return np.array([
    distance * math.cos(phi),
    distance * math.sin(phi) * math.cos(theta),
    distance * math.sin(phi) * math.sin(theta),
    ])
```

The quaternion path replaces matrix composition with Hamilton products — no 3×3 matrices, no trigonometric frame assembly. The comparison below summarizes the trade-offs as implemented (not in the abstract):

| Dimension | Classical (`make_coord` family) | Quaternion (`make_coord_Q` family) |
|---|---|---|
| Core functions | `make_axis_vectors`, `rotation_to_plane`, `make_coord`, `make_coord_from_angles` | `hamiltonian_multiplication_Q`, `make_coord_Q`, `make_coord_Q_planar`, `make_coord_Q_COO` |
| Rotation representation | 3×3 matrix (`np.dot(b, AXIS_111).T`) | Unit quaternion sandwich q·p·q* |
| Numba status | Pure NumPy, not JIT-compiled | `@njit`-decorated, compiled hot path |
| Matrix/quaternion allocations | Creates rotation matrix per call | Allocates only tuple components |
| Usage in tree | Planar-group placement (carbonyl geometry via frames) | Backbone extension, terminal groups, template alignment |

The quaternion kernels are the ones wired for performance — `make_coord_Q_planar` exists specifically because the classical path was too slow for per-residue carbonyl placement — while the classical functions remain as the reference semantics.

Sources: [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L109-L171), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L552-L569), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L79-L106)

## Orthonormal Frames from Three Atoms

The frame machinery answers: given three connected atoms A→B→C, what rotation matrix expresses "A at origin, A→B as X-axis, C defining the XY-plane"? `make_axis_vectors` constructs it in three steps: the bond vector `AB = A − B` normalized becomes the X direction; `parallel_ABC = AB × BC` (the plane normal, normalized) becomes one basis vector; and `perpendicular = AB × parallel_ABC` completes the right-handed triad. Every normalization is guarded by a zero-length check (`if Alen > 0.0`), so degenerate collinear inputs do not raise — they silently return unnormalized vectors, a deliberate soft-failure choice for a function called inside tight loops.

`rotation_to_plane` then stacks `[AB_vect, −perpendicular, parallel_ABC]` as rows of matrix `b` and returns `np.dot(b, AXIS_111).T` — multiplying by the identity constant `AXIS_111` (L17-21) is a no-op by value; it exists to force the 3×3 array shape and keep the transpose arithmetic explicit. The negated second row encodes the handedness fix that makes the downstream carbonyl placement land on the correct side of the backbone plane.

Sources: [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L17-L21), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L24-L76), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L79-L106)

## The Quaternion Engine: Hamilton Products and the Sandwich Product

Everything rotates through one 4-tuple arithmetic primitive. `hamiltonian_multiplication_Q(a1, b1, c1, d1, a2, b2, c2, d2)` implements the Hamilton product of quaternions as four scalar expressions — the components of `(w1q1)·(w2q2)`:

```python
return (
    (a1 * a2) - (b1 * b2) - (c1 * c2) - (d1 * d2),   # w
    (a1 * b2) + (b1 * a2) + (c1 * d2) - (d1 * c2),   # x
    (a1 * c2) - (b1 * d2) + (c1 * a2) + (d1 * b2),   # y
    (a1 * d2) + (b1 * c2) - (c1 * b2) + (d1 * a2),   # z
    )
```

A commented-out earlier variant operated on transposed arrays (`a2.T`, L281-288); the shipped version dropped the transposes to serve both scalar and vectorized call sites. Ancestors are hard-coded: the rotation of a pure quaternion `p = (0, x, y, z)` by unit quaternion `q` is computed as `HMQ(HMQ(q, p), q*)`, where the conjugate `q* = (q_w, −q_x, −q_y, −q_z)` is formed inline rather than stored.

`rotate_coordinates_Q` is the general-purpose batch rotator: for coordinates of shape `(N, 3)`, a unit rotation axis `rot_vec`, and angle `angle_rad`, it builds the half-angle quaternion — `b1 = cos(θ/2)`, `(b2, b3, b4) = sin(θ/2) · axis` — applies the sandwich product across all N atoms simultaneously (the pure-vector leading zero is passed as a literal `0` in the first Hamilton call, L447-450), and reassembles with `VSTACK((d2, d3, d4)).T`. The docstring states the contract the code does not enforce: **the axis must already be unitary**, otherwise the "rotation" becomes a rotation-plus-scale.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["coords N x 3, unit axis, angle_rad"] --> B["half-angle quaternion q<br/>b1 = cos theta/2, bxyz = sin theta/2 * axis"]
    B --> C["pure quaternions p = 0, x, y, z<br/>one per atom, vectorized"]
    C --> D["c = HMQ q, p"]
    D --> E["d = HMQ c, q_conjugate<br/>conjugate built inline: b1, -b2, -b3, -b4"]
    E --> F["rotated = vstack d2 d3 d4 transposed"]
```

Sources: [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L280-L299), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L412-L460)

## Atom-Placement Kernels: Geometry Conventions That Reward Close Reading

The three specialized kernels share a skeleton — origin transfer, cross-product axis, bend quaternion, second quaternion — but diverge in input conventions and axis construction. These conventions are documented in docstrings, not enforced in code, which makes them the primary source of integration bugs.

**`make_coord_Q`** places a new atom from predecessors `v1, v2, v3` with a bend and torsion. It transfers `o1 = v1 − v2` and `o2 = v3 − v2` to the origin, forms the rotation axis as the normalized cross `CROSS(o2, o1)` — note the comment `# changed`: the operand order defines chirality, and flipping it flips the torsion sense — rotates the `o2` unit vector by the bend quaternion, then rotates that result by the torsion quaternion built around `uo2` (the unit `v3−v2` axis, which is the chemical torsion axis). Finally the resulting unit vector is scaled by `distance` and translated by `v3`. The performance-sensitive final step is hand-rolled (`ARRAY((f2 * distance, f3 * distance, f4 * distance))`) with a benchmark note: 857 ns versus 1.8 µs for the idiomatic `np.array([f2, f3, f4]) * distance`.

> [!TIP]
> The kernel's angle contract is asymmetric and unforgiving: `bend` must arrive **pre-transformed as `(π − bend) / 2`** (docstring L494-497 — "this calculation must be computed outside this function"), while `torsion` is passed raw and halved internally at L529. Feeding a raw bend angle silently produces geometry bent by the wrong factor; no assertion catches it.

**`make_coord_Q_planar`** exists for carbonyl C=O placement: same origin-transfer and cross-product opening, but only one rotation — the `bend` "should be half of the desired value" (L581-582), rotating `o1`'s unit vector around the plane normal and translating by `center_point`.

**`make_coord_Q_COO`** builds the C-terminal carboxyl pair (O and OXT) from `CA_term` and `C_term`, with defaults pulled from `build_definitions`: `distance=distance_C_OXT` (1.27 Å) and `bend = 2π/3` (120°). Its trick is synthesizing a rotation axis from a single bond vector: `o2 = o1[::-1]` creates an "imaginary coordinate perpendicular to o1 and origin" (L653-655), whose cross product with `o1` yields a valid axis. Two mirror quaternions — one at `−bend`, one at `+bend` around the same axis — place O and OXT symmetrically, exactly the sp² carboxyl geometry.

| Kernel | Target geometry | njit | Bend input convention | Torsion handling | Axis construction |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `make_coord_Q` | Generic atom from 3 predecessors | Yes | `(π − bend) / 2` required | Passed raw, halved internally | `normalize((v3−v2) × (v1−v2))` |
| `make_coord_Q_planar` | Carbonyl O | Yes | Pre-halved ("half of desired value") | None | Same cross-product pattern |
| `make_coord_Q_COO` | C-terminal O + OXT pair | Yes | `(π − bend) / 2` if overridden | None (symmetric ± rotations) | `o1 × o1[::-1]` synthetic perpendicular |
| `rotate_coordinates_Q` | Batch (N, 3) rotation | Wrapped at L962 | n/a (angle + unit axis) | n/a | Axis supplied by caller |

Sources: [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L463-L549), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L552-L606), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L609-L693)

## Inverse Geometry: Torsion Recovery and Angle Binning

Placement has an inverse: given coordinates, recover the torsion angles that generated them — required for extracting statistics from database fragments and for validating built conformers. `calc_torsion_angles` computes signed dihedrals for an entire `(N, 3)` coordinate array in one vectorized pass, using the Azevedo-lab formulation (referenced at L188-189): bond vectors `q_vecs` from successive differences, adjacent cross products normalized into plane normals, then the four unitary components `u0, u1, u2, u3` combined through `cos_theta = DIAGONAL(MATMUL(u0.T, u1))` and `sin_theta = DIAGONAL(MATMUL(u0.T, u2))`, with the sign returned as `−ARCTAN2(sin, cos)` (L272). The `DIAGONAL` trick broadcasts per-atom-pair dot products along the whole chain without Python loops.

Because the backbone is stored as flattened N, CA, C triples, the output maps to physical torsions by stride slicing — a convention every consumer must respect:

| Torsion | Slice of output array | Chemical bond |
|---|---|---|
| `psi` | `[::3]` | CA−C |
| `omega` | `[1::3]` | C−N(i+1) |
| `phi` | `[2::3]` | N−CA |

Two auxiliary functions complete the inverse toolkit. `calc_angle` / `calc_angle_njit` return the angle between two vectors, clipping the cosine into `[−1.0, 1.0]` before `arccos` — the njit version replaces `np.clip` with explicit branches because Numba handles them more predictably. `round_radian_to_degree_bin_10` converts radians to degrees and snaps to the nearest 10° bin, implementing round-half-away-from-zero on exact `.5` cases by testing the parity of the tens digit (`x10 % 2` → `+5` else `−5`, L857-864); this is the discretization used when torsion libraries are binned (see [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling)).

Sources: [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L174-L272), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L302-L343), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L831-L866)

## Sidechain Template Alignment: A Two-Stage Quaternion Dock

`place_sidechain_template` is where the rotation kernels compose into an application-level operation: superimposing a pre-built sidechain template onto a newly built backbone. The tail of the function (visible from L400) reveals the algorithm: it computes plane normals for both the template's N-CA-C frame and the conformer's, measures the angle between them via `calc_angle_njit`, derives the rotation vector as the cross product of the two normals (`rv = CROSS(cross_ss, cross_cnf)`, normalized), and executes a second quaternion rotation `rot2 = rotate_coordinates_Q_njit(rot1, rvu, angle)` that aligns the template plane onto the conformer plane while "maintaining the N-CA in place" (L406). The final translation `rot2[:, :] + bb_cnf[1, :]` pins the template onto the conformer's CA atom. The result is a rigid-body dock: one rotation to match bond direction, one rotation about the common axis to match plane orientation, one translation — all quaternion operations, all Numba-compiled.

Sources: [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L346-L409)

## Performance Engineering: Numba as an API Constraint

The Numba strategy in `libcalc.py` is observable in its layout: a module-top comment declares *"numba.njit functions are defined at the end of the module"* (L14-15), and lines 959-966 deliver on it — six `njit` wrappers bound as module-level names:

```python
calc_all_vs_all_dists_njit = njit(calc_all_vs_all_dists)
multiply_upper_diagonal_raw_njit = njit(multiply_upper_diagonal_raw)
rotate_coordinates_Q_njit = njit(rotate_coordinates_Q)
rrd10_njit = njit(round_radian_to_degree_bin_10)
sum_upper_diagonal_raw_njit = njit(sum_upper_diagonal_raw)
unit_vec_njit = njit(unit_vector)
```

Wrapping at the tail (rather than decorating in place) keeps the plain-Python functions importable for testing and lets `libbuild.py` import only the compiled variants. Several kernels use a distinctive closure trick: NumPy callables (`CROSS`, `NORM`, `QM`, `SIN`, `COS`, `ARRAY`) are injected as default parameters so the compiled closure resolves them as constants instead of re-lookup. Distance computation avoids `scipy.spatial.distance.pdist` entirely — `calc_all_vs_all_dists_square` reproduces its upper-triangular output but skips the `sqrt`, returning squared distances suited to Lennard-Jones `r⁻¹²`/`r⁻⁶` terms; `calc_all_vs_all_dists` is the square-rooted twin. The pair-op helpers `sum_upper_diagonal_raw` and `multiply_upper_diagonal_raw` are aggressively in-place: they require the caller to pre-allocate `result` of length N(N−1)/2 and write into it, a design the docstrings justify explicitly — *"By passing the output array as a function argument, errors related to memory freeing are avoided"* (L884-888). `libbuild.py` consumes exactly this contract when assembling per-pair force-field coefficients in `create_LJ_params_raw` (sigma sums via `sum_upper_diagonal_raw_njit`, epsilon products via `multiply_upper_diagonal_raw_njit`, then mixing rules `eps_ij = sqrt(eps_i·eps_j)`, `sigmas_ij = sigma_sum × 5` for nm→Å conversion).

| Technique | Where | Rationale in code |
|---|---|---|
| Deferred `njit` wrappers at module tail | libcalc L959-966 | Keep plain functions importable; comment at L14-15 |
| NumPy callables injected as default args | `make_coord_Q`, `rotate_coordinates_Q`, etc. | Compile-time constant resolution |
| Squared-distance kernel (no sqrt) | `calc_all_vs_all_dists_square` L696-727 | Feed LJ r⁻¹²/r⁻⁶ directly |
| Caller-allocated output arrays | `sum/multiply_upper_diagonal_raw` L875-943 | Avoid large intermediate allocations / memory-freeing errors |
| Hand-rolled small-array construction | `make_coord_Q` L540-543 | 857 ns vs 1.8 µs benchmarked inline |

> [!TIP]
> One trap for contributors: `unit_vector` at L869-871 contains a typo — `np.linalgn.norm` — so calling `unit_vec_njit` (or `unit_vector`) would raise `AttributeError` at runtime. Working normalization is performed inline inside the kernels (`ocross / NORM(ocross)` pattern); treat `unit_vector` as dead-until-fixed code when auditing call paths.

Sources: [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L959-L966), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L696-L760), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L875-L943), [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L876-L921), [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L869-L871)

## Navigating the Mathematical Stack

The geometry layer described here is consumed upward in three directions. The backbone construction loop applies `make_coord_Q` semantics per residue with geometry drawn from the parameter tables covered in [Bond Geometry Strategies](8-bond-geometry-strategies); torsion values feeding those placements are sampled per [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling) using the binning function shown above. The distance kernels additionally underpin clash detection — `libbuild.py` wires `calc_all_vs_all_dists_njit` into `energycalculator_ij` at L745-748 — whose force-field terms are detailed in [Energy-Based Clash Filtering](12-energy-based-clash-filtering) and the compiled-kernel deep dive [C++ Extension & Numba Kernels](13-c-extension-and-numba-kernels). For the specialized closure problem — joining fragment-docked segments with analytic loop solutions — proceed to [Loop Closure Algorithms](15-loop-closure-algorithms), and for how sidechain templates like the one aligned by `place_sidechain_template` are generated, see [Sidechain Packing Methods](11-sidechain-packing-methods).


# Bond Geometry Strategies



Bond geometry — the planar bond angles (bend angles) and covalent bond lengths that fix local backbone rigidity — is a first-class, *pluggable* concern in IDPConformerGenerator. While torsion angles (φ/ψ) define the conformational freedom sampled from fragment databases, the bond geometry that "fleshes out" those torsions into 3D coordinates is supplied by one of four interchangeable strategies: `fixed`, `sampling` (the default), `exact`, and `int2cart`. This page explains the strategy registry architecture, the internal angle convention that all strategies must honor, the data provenance of each strategy, and how strategy data flows into the multiprocessing builder at runtime. Quaternion-based coordinate placement itself is covered in [Coordinate Geometry & Quaternion Math](7-coordinate-geometry-and-quaternion-math); torsion sampling is covered in [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling).

Sources: [bgeo_strategies/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py#L1-L76), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1-L29)

## Strategy Architecture: A Pluggable Registry

The entire strategy system is concentrated in a single registry module, `components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py`. It defines the canonical tuple of strategy names, designates `sampling` as the default, exposes `add_bgeo_strategy_arg()` so the `build` CLI (and LDRS clients) attach the `--bgeo-strategy` flag, and pairs it with a `-bgeo_path/--bgeo_path` option for supplying an externally generated bond geometry database. The help text explicitly scopes `--bgeo_path` to the `sampling` and `int2cart` strategies — `exact` obtains its geometry through the main `-db` input instead, and `fixed` needs no database at all.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    CLI["idpconfgen build<br/>--bgeo-strategy / --bgeo_path"]
    CLI --> REG["components/bgeo_strategies/<br/>bgeo_strategies tuple · default = sampling"]

    REG --> FIXED["fixed"]
    REG --> SAMP["sampling ★ default"]
    REG --> EXACT["exact"]
    REG --> INT2["int2cart"]

    FIXED -->|"get_cycle_bend_angles()"| BD["core/build_definitions.py<br/>per-residue mean bend angles"]
    SAMP -->|"bgeo_sampling_path"| TAR["bundled bgeo_sampling.tar<br/>(empirical distribution DB)"]
    EXACT -->|"aligndb(db, True)"| BGEODB["user DB built by<br/>idpconfgen bgeodb"]
    INT2 -->|"BGEO_Int2Cart"| MODEL["Int2Cart neural model<br/>PyTorch + CUDA (optional dep)"]

    INT2 -.->|"ImportError guard"| HAS["has_int2cart flag<br/>CheckBgeoInstallation blocks CLI"]
```

Dependency gating is handled by an `argparse` action class, `CheckBgeoInstallation`, which wraps the `choices` validation: if the user selects `int2cart` but the external `modelling`/PyTorch stack is absent (`has_int2cart` is `False`), the parser raises a descriptive error pointing to the installation docs rather than failing later at build time. Each strategy is a small package under `components/bgeo_strategies/` exporting a `name` constant that must match the registry tuple exactly — a convention shared with the sidechain-packing plugin system described in [Component Plugin Pattern](20-component-plugin-pattern).

Sources: [bgeo_strategies/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py#L17-L50), [bgeo_strategies/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py#L53-L76), [int2cart/bgeo_int2cart.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/int2cart/bgeo_int2cart.py#L6-L20)

**Strategy comparison at a glance:**

| Strategy | Geometry source | Granularity | External dependency | `--bgeo_path` | Relative cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fixed` | Curated means in `build_definitions.py` | One bend angle per residue type | None | Not applicable | Negligible |
| `sampling` ★ | Bundled `bgeo_sampling.tar` | Distribution per bond-type/residue/torsion-bin | None | Yes | Dict lookups + random draw |
| `exact` | Database from `idpconfgen bgeodb` | Fragment-exact angles **and** bond lengths | bgeodb-generated DB (via `-db`) | No (uses `-db`) | DB alignment step |
| `int2cart` | NVIDIA Int2Cart neural predictor | Predicted d1–d3 lengths, θ1–θ3 angles per torsion | PyTorch + `modelling` pkg + CUDA GPU | Yes | GPU inference |

Sources: [bgeo_strategies/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py#L17-L50)

## The (π − θ)/2 Bend Angle Convention

Every bond geometry store in this codebase — the fixed dictionaries, the sampling database, the Int2Cart predictions — expresses bend angles in the same *pre-transformed* unit: **half the planar supplement**, `(π − θ) / 2`, in radians. This is not a stylistic choice. The quaternion-based builder positions each new backbone atom by rotating about a bond axis, and the rotation angle required to land an atom on the planar-angle cone is exactly half the supplement of the planar angle. Storing angles pre-halved removes a per-atom division from the hot building loop and, more importantly, makes every geometry source drop-in compatible with the builder's rotation kernels.

The convention is enforced at three independent points, all of which must agree for a strategy to work: the `bgeo` CLI docstring states that angles are "in sync with the expectations of the `$ idpconfgen build` command" and documents the `(PI - angle) / 2` form; the extraction routine applies `(np.pi - calc_angle_njit(...)) / 2` to each backbone bend before storing it (with `Ca_C_O` stored as `angle / 2` since it is already a plain planar angle in the same family); and the fixed-strategy dictionaries are derived from raw means via the comprehension `{key: (pi - v) / 2}`.

| Backbone bend angle | Registry key (`core.definitions`) | Fixed-strategy dictionary | Ala mean (raw) | σ (raw) | Builder consumption phase |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C(m1)–N–CA | `bgeo_Cm1NCa` | `build_bend_angles_Cm1_N_CA` | 2.118 rad ≈ 121.4° | 0.028 | OMEGA step |
| N–CA–C | `bgeo_NCaC` | `build_bend_angles_N_CA_C` | 1.939 rad ≈ 111.1° | 0.036 | PHI step |
| CA–C–N(p1) | `bgeo_CaCNp1` | `build_bend_angles_CA_C_Np1` | 2.038 rad ≈ 116.8° | 0.022 | PSI step |
| CA–C–O | `bgeo_CaCO` | `build_bend_CA_C_O` (scalar) | 2.102 rad ≈ 120.4° | — | Carbonyl O placement |

A fourth scalar family completes the carbonyl and amide geometry: `build_bend_CA_C_OXT = (π − 2π/3) / 2` for the C-terminal OXT, `build_bend_H_N_C = radians(114) / 2` for the amide hydrogen, plus the fixed distances `distance_C_O`, `distance_C_OXT = 1.27 Å`, and `distance_H_N = 0.9 Å`. Note that the residue-indexed dictionaries carry the *raw* mean under a fraction-like name (`bend_angles_N_CA_C`) while the `(π − v)/2`-transformed counterpart lives under the `build_bend_angles_*` name that strategies actually consume.

> [!TIP]
> Feeding raw planar angles (instead of the half-supplement form) into any bgeo store will silently mirror backbone geometry around each placed atom — the builder never re-transforms. When authoring a custom strategy or converting third-party geometry tables, apply `(pi − θ)/2` at ingestion time, exactly as `read_trimer_torsion_planar_angles` does.

Sources: [cli_bgeo.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_bgeo.py#L26-L63), [libhigherlevel.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libhigherlevel.py#L824-L846), [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L495-L590), [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L668-L675)

## Strategy: `fixed` — Curated Per-Residue Means

The `fixed` strategy is the simplest contract in the system: it provides an infinite cycle over the three `build_bend_angles_*` dictionaries in builder-phase order — `build_bend_angles_Cm1_N_CA` for the OMEGA placement, `build_bend_angles_N_CA_C` for PHI, and `build_bend_angles_CA_C_Np1` for PSI. `get_cycle_bend_angles()` returns an `itertools.cycle` over that tuple, so the builder consumes one dictionary per placement step, round and round, for every residue of the template chain. No database, no randomness: every conformer built with `fixed` shares identical bond geometry, differing only through torsion sampling.

The underlying numbers in `core/build_definitions.py` are noteworthy for their representation: each mean is stored as an exact integer ratio (e.g., `8719677895929259 / 4503599627370496`), which reproduces the original float64 bit-for-bit and makes the curated values version-stable across platforms. Comments record the human-readable value and its observed standard deviation across the reference structure set — standard deviations that `fixed` deliberately discards. The per-residue-type spread is chemically meaningful: glycine's N–CA–C angle is the widest (1.977 rad), proline and isoleucine/valine the narrowest (≈1.914–1.968 rad), reflecting ring strain and β-branching respectively.

**Fixed bond lengths** (used alongside the bend angles by the distance iterators `get_cycle_distances_backbone`/`get_cycle_bond_type` from `libbuild.py`) follow the same pattern — per-residue dictionaries plus precomputed `average_distance_*` and `std_distance_*` aggregates:

| Bond | Dictionary | Range over 20 residue types (Å) | Comment on outliers |
|---|---|---|---|
| N–CA | `distances_N_CA` | 1.455 – 1.466 | Proline longest (ring geometry) |
| CA–C | `distances_CA_C` | 1.515 – 1.526 | Glycine shortest (no Cβ) |
| C–N(p1) | `distances_C_Np1` | 1.330 – 1.331 | Peptide bond, essentially invariant |
| C–O / C–OXT / H–N | scalars | 1.234 / 1.27 / 0.9 | Single values, residue-independent |

Sources: [fixed/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/fixed/__init__.py#L9-L22), [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L503-L546), [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L587-L676)

## Strategy: `sampling` — Empirical Distributions (Default)

`sampling` replaces single means with **observed distributions conditioned on sequence context and backbone torsions**, and it is the registry default. The database ships with the package as `bgeo_sampling.tar` (path exposed as `bgeo_sampling_path`), created from high-resolution PDB structures. The canonical authoring pipeline is the `idpconfgen bgeo` CLI: for every trimer in every input structure, it computes the middle residue's φ/ψ, rounds both to 10° bins, and records the four observed bend angles (`Cm1_N_Ca`, `N_Ca_C`, `Ca_C_Np1`, `Ca_C_O`) under the composite key `'<AAA>':'<phi>,<psi>'`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    PDB["High-resolution<br/>PDB/mmCIF corpus"] -->|"idpconfgen bgeo<br/>trimer walk · φ/ψ → 10° bins"| RAW["trimer-keyed library<br/>angles in (π−θ)/2 rad"]
    RAW -->|"bgeo --convert<br/>convert_bond_geo_lib()"| HIER["bond-type-first hierarchy<br/>bond → residue → DAE → torsion bin"]
    HIER --> TAR["bgeo_sampling.tar"]
    TAR -->|"populate_globals()"| FULL["BGEO_full (global)"]
    FULL -->|"bgeo_reduce()"| TRI["BGEO_trimer<br/>(context-dependent view)"]
    FULL -->|"bgeo_reduce()"| RES["BGEO_res<br/>(residue-only view)"]
    TRI --> B["Builder placement loop<br/>(quaternion kernels)"]
    RES --> B
```

After extraction, `idpconfgen bgeo --convert` invokes `convert_bond_geo_lib()` to restructure the library from trimer-first to **bond-type-first hierarchy** — the shape the builder actually queries. The five-level key schema is:

| Level | Example key | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — bond type | `N_Ca_C` | Which planar angle (exact-match keys, from `core.definitions` `bgeo_*` constants) |
| 2 — central residue | `A` | 1-letter code of the middle residue |
| 3 — adjacent pair (DAE) | `DE` | Previous/next residue letters flanking the central residue |
| 4 — torsion bin | `'10,-40'` | φ/ψ of the central residue, rounded to 10° |
| 5 — leaf | list of floats | Observed bend angles, already in `(π−θ)/2` rad |

At build time, `populate_globals()` loads the tar into the `BGEO_full` global, then calls `bgeo_reduce()` (from `libhigherlevel.py`) to split it into two query-optimized views, `BGEO_trimer` and `BGEO_res` — both retaining the same first-layer bond-type keys (asserted explicitly), differing in how deep the context hierarchy is retained for lookup. The test fixtures mirror this lifecycle one-to-one: `EXPL_A_bgeo.json` (raw), `EXPL_A_bgeo_converted.json` (post-`convert_bond_geo_lib`), and `EXPL_A_bgeo_trimer.json`/`EXPL_A_bgeo_res.json` (post-`bgeo_reduce`), making the data pipeline directly inspectable without touching the production tar. The extraction kernel itself, `read_trimer_torsion_planar_angles`, walks 7-atom windows labeled `CA C N CA C N CA`, computes φ/ψ via `calc_torsion_angles`, bins with `rrd10_njit`, and validates atom labels at every step — mismatched or non-standard residues are logged and skipped rather than poisoning the statistics.

Sources: [sampling/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/sampling/__init__.py#L1-L12), [cli_bgeo.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_bgeo.py#L1-L63), [libhigherlevel.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libhigherlevel.py#L725-L846), [libhigherlevel.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libhigherlevel.py#L849-L883), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L864-L881)

## Strategy: `exact` — Fragment-Consistent Geometry

`exact` closes the loop between torsion sampling and bond geometry: instead of re-drawing bend angles from a statistical database, it reads the **bond angles and bond lengths that physically accompanied the selected fragment** in its source structure. The divergence appears in `main()`: when the strategy is `exact`, the fragment database is opened with `aligndb(db, True)`, whose second positional flag extends the returned tuple with `BEND_ANGS` and `BOND_LENS` arrays alongside the usual `ANGLES` — module globals that otherwise stay `None`. This is why `exact` requires a database produced by the dedicated `bgeodb` CLI (the torsions+geometry superset of the plain `torsions` CLI); feeding a torsions-only database triggers an explicit `DATABASE ERROR` message instructing the user to regenerate with `bgeodb`.

The trade-off is representational rather than computational. With `exact`, every built conformer inherits bond geometry that is *self-consistent with its torsion context* — valuable when rebuilding from curated fragment sets or when reproducing specific experimental geometries — but the ensemble loses the intra-context geometric variability that `sampling` provides. Note the asymmetry in global-population: despite needing no `bgeo_path`, `exact` still triggers the `BGEO_full/BGEO_trimer/BGEO_res` load in `populate_globals()` (it shares the condition with `sampling` and `int2cart`), while `are_globals()` treats it like `fixed` — requiring only the atom labels, masks, and energy functions. Strategy-specific residue matching during fragment stitching is delegated to `get_adjacent_angles(...)`, which receives `bgeo_strategy` as a parameter so torsion-adjacency logic can adapt its geometry lookups.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L612-L633), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L130-L133), [exact/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/exact/__init__.py#L1-L4), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L864-L866)

## Strategy: `int2cart` — Neural Internal-Coordinate Prediction

`int2cart` delegates geometry prediction to the **Int2Cart** neural network (NVIDIA's `modelling` package): given a sequence and its torsion angles, the model regresses the six internal coordinates per residue — bond lengths `d1, d2, d3` and bend angles `theta1, theta2, theta3` — effectively *learning* the bond geometry distribution rather than tabulating it. The wrapper class `BGEO_Int2Cart` bundles a frozen checkpoint (`model.tar`) and YAML config (`int2cart.yml`) inside the strategy package; its single public method, `get_internal_coords(sequence, torsions)`, runs `predict()` with `units="radian"` and `build=False`, then slices the last-residue predictions (`[0, -1, 0]`) to return the 6-tuple for incremental chain extension.

This is the only strategy with an **optional hard dependency and hardware requirement**. The module guards its imports with `try/except ImportError`, setting `has_int2cart = False` so the rest of the package can import the name safely; the CLI blocks selection early via `CheckBgeoInstallation`; and at runtime `populate_globals()` instantiates the model inside a `try/except RuntimeError`, logging a warning to use CUDA-compatible GPUs if construction fails — the model checkpoint is loaded with `map_location=torch.device('cuda')`, making a GPU effectively mandatory. Because Int2Cart predicts geometry from torsions alone, it consumes the same `BGEO_*` globals as `sampling` (loaded for fallback/contextual use) plus its own `INT2CART` global, as codified in `are_globals()`.

Sources: [int2cart/bgeo_int2cart.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/int2cart/bgeo_int2cart.py#L6-L62), [bgeo_strategies/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py#L53-L70), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L882-L893)

## Runtime Data Flow: Globals, Validation, and Multiprocessing

Strategy selection ultimately resolves into **module-level globals** — the same performance pattern used for atom labels and energy functions, chosen because reading globals is the cheapest data-sharing mechanism across `multiprocessing.Pool` workers (fork inherits them; nothing is pickled per task). The lifecycle is: `main()` determines the strategy → `populate_globals()` materializes its data → `are_globals()` asserts completeness *per strategy* → the pool of `_build_conformers` workers consumes the globals read-only.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as build main()
    participant PG as populate_globals()
    participant G as module globals
    participant AG as are_globals()
    participant W as Pool workers

    M->>PG: bgeo_strategy, bgeo_path, forcefield
    alt strategy ∈ {sampling, exact, int2cart}
        PG->>PG: read DB (default: bundled bgeo_sampling.tar)
        PG->>G: BGEO_full.update(db)
        PG->>G: BGEO_trimer, BGEO_res ← bgeo_reduce(BGEO_full)
        PG->>PG: assert identical first-layer keys
    end
    alt strategy = int2cart
        PG->>G: INT2CART = BGEO_Int2Cart()  (CUDA; warn on RuntimeError)
    end
    PG->>G: ALL/TEMPLATE_LABELS, MASKS, EFUNC
    M->>AG: bgeo_strategy
    AG-->>M: per-strategy completeness check (AssertionError if partial)
    M->>W: Pool(ncores).imap(_build_conformers ...)
    W->>G: read-only access to BGEO_* / INT2CART per placement step
```

The validation matrix in `are_globals()` makes each strategy's runtime contract explicit and is worth reading as the authoritative spec: `sampling` requires `BGEO_full`, `BGEO_trimer`, `BGEO_res`; `exact` and `fixed` require only the labels/masks/energy-function trio; `int2cart` requires the `BGEO_*` trio *plus* the instantiated `INT2CART` model; and any unrecognized value raises with the registry's formatted `bgeo_error_msg`. In `--long` mode the same preparation runs per fragment, with each fragment's globals snapshot (`SLICEDICT_XMERS`, `XMERPROBS`, `BGEO_*`, labels, masks, energy functions) archived into `LONG_GLOBALS` and swapped in as fragments are processed sequentially.

> [!TIP]
> When debugging a strategy, check `are_globals()` first: a partially populated global set (e.g., `INT2CART` left `None` after a GPU RuntimeError under `int2cart`) fails the `all(...)` check *before* any pool work is dispatched, converting what would be a confusing mid-build worker crash into an immediate, attributable startup error.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L182-L222), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L829-L893), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L131-L155), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L694-L715)

## Strategy Selection Guide

For production IDP ensemble generation, the default `sampling` strategy offers the best realism-to-cost ratio: context-conditioned geometric variability from high-resolution structures with no external dependencies. Choose `fixed` for debugging the building pipeline itself (geometry ceases to be a random variable) or for extremely fast templated builds where geometric variation is unwanted. Choose `exact` when rebuilding must preserve the bond geometry of specific source fragments — typically with a curated `bgeodb` database. Reserve `int2cart` for GPU-equipped environments where learned geometry generalization (especially around non-canonical torsion regimes) justifies the dependency; note that its quality depends on the bundled checkpoint, and it is the only strategy whose failure mode is environmental (missing CUDA) rather than logical.

All strategies feed the same downstream contract — half-supplement bend angles plus Å-scale bond lengths consumed by the quaternion placement kernels — so switching strategies never changes the builder's control flow, only its numeric sources. That contract, and the full fixed-value tables, are itemized in [Build Definitions Reference](21-build-definitions-reference); the placement math consuming these values is derived in [Coordinate Geometry & Quaternion Math](7-coordinate-geometry-and-quaternion-math); and how sampled torsion contexts select which bgeo entries to query next is covered in [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling).


# K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling



This page explains how IDPConformerGenerator decides **how many residues to grow per sampling step** during conformer construction. Instead of adding one residue at a time, the builder draws backbone torsion segments of variable length — *k*-mers ("x-mers") — from an empirical torsion database, and the probability of each fragment length is governed by a small, self-contained component: `idpconfgen.components.xmer_probs`. We cover the data contract, the input file format, CLI integration, the database-matching pipeline that validates k-mer availability, and the dynamic renormalization that keeps the distribution valid when the database cannot satisfy every requested size.

## Why Fragment Length Is a Random Variable

The `idpconfgen build` command constructs conformers from a torsion-angle database previously generated by `idpconfgen torsions` ([cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1-L10)). At each growth step, the engine does not commit to a fixed segment size: it selects a fragment of *k* consecutive residues from the input sequence, locates all matching fragments in the database, and samples one of their stored torsion sets. The value of *k* is itself drawn from a weighted distribution, which is exactly what the `XmerProbs` object encodes. The component's docstring states its dual responsibility plainly: *"Define fragment probability distribution for CLI and building"* ([xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L1)).

The shipped default allows fragments of 1 to 5 residues with relative weights `(1, 1, 3, 3, 2)`, meaning trimers and tetramers are three times as likely as monomers or dimers, and pentamers twice as likely ([xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L28-L30)). This bias toward mid-sized fragments reflects a deliberate trade-off between local torsion realism (longer fragments capture residue-to-residue angle correlations) and database coverage (shorter fragments match more often).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["xmer_probs file (.col)<br>or built-in default"] --> B["read_xmer_probs_from_file"]
    B --> C["convert_int_float_lines_to_dict"]
    C --> D["make_xmerprobs<br>normalize weights to sum=1"]
    D --> E["XmerProbs(sizes, probs)"]
    E --> F["cli_build.py global<br>XMERPROBS"]
    G["torsions database<br>primary + secondary strings"] --> H["prepare_slice_dict<br>search k-mers of every size"]
    F --> H
    H --> I["SLICEDICT_XMERS<br>size → fragment → slice objects"]
    I --> J["build_conformer<br>draw k by probs, pick slice"]
    J --> K["backbone torsion segments<br>omega / phi / psi"]
```

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1-L10), [xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L28-L30)

## The XmerProbs Data Contract

The entire distribution is carried by a two-field namedtuple: `_XmerProbs = namedtuple('XmerProbs', ['sizes', 'probs'])` ([xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L18)). The constructor function `make_xmerprobs(sizes, probs)` copies the sizes into a list and delegates normalization to `make_seq_probabilities(probs, reverse=False)`, which divides every weight by the total so the probabilities sum to exactly 1 ([libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L946-L957)). Weights may be any integers — the help text notes that `10` and `90` become 10% and 90% ([xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L91-L92)).

| API element | Location | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `XmerProbs(sizes, probs)` | [xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L18) | Immutable distribution container |
| `make_xmerprobs(sizes, probs)` | [xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L21-L25) | Validates/normalizes into a distribution |
| `default_XmerProbs` | [xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L28-L30) | Sizes `(1..5)`, weights `(1, 1, 3, 3, 2)` |
| `read_xmer_probs_from_file(fpath)` | [xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L33-L38) | File → dict → distribution |
| `prepare_xmer_probs(value)` | [xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L113-L118) | Type-dispatching adapter for the build engine |
| `compress_xmer_to_bool/_key` | [xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L121-L134) | Restrict sizes & renormalize |
| `make_seq_probabilities(seq)` | [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L946-L957) | Divide-by-sum normalization |

The file reader is a functional pipeline: `chainf(fpath, read_lines, convert_int_float_lines_to_dict)` streams lines into an ordered `{size: weight}` dict, from which the distribution is assembled and logged ([xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L33-L38)). `prepare_xmer_probs` then acts as the single entry point consumed by the builder: it passes through an existing `XmerProbs` instance (guarded by `is_XmerProbs`), falls back to `default_XmerProbs` for `None`, and otherwise attempts a file read ([xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L52-L62), [xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L112-L118)). Both fallback behaviors are pinned by tests: `prepare_xmer_probs(None)` and `read_xmer_probs_file_or_default(None)` must return the default object *by identity* ([test_xmer_probs.py](tests/test_xmer_probs.py#L46-L55)).

Sources: [libcalc.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcalc.py#L946-L957), [test_xmer_probs.py](tests/test_xmer_probs.py#L46-L55)

## Input File Format and CLI Integration

The distribution is configured through `-xp / --xmer-probs`, a two-column text file where the first column is the fragment size and the second its relative probability; `#` starts a comment line ([xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L83-L98)). The repository's test fixture `xmer_prob.col` encodes sizes 1, 2, 5 with weights 2, 4, 6, and the test suite verifies it normalizes identically to `make_xmerprobs([1, 2, 5], [2, 4, 6])` ([test_xmer_probs.py](tests/test_xmer_probs.py#L25-L34)).

```text
# size    weight
1         2
2         4
5         6
```

CLI parsing is handled by `XmerProbsAction`, an `argparse.Action` subclass that eagerly converts the file path into an `XmerProbs` object at parse time and translates failure modes into precise parser errors ([xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L65-L80)):

| Failure | CLI response |
|---|---|
| `ValueError` / `TypeError` (malformed file) | `Not a compatible '<dest>' format.` |
| Missing file | `File <value> not found for parameter <dest>.` |
| Directory passed | `<value> is a directory. We expect a file...` |

This fail-fast design means invalid distributions are rejected before any expensive database preparation begins. The action is attached to the build parser via `add_xmer_arg(ap)` ([cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L352)), itself a functional composition over `add_general_arg` with the flags and kwargs defined in the component ([xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L98-L110)). A test confirms `add_xmer_arg` yields `None` by default and a valid `XmerProbs` when given `-xp <file>` ([test_xmer_probs.py](tests/test_xmer_probs.py#L81-L94)).

> [!TIP]
> Because `XmerProbsAction` validates at *argument-parse* time, you get distribution errors in the CLI usage phase, not minutes later inside the multiprocessing pool — a deliberate placement of the validation boundary as early in the pipeline as possible.

Sources: [xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L65-L80), [test_xmer_probs.py](tests/test_xmer_probs.py#L81-L94)

## Database Matching: `prepare_slice_dict`

A user-requested distribution only matters if the torsion database actually contains fragments of those sizes for the target sequence. This reconciliation happens in `prepare_slice_dict` in [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L479-L488). Its documented protocol has three stages ([libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L492-L518)):

1. **Enumerate x-mers** — the input sequence is split into every overlapping fragment of each size in `mers_size` ([libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L570-L574)).
2. **Search the database** — for each x-mer, the concatenated `primary` sequence string is searched for all matches, honoring the `res_tolerance` substitution dictionary (e.g., `{"A": "AIL"}` lets Ala match Ile/Leu sites). The search is repeated for the variant where the x-mer is followed by a proline, and only entries with at least one match survive ([libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L499-L509)).
3. **Optional CSSS layer** — when custom secondary-structure sampling is active, surviving slices are re-indexed by their DSSP code from the concatenated `secondary` string, so the builder can sample specific secondary structure per region ([libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L511-L518)).

The returned dictionary is nested: the first key level is the fragment *length*, the second level is the fragment sequence, and the values are slice objects pointing into the torsion database ([libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L555-L566)). Matching is parallelized with `pool_function` across cores, one work unit per x-mer size ([libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L579-L590)). Notably, if the user never requested size 1, a single-residue layer is force-added anyway, guaranteeing the builder always has a maximal-coverage fallback ([libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L592-L599)).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    S["input sequence (1-letter)"] -->|"get_mers(seq, k)<br>for each k"| X["x-mers per size"]
    T["torsions database<br>primary / secondary"] --> P
    X --> P["populate_dict_with_database<br>regex match + res_tolerance"]
    P -->|"matches only"| D["slice_dict<br>k → fragment → slices"]
    P -->|"+Pro lookahead"| D
    D --> R{"CSSS enabled?"}
    R -->|yes| D2["re-index slices<br>by DSSP key"]
    R -->|no| D3["SLICEDICT_XMERS global"]
    D2 --> D3
```

Sources: [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L492-L518), [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L570-L599)

## Dynamic Renormalization: Compressing the Distribution

After database matching, some requested sizes may have zero available fragments. The component handles this with two compression functions. `compress_xmer_to_bool` filters an existing `XmerProbs` by a boolean mask over its sizes, while `compress_xmer_to_key` derives that mask by testing which sizes appear in a list of available keys — both re-run `make_xmerprobs` on the survivors, which automatically renormalizes the weights ([xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L121-L134)). This is the implementation of the promise in the CLI help: *"Fragment sizes will be ignored if no matches are found in the database and the probabilities renormalized"* ([xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L95-L96)).

The test suite pins exact numbers. Compressing the default distribution `(1,2,3,4,5)` with weights `(1,1,3,3,2)` down to keys `[3, 4, 5]` yields sizes `[3, 4, 5]` and probabilities `[0.375, 0.375, 0.25]` — the retained raw weights `3, 3, 2` (sum 8) redistributed over the reduced support ([test_xmer_probs.py](tests/test_xmer_probs.py#L108-L114)):

| State | sizes | probs |
|---|---|---|
| Default | `(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)` | `(0.1, 0.1, 0.3, 0.3, 0.2)` |
| After compress to `[3,4,5]` | `[3, 4, 5]` | `(0.375, 0.375, 0.25)` |
| Fixture file (sizes 1,2,5) | `[1, 2, 5]` | `(≈0.167, ≈0.333, ≈0.5)` |

Sources: [xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L121-L134), [test_xmer_probs.py](tests/test_xmer_probs.py#L97-L114)

## Consumption in the Build Engine

Inside [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L110-L137), the reconciled artifacts live in module-level globals: `ANGLES` holds the torsion database slices, `SLICEDICT_XMERS` the k-mer → slice index, and `XMERPROBS` the (possibly compressed) size distribution. The file explains why these are globals: *"I use global variables to facilitate distributing conformer creation processes across multiple cores... cores can read global variables fast and with non-significant overhead"* ([cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L110-L114)). Worker processes therefore sample a fragment size from `XMERPROBS`, look up candidate slices in `SLICEDICT_XMERS`, and extract the corresponding torsion triplet sequence from `ANGLES`.

The torsion extraction follows the backbone cycle documented in libbuild: bond geometry and distance iterators cycle through N–CA (omega), CA–C (phi), and C–N(+1) (psi) in a fixed, order-synced pattern ([libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L449-L477)). A second lookahead rule, encoded in the CLI help, extends sampling: *"If a Proline residue follows the fragment being built, the extra Proline angles will also be consider regardless of the selected fragment size"* ([xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L93-L94)) — so a drawn k-mer may materialize a k+1-residue torsion segment when proline stacking demands it.

For long disordered chains, the `--long` mode scopes a *separate* set of these globals per 150-residue fragment: `LONG_GLOBALS` enumerates exactly the per-fragment identities, including `SLICEDICT_XMERS` and `XMERPROBS` ([cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L157-L173)). Each fragment thus gets its own database-matched distribution, reflecting that residue windows far apart in a long IDP may have different k-mer coverage in the empirical database.

> [!TIP]
> When debugging sampling behavior, read the log lines emitted by `logxmerprobs` — they print both the *original* and the *"corrected fragment selection probabilities"* ([xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L41-L49), [xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L121-L128). If the corrected sizes differ from your input file, the database simply lacks matches for the missing sizes, not a parsing bug.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L110-L137), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L157-L173), [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L449-L477)

## Summary and Where to Go Next

K-mer torsion probability sampling is a three-layer design: a **pure data component** (`XmerProbs`) owning normalization and compression; a **database reconciliation layer** (`prepare_slice_dict`) that intersects the requested support with empirically available fragments; and a **consumption layer** of build-engine globals that makes the distribution readable at zero cost from every worker process. The design keeps probability semantics testable in isolation — the entire behavioral surface is pinned by a 115-line test module ([test_xmer_probs.py](tests/test_xmer_probs.py#L1-L115)).

To continue through the building engine:

- See where the sampled torsion segments are consumed end-to-end in [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble)
- Understand how per-bond angles/bonds around the sampled torsions are resolved in [Bond Geometry Strategies](8-bond-geometry-strategies)
- Explore the alternative geometry backends (exact/fixed/int2cart/sampling) referenced by the same build globals in [Component Plugin Pattern](20-component-plugin-pattern)
- For the CLI plumbing behind `-xp`, `-db`, and subcommand registration, see [CLI Subcommand System](17-cli-subcommand-system)
- To run the fixtures used in this page (`xmer_prob.col`, `test_xmer_probs.py`), consult [Testing Strategy & Fixtures](22-testing-strategy-and-fixtures)


# NMR Chemical Shift Matching



This page explains how IDPConformerGenerator bridges the gap between **experimental NMR chemical shift data** and **conformer ensemble generation**. Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) defy single-structure characterization, so the toolkit converts chemical-shift-derived secondary structure populations into per-residue sampling probabilities (CSSS — *Custom Secondary-Structure Sampling*), injects them into the build engine, and closes the loop by back-calculating NMR J-coupling observables from the resulting ensembles. We cover the `csssconv` standardization layer, the `makecsss` authoring tool, the CSSS JSON contract consumed by `build`, and the `torsionsJ` validation subcommand — all at the implementation level relevant to intermediate developers. Fragment-selection mechanics themselves are deferred to [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling).

## From NMR Observables to Sampling Constraints

IDPConformerGenerator does **not** predict chemical shifts itself. Instead, it occupies the two integration points of a chemical-shift-driven workflow: *constraint injection* (converting shift-derived populations into build-time sampling biases) and *ensemble validation* (computing shift-related observables from generated structures). NMR chemical shifts for an IDP (e.g., BMRB entry 25501, the unfolded drkN SH3 domain) are first processed by external inference tools — CheSPI or δ2D — which translate shifts into per-residue secondary structure populations. The `csssconv` subcommand standardizes those heterogeneous outputs into a single CSSS JSON schema, which the `build` subclient consumes via its `-csss` flag.

Sources: [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L1-L10), [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L13-L20)

The concept map below shows both data directions: the forward (constraints) path in solid arrows and the validation (back-calculation) path with the dashed feedback edge.
