Note that `makecsss` provides an alternative authoring path that bypasses chemical shift data entirely when only qualitative structural intuition is available.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Experimental["Experimental NMR Data"]
        CS["BMRB chemical shifts<br/>(e.g. BMRB 25501)"]
    end

    subgraph Inference["Chemical-Shift Inference (external tools)"]
        CHESPI["CheSPI<br/>probs8_[ID].txt<br/>8 DSSP-state probabilities"]
        D2D["δ2D<br/>*.TXT<br/>Helix/Beta/Coil/PPII populations"]
    end

    subgraph IDPConfGen["IDPConformerGenerator"]
        CONV["csssconv<br/>(cli_csssconv.py)"]
        MAKE["makecsss<br/>(cli_makecsss.py)"]
        CSSS["CSSS.JSON<br/>{residue: {'L'/'H'/'E': prob}}"]
        BUILD["build -csss<br/>(cli_build.py)"]
        TJ["torsionsJ<br/>(cli_torsionsJ.py)"]
    end

    ENSEMBLE["Conformer ensemble (.pdb)"]
    EXPJ["Experimental ³J HN-CαHA"]

    CS --> CHESPI
    CS --> D2D
    CHESPI -->|"-p8"| CONV
    D2D -->|"-d2D"| CONV
    CONV --> CSSS
    MAKE -->|"author / edit"| CSSS
    CSSS --> BUILD
    BUILD --> ENSEMBLE
    ENSEMBLE -->|"back-calculate"| TJ
    TJ -->|"torsionsJ_HN-CaHA.json"| EXPJ
    EXPJ -.->|"ensemble validation loop"| ENSEMBLE
```

Sources: [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L11-L21), [cli_torsionsJ.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_torsionsJ.py#L1-L11), [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L130-L170)

## The External Inference Layer: CheSPI and δ2D

Two published tools serve as the canonical chemical shift interpreters, and the module header records both citations as the expected provenance of input files. **CheSPI** (Nielsen & Mulder, *J Biomol NMR* 2021) infers populations over the full 8-state DSSP alphabet, while **δ2D** (Camilloni et al., *Biochemistry* 2012) predicts a coarser 4-state model that includes polyproline-II (PPII) — a state of particular relevance for disordered chains. The repository ships real outputs for both tools in the drkN SH3 example so developers can test the converters without access to a BMRB pipeline.

| Aspect | CheSPI | δ2D |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Nielsen & Mulder, J Biomol NMR 75(6-7):273-291 (2021) | Camilloni et al., Biochemistry 51(11):2224-2231 (2012) |
| `csssconv` flag | `-p8` / `--chespi_p8` | `-d2D` / `--delta2D` |
| Native file | `probs8_[ID].txt` | `.TXT` |
| Predicted states | 8 DSSP codes: H, G, I, E, ' ' (coil), T, S, B | 4 states: Helix, Beta, Coil, PPII |
| Grouped output mapping | H = α-helix + 3₁₀-helix; E = β-strand; L = everything else | H = Helix; E = Beta; L = Coil + PPII |
| Unreliable-residue fallback | not handled | uniform 0.25 (full) / 0.333 (grouped) |
| Input validation | regex on first line | marked TODO in source |

Sources: [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L1-L10), [probs8_25501_unfolded.txt](example/drksh3_example/probs8_25501_unfolded.txt#L1-L10), [drk_d2D.txt](example/drksh3_example/drk_d2D.txt#L1-L14)

## Input Contract: Native File Formats

The **CheSPI `probs8` format** is whitespace-delimited with three leading tokens per line: a one-letter residue code, the residue number, and eight probability floats whose column order matches the DSSP sequence `H, G, I, E, ' ', T, S, B` (the order hardcoded in the full converter). For example, residue 1 of the drkN SH3 file reads `M 1 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 0.5370 0.4630 0.0000 0.0000` — 53.7% coil and 46.3% turn. Each row sums to 1.0 across the eight states.

Sources: [probs8_25501_unfolded.txt](example/drksh3_example/probs8_25501_unfolded.txt#L1-L10), [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L89)

The **δ2D format** mixes header/comment lines (prefixed `#`, including a summary block with total populations such as `#Helix(H): 3.1%`) with data rows containing: residue number, residue letter, Helix, Beta, Coil, and PPII probabilities, plus a trailing consensus SS letter. Crucially, residues that δ2D deemed unreliable are *commented out* with a `#<resnum>` prefix (residues 1, 2, 58, 59 in the example) — the converters detect these via regex and substitute uniform probabilities rather than failing.

Sources: [drk_d2D.txt](example/drksh3_example/drk_d2D.txt#L1-L60), [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L178-L180)

## csssconv: The Standardization Layer

### CLI Surface

The subcommand accepts either (or both) prediction files plus an optional `--output` path; without it, the JSON is printed to stdout so it can be redirected. The `--full` flag preserves the native state alphabet instead of grouping into the builder's three-state model. Before parsing CheSPI input, `main()` applies a light sanity check — a `re.fullmatch` against the expected first-line shape — and aborts with a log message directing the user to `probs8_[ID].txt` files; the δ2D path carries an explicit `TODO` for equivalent validation.

| Flag | Long form | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `-p8` | `--chespi_p8` | path to CheSPI `probs8_[ID].txt` |
| `-d2D` | `--delta2D` | path to δ2D `.TXT` |
| `-f` | `--full` | keep all native DSSP codes, skip grouping |
| (libcli) | `--output` | write JSON to file instead of stdout |

Sources: [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L46-L67), [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L264-L292)

### Parser Functions and Module Interaction

Four sibling functions implement the 2×2 matrix of {CheSPI, δ2D} × {full, grouped}. All return the same nested-dictionary shape (residue number → state → probability), differing only in the second key layer. The interaction diagram below annotates each parser with its exact data contract, including the index arithmetic that constitutes the modules' most subtle behavior.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph cli_csssconv["cli_csssconv.py"]
        MAIN["main()"]
        FULL8["chespi_probs8_convert_full()"]
        GRP8["chespi_probs8_convert_grouped()"]
        FULLD["d2D_convert_full()"]
        GRPD["d2D_convert_grouped()"]
        RX["first-line regex check"]
    end
    P8["probs8_[ID].txt"] --> RX
    RX --> FULL8
    RX --> GRP8
    D2D["δ2D .TXT"] --> FULLD
    D2D --> GRPD
    FULL8 -->|"pop resid; keys H,G,I,E,' ',T,S,B"| MAIN
    GRP8 -->|"resid stays at data[0]; H=data[1]+data[2], E=data[4], L=data[3]+data[5..8]"| MAIN
    FULLD -->|"pop resid; keys H,E,' ',P; #N → 0.25"| MAIN
    GRPD -->|"pop resname+SS letter; H=data[1], E=data[2], L=data[3]+data[4]; #N → 0.333"| MAIN
    MAIN --> OUT["CSSS.JSON (stdout or --output)"]
```

Sources: [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L70-L102), [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L105-L141), [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L144-L187), [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L190-L235)

| Function | Input | Second key layer | Residue-number handling | Rounding |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `chespi_probs8_convert_full` | probs8 file | H/G/I/E/' '/T/S/B | `data.pop(0)` after `resid` read | none |
| `chespi_probs8_convert_grouped` | probs8 file | L/H/E | kept at `data[0]`, probs occupy `data[1..8]` | L, H to 4 decimals |
| `d2D_convert_full` | δ2D txt | H/E/' '/P | `data.pop(0)` after `resid` read | none |
| `d2D_convert_grouped` | δ2D txt | L/H/E | kept at `data[0]`; pops resname + trailing SS letter | L to 3 decimals |

Sources: [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L87-L102), [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L124-L141), [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L161-L187), [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L209-L235)

### Grouping Semantics

**Grouping is not a simple collapse** — it implements idpconfgen's biological definitions of the three build states. For CheSPI input, helix probability `H` aggregates α-helix (H) and 3₁₀-helix (G) columns; `E` takes the β-strand column directly; `L` absorbs π-helix (I), coil (' '), turn (T), bend (S), and β-bridge (B) — meaning π-helix propensity is deliberately routed into loop sampling, a defensible choice since π-helices are vanishingly rare in disordered ensembles. The three grouped values sum to exactly 1.0 because they partition all eight input columns. δ2D grouping is analogous but simpler: `L` = Coil + PPII, treating polyproline-II as loop-phase backbone sampling.

Sources: [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L133-L137), [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L220-L223)

> [!TIP]
> Watch the **index-arithmetic asymmetry** between full and grouped converters. In *grouped* modes, the residue number is read from `data[0]` but never popped, so probabilities occupy `data[1..N]`; in *full* modes, `data.pop(0)` shifts probabilities down to `data[0..N-1]`. δ2D additionally strips the residue letter with `pline.pop(1)` and the consensus SS letter with a trailing `pline.pop()` *before* numeric conversion. Any extension of these parsers (e.g., adding a fifth δ2D state) must re-derive every index from scratch.

### Unreliable-Residue Fallback

δ2D emits `#<resnum>` lines for residues whose chemical shift coverage was insufficient (terminal and some internal residues). The converters intercept these with `re.match(r"\#+\d", line)`, parse the residue number from the comment, and assign **maximum-entropy uniform priors**: 0.25 per state in full mode, 0.333 in grouped mode. This guarantees the builder receives a complete residue-indexed map even where experimental data is sparse, rather than silently truncating the sequence.

Sources: [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L178-L186), [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L226-L234)

## The CSSS.JSON Contract

The standardized output is a nested dictionary serialized with `json.dumps(..., indent=4)`: the first key layer is the **residue number** (as an integer key pre-serialization, string after JSON round-trip), and the second layer maps state codes to probabilities. Grouped mode yields exactly three keys per residue (`L`, `H`, `E`) summing to 1.0; full mode yields the native 8-key (CheSPI) or 4-key (δ2D) alphabet that downstream tooling may use for finer-grained analysis.

```json
{
    "15": {"L": 0.7803, "H": 0.1008, "E": 0.0007},
    "16": {"L": 0.7124, "H": 0.2141, "E": 0.0004},
    "17": {"L": 0.6690, "H": 0.2994, "E": 0.0003}
}
```

Sources: [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L119-L123), [cli_csssconv.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_csssconv.py#L271-L277)

## makecsss: Authoring Propensities Without Shift Data

When chemical shift data is unavailable — or when a shift-derived file needs surgical edits — `makecsss` generates or modifies CSSS JSON from a declarative pattern string. The `-cp/--custom-pattern` grammar is pipe-separated triples of `<RESIDUE|RANGE> <DSSP_REGEX> <PROBABILITY>`, e.g. `-cp '1-14 L 1.0|15-25 H 1.0|26-59 L 1.0'` forces helix sampling for residues 15–25 and loop elsewhere; ranges expand in a single loop, and `X` acts as an any-state wildcard in the documented examples. Overlapping entries are legal but warn via the logger (`propensities for residue {i} have been changed due to overlap`), with later entries winning.

Sources: [cli_makecsss.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_makecsss.py#L34-L55), [cli_makecsss.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_makecsss.py#L76-L93), [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L132-L146)

The `-fc/--file-csss` flag turns the tool into an **editor**: an existing CSSS JSON is loaded with `read_dict_from_json`, each parsed propensity is merged per residue/state, and residues absent from the original file are appended with a `new residue {resid} has been appended` warning triggered by the `KeyError` branch. This round-trip path (csssconv → makecsss → build) is the recommended chain for refining shift-derived priors with manual domain knowledge.

Sources: [cli_makecsss.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_makecsss.py#L96-L148), [cli_makecsss.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_makecsss.py#L17-L18)

## Build-Time Integration: The -csss Handoff

The `build` subclient accepts the standardized file via `-csss <file>.json`, replacing the default discrete helix/strand/loop database selection with **per-residue probabilistic fragment sampling** driven by the shift-derived populations. Two interface rules from the reference workflow matter for developers: CSSS sampling requires the default loop database to be disabled (`--dloop-off`), and it composes with the energy filter (`-et 'pairs'`) and custom k-mer fragment-size distributions (`-xp`) — the sampling mechanics that consume these probabilities are documented in [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling), while the surrounding pipeline stages are covered in [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble).

```bash
idpconfgen build \
    -db idpconfgen_database.json \
    -seq drksh3.fasta \
    -nc 100 \
    -csss csss_drk_d2D.json \
    --dloop-off \
    -et 'pairs' \
    -of ./drk_CSSSd2D_nosub \
    -n
```

Sources: [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L158-L175)

## torsionsJ: Back-Calculating the ³J HN-CαHA Observable

Validation reverses the data flow: instead of pushing experimental information into sampling, `torsionsJ` computes an NMR-sensitive geometric observable **from generated conformers** so it can be compared against experimental values. The subcommand calculates the HN–CαHA dihedral (H–N–CA–HA, right-hand rule with the thumb pointing N→CA) for every residue of every input structure — the torsion governing the ³J HN-CαHA Karplus relation used in IDP NMR studies — and writes `torsionsJ_HN-CaHA.json` with one angle list per structure, keyed by file stem. Angles may exceed 180° and are reported as their negative-angle equivalents; proline positions receive `np.nan` by default since they lack an amide proton.

Sources: [cli_torsionsJ.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_torsionsJ.py#L1-L26), [cli_torsionsJ.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_torsionsJ.py#L130-L135)

| Flag | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `-deg` / `--degrees` | via libcli | report angles in degrees instead of radians |
| `-dec` / `--decimals` | 3 | rounding precision |
| `--no_hn_term` | True | structures lack N-terminal amide protons; first torsion then corresponds to residue 2 |
| `--hn_labels` | `('H', 'H1')` | alternative amide-proton atom names (e.g. add `HN`) |
| `--proline_value` | `np.nan` | placeholder for proline positions |
| `-n` / `--ncores` | 1 | worker count for the multiprocessing pool |

Sources: [cli_torsionsJ.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_torsionsJ.py#L66-L93), [cli_torsionsJ.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_torsionsJ.py#L16-L26)

### get_torsionsJ Internals

The heavy lifting lives in `libs/libhigherlevel.py::get_torsionsJ`, orchestrated per-file by the thin `cli_helper_calc_torsionsJ` wrapper. The implementation must solve a **residue-alignment problem**: atoms are selected from four independent name-based masks (amide protons, N, CA, HA/HA2), and any length mismatch — typically an N-terminal proton expectation error — is caught by a descriptive assertion before computation. Prolines enter the picture through a clever placeholder mechanism visible in the masking step below.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A["PDB/mmCIF structure"] --> B["mask: hn_labels (H/H1) ∪ PRO-CD atoms"]
    B --> C["column-slice N, CA, HA/HA2 arrays<br/>offset by hn_idx (from --no_hn_term)"]
    C --> D["shape assertion: hs == n == ca == ha"]
    D --> E["np.hstack([hs, n, ca, ha]).reshape()<br/>interleave H,N,CA,HA rows per residue"]
    E --> F["calc_torsion_angles(coords)"]
    F --> G["stride slice [0::4] — keep HN-CαHA dihedrals only"]
    G --> H["FASTA proline indices ← proline_value (NaN)"]
    H --> I["degrees conversion → np.round"]
    I --> J["pool_function + report_on_crash"]
    J --> K["torsionsJ_HN-CaHA.json<br/>{pdb_stem: [angles...]}"]
```

Sources: [libhigherlevel.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libhigherlevel.py#L300-L354), [libhigherlevel.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libhigherlevel.py#L505-L507), [cli_torsionsJ.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_torsionsJ.py#L109-L133)

> [!TIP]
> The **PRO-CD placeholder trick** is the key implementation insight: proline CD atoms are injected into the atom mask purely so that every residue — prolines included — contributes one row group to the hstacked array, preserving per-residue alignment between the four atom-class arrays. The placeholder angles are then discarded by the `[0::4]` stride extraction, and NaN values are re-injected afterward at FASTA-derived proline indices. Removing this mask branch would silently shift every subsequent residue's torsion by one position.

Parallelization follows the toolkit's standard pattern: a `FileReaderIterator` streams `.pdb` inputs, `functools.partial` binds the conversion parameters (`degrees`, `decimals`, `hn_terminal=not no_hn_term`), `report_on_crash` isolates per-file failures so one malformed structure cannot kill the batch, and `pool_function` fans work across cores — the same architecture detailed in [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture).

Sources: [cli_torsionsJ.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_torsionsJ.py#L109-L128), [libhigherlevel.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libhigherlevel.py#L505-L507)

## End-to-End Reference Workflow

The drkN SH3 example (a well-studied IDP with BMRB shifts 25501) exercises the full loop and doubles as an executable regression scenario. The flowchart traces the command sequence shipped in the example README; note that the same CSSS file composes with custom fragment-size distributions (`-xp customFragments.txt`, a two-column size/probability table) without modification.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S0["BMRB 25501 shifts<br/>(unfolded drkN SH3)"] --> S1["CheSPI / δ2D inference<br/>(external tools)"]
    S1 --> S2["idpconfgen csssconv -d2D drk_d2D.txt<br/>-o csss_drk_d2D.json"]
    S1 --> S3["idpconfgen csssconv -p8 probs8_25501_unfolded.txt<br/>-o csss_drk_chespi.json"]
    S2 --> S4["idpconfgen build -db idpconfgen_database.json<br/>-seq drksh3.fasta -nc 100<br/>-csss csss_drk_d2D.json --dloop-off<br/>-et 'pairs' -of ./drk_CSSSd2D_nosub -n"]
    S3 --> S4
    S4 --> S5["idpconfgen torsionsJ ./ensemble/*.pdb -deg"]
    S5 --> S6["torsionsJ_HN-CaHA.json<br/>vs experimental ³J couplings"]
```

Sources: [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L29-L60), [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L148-L182)

Because the toolkit is deterministic under a fixed seed, CSSS-driven runs are reproducible bit-for-bit, which makes A/B comparisons between `csss_drk_d2D.json` and `csss_drk_chespi.json` ensembles a clean way to quantify the divergence between the two inference tools on identical data. The full research context for this example, including residue-tolerance substitutions (`-urestol`) layered on top of `--dany` sampling, is covered in [Research Examples Library](23-research-examples-library).

Sources: [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L60-L63), [customFragments.txt](example/drksh3_example/customFragments.txt#L1-L5)

## Where to Go Next

Within the Conformer Building Engine track, the natural continuation is [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling) for the fragment-selection mechanics that consume CSSS probabilities, followed by [Sidechain Packing Methods](11-sidechain-packing-methods) and [Energy-Based Clash Filtering](12-energy-based-clash-filtering) for the downstream ensemble refinement stages that accept CSSS-built backbones. For a hands-on entry point before tackling shift data, start with [Tutorial: First Conformer Ensemble](4-tutorial-first-conformer-ensemble).

# Sidechain Packing Methods



IDPConformerGenerator builds conformers on a backbone-first template that only contains Ala/Gly/Pro sidechain atoms; full sidechains are added in a second, pluggable stage. This page documents the **sidechain packing component**: its strategy-pattern registry, the strict API contract every packing method must honor, the two shipped implementations (FASPR and MCSCE), their CLI surface, and their integration points inside the `build` pipeline. Everything here is verifiable in `src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/` and its wiring in `cli_build.py`.

Sources: [__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L1-L23), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L137-L142)

## Architectural Pattern: Strategy Registry

The package docstring states the design explicitly: *it implements a strategy pattern where depending on the sidechain option (str) the building workflow will use one function or another*. The registry is a plain dictionary mapping the CLI-facing method name to its initializer, with `'faspr'` as `DEFAULT_SDM`. Because the build worker processes never see concrete classes — only the selected callable — adding a third method requires exactly one registry entry and one initializer that respects the contract.

Sources: [__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L1-L38)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A["idpconfgen build<br/>-scm {faspr | mcsce}"] --> B["sidechain_packing_methods registry<br/>__init__.py#L30-L33"]
    B -->|"faspr (default)"| C["init_faspr_sidechains<br/>faspr.py"]
    B -->|"mcsce"| D["init_mcsce_sidechains<br/>mcsce.py"]
    C --> E["idpcpp.faspr_sidechains<br/>C++ extension kernel"]
    E --> F["dun2010bbdep.bin<br/>Dunbrack 2010 BB-dep rotamer library"]
    D --> G["mcsce package (external)<br/>create_side_chain"]
    G --> H["Amberff14SB forcefield<br/>LJ + clash energy terms"]
```

The registry module also owns the CLI plumbing so that method-specific arguments travel with the method, not with `cli_build`: `add_sidechain_method(parser)` attaches the `-scm/--sidechainmethod` choice, and `add_mcsce_subparser(ap)` attaches the MCSCE-only option group. This mirrors the plugin style used across the components package (see [Component Plugin Pattern](20-component-plugin-pattern)).

Sources: [__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L41-L48), [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L21-L50)

## The Packing Contract: init → calc Closures

Every packing method is exposed as a two-phase API. The `init_*` function is called **once per sequence** and receives the identity of the target protein: `input_seq` (FASTA string), `template_masks` (the Ala/Gly/Pro building template, a `libbuild.ConfMasks` tuple), and `all_atom_masks` (the full all-atom coordinate system). It returns a closure — `calc(coords)` — which the builder invokes **once per conformer** against backbone coordinates.

The return contract is a `(mask, coords)` pair. The mask is a boolean array over the all-atom system telling `cli_build` which atom columns the returned coordinates populate; the coords array holds the heavy-atom positions in the method's native layout. This asymmetry is what lets two very different algorithms plug into one builder:

| Method | Consumed slice | Returned mask | Returned coordinates |
|---|---|---|---|
| FASPR | `coords[template_masks.bb4]` (N, CA, C, O) | `all_atom_masks.non_Hs_non_OXT` | Full heavy-atom array (backbone + sidechains) |
| MCSCE | `coords[template_masks.non_sidechains]` | `all_atom_masks.all_sidechains` | Sidechain-only atoms |

Sources: [__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L8-L23), [faspr.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/faspr.py#L20-L55), [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L53-L84)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Main as cli_build.main()
    participant W as Builder process
    participant I as init_*_sidechains(seq, masks)
    participant A as FASPR / MCSCE algorithm
    Main->>W: sidechain_parameters + global label/mask objects
    W->>I: called once per sequence (or per fragment)
    I-->>W: calc(coords) closure
    loop per conformer
        W->>W: build Ala/Gly/Pro backbone template
        W->>A: calc(backbone coords)
        A-->>W: (sidechain mask, coords)
        W->>W: assemble + write all-atom PDB
    end
```

The contract also documents error handling as part of the interface: if MCSCE cannot place sidechains, its closure returns `(None, None)`, which the builder treats as a rejected conformer rather than a crash — a deliberate soft-fail for stochastic sampling.

Sources: [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L143-L146), [__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L8-L14)

## FASPR: Deterministic Rotamer Packing on the C++ Kernel

FASPR (*Fast and Accurate Side-chain Prediction and Relaxation*) is the default method. The Python layer is a thin shim: it resolves `idpcpp.faspr_sidechains` — the project's C++ extension (detailed in [C++ Extension & Numba Kernels](13-c-extension-and-numba-kernels)) — and binds the path of the bundled rotamer library, `dun2010bbdep.bin`. The import is deliberately placed inside the init function to avoid problems under tox, keeping the heavyweight native dependency out of the import graph of every other module.

Sources: [faspr.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/faspr.py#L43-L46)

Per conformer, the closure slices the four backbone atoms via `template_masks.bb4`, passes them to the C++ kernel together with the sequence and rotamer-library path, and returns the result masked with `non_Hs_non_OXT` — i.e., FASPR rewrites the complete heavy-atom picture, hydrogens and the C-terminal OXT excluded. The rotamer data itself, `dun2010bbdep.bin`, is the Dunbrack 2010 backbone-dependent rotamer library taken from the upstream FASPR repository (MIT licensed, attribution preserved verbatim in the component README), so packing statistics are reproducible without network access.

Sources: [faspr.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/faspr.py#L48-L55), [README.md](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/README.md#L1-L10)

Because FASPR is a deterministic graph-based rotamer assignment, it accepts no tunable parameters: note that `init_faspr_sidechains` has no `user_parameters` argument and simply ignores extra kwargs. Its cost profile is therefore constant per conformer, which is why it serves as the default sampling backend.

Sources: [faspr.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/faspr.py#L11-L12), [__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L38)

## MCSCE: Monte Carlo Energy-Based Packing

MCSCE integrates the external [THGLab/MCSCE](https://github.com/THGLab/MCSCE) package and is the physically-expensive, energetically-aware alternative. The init function constructs an MCSCE `Structure` from the FASTA sequence (backbone-only build), then selects the **Amberff14SB** forcefield with terminal capping conventions matching IDPConformerGenerator's own builder (`Cterminal='OXT'`, `Nterminal='HN'`), and installs an energy function factory via `initialize_func_calc` using the terms `('lj', 'clash')`.

Sources: [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L104-L129)

Two sampling modes exist, mapped onto MCSCE's `return_first_valid` flag: `'simple'` returns the first sterically valid placement found, while `'exhaustive'` performs `n_trials` sampling rounds. User-tunable knobs — `mode`, `n_trials`, `batch_size`, `temperature` — are defined in `mcsce_defaults` and overridable both programmatically and via CLI flags.

Sources: [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L10-L18), [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L111-L120), [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L21-L50)

> [!TIP]
> MCSCE keeps the *last-initialized* energy functions in its own module globals (`sidechain_placeholders`, `energy_calculators`). Because one worker process can build several sequences — the overlapping fragments of `build --long` and the `ldrs` workflow — `init_mcsce_sidechains` snapshots this state per sequence and the `calc` closure restores it before every call. Removing this bookkeeping silently corrupts energy evaluation when fragment builders interleave within a process.

Sources: [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L130-L138)

The per-conformer closure is asymmetric compared to FASPR: it only feeds MCSCE the non-sidechain coordinates (`template_masks.non_sidechains`), receives a complete MCSCE `Structure` back, and derives the sidechain coordinate block by *excluding* backbone and terminal-H atom names (`N, CA, C, O, H1, H2, H3, OXT, H`) from the structure's data array. The result is returned against `all_atom_masks.all_sidechains`, so `cli_build` writes only the newly placed atoms — preserving the builder's own backbone coordinates exactly.

Sources: [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L139-L162)

## CLI Surface and Parameter Routing

All packing behavior is configured from the `build` subcommand. Three controls belong to the packing stage itself, and four more configure MCSCE specifically:

| Flag | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `-scm` / `--sidechainmethod` | `faspr` | Selects the packing method from the registry |
| `-dsd` / `--disable-sidechains` | off | Skips sidechain computation entirely (backbone-only conformers) |
| `-etss` / `--energy-threshold-sidechains` | `250.0` kJ | Rejects conformers whose energy exceeds the threshold *after* packing |
| `--mcsce-mode` | `simple` | `simple` (first valid) vs `exhaustive` sampling |
| `--mcsce-n_trials` | `10` | Trials per residue in exhaustive mode |
| `--mcsce-batch_size` | `16` | MCSCE energy-function batch size |
| `--mcsce-temperature` | `300` | Monte Carlo sampling temperature |

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L265-L275), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L340-L350), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L365-L366), [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L21-L50)

> [!TIP]
> Parameter routing uses a **name-prefix convention**: every MCSCE-related kwarg arriving in `main()` is named `mcsce_<param>`, and `get_sidechain_packing_parameters(kwargs, mode)` strips the prefix before passing the dict to the method initializer. This is how `--mcsce-temperature` becomes `temperature=300` without `cli_build` knowing anything about MCSCE's schema — the same extensibility contract a third-party packing plugin would follow.

Sources: [__init__.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L51-L58)

The sidechain energy threshold (`-etss`) is distinct from the backbone threshold (`-etbb`, default 100 kJ): conformers are rejected *after* sidechains are placed, making this knob the primary lever controlling the trade-off between packing strictness and yield. Its downstream consumption belongs to the rejection stage described in [Energy-Based Clash Filtering](12-energy-based-clash-filtering).

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L329-L350)

## Integration Points in the Build Pipeline

The packing method flows through `build` in four hops. First, `main()` accepts `sidechain_method=DEFAULT_SDM` and extracts method-specific parameters from the raw kwargs. Second, `populate_globals()` materializes the shared identity objects both methods depend on: `ALL_ATOM_LABELS/MASKS/EFUNC` for the real sequence and `TEMPLATE_LABELS/MASKS/EFUNC` for the Ala/Gly/Pro template — these globals exist because reading module globals is the cheap cross-process communication channel of the multiprocessing design (see [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture)). Third, `_build_conformers()` passes `sidechain_parameters` into the `conformer_generator` builder, which resolves the registry entry once per process. Fourth, in long-IDP mode, `_build_long_conformers()` maintains one builder per fragment, each initialized with the same `sidechain_parameters` but fragment-specific globals.

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L447-L472), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L679-L681), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L816-L894), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L897-L943), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L945-L999)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    M["main()<br/>sidechain_method, kwargs"] -->|"get_sidechain_packing_parameters"| P["sidechain_parameters dict<br/>(prefix-stripped)"]
    M --> PG["populate_globals()<br/>ALL_ATOM_* / TEMPLATE_* labels, masks, efuncs"]
    P --> BC["_build_conformers()<br/>conformer_generator(...)"]
    PG --> BC
    BC --> REG["init_faspr_sidechains /<br/>init_mcsce_sidechains"]
    REG --> CL["calc(coords) closure<br/>(mask, coords) per conformer"]
    CL --> OUT["all-atom PDB + energy log"]
```

For `--long` sequences, the docstring of `_build_long_conformers` documents the fragment protocol precisely: every conformer is built fragment by fragment, aligned onto the chain built so far and rejected on clash; after 20 failed fragment conformers, the builder retreats and rebuilds the previous fragment. Packing consequently runs per-fragment, which is exactly why the MCSCE global-state snapshotting covered above is load-bearing.

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L951-L958)

## Choosing Between Methods

The two implementations occupy opposite corners of the speed/fidelity space, and the choice is a pure runtime decision — no code changes:

| Dimension | FASPR (default) | MCSCE |
|---|---|---|
| Algorithm class | Rotamer-library graph assignment | Monte Carlo sidechain placement |
| Dependency | Built-in C++ extension (`idpcpp`) | External `mcsce` pip package |
| Energy model | None (statistical rotamer priors) | Amberff14SB, `lj` + `clash` terms |
| Determinism | Deterministic given backbone | Stochastic (temperature, trials) |
| Tunables | None | mode, n_trials, batch_size, temperature |
| Failure mode | Always returns a placement | Soft-fail `(None, None)` → conformer rejected |
| Coordinate return | Full heavy-atom array | Sidechain-only atoms |

Sources: [faspr.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/faspr.py#L43-L55), [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L10-L18), [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L104-L129)

Operationally: use FASPR for high-throughput ensemble generation where the subsequent energy filter (default `-etss 250` kJ) provides the quality gate; switch to `mcsce` when sidechain realism matters more than throughput, tuning `--mcsce-mode exhaustive` with `--mcsce-n_trials` at the cost of per-conformer runtime.

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L340-L350)

## Verification Assets

The component is covered by a dedicated test module, `tests/test_component_sidechain_packing.py`, and exposes its API reference through the Sphinx page `docs/reference/component_sidechain.rst` — both are the canonical entry points when extending the registry with a new method. The interplay between the packing stage and torsion/geometry sampling upstream is documented in [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble) and [Bond Geometry Strategies](8-bond-geometry-strategies).

Sources: [tests/test_component_sidechain_packing.py](/tests/test_component_sidechain_packing.py), [docs/reference/component_sidechain.rst](/docs/reference/component_sidechain.rst)

## Continue the Deep Dive

Natural next pages in this module: [Energy-Based Clash Filtering](12-energy-based-clash-filtering) explains how `-etss` consumes the energies produced after packing; [C++ Extension & Numba Kernels](13-c-extension-and-numba-kernels) details the `idpcpp` binary FASPR delegates to; and [Component Plugin Pattern](20-component-plugin-pattern) generalizes the registry contract you saw here to the bgeo-strategy and residue-tolerance components.

# Energy-Based Clash Filtering



Energy-based clash filtering is the physics gate of the IDPConformerGenerator build pipeline: every fragment grown onto the conformer, and every conformer after sidechain packing, is scored with a pairwise (ij) non-bonded energy function. Conformers—or individual atom pairs—whose energy exceeds configurable thresholds are discarded before ever reaching the output folder. This page explains the mathematical model, the Numba closure architecture that implements it, the ij-pair exclusion logic that prevents covalent neighbors from poisoning the score, and the `whole` vs. `pairs` threshold semantics that control filtering strictness.

## Architectural Position: A Two-Phase Energy Gate

The filtering system is deliberately split into three layers with clean dependency edges: a **kernel layer** (`libenergyij.py`) containing pure numerical closures, an **assembly layer** (`libbuild.py`) that parameterizes those kernels from a force field and topology masks, and an **orchestration layer** (`cli_build.py`) that wires the assembled functions into the multiprocessing build loop and applies the thresholds. Two independent energy functions exist per build: `TEMPLATE_EFUNC` scores the Ala/Gly/Pro backbone template during fragment growth (gated by `-etbb`), and `ALL_ATOM_EFUNC` scores the fully packed structure (gated by `-etss`).

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph CLI["cli_build.py — Orchestration"]
        ARGS["CLI args<br/>-etbb 100 kJ<br/>-etss 250 kJ<br/>-et --et-type"]
        ELOG["EnergyLogSaver<br/>energies.log"]
        PROC["_concurent_build workers"]
    end

    subgraph ASM["libbuild.py — Assembly"]
        PEF["prepare_energy_function"]
        MASK["create_bonds_apart_mask_for_ij_pairs"]
        LJP["create_LJ_params_raw"]
        CP["create_Coulomb_params_raw"]
    end

    subgraph KERNEL["libenergyij.py — Numba kernels"]
        LJ["init_lennard_jones_calculator"]
        COU["init_coulomb_calculator"]
        EC["energycalculator_ij"]
    end

    subgraph DATA["Parameter provenance"]
        FF["protein.ff14SB.xml<br/>sigma / epsilon / charge"]
        CALC["libcalc.py<br/>calc_all_vs_all_dists_njit"]
    end

    ARGS --> PEF
    FF --> LJP
    FF --> CP
    LJP --> PEF
    CP --> PEF
    MASK --> PEF
    PEF --> EC
    LJ --> EC
    COU --> EC
    CALC --> EC
    EC --> PROC
    PROC -->|"energy vs. threshold"| ARGS
    PROC --> ELOG
```

The layering pays off in two ways. Because kernels are stateless closures parameterized once at startup, worker processes only read immutable module-level globals—this is an explicit design decision documented in `cli_build.py` to avoid IPC overhead during multiprocessing. And because `prepare_energy_function` receives `lj_term`/`coulomb_term` booleans, the energy model is reconfigurable without touching kernel code.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L110-L155), [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L654-L680), [libenergyij.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libenergyij.py#L1-L18)

## The Physics Model: Lennard-Jones + Coulomb

The filter evaluates two classical non-bonded energy terms over all non-redundant atom pairs. The Lennard-Jones term models short-range repulsion and dispersion attraction as `E_ij = A/r¹² − B/r⁶`, computed in full (no infinite-distance approximation) by the Numba kernel:

```python
@njit
def calculate(distances_ij):
    ar = acoeff / (distances_ij ** 12)
    br = bcoeff / (distances_ij ** 6)
    return ar - br
```

The Coulomb term adds electrostatics as `E_ij = q_i·q_j·κ/r` with a fixed dielectric scaling of `0.25` (i.e., κ = 4.0), applied directly to the pair-charge product at parameterization time.

| Term | Formula | Pair parameters | Scaling constants |
|------|---------|-----------------|-------------------|
| Lennard-Jones | `A/r¹² − B/r⁶` | `A = 4εσ¹²`, `B = 4εσ⁶` (Å) | 1-4 pairs × `lj14scale × 0.2` |
| Coulomb | `q_i·q_j / r` | `q_i·q_j × 0.25` (dielectric 4.0) | 1-4 pairs × `coulomb14scale` |

Parameter provenance follows the Amber ff14SB force field, read from `core/data/protein.ff14SB.xml`. The mixing rules are implemented in `create_LJ_params_raw` with a notable arithmetic trick: rather than iterating over pairs in Python, `sigma` values are **summed** over the upper diagonal by `sum_upper_diagonal_raw_njit` and `epsilon` values are **multiplied** by `multiply_upper_diagonal_raw_njit`—from which the geometric-mean ε (`ε_ij ** 0.5`) and arithmetic-mean σ (`sigma_pre * 5`, which folds the `/2` mean and the nm→Å `×10` unit conversion into one scalar) are derived vectorially.

Sources: [libenergyij.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libenergyij.py#L23-L78), [libenergyij.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libenergyij.py#L81-L125), [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L876-L944), [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L704-L742)

## Topology Awareness: The ij-Pair Exclusion Scheme

A naive all-pairs energy would assign enormous (often infinite) penalties to covalently bonded neighbors and 1-3 pairs, which sit at fixed short distances by construction. The filter solves this with two boolean masks over the `N·(N−1)/2` upper-diagonal pair space, built by `create_bonds_apart_mask_for_ij_pairs` from the Amber bond topology tables (`forcefield.bonds_le2_intra`, `bonds_equal_3_intra` plus their inter-residue counterparts):

| Bond separation | Mask | LJ treatment | Rationale |
|-----------------|------|--------------|-----------|
| 1-2 and 1-3 (`bonds_le_2_mask`) | `base_bool=False` → True | `np.nan` on A and B coefficients | Covalent geometry; excluded via NaN-aware summation |
| Exactly 1-4 (`bonds_exact_3_mask`) | True | `× lj14scale × 0.2` | Standard Amber 1-4 correction, damped 5× further for IDP tolerance |
| > 3 bonds | neither mask | unscaled full potential | The pairs that actually signal clashes |

Mask construction is itself a generator pipeline: `gen_ij_pairs_upper_diagonal` streams `(atom_i, atom_j)` tuples, `gen_atom_pair_connectivity_masks` yields the integer index of each pair satisfying the connectivity criterion via `are_connected`, and the consumer writes these indices into a pre-allocated `np.full(num_ij_pairs, base_bool)` array. Inter-residue connectivity is only considered for consecutive residues, keeping the mask construction O(N²) but with a lightweight per-pair dictionary lookup.

The exclusion scheme is the reason the `np.nansum` reduction exists: bonded pairs contribute `NaN`, which `nansum` silently skips, so the "exclusion" costs zero branches in the hot loop.

Sources: [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L681-L718), [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L753-L873), [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L947-L1000)

> [!TIP]
> The 1-4 damping factor in `acoeff[bonds_exact_3_mask] *= _lj14scale * 0.2` contains a hardcoded `0.2` on top of the force field's own `lj14scale`. If you port these energies to compare against external Amber tools, remember IDPConformerGenerator's 1-4 LJ term is 5× weaker than stock ff14SB—an intentional loosening that lets slightly strained torsion fragments pass the `-etbb` gate instead of triggering infinite rebuild loops.

## The Closure Factory Pattern

`libenergyij.py` implements a **factory-of-factories** design: `init_lennard_jones_calculator` and `init_coulomb_calculator` each return a fresh `@njit`-compiled closure with the pair coefficients baked into its lexical scope. Because Numba specializes compiled code per closure instantiation, the pair coefficients are constants at JIT time and the kernel reduces to a pure vectorized array expression with no global lookups. The `energycalculator_ij` combinator then closes over a distance function (`calc_all_vs_all_dists_njit`, which flattens coordinates into the same `N·(N−1)/2` upper-diagonal layout) and a list of energy terms, producing the final `calculate(coords) → float` callable that the build workers invoke.

```mermaid
graph LR
    COORDS["coords (N,3)"] --> DIST["calc_all_vs_all_dists_njit"]
    DIST -->|"dist_ij (N(N−1)/2,)"| LJ["LJ closure<br/>acoeff, bcoeff in scope"]
    DIST --> COU["Coulomb closure<br/>charges_ij in scope"]
    LJ -->|"pair energies / nansum"| SUM["energy sum"]
    COU --> SUM
    SUM --> THR{"energy > threshold?"}
    THR -->|"yes"| REJ["discard conformer"]
    THR -->|"no"| ACC["accept conformer"]
```

The dispatch between per-pair and summed output is controlled by a `postf` string index into an options dictionary that must remain aligned with `post_calc_options = ['pairs', 'whole']`—the module docstring at the top of the file warns about this invariant, and the CLI component enforces it through argparse `choices`.

Sources: [libenergyij.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libenergyij.py#L14-L20), [libenergyij.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libenergyij.py#L58-L78), [libenergyij.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libenergyij.py#L128-L180), [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L744-L750)

## Threshold Semantics: `whole` vs. `pairs`

The `-et/--et-type` argument (bound to `energy_type_ij`) selects how pair energies collapse into a rejection decision, and the two modes are not merely cosmetic—they define fundamentally different failure criteria:

| Dimension | `pairs` (default) | `whole` |
|-----------|-------------------|---------|
| Aggregation | none—each pair checked individually | `np.nansum` → single conformer float |
| Rejection rule | **any** single pair above threshold rejects the whole conformer | total energy above threshold rejects |
| Safe threshold range | ≥ 2–3 kJ mandatory | even negative values valid |
| Failure mode at 0 | infinite loop: 1-4 pairs always carry small positive energy | none |
| Strictness | catches localized clashes anywhere | tolerates one clash if the rest is favorable |

The constraint on `pairs` mode is documented in the component's help text: because exactly-3-bonds-apart pairs always contribute a small positive Lennard-Jones energy (their equilibrium distance sits on the repulsive wall), setting `-etbb` or `-etss` to `0` under `pairs` makes *every* conformer fail, and the builder will churn forever without ever accepting a structure.

The two thresholds apply at different pipeline stages: `-etbb/--energy-threshold-backbone` (default **100.0**) gates fragments during **backbone** growth against `TEMPLATE_EFUNC`, while `-etss/--energy-threshold-sidechains` (default **250.0**, ignored with `-dsd`) gates the fully **sidechain-packed** conformer against `ALL_ATOM_EFUNC`. The higher sidechain default reflects the larger contact surface once heavy atoms are added.

Sources: [energy_threshold_type.py](src/idpconfgen/components/energy_threshold_type.py#L11-L32), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L328-L351), [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L669-L675)

## Operational Integration: Logging and Multiprocessing

Accepted conformer energies are streamed to disk by `EnergyLogSaver`, a main-process-owned writer (default path `energies.log`, configurable via `-el/--energy-log`) that emits `confname,energy` lines and flushes after each write so partially completed runs leave a usable record. The class is intentionally *not* sent to worker processes—it accumulates results returned through the multiprocessing pipeline, avoiding concurrent-write races.

The energy functions themselves follow the opposite pattern: `ALL_ATOM_EFUNC`, `TEMPLATE_MASKS`, `TEMPLATE_EFUNC`, and their all-atom siblings live as module-level globals that worker processes read directly. Since Python multiprocessing forks share the parent's memory at spawn time, this turns per-worker initialization of the ~O(N²) parameter arrays into a zero-copy read—an optimization the code comments explicitly justify.

Per-atom parameters are resolved in `extract_ff_params_for_seq`, which walks every atom of the input sequence through the force field dictionary with two residue-context rules worth knowing when debugging parameter errors: terminal residues are remapped to `NXXXX`/`CXXXX` force field blocks, and histidine is force-protonated (`HIS` → `HIP`) regardless of local environment.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L371-L395), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L355-L361), [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L977-L994)

## Comparison with Alternative Clash-Detection Strategies

The energy-gate design contrasts sharply with the distance-cutoff clash detectors common in other tools. Understanding the trade-offs clarifies why this codebase commits to physics:

| Criterion | Energy-based (this system) | Distance-cutoff (typical) |
|-----------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| Signal | continuous, physically grounded | binary overlap flag |
| Tunes via | `-etbb`, `-etss`, force field, `-et` type | cutoff radius only |
| Distinguishes 1-4 strain from real clash | yes (via masks + scaling) | requires manual neighbor exclusion |
| Cost | O(N²) with per-pair exponentials | O(N²) comparisons, cheaper constants |
| Extensible to electrostatics | yes (Coulomb term toggle) | no |

The Numba kernels keep the O(N²) exponentials inside JIT-compiled loops over contiguous float64 arrays, so the energy model's runtime overhead against a plain distance check is largely the two extra fused-multiply operations per pair.

Sources: [libenergyij.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libenergyij.py#L58-L78), [libbuild.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libbuild.py#L744-L750)

> [!TIP]
> When a build run stalls producing no output, inspect `energies.log` first: it is written even for the accepted subset only after threshold evaluation, so an empty file under `pairs` mode almost always means your `-etbb`/`-etss` values sit below the 1-4 repulsive floor. Switch `-et whole` or raise thresholds to 2–3+ to restore progress—the failure is diagnosable entirely from the log, no debugger needed.

## Verification and Testing Surface

The kernel layer is directly unit-tested in `tests/test_libenergyij.py`, which exercises both calculator factories and the post-calculation dispatch, while `tests/test_build_definitions.py` and `tests/test_libbuild.py` cover the assembly layer including mask generation and parameter extraction. Because the closures capture their coefficients at definition time, tests can verify the exact numerical contract—that `calculate(distances)` returns `acoeff/d¹² − bcoeff/d⁶` element-wise—without constructing protein structures.

Sources: [tests/test_libenergyij.py](tests/test_libenergyij.py#L1-L50), [tests/test_libbuild.py](tests/test_libbuild.py#L1-L50)

## Where to Go Next

The energy gate sits downstream of fragment sampling and upstream of output validation, so its behavior is best understood in context. For how conformers are grown from torsion fragments before the `-etbb` gate fires, continue to [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble); for the speed-critical Numba and C++ kernels behind `calc_all_vs_all_dists_njit`, see [C++ Extension & Numba Kernels](13-c-extension-and-numba-kernels). To understand how the sidechain atoms that trigger the `-etss` gate get packed in the first place, read [Sidechain Packing Methods](11-sidechain-packing-methods), and for the CLI plumbing that binds `-etbb`/`-etss`/`-et` into the `build` subcommand, consult [CLI Subcommand System](17-cli-subcommand-system).

# C++ Extension & Numba Kernels



This page documents the two native/compiled acceleration layers inside IDPConformerGenerator: the **`idpcpp` pybind11 C++ extension** (a vendored copy of the FASPR sidechain-packing algorithm) and the **Numba `@njit` kernels** that power per-pair energy evaluation and sequence/geometry utilities. As an advanced-level reference, it covers provenance, build configuration, the Python↔C++ data marshaling contract, the GMEC search pipeline inside FASPR, and the closure-factory pattern used to compile Numba kernels. For how these components slot into the overall build workflow, see [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble) and [Sidechain Packing Methods](11-sidechain-packing-methods).

## Architectural Context: Two Acceleration Strategies

IDPConformerGenerator generates thousands of conformers per ensemble, and two workloads dominate runtime: (1) **sidechain packing** — a combinatorial search for the Global Minimum Energy Conformation (GMEC) over rotamer libraries, and (2) **pairwise energy evaluation** — Lennard-Jones and Coulomb terms computed over all atom i-j pairs for clash filtering. The project solves these with different tools: a compiled C++ extension for the combinatorial search, and JIT-compiled Numba closures for array-heavy numeric loops.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Python["Python orchestration layer"]
        CB["cli_build.py<br/>(build command)"]
        SP["sidechain_packing registry<br/>{'faspr', 'mcsce'}"]
        LE["libenergyij.py<br/>closure factories"]
        FM["faspr.py<br/>init_faspr_sidechains()"]
    end

    subgraph Native["Native / JIT layer"]
        PYB["pybind11 boundary<br/>faspr_sidechains()"]
        CPP["idpcpp.cpp<br/>FASPR algorithm (C++)"]
        BIN[("dun2010bbdep.bin<br/>rotamer library")]
        NJIT["Numba @njit closures<br/>LJ / Coulomb kernels"]
    end

    CB --> SP
    SP -->|'-scm faspr (default)'| FM
    FM -->|coords, seq, bin path| PYB
    PYB --> CPP
    BIN -.->|"global ifstream,<br/>seekg(0) per call"| CPP
    CB -->|"prepare_energy_function()"| LE
    LE --> NJIT
```

**Prerequisite note**: the diagram above shows the two entry points — the strategy-pattern registry in `sidechain_packing/__init__.py` dispatches to either FASPR (via pybind11) or MCSCE (an external package), while energy kernels are wired through closure factories at build time.

Sources: [sidechain_packing/\_\_init\_\_.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L18-L33), [faspr.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/faspr.py#L1-L10), [libenergyij.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libenergyij.py#L1-L11), [requirements.txt](/requirements.txt#L1-L8)

## The `idpcpp` C++ Extension: Vendored FASPR

The single translation unit `src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp` (~4,000 lines) contains a **vendored copy of the FASPR algorithm** taken from the original repository at a pinned commit, licensed under MIT (a copy ships alongside in the `FASPR_License` file). FASPR (Fast Protein Side-chain Repacking) predicts sidechain conformations from backbone coordinates using a rotamer library and an energy-based search.

The vendoring introduced deliberate structural deviations from upstream, all documented in the file header: the original multi-file layout was merged into one file, I/O routines not needed by IDPConfGen were stripped or commented out, message output was disabled, `One2Three` residue-code mapping was rewritten, and — critically — the `dun2010bbdep.bin` rotamer file handling was redesigned to be read **once and held as a global variable** managed by `faspr_sidechains()`. All algorithmic parts are maintained "EXACTLY as in the original code, in both execution and presentation." The pybind11 adapter functions were authored by `@joaomcteixeira` and are signed in docstrings accordingly.

Sources: [idpcpp.cpp](/src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp#L1-L44), [idpcpp.cpp](/src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp#L71-L137)

## Build System Integration

The extension is compiled at install time via setuptools. In `setup.py`, a `Pybind11Extension` named `idpcpp` is created from the single source file, paired with the standard pybind11 `build_ext` command class. This wiring is **conditional**: when `TOX_ENV_NAME` is present in the environment (and `TOXTESTING` is not), `ext_modules` and `cmdclass` are left empty so test environments never invoke a C++ compiler. This design choice explains a downstream pattern — the consumer module imports `idpcpp` *lazily inside* the factory function with the comment "we import idpcpp here to avoid problems with tox," ensuring module import never fails in tox environments where the extension does not exist. Version pins in `requirements.txt` scope the binding library to `pybind11>=2.9.2, <2.13.6`.

Sources: [setup.py](/setup.py#L14-L30), [setup.py](/setup.py#L91-L99), [faspr.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/faspr.py#L49-L52), [requirements.txt](/requirements.txt#L1-L8)

## The pybind11 Boundary: Data Marshaling Contract

The extension exports exactly **one Python-visible function**, registered in the `PYBIND11_MODULE(idpcpp, m)` block:

| Element | Detail |
|---|---|
| Python name | `idpcpp.faspr_sidechains` |
| Signature | `(conf_xyz: array_t<double, c_style \| forcecast>, reslabel: str, dunbbdepfile: str) -> np.ndarray` |
| Input array | Flattened `(N, 3)` double coordinates of **only** N, CA, C, O backbone atoms, atoms and residues sorted |
| Return | 2-D `py::array` of heavy-atom coordinates with sidechains built |

The marshaling path is explicit and worth understanding for anyone extending the binding. On entry, the pybind11 type caster `py::array_t<double, py::array::c_style | py::array::forcecast>` guarantees a C-contiguous, cast-to-double array (the `forcecast` flag silently converts mismatched dtypes). The body then allocates a `std::vector<double>` and bulk-copies via `std::memcpy`, calls the pure C++ pipeline, and finally wraps the result vector's raw pointer in a `py::buffer_info` describing a `(len/3, 3)` NumPy array with explicit strides — a zero-copy handoff of the returned `std::vector` storage.

**Critical contract**: the docstring warns that "Failure to comply may result in unexpected errors or Segmentation Fault," because for efficiency several input checks performed by original FASPR were deactivated in this adaptation. Callers must supply the exact N→CA→C→O atom ordering per residue. This invariant is honored by the Python side, which slices the full coordinate system with the `template_masks.bb4` boolean mask before calling.

A subtle performance mechanism: the module keeps a global `ifstream infile` for the rotamer binary. On every call, if the file is already open it calls `clear()` + `seekg(0)` to rewind instead of reopening — eliminating repeated file-open syscalls across the thousands of invocations a build performs.

Sources: [idpcpp.cpp](/src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp#L3931-L3994), [idpcpp.cpp](/src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp#L3999-L4007), [idpcpp.cpp](/src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp#L3838-L3902), [faspr.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/faspr.py#L49-L64)

## FASPR Execution Pipeline

The adapter function `main_faspr()` reproduces the original FASPR workflow in six stages, bridged in/out by two helper functions: `inject_coords()` (replaces the original `Structure::ReadPDB`, constructing internal `Residue` records from the flat coordinate vector and one-letter labels, stride-12 indexing for 4 atoms × 3 coordinates) and `extract_coordinates()` (flattens `Structure.pdb` back to a vector of doubles).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["inject_coords()"] --> B["LoadSeq()"]
    B --> C["BuildSidechain()"]
    C --> D["CalcSelfEnergy()"]
    D --> E["CalcPairEnergy()"]
    E --> F["Search()"]
    F --> G["extract_coordinates()"]

    subgraph Search internals
        F --> F1["DEE search<br/>(Dead-End Elimination)"]
        F1 --> F2["Graph edge decomposition"]
        F2 --> F3["Subgraph → tree decomposition<br/>(treewidth ≤ 5 solved exactly)"]
        F3 --> F4["GMEC rotamer assignment"]
    end
```

**Prerequisite note**: the `Search()` stage implements combinatorial optimization — Dead-End Elimination prunes rotamers that provably cannot appear in the GMEC; interaction graph edges that admit bounded energy decomposition are removed; remaining residue-interaction subgraphs are converted to tree decompositions, and trees with treewidth ≤ `TREEWIDTH_CUT` (5) are solved exactly by bottom-up energy calculation and top-down assignment, with a `goto LOOP` retry in "hardmode" for trees exceeding the cut after threshold doubling.

The energy model is encoded as `#define` constants at the top of the file: per-atom-type VDW radii and depth parameters, hydrogen-bond and disulfide-bond distance/angle optima and cutoffs, per-amino-acid energy weights (`WGT_CYS` 5.5 … `WGT_GLU` 1.0), and rotamer probability thresholds (`ROT_PROB_CUT_MIN` 0.01, `ROT_PROB_CUT_ACC` 0.97) that govern which library rotamers are considered per residue.

Sources: [idpcpp.cpp](/src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp#L3905-L3928), [idpcpp.cpp](/src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp#L3764-L3832), [idpcpp.cpp](/src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp#L73-L164), [idpcpp.cpp](/src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp#L3841-L3882)

## Numba JIT Kernels

The second acceleration layer uses Numba (`numba>=0.53.0, <1` pinned in `requirements.txt`) with `@njit` (no-Python-mode) compilation. The kernels follow a distinctive **closure-factory pattern**: an `init_*` function captures problem-specific coefficient arrays in a closure, compiles specialized `@njit` functions against them, and returns the configured variant. Because the coefficients are compile-time closure state rather than runtime arguments, Numba specializes the machine code per coefficient set, avoiding argument-passing overhead in the hot loop.

`libenergyij.py` — the module docstring states it "Contains only energy terms that evaluate energy for each atom-atom pair separately" — provides two factories:

| Factory | Captured state | `@njit` kernels | Formula |
|---|---|---|---|
| `init_lennard_jones_calculator` | `acoeff`, `bcoeff` (ij-pair LJ coefficients) | `calculate`, `calculate_nansum` | `a/r¹² − b/r⁶` |
| `init_coulomb_calculator` | `charges_ij` (ij-pair charges) | `calculate`, `calculate_nansum` | `q/r` |

Each factory supports two `post_calc_options`: `'pairs'` (default — returns the energy per pair, preserving per-interaction diagnostics) and `'whole'` (applies `np.nansum` for a single scalar). The docstrings stress that it is the caller's responsibility to encode irrelevant pairs (covalently bonded, or 2 bonds apart) as `np.nan`, which the nansum reduction then ignores. The returned object is documented as a `numba.njitted func` — a closure with registered coefficients expecting an `(N,)` distances array.

Sources: [requirements.txt](/requirements.txt#L1-L8), [libenergyij.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libenergyij.py#L1-L78), [libenergyij.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libenergyij.py#L81-L120)

### Kernel inventory across the library

Beyond energy terms, Numba-prefixed functions appear throughout the computational libs. Their names are imported directly into the build command, confirming the JIT path is load-bearing in the main pipeline:

| Module | Numba functions (imported by `cli_build.py`) | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `libs/libcalc.py` | `rotate_coordinates_Q_njit`, `rrd10_njit` | Quaternion coordinate rotation; residue-residue distance (r<sup>10</sup>-scaled) evaluation |
| `libs/libparse.py` | `get_seq_chunk_njit`, `get_trimer_seq_njit` | Fast k-mer sequence chunking for torsion-probability sampling |
| `libs/libenergyij.py` | (closure-generated) `calculate`, `calculate_nansum` | Per-pair LJ/Coulomb energy terms |

The `_njit` naming suffix acts as an inline marker distinguishing compiled variants from their NumPy-eager counterparts — a convention visible in the import lists of the build command.

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L74-L84), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L92-L100), [libenergyij.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libenergyij.py#L14-L20)

## Integration: The Sidechain Packing Strategy Pattern

Both native paths meet at a uniform strategy interface. The `sidechain_packing` package implements "a strategy pattern where depending on the sidechain option (str) the building workflow will use one function or another," with all methods returning "an array mask to be used in `all_atom_coords` and … the coordinate compatible with such a mask." The registry maps `'faspr'` → the pybind11-backed factory (the default, `DEFAULT_SDM = 'faspr'`) and `'mcsce'` → the external-package-backed factory.

The `init_faspr_sidechains()` factory binds three things into its returned closure: the input FASTA sequence, the path to the packaged `dun2010bbdep.bin` rotamer binary (resolved from the installed package via `source_folder`), and the callable `idpcpp.faspr_sidechains`. Its `compute_faspr_sidechains(coords)` inner function slices backbone coordinates with `template_masks.bb4`, invokes the extension, and returns the `all_atom_masks.non_Hs_non_OXT` mask paired with the extended coordinates — satisfying the shared contract without the caller knowing which engine ran.

MCSCE takes a different native strategy: rather than vendoring, it imports the external `mcsce` package (`Structure`, `side_chain_builder`, `prepare_energy_function`, Amberff14SB forcefield definitions) at factory-call time. One integration detail matters for this repo's multiprocessing architecture: MCSCE keeps energy functions of the last-initialized structure in **module globals**, so the adapter explicitly saves/restores `(sidechain_placeholders, energy_calculators)` state — "one process may build several sequences (the fragments of long IDRs in `build --long` and `ldrs`)." MCSCE offers `simple`/`exhaustive` sampling modes, configurable trials, batch size, and temperature via `--mcsce-*` CLI flags. See [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture) for how per-process state isolation makes this necessary.

Sources: [sidechain_packing/\_\_init\_\_.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L1-L58), [faspr.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/faspr.py#L5-L64), [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L1-L18), [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L97-L150), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L36-L42)

## Design Trade-offs at a Glance

| Dimension | `idpcpp` (pybind11 C++) | Numba `@njit` closures | MCSCE (external pkg) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Technique | Ahead-of-time compiled C++ | JIT-compiled Python closures | External package internals |
| Hot path | Combinatorial GMEC rotamer search | Per-pair energy terms, geometry ops | Monte-Carlo sidechain sampling |
| Data transfer | `memcpy` in, zero-copy `buffer_info` out | Native NumPy arrays (no boundary) | Python-level structure objects |
| State handling | Global `ifstream` + rewind per call | Coefficients frozen in closure | Module globals, manually saved/restored |
| Fragility | Strict ABI contract; segfault on misuse | First-call compile latency | Cross-initialization state leakage |
| Test-path behavior | Compiled only outside tox; lazy import | Compiles normally | Deferred import inside factory |

Sources: [idpcpp.cpp](/src/idpconfgen/cpp/idpcpp.cpp#L3931-L3994), [libenergyij.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libenergyij.py#L23-L78), [mcsce.py](/src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L133-L142), [setup.py](/setup.py#L14-L30)

## Key Takeaways

The acceleration layer reflects three deliberate engineering decisions. First, **vendoring with pinned provenance**: the FASPR copy preserves upstream algorithm semantics exactly while stripping I/O, keeping citation obligations visible in the header and license file. Second, **boundary minimization**: `idpcpp` exports one function, marshals data through a single documented contract (bb4-sorted, C-contiguous doubles), and caches the rotamer file handle globally — trading input validation for per-call efficiency in a context where the trusted Python caller guarantees the invariant. Third, **closure-specialized JIT**: Numba kernels bake coefficient arrays into compiled closures at setup time, a pattern that keeps the numeric kernels small, allocation-free, and reconfigurable per energy model. Together these layers let a pure-Python orchestration pipeline sustain ensemble-scale throughput, as consumed by the clash-filtering stage described in [Energy-Based Clash Filtering](12-energy-based-clash-filtering).

To go deeper: the FASPR/MCSCE consumer contracts are detailed in [Sidechain Packing Methods](11-sidechain-packing-methods); the Numba energy kernels' role in rejection sampling is covered in [Energy-Based Clash Filtering](12-energy-based-clash-filtering); the quaternion math behind `rotate_coordinates_Q_njit` is explained in [Coordinate Geometry & Quaternion Math](7-coordinate-geometry-and-quaternion-math); and how per-process isolation enables these stateful native libraries is covered in [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture).


# LDRS Workflow Overview



The **LDRS module** is IDPConformerGenerator's system for attaching Intrinsically Disordered Regions (IDRs) onto experimentally solved folded protein structures — filling N-terminal tails, C-terminal tails, and internal linkers between folded domains with all-atom disordered conformers. This page explains the end-to-end workflow: how inputs are classified, how IDR conformers are generated per disorder type, how loop closure works at the orchestration level, and how the final stitched ensembles are produced. Deeper algorithmic treatment of loop closure and multi-chain modeling is deferred to [Loop Closure Algorithms](15-loop-closure-algorithms) and [Multi-chain Complex Modeling](16-multi-chain-complex-modeling).

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1-L23), [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L1-L7)

## Module Identity and Naming

The module's conceptual lineage is documented directly in `ldrs_helper.py`, which describes itself as "Client for building IDRs on PDB files in the cartesian coordinate space" and names the methodology **FLDR/S — Folded disordered region/structure sampling**. The two entry points split responsibilities cleanly: `cli_ldrs.py` (~3,300 lines) is the CLI client and orchestrator that owns the workflow phases and multiprocessing pools, while `ldrs_helper.py` (~2,600 lines) holds the pure coordinate-space mechanics — alignment, clash counting, overlap attachment, junction finding, and the grafting "surgeon" itself.

Sources: [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L1-L7), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1-L23)

A central vocabulary term is the **disorder case taxonomy**, defined as a simple integer-keyed dictionary in `ldrs_helper.py`: case `0` is an **N-IDR** (disorder at the chain's start), case `1` is a **Linker-IDR** (disorder sandwiched between two folded segments — the hardest case, since it requires loop closure), and case `2` is a **C-IDR** (disorder at the chain's end). Every downstream decision in the workflow keys off this classification, and the internal residue numbering deliberately includes two extra residues flanking each IDR "to facilitate reconstruction later on" — a detail the CLI logs explicitly to users.

Sources: [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L49-L55), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L772-L784), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1088-L1092)

## Workflow Architecture

The `main()` function in `cli_ldrs.py` executes a strict phase pipeline: validate inputs → parse the folded template → classify disorder → generate IDR fragment conformers in parallel → stitch and clash-check combinations → write final conformers and clean up. The following diagram maps the phases to their implementing functions:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Inputs: -db torsions DB, -seq FASTA, -fld folded PDB/mmCIF"] --> B["Phase 0: Validation<br/>tolerance_calculator, sampling-option exclusivity"]
    B --> C["Phase 1: Template Parsing<br/>Structure.build, CIF→PDB conversion,<br/>get_fasta_from_PDB, process_multichain_pdb"]
    C --> D["Phase 2: Disorder Detection<br/>break_check + overlap masking ('*'),<br/>consecutive_grouper → DISORDER_BOUNDS,<br/>classify → DISORDER_CASES (0/1/2)"]
    D --> E{"Per-IDR dispatch<br/>(per chain)"}
    E -->|"Linker-IDR, ccd (default)"| F["_close_linker_ccd<br/>torsion-space closure rounds<br/>libccd.RamachandranReference"]
    E -->|"Linker-IDR, next_seeker"| G["_close_linker_next_seeker<br/>grow halves from both ends,<br/>KD-tree match meeting pairs"]
    E -->|"N-IDR / C-IDR"| H["_build_conformers /<br/>_build_long_conformers<br/>Pool(ncores)"]
    F --> I["Phase 4: Stitching<br/>create_all_combinations,<br/>inter_chain_cc (multichain),<br/>psurgeon grafting pool"]
    G --> I
    H --> I
    I --> J["Output: conformer_1..N.pdb<br/>+ energies.log"]
```

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L497-L548), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L656-L784), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L887-L1140), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1144-L1210)

## Phase 1 — Template Parsing and Multi-Chain Reconciliation

The folded structure is loaded through the generic `Structure` parser, so both PDB and PDBx/mmCIF inputs work; mmCIF files are transparently converted to a temporary PDB (`structure_to_pdb`) because the FASTA extraction helper expects PDB formatting. Chain identity is read from `col_chainID`, with a fallback to segment IDs (`col_segid`) when chain IDs are blank — a common occurrence in membrane-style files.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L656-L681)

Multi-chain handling is where LDRS reconciles two sources of truth: the user's sequence dictionary and the template's actual chains. If the input FASTA contains multiple sequences, `MULTICHAIN` is set and a log message announces "multiple sequences detected, assuming they are in a multi-chain complex." Conversely, if the template holds several chains but only one sequence was given, `process_multichain_pdb` (from `libmultichain`) attempts to match each chain against the input and marks chains whose sequence perfectly matches (needing no modeling) as skipped — the changelog records this behavior landing in v0.7.21 and a fix for 3+ chains in v0.7.28.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L576-L591), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L682-L724), [CHANGELOG.rst](/CHANGELOG.rst#L59-L71)

## Phase 2 — Disorder Detection and Case Classification

For each chain, LDRS converts the full-length input sequence into a masked version where every residue belonging to the folded template is replaced with `'*'`. This masking is the workflow's core trick: it folds template-identity matching, PPM/CHARMM-GUI membrane segments (kept only for clash-checking context), and chain-break detection (`break_check`) into one uniform representation, after which `consecutive_grouper` collapses the remaining unmasked indices into contiguous disorder intervals — `DISORDER_BOUNDS` — and each interval is tagged with its case in `DISORDER_CASES`.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L743-L784), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L690-L702)

| Case | Tag | Position in chain | Build strategy |
|------|-----|-------------------|----------------|
| 0 | N-IDR | Start of chain | Grow from template N-terminus (C–N–CA anchor) |
| 1 | Linker-IDR | Between two folded regions | Loop closure: `ccd` or `next_seeker` |
| 2 | C-IDR | End of chain | Grow from template C-terminus (N–CA–C anchor) |

Sources: [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L49-L55), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1030-L1070)

The torsion-angle database loaded here is the same artifact produced by the classical pipeline's `torsions` command (verified via `aligndb`), which means LDRS reuses the sampling infrastructure documented in [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling) rather than defining its own fragment statistics. Secondary-structure sampling flags (`-dloop`, `-dhelix`, `-dstrand`, `-dany`, `-duser`) are validated to be mutually exclusive groups at startup — the same contract as the `build` client.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L788-L807), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L553-L570)

## Phase 3 — Per-IDR Generation Dispatch

The heart of `main()` is a per-chain loop over `DISORDER_SEQS` that routes each region down one of three paths. The dispatch is worth reading as a pattern: **each path produces fragment conformers into a temporary directory tree** (`{TEMP_DIRNAME}/chain{X}/{case}/...`), and none of them write the final structure — stitching is deliberately deferred to Phase 4. This separation lets the stitcher explore the combinatorial product of all per-region libraries.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L884-L1142)

### Path A: Linker-IDR + CCD (the default)

When `--loop-closure ccd` is selected (default), each Linker-IDR is closed in **torsion space** using `libccd`: the backbone conformer is attached to the first folded end and small φ/ψ perturbations steer the free end onto the second folded end via a clash-aware damped least-squares solver. The orchestrator instantiates a single shared `RamachandranReference` (lazily, on first linker) and packages the folded-structure context through `prepare_ccd_context`. `_close_linker_ccd` then runs **round-based closure**: each round dispatches worker quotas across cores, prunes duplicate loops with `prune_duplicate_loops`, and logs rejection reasons; it stops when the target conformer count is met or when `LOOP_STALL_ROUNDS` (5) consecutive rounds add no new distinct loop. Worker seeds are made deterministic per region/round/worker (`random_seed + 104729*index + 7919*round_ + worker`), keeping ensembles reproducible. The changelog dates this solver to v0.10.0 and recommends it for L-IDRs longer than ~40 residues (~17× faster than the alternative).

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L279-L286), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L898-L947), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1213-L1344), [CHANGELOG.rst](/CHANGELOG.rst#L12-L23)

### Path B: Linker-IDR + next_seeker

The `next_seeker` method instead grows conformer **halves from each folded end independently** and keeps pairs that meet with correct peptide-bond geometry. `main()` extracts the six flanking backbone atoms (C, N, CA on both sides of the break) into `fld_coords_C`/`fld_coords_N` anchor frames, prepares per-half fragment plans (`long_fragments(seq, case, 2)` for both directions), and hands everything to `_close_linker_next_seeker`. Per v0.10.1, halves are built backbone-only first and all halves compared at once via a KD-tree, with sidechains packed only on completed loops; `NEXT_SEEKER_HALVES = 640` sets the per-round half budget. This method needs very large libraries for long linkers, which is why it is not the default.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L949-L1028), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L283-L286), [CHANGELOG.rst](/CHANGELOG.rst#L12-L23)

### Path C: N-IDR / C-IDR terminal growth

Terminal tails are the classical case: `main()` locates the two template residues adjacent to the disorder boundary, captures their C–N–CA coordinates as the rotation/alignment anchor, seeds per-core `RANDOMSEEDS` and a `CONF_NUMBER` queue, and fans out `_build_conformers` (or `_build_long_conformers` for fragmented builds) over a `Pool(ncores)`. Any leftover conformers (`nconfs % ncores`) are built inline on the main process afterward. Alignment onto the template is then handled during stitching via `align_coords`/`attachment_overlaps` from `ldrs_helper.py`.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1030-L1141), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L82-L111)

| Aspect | `ccd` (default) | `next_seeker` |
|--------|-----------------|---------------|
| Closure space | Torsion (φ/ψ perturbation) | Cartesian meeting of grown halves |
| Growth pattern | Single backbone, steered both ends | Two independent halves |
| Pair selection | Damped least-squares target capture | KD-tree batch comparison of all halves |
| Sidechain timing | After loop accepted | Only after loop completed (v0.10.1) |
| Long-linker guidance | Recommended > 40 residues | Needs very large libraries |
| Stop criterion | nconfs met or 5 stalled rounds | Pair matches found in rounds |

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L352-L381), [CHANGELOG.rst](/CHANGELOG.rst#L12-L23)

## Long-IDR Fragmentation
