IDRs longer than `LONG_IDR_FRAGMENT` (150 residues) are never built as a single growing chain. `split_long_idr` partitions the disorder sequence into ≤150-residue fragments, and for N-IDRs, C-IDRs, and `next_seeker` linker halves these fragments are attached one to the next — the same "build in fragments" logic introduced for `build --long` in v0.10.0. Correspondingly, the per-region sampling tables (`SLICEDICT_XMERS`, `XMERPROBS`, `GET_ADJ`) are either populated per fragment or set to `None` when a path delegates to the fragment builder. Fragment-level build state is tracked in `FRAGMENT_GLOBALS`, indexed by position in `GET_ADJ`, so each worker process reads only its fragment's labels, masks, and energy functions.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L14-L15), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L219-L229), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L862-L876), [CHANGELOG.rst](/CHANGELOG.rst#L18-L23)

> [!TIP]
> Notice that CCD Linker-IDRs are explicitly excluded from fragmentation-based sampling-table setup (`not linker or loop_closure == 'next_seeker'`): the CCD solver consumes the whole linker sequence at once through `populate_globals`, so only terminal IDRs and next_seeker halves get fragment-indexed tables. Misreading this conditional is the fastest way to get lost in `SLICEDICT_XMERS` initialization.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L862-L876), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L915-L920)

## Phase 4 — Stitching and Clash Validation

Stitching converts per-region fragment libraries into final full-length conformers. `create_all_combinations` enumerates every possible pairing of fragment files across the temporary directory tree (per chain), and for multi-chain systems `inter_chain_cc` filters combinations so that inter-chain clashes are actually checked — the changelog records inter-chain clash-checking being added in v0.7.22 and made compatible with `mcsce`-packed sidechains in v0.7.23. Each surviving combination is then handed to **`psurgeon`** — the grafting function named for its surgical role — which receives the folded `Structure`, the per-chain `DISORDER_CASES` and `DISORDER_BOUNDS`, and produces a completed coordinate array that `main()` serializes as `conformer_{i}.pdb`.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1150-L1205), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L82-L111)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Temp["Temporary fragment libraries (.ldrs_temp/)"]
        T1["N-IDR<br/>conformer pool"]
        T2["Linker-IDR<br/>closed loops"]
        T3["C-IDR<br/>conformer pool"]
    end
    T1 --> CC["create_all_combinations<br/>(+ inter_chain_cc for complexes)"]
    T2 --> CC
    T3 --> CC
    CC --> PS["psurgeon: graft onto fld_struc,<br/>renumber residues/serials,<br/>intra+inter chain clash-check"]
    PS --> OUT["conformer_1..N.pdb"]
    PS -.->|"kept if -kt / --stitching-off"| TEMP["ldrs_temp/ retained"]
```

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1144-L1208)

Two cleanup semantics are worth memorizing: temporary directories are hidden (`.ldrs_temp/`) and deleted at the end unless `--keep-temporary` was passed, and `--stitching-off` both renames the temp directory and disables grafting entirely — IDRs are then only "aligned and clash-checked," which is useful for debugging fragment libraries in isolation. Clash tolerance itself is a single scalar: `tolerance_calculator` maps the `--clash-tolerance` float (default 0.5) onto `max_clash = int(tolerance * 80)` and `dist_tolerance = tolerance * 0.8` (i.e., 40 allowed clashes, 0.4 Å vdW headroom by default).

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L343-L350), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L548-L551), [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L58-L79)

> [!TIP]
> When debugging why a stitched conformer looks broken, check `energies.log` first — `EnergyLogSaver` runs on the main process only (worker-safe via flush-per-line) and pairs every conformer name with its kJ energy, letting you correlate rejection patterns with `-etbb`/`-etss` thresholds before diving into geometry.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L454-L494), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L878-L878)

## CLI Parameter Surface

The `ldrs` subcommand registers its parser through the same `libcli` conventions as every other client, which means the flags documented in [CLI Subcommand System](17-cli-subcommand-system) apply here too. The table below summarizes the LDRS-specific surface; component flags (bgeo strategy, xmer probabilities, residue tolerance, sidechain packing) delegate to the shared plugin arguments.

| Flag | Default | Role in workflow |
|------|---------|------------------|
| `-db` / `-seq` / `-fld` | required | Torsion DB, full-length FASTA, folded template |
| `-nc` `--nconfs` | 1 | Conformers per disorder case (drives round quotas) |
| `--loop-closure` | `ccd` | Linker closure method (`ccd` \| `next_seeker`) |
| `--ccd-max-trials` | 100 | Backbones each core tries per delivered loop |
| `-tol` `--clash-tolerance` | 0.5 | Maps to max clashes (×80) and Å tolerance (×0.8) |
| `--stitching-off` | off | Skip grafting; IDRs only aligned + clash-checked |
| `-kt` `--keep-temporary` | off | Retain fragment libraries after stitching |
| `--membrane` | off | Filter to PRO segids (PPM/CHARMM-GUI output) |
| `-dsd` | off | Disable sidechain packing |
| `-etbb` / `-etss` | 100 / 250 kJ | Backbone / post-packing energy rejection gates |
| `-el` | `energies.log` | Per-conformer energy log |

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L288-L467), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L352-L409)

## Where LDRS Sits in the Codebase

The module's dependency graph is intentionally shallow toward libraries and deep toward the build engine: `cli_ldrs.py` imports the conformer-generation machinery directly (`gen_PDB_from_conformer`, `get_adjacent_angles` from `cli_build`), the component plugin system (`bgeo_strategies`, `sidechain_packing`, `xmer_probs`, `residue_tolerance`), `libccd` for torsion-space closure, and `libmultichain`/`libmulticore` for complex handling and pool management. This mirrors the global-variable multiprocessing strategy inherited from the `build` client — sampling globals (`BGEO_*`, `ANGLES`, `INT2CART`) are populated once in `main()` and read cheaply by forked workers, a pattern explained further in [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture).

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L39-L155), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L161-L229)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    CL["cli_ldrs.py<br/>(orchestrator)"] --> LH["ldrs_helper.py<br/>(coordinate mechanics)"]
    CL --> CB["cli_build.py<br/>(gen_PDB_from_conformer)"]
    CL --> CCD["libs/libccd.py<br/>(RamachandranReference, CCDParameters)"]
    CL --> MC["libs/libmultichain.py<br/>(process_multichain_pdb)"]
    CL --> COMP["components/*<br/>(bgeo, sidechains, xmer, tolerance)"]
    LH --> LS["libs/libstructure.py<br/>libs/libcalc.py"]
    LH --> BD["core/build_definitions.py"]
```

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L39-L155), [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L8-L46)

## Recommended Reading Path

To build working knowledge of LDRS, read in this order: start with the module docstrings of `cli_ldrs.py` and `ldrs_helper.py` (both quoted above), then trace `main()` phase-by-phase using the architecture diagram, and finally study `_close_linker_ccd`'s round/stall logic as the canonical example of the module's concurrency style. Working test fixtures live in `tests/test_cli_ldrs.py` and `tests/test_ldrs_helper.py`, and runnable command sequences are in `example/slc26a9_example/` (terminal IDR stitching) and `example/complex_example/` (multi-chain D1D2 with linker closure).

Continue with: [Loop Closure Algorithms](15-loop-closure-algorithms) for the CCD and next_seeker internals, [Multi-chain Complex Modeling](16-multi-chain-complex-modeling) for `inter_chain_cc` and template matching, or revisit [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble) for the fragment-generation machinery LDRS reuses.


# Loop Closure Algorithms



This page documents the two strategies by which the LDRS module bridges a disordered region between two **fixed folded domains**: the default `ccd` method — a torsion-space, clash-aware damped least-squares closure engine implemented in `libs/libccd.py` — and the alternative `next_seeker` method, a meet-in-the-middle growth strategy coordinated through `ldrs_helper.py`. The material below covers the position of closure in the build pipeline, the four-stage CCD algorithm, its solver mechanics, its contact model, its acceptance gate, and the verified functional vocabulary of the `next_seeker` path. It assumes familiarity with the fragment-growth concepts introduced in [LDRS Workflow Overview](14-ldrs-workover-overview) and the torsion databases described in [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling).

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1-L23), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L1-L42)

## Position in the LDRS Pipeline

LDRS classifies every disordered region into one of three **disorder cases** — `N-IDR` (a tail before the first folded region), `Linker-IDR` (a region between two folded regions), and `C-IDR` (a tail after the last folded region). Only the `Linker-IDR` case requires loop closure: the chain must connect two anchors whose coordinates are fixed by the input folded structure. N- and C-terminal tails are simply grown outward from a single folded domain, so no closure problem exists for them. The long-IDR policy is uniform across the module — N-IDRs, C-IDRs, and `next_seeker` Linker-IDR halves longer than 150 residues are built in fragments of at most 150 residues, attached one to the next.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Torsion database<br/>(idpconfgen torsions)"] --> B["Fragment growth<br/>≤ 150-residue fragments"]
    B --> C{"Disorder case"}
    C -->|"N-IDR / C-IDR"| D["Grow outward from one<br/>folded domain — no closure"]
    C -->|"Linker-IDR"| E{"--loop-closure"}
    E -->|"ccd (default)"| F["CCD torsion-space closure<br/>libs/libccd.py"]
    E -->|"next_seeker"| G["Meet-in-the-middle growth<br/>ldrs_helper.py"]
    F --> H["Closed Linker-IDR bridging<br/>two folded domains"]
    G --> H
    H --> I["Combination clash check<br/>(> 40 contacts rejected)"]
    I --> J["Ensemble output"]
```

The `cli_ldrs` module is the orchestrator: it imports the closure context builder (`prepare_ccd_context`), the junction/reachability helpers, and `libccd` itself, exposing the choice of method via the `--loop-closure` argument with `ccd` as the default. After closure, fragment combinations are cross-checked for steric incompatibility: every IDR fragment of a combination is checked against every other one, and a combination is rejected when any pair exceeds 40 contacts within the van der Waals radii sum + 1.0 Å.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1-L23), [cli_ldrs.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L82-L112), [ldrs_helper.py](src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L49-L55), [ldrs_helper.py](src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L136-L167), [ldrs_helper.py](src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L289-L327)

## Two Closure Strategies at a Glance

The two methods represent fundamentally different closure philosophies. The `libccd.py` module docstring frames the distinction precisely: `next_seeker` "searches for two independently grown halves whose ends happen to meet," whereas CCD "closes every IDPConformerGenerator backbone individually" by adjusting torsions of an already-built chain until its endpoint lands on the second folded domain. Both operate on a backbone that includes two overlapping folded residues on each side of the IDR — the same context sequence.

| Dimension | `ccd` (default) | `next_seeker` |
|---|---|---|
| Closure mechanism | Damped least-squares (Levenberg-Marquardt IK) adjusts IDR phi/psi until the endpoint N, CA, C lands on the folded domain | Conformers grown from each folded region are joined where their ends meet |
| Torsion budget vs. source | Bounded: ≤ 25° RMS / 90° max change per phi/psi, 90° cumulative rotation cap | Unbounded relative to the source; halves grow independently |
| Geometry preservation | Bond lengths, angles, omega, and chirality kept exactly — rotations act on rigid sub-trees | Determined by fragment growth geometry |
| Failure reporting | Reason-coded `CCDResult` with per-closure statistics | Governed by reachability heuristics in the helper functions |
| Fragment policy | Per-backbone closure | Linker halves > 150 residues split into ≤ 150-residue fragments |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph CCD["ccd — pull to target"]
        direction TB
        A1["Grow one backbone"] --> A2["Anchor to folded domain 1"] --> A3["LM iterations move IDR phi/psi<br/>until endpoint reaches domain 2"]
    end
    subgraph NS["next_seeker — meet in the middle"]
        direction TB
        B1["Grow half from domain 1"] --> B3["Join where the halves meet"]
        B2["Grow half from domain 2"] --> B3
    end
```

Sources: [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L1-L14), [cli_ldrs.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L7-L15)

## The CCD Engine: `libs/libccd.py`

### Design Contract

The CCD implementation is built on a strict invariance contract: **rotations act only on rigid sub-trees around N–CA (phi) and CA–C (psi) bonds**, so bond lengths, bond angles, omega angles, and chirality of the source conformer are preserved exactly. Only phi/psi *inside the IDR* change, and only by bounded amounts — meaning the torsion sampling statistics of IDPConformerGenerator are preserved through closure. This is what distinguishes it from Cartesian-minimization approaches that would distort the input geometry. All coordinates are in Angstroms; all angle parameters are in degrees.

The module carries provenance annotations: the phi/psi limits, contact criteria, omega policy, and backbone geometry windows derive from the **AlphaFlex loop builders**, while the endpoint targets are deliberately tighter so that the peptide junctions keep ideal geometry *without* a final minimization step.

Sources: [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L35-L42), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L131-L137)

### Stage 1 — Geometry Normalization

Before closure, the source backbone (IDR plus two overlapping folded residues on each side) must pass a geometry audit against `GEOMETRY_WINDOWS`, a dict of nine accepted bond lengths (Å) and angles (°) for N–CA, CA–C, C=O, and the peptide bond C–N plus its three flanking angles — explicitly the windows of the AlphaFlex loop builders' backbone check. Additionally, every peptide bond must be trans (or cis before a proline). Backbones failing the windows are rebuilt by `idealize_backbone`, a NeRF-style (`_place`) sequential reconstruction that recovers phi/psi/omega from the input coordinates and re-lays the chain using the **fixed bond geometry** of IDPConformerGenerator — per-residue-type averages defined in `core/build_definitions` — then Kabsch-superimposes the result onto residue 1. This repairs stretched bonds and malformed peptide planes (for example at fragment junctions of `build --long` conformers) while keeping the sampled torsions.

| Key | Window | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `N_CA` | 1.35–1.56 Å | N–CA bond length |
| `CA_C` | 1.40–1.63 Å | CA–C bond length |
| `C_O` | 1.15–1.33 Å | Carbonyl bond length |
| `C_N` | 1.20–1.47 Å | Peptide bond to next residue |
| `N_CA_C` | 98–128° | Bend at CA |
| `CA_C_O` | 102–138° | Bend at C toward O |
| `CA_C_N` | 98–145° | Bend at C toward next N |
| `O_C_N` | 98–145° | Peptide-plane complement |
| `C_N_CA` | 102–145° | Bend at next N |

Sources: [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L9-L14), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L67-L108), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L1008-L1098)

### Stage 2 — Anchoring the Lower Junction

The loop is then anchored to the first folded domain in two moves. First, the N, CA, C atoms of the residue preceding the IDR are superimposed onto the folded domain using `kabsch`, an SVD-based superposition constrained to proper rotations (the reflection determinant is corrected to `+1` before assembling the rotation matrix), which returns rotation, translation, and the residual RMSD. Second, psi of that residue is rotated so its carbonyl O matches the folded one — this preserves the folded peptide plane, ensuring the covalent junction does not perturb the experimental geometry of the folded domain.

Sources: [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L15-L17), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L224-L251)

### Stage 3 — The Damped Least-Squares Solver

The core of the algorithm is the `dls` method: **clash-aware damped least-squares** (Levenberg-Marquardt inverse kinematics) over the IDR phi/psi angles. Each iteration linearizes two objectives. The first is the weighted endpoint error — the deviation of the following residue's N, CA, C from the folded target, weighted 8 : 4 : 2 respectively — clamped to `dls_max_move` (2.0 Å) per iteration. The second objective is contact avoidance: backbone atoms coming within a margin of each other or of the fixed environment produce Jacobian rows that push the overlapping pairs apart, where the gradient of a contact distance with respect to a torsion is the torque of the pair's separating unit vector about that torsion's axis (`d|xj − xi|/dθk = uk · ((xj − pk) × unit)` for the pivot moving atom j but not atom i). The step solves the minimum-norm damped system `(J Jᵀ + λ²I) s = Jᵀ r`, with `dls_prior` pulling accumulated changes back toward the source conformer where constraints allow.

Three safety mechanisms bound every step: no torsion turns more than `dls_max_step` (4°) per iteration and no atom moves more than `dls_max_displacement` (1.0 Å); torsions that reach a cumulative `dls_torsion_cap` (60°) are **frozen** while the remaining pivots are re-solved; and a dedicated **finishing pass** (no prior, tightened margins of 0.1 Å, `dls_finish_*` budget) refines near-closed loops using a 16-residue C-terminal window of pivots. A subsequent `polish` phase — triggered when endpoint RMSD is below `polish_trigger_rmsd` (3.0 Å) — runs a plain endpoint-least-squares LM with adaptive damping (λ halved on accepted steps, quadrupled on rejected ones, abandoned at 10⁴) at a higher clash weight (2.0), restoring the pre-polish state if the final target is not met.

| Solver group | Parameters (default) | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Iteration budget | `dls_iterations` (600), `dls_stall` (100) | Main loop length and stall detection |
| Damping | `dls_damping` (0.3), `dls_prior` (0.05) | LM regularization, source-attraction |
| Step bounds | `dls_max_step` (4°), `dls_max_displacement` (1.0 Å), `dls_max_move` (2.0 Å) | Per-torsion, per-atom, per-iteration limits |
| Torsion freezing | `dls_torsion_cap` (60°) | Cumulative cap before a pivot is frozen |
| Contact margins | `dls_clash_weight` (1.0), `dls_self_margin` (0.4 Å), `dls_env_margin` (0.8 Å) | Solver-time contact gradients |
| Finishing pass | `dls_finish_window` (16), `dls_finish_iterations` (150), `dls_finish_stall` (40), `dls_finish_margin` (0.1 Å) | Near-closure refinement, no prior |
| Polishing | `polish_trigger_rmsd` (3.0 Å), `polish_iterations` (60), `polish_max_step` (10°), `polish_damping` (1.0), `polish_tolerance` (0.05 Å), `polish_clash_weight` (2.0), `polish_clash_margin` (0.05 Å) | Endpoint-only LM for close misses |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Snapshot current state"] --> B["Compute anchors/axes<br/>for active pivots"]
    B --> C["Linearise endpoint error<br/>weighted 8:4:2 for N:CA:C<br/>clamped to dls_max_move"]
    C --> D["Linearise clash gradients<br/>self 0.4 A / env 0.8 A margins"]
    D --> E["Solve damped LS:<br/>(J J' + lambda^2 I) s = J' r"]
    E --> F["Clip to dls_max_step and<br/>dls_max_displacement"]
    F --> G{"Cumulative rotation > 60°?"}
    G -->|"Yes"| H["Freeze capped pivots,<br/>re-solve the rest"]
    G -->|"No"| I["Apply step, book delta"]
    H --> I
    I --> J{"Closed without overlaps,<br/>or iterations/stall exhausted?"}
    J -->|"No"| B
    J -->|"Yes"| K["Finishing pass + polish<br/>for near-closed loops"]
```

Sources: [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L163-L179), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L1395-L1453), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L1455-L1474), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L1482-L1554), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L1556-L1599)

> [!TIP]
> The solver never re-derives geometry from internal coordinates during iterations — it rotates exact coordinate sub-trees via `rotate_torsions`, which composes all pivot rotations into per-atom affine transforms so that *every torsion changes exactly by its solved angle*, applied as if one by one from the C-terminal end. This composition is what makes the linearized Jacobian consistent with the applied finite steps, and why the geometry invariants (bonds, angles, omega) survive hundreds of iterations.

### Rotation Algebra and Linearization

Three NumPy-vectorized primitives support the solver. `rotation_matrices` builds P rotation matrices at once via the Rodrigues formula from unit axes and angles. `rotate_torsions` applies P torsion changes to a flat coordinate array in a single pass: it orders pivots by start index, accumulates composed linear/shift maps, and updates every moved atom with one `einsum` contraction. `torsion_displacement` computes the first-order displacement of selected atoms for small torsion changes using cumulative sums of spin and moment terms — the analytic Jacobian supplier behind the endpoint and clash rows. Geometric primitives (`dihedral` with IUPAC sign convention, `bend_angle`, `backbone_phi_psi`, `wrap_angle` to [−π, π)) round out the torsion-space toolkit, mirroring the coordinate machinery documented in [Coordinate Geometry & Quaternion Math](7-coordinate-geometry-and-quaternion-math).

Sources: [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L254-L310), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L313-L421)

### The Contact Model

Clash awareness during closure rests on two classes. **`ClashEnvironment`** holds the fixed heavy atoms the loop must not overlap with — folded domains, other chains, membranes — indexed in a `cKDTree` built on first use, with bounding-box early rejection and boolean masks that exempt covalently bonded junction atoms from contact checks. **`ContactModel`** constructs the moving atom set from the backbone: besides N, CA, C, O it builds each residue's amide H (bisector direction, 0.9 Å from N — the same construction IDPConformerGenerator uses, skipped for proline) and an ideal C-beta pseudo-atom of radius 2.4 Å (skipped for glycine) that **keeps room for the side chains packed afterwards** — the coupling to [Sidechain Packing Methods](11-sidechain-packing-methods). Each pseudo-atom rigidly follows the backbone atom it hangs on (H follows N, CB follows C, so phi moves CB but psi does not), recorded in the `follows` array that the Jacobian machinery uses to decide which pivots can resolve which contact.

Self-contact rules encode polymer physics: pairs up to three bonds apart along the chain are never compared, and C-alpha pairs more than `self_ignore_window` (2) residues apart must respect a dedicated `self_ca_cutoff` of 2.85 Å in addition to the scaled van der Waals criterion (`clash_scale` = 0.65 of the radii sum).

Sources: [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L424-L549), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L552-L725), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L578-L617)

### Stage 4 — The Acceptance Gate

A closed loop is only accepted if **all** of the following checks pass, evaluated by `CCDParameters` thresholds and dedicated measurement functions:

| Check | Function/threshold | Criterion |
|---|---|---|
| Endpoint residuals | `target_rmsd` 0.10 Å, `target_n_residual` 0.05 Å, `target_max_residual` 0.20 Å, weights (8, 4, 2) | N, CA, C of the residue following the IDR land on the folded domain |
| Torsion drift | `max_phipsi_rms_delta` 25°, `max_phipsi_delta` 90°, `max_total_rotation` 90° | Every phi/psi stays near the source conformer |
| Peptide bonds | `omega_tolerance` 20°, `allow_nonpro_cis` False | Every omega trans (cis allowed before Pro) |
| Junction geometry | `junction_distance_tolerance` 0.05 Å, `junction_angle_tolerance` 10° | Both C–N junctions within windows of `IDEAL_GEOMETRY` (`junction_geometry`/`junction_failure` report the first violation) |
| Contacts | `clash_scale` 0.65, `max_self_clashes` 0, `max_env_clashes` 0 | Zero nonlocal self/environment overlaps |
| Torsion statistics | `max_rama_outlier_fraction` 0.05 | ≤ 5% of residues in (phi, psi) bins unobserved in the torsion database |

The Ramachandran check is implemented by `RamachandranReference`, which consumes the (omega, phi, psi) arrays and sequences produced by `idpconfgen.libs.libfilter.aligndb` — i.e., the torsion database itself. Occupancy is counted in 10° bins, smoothed over the 3×3 neighborhood, and thresholded relative to total observations; residue types with fewer than 2000 observations fall back to pooled references, with glycine and proline pooled separately from all other residues.

Sources: [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L139-L208), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L732-L799), [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L1101-L1199)

### Result Contract

Closure returns a `CCDResult` dataclass: an `accepted` flag, a human-readable `reason` for rejection, the closed `backbone` (L, 4, 3 array), optional `extra` atoms, the superposition `rotation`/`translation` applied at anchoring, and a `stats` dict for per-closure diagnostics. This reason-coded contract is what allows the LDRS driver to retry with fresh conformers and aggregate rejection statistics.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CLI["cli_ldrs.py<br/>--loop-closure ccd"] --> CTX["ldrs_helper.py<br/>prepare_ccd_context"]
    CTX --> CL["libccd.py<br/>close_loop"]
    CL --> P["CCDParameters<br/>(all thresholds)"]
    CL --> ST["rotate_torsions /<br/>torsion_displacement"]
    CL --> CM["ContactModel<br/>H + CB pseudo-atoms"]
    CL --> CE["ClashEnvironment<br/>fixed-atom KD-tree"]
    CL --> RR["RamachandranReference<br/>torsion-db occupancy"]
    CL --> RES["CCDResult<br/>accepted / reason / stats"]
    ST --> CM
    CM --> CE
```

Sources: [libccd.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libccd.py#L211-L221), [cli_ldrs.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L82-L112)

> [!TIP]
> The contact criteria are stricter than physical van der Waals overlap: `clash_scale` = 0.65 means a pair "overlaps" below 65% of its radii sum, and `max_self_clashes`/`max_env_clashes` are both zero — no tolerated clashes at all. Combined with the C-beta pseudo-atoms reserving side-chain volume, a CCD-accepted loop is pre-cleared for the downstream energy-based filtering of [Energy-Based Clash Filtering](12-energy-based-clash-filtering) rather than merely vdW-legal.

## `next_seeker`: Meet-in-the-Middle Growth

The alternative strategy avoids torsion adjustment entirely. Per the `cli_ldrs` module documentation, `next_seeker` grows conformers from **each** folded region and joins them where their ends meet — a stochastic meet-in-the-middle search whose success depends on the two independently grown halves reaching a common endpoint. Linker-IDR halves longer than 150 residues are built as ≤ 150-residue fragments attached one to the next, matching the long-IDR fragment policy of the tails.

The verified import surface of `cli_ldrs` reveals the functional vocabulary this strategy is assembled from, all defined in `ldrs_helper.py`:

| Functional role | Imported helpers |
|---|---|
| Junction discovery | `find_junctions`, `junction_runs`, `linker_numbered` |
| Reachability analysis | `linker_reach`, `linker_stop`, `reachable_residues`, `unreachable_end` |
| Half-building | `half_backbone`, `build_in_fragments`, `split_long_idr`, `splice_folded_rows` |
| Join validation & repair | `break_check`, `prune_duplicate_loops`, `attachment_overlaps`, `align_coords`, `psurgeon` |
| CCD context | `prepare_ccd_context`, `inter_chain_cc` |

The last row foreshadows the multi-chain setting: `inter_chain_cc` and the environment-aware design of `ClashEnvironment` (which explicitly lists "other chains, membrane" among fixed atoms) connect closure to the scenarios documented in [Multi-chain Complex Modeling](16-multi-chain-complex-modeling). Notably, `ldrs_helper.py` self-describes as a "client for building IDRs on PDB files in the cartesian coordinate space" whose "methodology deviates from traditional IDP or beads-on-a-string FLDR/S approach" — closure exists precisely because full-chain FLDR/S sampling does not respect fixed anchors.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L7-L15), [cli_ldrs.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L82-L112), [ldrs_helper.py](src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L1-L7)

## Cross-Cutting Shared Machinery

Both strategies draw on the same supporting infrastructure in `ldrs_helper.py`. The `consecutive_grouper` utility partitions disordered residue indices into contiguous `(first, last)` bounds — the segmentation input for building and closure. Steric verification of finished combinations is handled by `_AtomSet` (coordinates + van der Waals radii with a lazily built `cKDTree` and bounding box) and `_count_contacts` (sparse distance matrix, per-pair radii-sum cutoffs), which `combinations_clash_check` applies pairwise across every mix of N-IDR, Linker-IDR, and C-IDR fragments, rejecting any pair with more than 40 contacts at vdW sum + 1.0 Å. This is the combinatorial post-filter that complements the per-loop zero-tolerance contact gate of CCD, and it operates before the ensemble-level energy evaluation of [Energy-Based Clash Filtering](12-energy-based-clash-filtering).

Sources: [ldrs_helper.py](src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L136-L167), [ldrs_helper.py](src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L223-L279), [ldrs_helper.py](src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L289-L327)

## Reading Progression

To contextualize this page within the engine: the torsion databases consumed by `RamachandranReference` and by the fragment builders are produced by the pipeline in [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling); the bond geometry tables underlying `IDEAL_GEOMETRY` and `idealize_backbone` are specified in [Bond Geometry Strategies](8-bond-geometry-strategies); the per-backbone growth machinery that CCD operates on is covered in [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble); and the end-to-end orchestration of fragments, combinations, and closure belongs to [LDRS Workflow Overview](14-ldrs-workover-overview). Continue to [Multi-chain Complex Modeling](16-multi-chain-complex-modeling) for the multi-chain environment contexts that `ClashEnvironment` and `inter_chain_cc` serve.


# Multi-chain Complex Modeling



Protein complexes rarely consist of a single chain, and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) frequently decorate multiple chains of the same assembly simultaneously. This page explains how IDPConformerGenerator's LDRS (Local Disordered Region Sampling) subsystem handles **multi-chain complexes**: how it identifies which chains exist in a folded template, matches them against the sequences supplied in a FASTA file, partitions disordered regions per chain, generates IDR conformers for every chain in parallel, and then grafts and clash-governs the results into coherent ensemble members. The material here builds directly on the machinery described in [LDRS Workflow Overview](14-ldrs-workflow-overview) and [Loop Closure Algorithms](15-loop-closure-algorithms); here we focus exclusively on what changes — and what becomes possible — when more than one chain is involved.

## The Multi-chain Detection Pipeline

The multi-chain workflow is orchestrated by `main()` in `cli_ldrs.py` and relies on a dedicated library module, `libmultichain.py`, which exists for exactly one purpose: "recognizing and processing multiple protein chains". The pipeline activates through two independent signals. First, when the input FASTA parses to a dictionary with more than one sequence, the client logs "multiple sequences detected. assuming they are in a multi-chain complex" and sets the module-level `MULTICHAIN` flag. Second, independently of the FASTA, the folded template is inspected by extracting the `chainID` column — falling back to `segid` when chain IDs are absent — and counting unique chains; more than one unique chain triggers the "Processing multiple protein chains" branch. This dual-signal design means a single-chain template with a multi-sequence FASTA, or a multi-chain template with one sequence, both degrade gracefully to single-chain behavior with informative logging.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["FASTA input (dict of sequences)"] -->|">1 sequence"| B["MULTICHAIN = True"]
    C["Folded template PDB/mmCIF"] --> D["Extract chainID column<br/>(fallback: segid)"]
    D --> E{"unique chains > 1?"}
    E -->|no| F["Single-chain path<br/>fld_chainseq = {chain: (fasta, 0, array)}"]
    E -->|yes| G["process_multichain_pdb()"]
    G --> H["Per-chain sequence extraction"]
    H --> I["SequenceMatcher.ratio()<br/>vs. every FASTA entry"]
    I -->|"ratio == 1.0"| J["Chain skipped<br/>(skipped_chains)"]
    I -->|"ratio < 1.0"| K["(fld_fasta, match_index, chain_arr)"]
    J & K --> L["Per-chain loop:<br/>temp dir chain{chain}/"]
    L --> M["IDR detection per chain<br/>(masking → consecutive_grouper)"]
    M --> N["N-IDR / Linker-IDR / C-IDR<br/>conformer generation"]
    N --> O["Grafting stage:<br/>chainID normalization, resSeq continuity, serial consistency"]
```

Sources: [libmultichain.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libmultichain.py#L1-L14), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L196-L198), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L576-L591), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L677-L724)

## Sequence-to-Chain Matching Semantics

The function `process_multichain_pdb` is the identity-resolution core of multi-chain modeling. It walks the template's `resSeq` column, appending a residue to the current chain's sequence only when the next row starts a new residue number — an efficient way to collapse the all-atom representation into one-letter sequences without re-parsing atom names. Each chain sequence is then scored against **every** FASTA entry with `difflib.SequenceMatcher(...).ratio()`, and the best-scoring entry wins. The return value encodes a complete assignment plan: `fld_chainseq[chain] = (fld_fasta, match_index, chain_arr)`, where `chain_arr` is the atom-array slice belonging to that chain, plus a `skipped_chains` list.

The skip logic deserves precise attention: a chain whose sequence matches a FASTA entry with ratio `1.0` is treated as *fully folded* and moved wholesale into `skipped_chains` — the client log states "Identical sequence found, skipping chain {chain}." This is how users exclude chains they do not want to model: the `-fld` argument documentation makes it explicit that "If you would like to skip chains in a multi-chain template you must have its identical sequence .fasta submitted in the -seq flag". After matching, the client filters `fld_chainseq` down to chains that are strings (skipped) versus tuples (to be modeled) and logs each `sequence {seq_id} is matched with chain {chain}` pairing. Two implications follow for complex systems: identical-sequence chains (e.g., homo-dimers) can be selectively skipped by providing one shared sequence, and mismatched-but-similar sequences (mutants, tags, constructs) are tolerated up to SequenceMatcher's fuzzy threshold — verified identity is never required for chains you *do* want to model.

| Matching outcome | `fld_chainseq[chain]` value | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Perfect match (ratio = 1.0) | `fld_fasta` (a plain string) | Chain appended to `skipped_chains`; left untouched in output |
| Partial match (best of all entries) | `(fld_fasta, match_index, chain_arr)` tuple | Chain selected for IDR building; IDR boundaries derived from `match_index` sequence |
| No chains skipped | `skipped_chains = None` | All chains proceed to modeling |

Sources: [libmultichain.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libmultichain.py#L17-L78), [libmultichain.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libmultichain.py#L45-L55), [libmultichain.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libmultichain.py#L57-L76), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L322-L332), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L703-L717)

## Per-chain Disorder Region Detection

Once chains are assigned, `main()` iterates `for chain in fld_chainseq` and computes each chain's disordered regions in isolation. The mechanism is sequence masking: the input sequence has every residue covered by the folded template replaced with `*`, and any remaining non-`*` indices are collected as the disordered set. Two masking sources are combined. First, `break_check(chain_pdb, membrane)` detects internal chain breaks in the template and masks those linker stretches — critically, in the multi-chain path `chain_pdb` is regenerated from *only that chain's* rows (`structure_to_pdb(chain_arr)`), with an explicit code comment explaining why: "Folded regions of this chain only: those of other chains with the same sequence but other IDRs would hide this chain's IDRs". Second, the chain's own folded FASTA is masked. In membrane-mode templates (produced by PPM v3 / CHARMM-GUI bilayer builders), rows whose `segid` contains "PRO" are retained while bilayer atoms are filtered out before coordinates are extracted.

> [!TIP]
> Masking runs per chain against that chain's own PDB slice, not the whole complex — this prevents duplicate-sequence chains (a homo-oligomer with IDRs on only one copy) from hiding each other's disordered regions during boundary detection.

The resulting disordered index list is converted to contiguous `(lower, upper)` bounds by `consecutive_grouper`, which groups consecutive integers using run-merging logic, producing the per-chain `DISORDER_BOUNDS[chain]` and a `DISORDER_CASES[chain]` classification. A chain whose sequence is completely overlapped by the template triggers the log message "Skipping chain {chain} because of complete overlap." Each bound is then classified by position: bounds starting at index 0 become N-IDRs (internally extended by 2 residues at the C-side for stitching), bounds ending at the sequence end become C-IDRs (extended 2 residues on the N-side), and interior bounds become Linker-IDRs (extended 2 residues on both sides). The extension rule is documented in the code as a necessity "to facilitate reconstruction later on" — the extra folded residues give the stitching stage real backbone context on each side of a junction.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L728-L786), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L743-L749), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L689-L703), [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L50-L59), [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L131-L163)

## Disorder Case Strategies Within a Complex

Each detected region is dispatched to a case-specific generation strategy, and per-chain temporary folder trees keep intermediate fragments organized: `ldrs_temp/chain{chain}/{case}/`, with Linker-IDRs further nested under `linker_{n}/{n}_match/` where `linkeridr_num` numbers linkers in sequence order. The three cases interact with the loop-closure subsystem differently, as summarized below.

| Case | Trigger condition | Generation strategy | Multi-chain relevance |
|---|---|---|---|
| **N-IDR** (`disorder_cases[0]`) | Bound starts at residue 0 | Conformer growth attached via the second folded residue's C–N–CA frame; `fld_coords` boundary recorded for stitching | Fragment pool per chain; later combined across chains |
| **Linker-IDR** (`disorder_cases[1]`) | Interior bound | `--loop-closure ccd` (default): attach to first folded end, close onto second via clash-aware damped least squares over φ/ψ, with `RamachandranReference` steering; or `next_seeker`: grow halves from both folded ends and keep pairs meeting with peptide-bond geometry | Junction atoms (`CC/NC/CAC`, `CN/NN/CAN`) located per chain; context prepared by `prepare_ccd_context` on the chain array plus the full complex array |
| **C-IDR** (`disorder_cases[2]`) | Bound ends at sequence end | Conformer growth from the terminal folded residue's N–CA frame (scanning backward from `last_seq`) | Same fragment-pool semantics as N-IDR |

Two additional multi-chain-relevant mechanics apply uniformly. IDRs longer than `LONG_IDR_FRAGMENT` (150 residues, per the module docstring) are split by `split_long_idr` and built in fragments attached one to the next — N-IDRs, C-IDRs, and `next_seeker` Linker halves; CCD-closed Linker-IDRs are built whole but checked as loops. And all fragment generation for terminal cases runs through the multiprocessing `Pool(ncores)` with `pool.imap(execute, range(ncores))`, the same global-variable-based distribution pattern documented in [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture) — meaning complex-scale ensembles scale out linearly with `-n` across all chains' IDRs simultaneously.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L886-L1028), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1030-L1142), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L862-L876), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1-L16), [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L50-L59)

## Combination Assembly: Cross-chain Clash Governance

The genuinely multi-chain coupling point arrives after individual IDR fragments exist. For a complex with, say, an N-IDR on chain A and a Linker-IDR on chain B, an ensemble member is not "one fragment per IDR" chosen independently — it is a *combination* drawing one fragment from each IDR's pool, and those fragments must not collide with each other across the complex interface. `ldrs_helper.py` implements this as a three-layer assembly system:

- **`combinations_clash_check(selected, cases)`** — takes one combination (one item per IDR list) and checks every pair of IDR fragments against each other using scipy `cKDTree` sparse distance matrices, accepting the combination only if no pair exceeds 40 contacts within vdW-radii sum + 1.0 Å. The `cases` argument lets it strip the 2-carried folded residues (`_idr_rows`) so that IDRs a few folded residues apart — which legitimately share those residues — are not falsely rejected. The `_combination_fragments` helper flattens the nested shape combinations take, e.g. `(N-IDR, [Linker-IDR 0, Linker-IDR 1], C-IDR)`.
- **`_random_combinations(lst)`** — enumerates the product space of one-item-per-list combinations; products of ≤ 100,000 are materialized and shuffled exhaustively, while larger spaces are sampled index-by-index with a `seen` set to avoid duplicates without memory blow-up.
- **`_assemble_combinations(sizes, num, passes, max_trials, attempts)`** — the driver, which selects up to `num` distinct combinations passing a caller-supplied predicate (the clash check), memoizing predicate results per index tuple so repeated candidates are never re-checked, and retrying across up to 4 assembly attempts.

The clash tolerance that governs final output is configured through `-tol/--clash-tolerance` (default 0.5), which `tolerance_calculator` maps linearly: `max_clash = int(tolerance × 80)` and `dist_tolerance = tolerance × 0.8` Å — so the default yields 40 allowed spherical clashes and 0.4 Å distance tolerance, exactly as the CLI help text documents. Note that CCD Linker closure deliberately doubles the clash budget (`max_clash * 2`) "2 fixed ends, as for linkers", reflecting the harder constraint problem of closing a loop between two rigid anchors. The underlying spatial-indexing machinery (`_AtomSet` with lazy KD-tree construction and bounding-box early rejection in `_count_contacts`) is shared with the broader clash validation stack described in [Energy-Based Clash Filtering](12-energy-based-clash-filtering).

Sources: [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L289-L327), [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L330-L399), [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L58-L79), [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L223-L279), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L392-L402), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L939)

## Grafting, Stitching, and the psurgeon API

After all per-chain conformers are built and moved, the pipeline enters its grafting stage, announced in code with the invariant checklist: "`col_chainID` and `col_segid` → make all chain A", residue numbers (`col_resSeq`) "need to be continuous", and `col_serial` "consistent as well" — i.e., internally the joined IDR chains are renumbered into a single continuous polymer before final per-chain IDs are written. Users can bypass stitching with `--stitching-off`, in which case "IDRs modeled will only undergo alignment and clash-checking" and temporary fragments are kept for manual assembly. The programmatic entry point for manual stitching is `psurgeon` in `ldrs_helper.py`, exported alongside structural helpers like `splice_folded_rows` and `find_junctions`. The repository ships a complete worked use in `slc26a9_stitching.py`, where pre-generated Linker-IDR conformer matches are spliced onto the folded 7CH1 SLC26A9 structure one at a time:

```python
combined_struc = psurgeon([[Path(idr)]], Path(fld), ["Linker-IDR"], [(lower, upper)])
combined_pdb = structure_to_pdb(combined_struc)
write_PDB(combined_pdb, output_stitched + f"conformer_{i + 1}.pdb")
```

The call signature visible here — fragment-list, folded structure path, disorder-case labels, and junction residue ranges — mirrors the internal disorder-cases vocabulary (`"Linker-IDR"` is `disorder_cases[1]`), making `psurgeon` the reusable surgical core that the automated `ldrs` pipeline drives in bulk. This two-tier design (automated end-to-end command vs. scriptable stitching API) is what the research examples exploit for custom pipelines; the slc26a9 case pairs a folded STAS domain FASTA with an IDR FASTA across two entries in the same input file, exercising the same matching machinery described above.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1144-L1147), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L343-L350), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L82-L111), [slc26a9_stitching.py](/example/slc26a9_example/slc26a9_stitching.py#L1-L23)

## Worked Example: The D1D2 Multi-chain Tutorial

The canonical demonstration lives in `example/complex_example/`, modeling IDRs on *both* chains A and B of the D1D2 sub-complex from the human SNRNP core domain (RCSB PDB 1B34) — deliberately combining all three cases (N-IDR, Linker-IDR, C-IDR) on both chains. Two formatting requirements are stated up front in the tutorial: every chain of the complex must appear in the FASTA file "even for chains you are not interested in LDRS processing", because LDRS uses the FASTA to determine which chains to process; and `D1D2.fasta` serves as the formatting reference. The entire ensemble is then produced by a single command:

```
idpconfgen ldrs \
    -db <PATH TO DATABASE.JSON> \
    -seq D1D2.fasta \
    -nc 10 \
    -fld 1B34.pdb \
    --dloop-off \
    --dany \
    -of ./D1D2_ldrs_ANY_faspr \
    -n
```

The tutorial notes that "the `ldrs` subclient will automatically detect all IDRs and their corresponding chains based on sequence similarity and mismatches in the primary sequence" between FASTA and PDB — the SequenceMatcher machinery — and reports roughly one hour of runtime on a 64 GB workstation with 10 threads at 3.0 GHz for 10 structures. The key multi-chain CLI parameters are summarized below.

| Flag | Purpose | Multi-chain behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `-fld / --folded-structure` | Template PDB/mmCIF of the folded complex | Required; multi-chain templates need identical FASTA entries for chains to be skipped |
| `-seq` | FASTA with one entry per chain | >1 entry activates `MULTICHAIN`; entries fuzzy-matched to chains |
| `--membrane` | Template built with PPM v3 / CHARMM-GUI bilayer | Filters non-"PRO" segids (lipids/waters) from all chain processing |
| `--stitching-off` | Skip automatic grafting | Outputs remain alignment+clash-checked fragments; enables `-kt` |
| `--loop-closure` | `ccd` (default) or `next_seeker` for Linker-IDRs | `ccd` practical for loops of hundreds of residues; `next_seeker` needs large libraries for long linkers |
| `--ccd-max-trials` | Trials per core per Linker conformer (default 100) | Stops if round 1 closes nothing; proceeds until complete or 5 stall rounds |
| `-tol / --clash-tolerance` | 0.0–1.0 (default 0.5) | Scales both allowed clashes (0–80) and Å tolerance (0–0.8) globally across the complex |
| `-nc / --nconfs`, `-n` | Ensemble size, core count | Distributed across all chains' IDR builds via multiprocessing Pool |

Sources: [complex_example/README.rst](/example/complex_example/README.rst#L1-L52), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L322-L467)

## Module Interaction Summary

The multi-chain capability is deliberately distributed across small, single-purpose modules rather than concentrated in one file — `libmultichain.py` holds identity resolution, `ldrs_helper.py` holds disorder bookkeeping and surgical assembly, and `cli_ldrs.py` holds orchestration. The following interaction map shows how a single complex build flows through them.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph cli_ldrs.py
        M["main() orchestration<br/>MULTICHAIN flag, per-chain loop,<br/>Pool distribution"]
    end
    subgraph libmultichain.py
        P["process_multichain_pdb()<br/>chain detection + SequenceMatcher<br/>+ skipped_chains"]
    end
    subgraph ldrs_helper.py
        B["break_check / consecutive_grouper<br/>disorder_cases / split_long_idr"]
        C["combinations_clash_check<br/>_random_combinations / _assemble_combinations"]
        S["psurgeon<br/>(splice fragments onto folded template)"]
    end
    subgraph Supporting libs
        ST["libstructure<br/>Structure, structure_to_pdb, write_PDB"]
        CCD["libccd<br/>RamachandranReference, CCDParameters"]
    end
    FASTA["D1D2.fasta"] --> M
    PDB["1B34.pdb"] --> P
    M --> P
    P -->|"fld_chainseq, skipped_chains"| M
    M --> B
    B -->|"DISORDER_BOUNDS / CASES"| M
    M --> CCD
    B --> C
    C --> S
    S --> ST
    ST --> OUT["Multi-chain ensemble .pdb"]
```

The result is a system where adding a chain to a complex does not require any new code path — only additional FASTA entries — because every downstream stage (boundary detection, generation, combination assembly, grafting) already operates on per-chain data structures keyed by chain ID.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L576-L786), [libmultichain.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libmultichain.py#L17-L78), [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L1-L59)

## Where to Go Next

This page covered the orchestration and identity-resolution layers unique to multi-chain systems. To go deeper into the machinery referenced here: the two Linker-IDR closure strategies (`ccd` damped least squares and `next_seeker` pairwise meeting) are analyzed in [Loop Closure Algorithms](15-loop-closure-algorithms); the overall fragment-to-ensemble lifecycle is framed in [LDRS Workflow Overview](14-ldrs-workflow-overview); the clash metrics reused by `combinations_clash_check` are detailed in [Energy-Based Clash Filtering](12-energy-based-clash-filtering); the `Pool`/global-variable distribution used for per-chain fragment generation is dissected in [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture); and both the D1D2 and slc26a9 workflows sit within the broader collection of runnable case studies in [Research Examples Library](23-research-examples-library).

# CLI Subcommand System



This page explains how IDPConformerGenerator transforms a single console command into one of **twenty specialized routines** without a framework — just disciplined `argparse` conventions. The entire system rests on three artifacts: a root dispatcher (`cli.py`), a shared infrastructure library (`libcli.py`), and a strict module contract enforced across every `cli_*.py` file. Understanding this system is prerequisite reading for contributing new commands, and it underpins how the build engine, LDRS module, and database-preparation utilities all expose themselves to users.

Sources: [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L1-L148), [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L1-L16)

## System at a Glance

The architecture operates in two distinct phases. At **import time**, `cli.py` imports all subcommand modules and asks `libcli.add_subparser()` to graft each module's parser onto the root parser tree. At **run time**, the parsed namespace carries a `func` default pointing at the selected module's `main()` — dispatch is simply calling it. No registry, no metaprogramming, no discovery: registration is explicit, ordered, and visible in one place.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph IT["Import Time — Registration Phase"]
        M1["cli_pdbdownloader: _name, _help, ap, main"]
        M2["cli_build: _name, _help, ap, main"]
        M3["... 18 more cli_ modules"]
        R["libcli.add_subparser"]
        R --> SP["subparsers action on root parser"]
        SP --> ROOT["cli.py — root CustomParser"]
        M1 --> R
        M2 --> R
        M3 --> R
    end
    subgraph RT["Run Time — Dispatch Phase"]
        U["$ idpconfgen build -db torsions.json -seq ..."]
        EP["console script → cli:maincli"]
        P["ap.parse_args → namespace"]
        D["cmd.func ** vars cmd"]
        MM["cli_build.main with keyword args"]
        U --> EP --> P --> D --> MM
    end
    ROOT -.->|"entry point binds maincli"| EP
```

The two phases are connected by a single convention: modules expose attributes at their top level, and the dispatcher reads them verbatim. This is why every subcommand's help text, usage string, and execution target lives inside its own module — the root `cli.py` only orchestrates.

Sources: [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L18-L43), [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L239-L267)

## Entry Point Chain: From Console Script to Dispatch

Packaging wires the `idpconfgen` command to `cli:maincli` through setuptools console scripts. The `entry_points` declaration in `setup.py` is the only packaging-level involvement — everything downstream is ordinary Python.

Sources: [setup.py](/setup.py#L93-L97)

Two invocation paths converge on the same function. Installed console scripts call `idpconfgen.cli:maincli` directly, while `python -m idpconfgen` routes through `__main__.py`, which imports and calls the identical `maincli`. This dual-path design costs one 16-line module and guarantees behavioral parity between both launch modes.

Sources: [\_\_main\_\_.py](/src/idpconfgen/__main__.py#L10-L15)

Inside `maincli()`, three things happen in sequence. First, a guard prints the root help and exits when fewer than two `argv` entries exist — invoking bare `idpconfgen` is never an error, it is a help screen. Second, after successful parsing, the tool writes an `idpconfgen.version` file into the current working directory as a provenance side effect. Third — and this is the entire dispatch mechanism — the command executes as `cmd.func(**vars(cmd))`, then logs a confirmation through the shared logger.

Sources: [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L125-L147)

## The Subcommand Module Contract

Every `cli_*.py` module is a self-contained parser-plus-logic unit. `libcli.add_subparser()` documents the required attributes explicitly, and all twenty modules conform: a docstring in a fixed format, metadata names, a `CustomParser` instance named `ap`, and a `main()` function. The contract is convention-based — nothing enforces it except consistency and tests.

| Attribute | Type | Role in the system |
|---|---|---|
| `__doc__` | str | Line 1 → program name; `USAGE:` marker → usage block; remainder → description |
| `_name` | str | The literal subcommand string typed by users (e.g. `'pdbdl'`, `'build'`) |
| `_help` | str | One-line summary shown in the root command listing |
| `_prog`, `_usage` | str | Derived from docstring; feed the parser's `prog` and `usage` |
| `ap` | `libcli.CustomParser` | Module-owned argument parser, inherited by the root via `parents` |
| `main()` | function | Execution target, bound via `set_defaults(func=module.main)` |

Sources: [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L245-L267), [cli_pdbdownloader.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_pdbdownloader.py#L48-L66)

The docstring is not decoration — it is parsed. `parse_doc_params()` splits the module docstring on the literal `USAGE:` marker, returning a `(prog, description, usage)` tuple in one pass. This means the module's documentation *is* its `--help` output; there is exactly one place where the command is described, and the CLI renders it directly.

Sources: [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L215-L236)

A minimal module like `cli_pdbdownloader.py` shows the full anatomy in 77 lines: metadata at lines 48–52, parser construction at 54–59, argument attachment via `libcli` factories at 61–66, a thin `main()` delegating to `download_pipeline`, and a standalone execution guard. Notably, `main()` accepts `func=None` explicitly — a requirement whose reason becomes clear in the dispatch protocol section below.

Sources: [cli_pdbdownloader.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_pdbdownloader.py#L48-L77)

## Registration Mechanics: add_subparser Under the Hood

The registration function is eight lines of dense design. It creates a child parser whose name is `module._name`, whose description concatenates the program name with the module's parsed description, and — critically — whose **argument set is inherited via `parents=[module.ap]`**. The `add_help=False` flag prevents the parent parser's own `-h` handler from conflicting with the child's. Finally, `new_ap.set_defaults(func=module.main)` plants the execution target in the namespace: whichever subcommand wins parsing, its `main` arrives as a namespace default.

Sources: [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L239-L267)

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class cli_module {
        <<module convention>>
        +__doc__ str
        +_name str
        +_help str
        +ap CustomParser
        +main function
    }
    class libcli {
        <<shared infrastructure>>
        +parse_doc_params docstring
        +add_subparser parser, module
        +add_version parser
        +CustomParser class
        +add_argument_X parser factories
        +maincli ap, main
    }
    class cli {
        <<root dispatcher>>
        +ap root parser
        +subparsers
        +maincli
    }
    cli_module --> libcli : parses own docstring, uses factories
    libcli --> cli_module : reads _name, _help, ap, main
    cli --> libcli : add_subparser, add_version
    cli --> cli_module : imports all 20 modules
```

Registration order in `cli.py` is meaningful — it is the order users see in `idpconfgen -h`. The six **core pipeline** routines (`pdbdl`, `sscalc`, `torsions`, `torsionsJ`, `build`, `ldr`) register first, mirroring the database-preparation-to-ensemble workflow; the fourteen **secondary utilities** follow. The root description block is likewise composed at import time by interpolating each module's `_name`, so the overview text and the subparser listing can never drift apart.

Sources: [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L50-L117)

## Shared Parser Infrastructure in libcli

`CustomParser` overrides `error()` to print the full help text before writing the error to stderr and exiting with code 2. For a scientific tool with dozens of flags per command, this "help-on-error" behavior dramatically reduces the need to consult documentation — the parser itself teaches the user.

Sources: [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L204-L212)

Rather than repeating `add_argument` calls with hand-crafted flags, modules pull **argument factories** from `libcli`. This standardizes the entire CLI vocabulary: `-n/--ncores` means the same thing in every routine that accepts it, and `-d/--destination` always produces a `Path` defaulting to the working directory. An in-code "arguments index" comment block serves as the living style guide for this vocabulary.

Sources: [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L291-L317)

| Factory | Produces | Notable behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `add_argument_ncores` | `int` | `nargs='?'` with `const = cpu_count() - 1` — bare `-n` means "all cores minus one" |
| `add_argument_seq` | str/dict | `SeqOrFasta` action accepts a raw sequence or FASTA file, supports multi-chain dicts |
| `add_argument_db` / `add_argument_idb` | `Path`/str | Output databases get `.json` extension enforcement via `CheckExt`; input DBs are `required=True` |
| `add_argument_destination_folder` | `Path` | Defaults to `Path.cwd()`; accepts TAR targets |
| `add_argument_random_seed` | `int` | Default `0`, present in every stochastic routine |
| `add_argument_chunks` | `int` | Memory-batching size, default `5_000` |

Sources: [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L533-L548), [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L448-L462), [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L359-L376)

Where standard `argparse` types fall short, **custom `Action` classes** perform validation and type coercion at parse time. This pushes failure detection to the earliest possible moment — a malformed probability list or unreadable dictionary is rejected before any pipeline code executes, using `parser.error()` for uniform messaging through `CustomParser`.

| Action | Purpose | Example coercion |
|---|---|---|
| `SeqOrFasta` | Accept sequence string or FASTA path | `'MMM...'` or `seq.fasta` → sequence dict |
| `FolderOrTar` | Normalize input container | `['archive.tar']` → `'archive.tar'` |
| `ReadDictionary` | JSON from file path or inline literal | `'{"a":1}'` or `data.json` → dict |
| `ListOfIntsPositiveSum` | Probability-like digit lists | `'3','2'` → `[3, 2]`, sum ≥ 1 enforced |
| `minimum_value(n)` | Parameterized bound factory | `-vdWb` cannot drop below 3 |
| `CheckExt(exts)` | Parameterized extension gate | `.json` databases |
| `ParamsToDict` | Inline `key=value` plotting kwargs | `xlabel=X color=b` → dict |
| `CSV2Tuple`, `ArgsToTuple`, `AllParam`, `ListOfPositiveInts` | Shape normalization | `'a,b'` → `('a','b')` |

Sources: [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L31-L168), [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L171-L201)

## The Dispatch Protocol and the func=None Convention

The one-line dispatcher `cmd.func(**vars(cmd))` has a subtle consequence: `vars(cmd)` — the namespace dictionary — **contains `func` itself**, because `set_defaults` planted it there. Every `main()` therefore receives a keyword argument named `func` holding its own callable. The codebase handles this with a universal convention: declare `func=None` in the signature and ignore it.

> [!TIP]
> Forgetting `func=None` in a new subcommand's `main()` produces a confusing `TypeError: main() got an unexpected keyword argument 'func'` at runtime — not at registration time. When writing a new `cli_*` module, treat `func=None` as part of the signature boilerplate, exactly as `cli_build.py` and `cli_pdbdownloader.py` do. The most defensive pattern is `cli_pdbdownloader.py`'s `main(*args, func=None, **kwargs)`, which absorbs any namespace residue.

Sources: [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L137-L143), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L439-L464), [cli_pdbdownloader.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_pdbdownloader.py#L69-L72)

The keyword-argument plumbing means `main()` signatures are hand-mirrored from parser destinations. `cli_build.py`'s `main()` declares `input_seq`, `database`, `dloop_off`, `bgeo_strategy`, `ncores`, `func=None`, and a trailing `**kwargs` for extension points — argparse converts `--dloop-off` to `dloop_off` and the signature must match exactly. Complex validation that argparse cannot express, such as mutual-exclusion checks between sampling modes, executes at the top of `main()` as explicit `ValueError` guards.

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L439-L483)

Every module also carries a **standalone twin path**: `if __name__ == '__main__': libcli.maincli(ap, main)`. This uses `libcli.maincli(ap, main)` — the per-module analog of the root dispatcher — so developers can run `python -m idpconfgen.cli_build ...` during development without touching the full registration tree. The same parse-and-call protocol applies, which is why the `func=None` convention is load-bearing in both paths.

Sources: [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L25-L28), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L1930-L1932)

Execution setup follows a shared lifecycle: each module defines a `LOGFILESNAME` (e.g. `'.idpconfgen_build'`, `'.idpconfgen_pdbdl'`), and `main()` initializes per-command log files via `init_files()` before issuing `T()`/`S()` prefixed log messages. This gives every subcommand consistent logging semantics with zero per-module logging logic.

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L108-L110), [cli_pdbdownloader.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_pdbdownloader.py#L48-L48), [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L489-L495)

## Extending the CLI: Adding a New Subcommand

The system's extensibility is best demonstrated by its own evolution: `cli_build.py` delegates portions of its parser to **component plugins** — `add_bgeo_strategy_arg`, `add_et_type_arg`, `add_xmer_arg`, `add_res_tolerance_groups`, `add_sidechain_method`, and `add_mcsce_subparser` all attach arguments to the module's `ap`. This is the seam where the CLI system meets the [Component Plugin Pattern](20-component-plugin-pattern): plugins own their flags, modules own registration.

Sources: [cli_build.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L326-L368)

Adding a new subcommand is a five-step checklist with no dispatcher-side surprises beyond the import and one `add_subparser` line:

| Step | Location | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | New `cli_<name>.py` | Docstring with `USAGE:` section; define `_name`, `_help`; run `parse_doc_params(__doc__)` |
| 2 | Same module | Build `ap = libcli.CustomParser(...)`, attach arguments via `libcli.add_argument_*` factories |
| 3 | Same module | Write `main()` with keyword params matching parser destinations **plus `func=None`** |
| 4 | Same module | Append `if __name__ == '__main__': libcli.maincli(ap, main)` |
| 5 | `cli.py` | Import the module, reference `_name` in the description block, call `libcli.add_subparser(subparsers, cli_<name>)` |

Sources: [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L18-L117), [cli_pdbdownloader.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_pdbdownloader.py#L48-L77)

## Design Assessment: Strengths and Trade-offs

| Dimension | Strength | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Discoverability | Help-on-error `CustomParser`; docstring-driven help keeps docs and CLI in lockstep | `USAGE:` marker parsing breaks silently if docstring format drifts |
| Consistency | Argument factories enforce a shared CLI vocabulary (ncores, random-seed, destination) across 20 commands | New contributors must learn the factory catalog before writing valid modules |
| Extensibility | Explicit registration list; component plugins inject their own arguments into `cli_build` | No auto-discovery — every new command edits `cli.py` in three places (import, description, registration) |
| Dispatch simplicity | One namespace default (`func`) replaces dispatcher branching entirely | The invisible `func` keyword leaks into every `main()` signature |
| Developer ergonomics | Per-module standalone execution via `libcli.maincli(ap, main)` | Module-level globals in `cli_build` exist for multiprocessing reasons (see [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture)) |

The system exemplifies a deliberate philosophy: **convention over configuration, but with the conventions written down**. The required-attributes contract is documented in `add_subparser`'s docstring, the argument vocabulary is indexed in-code, and the two-tier registration (pipeline vs. secondary) encodes architectural intent directly into help output ordering.

Sources: [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L239-L267), [libcli.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L291-L317)

> [!TIP]
> When debugging CLI behavior, remember that `cli.py` evaluates module attributes (`cli_build._name`, `cli_pdbdl._name`, ...) at import time to compose its description block. Any syntax error or import failure in any of the twenty `cli_*.py` modules breaks the entire `idpconfgen` command — not just the affected subcommand — because registration is a single eager import pass.

## Where to Go Next

The CLI layer is the front door to everything else in this catalog. To trace what happens after `main()` is invoked, continue with:

- **Command internals**: [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble) for `build`, or [LDRS Workflow Overview](14-ldrs-workover-overview) → [LDRS Workflow Overview](14-ldrs-workflow-overview) for `ldrs`
- **How plugins inject flags into parsers**: [Component Plugin Pattern](20-component-plugin-pattern)
- **What `-n/--ncores` activates underneath**: [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture)
- **Testing these parsers**: [Testing Strategy & Fixtures](22-testing-strategy-and-fixtures) includes `test_libcli.py` coverage of the shared infrastructure


# Multiprocessing Architecture



IDPConformerGenerator converts embarrassingly parallel scientific workloads — torsion extraction, secondary-structure calculation, and conformer building — into multi-core executions. Rather than adopting a single monolithic framework, the project layers two complementary parallelization mechanisms: a **generic, reusable Pool utility library** (`libmulticore`) for data-parallel batch jobs, and an **application-specific worker-replica orchestration** embedded in the `build` CLI, which coordinates long-lived builder processes through shared module globals and `multiprocessing.Queue` channels. This page dissects both mechanisms, the observability tooling that wraps them, and the design constraints (pickling, determinism, crash tolerance) that shaped their implementation.

Sources: [libmulticore.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L1-L131), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L110-L173)

## Architecture Overview: Three Layers

The multiprocessing stack is organized as a deliberate separation of concerns. At the base sits the **execution utility layer** (`libs/libmulticore.py`), a 131-line module exposing functional wrappers around `multiprocessing.Pool` that yield results as generators. Above it, the **orchestration layer** in CLI modules (most prominently `cli_build.py`) decides *what* runs in parallel — either individual data items or whole worker replicas — and wires consumers together with `functools.partial`. The **observability layer** (`libs/libtimer.py` `ProgressWatcher` plus the logger's `report_on_crash`) provides terminal-adaptive progress rendering and crash-tolerant error reporting that wraps every dispatched task. CLI conventions documented in `libcli.py` — the `-n, --ncores` flag and the `-c, --chunks` fragment size (default `5_000`) — form the user-facing entry points that feed parameters down into these layers.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "CLI / Argument Layer"
        A["libcli.py<br/>-n / --ncores flag<br/>-c / --chunks (default 5000)"]
    end
    subgraph "Orchestration Layer"
        B["cli_build.py main()<br/>partial(...) composition<br/>nconfs // ncores partitioning"]
        C["CONF_NUMBER Queue<br/>RANDOMSEEDS Queue"]
    end
    subgraph "Execution Utility Layer"
        D["libmulticore.pool_function<br/>Pool + imap_unordered generator"]
        E["libmulticore.pool_function_in_chunks<br/>chunked fragment execution"]
        F["libmulticore.consume_iterable_in_list<br/>picklable generator wrapper"]
    end
    subgraph "Observability Layer"
        G["libtimer.ProgressWatcher<br/>ProgressBar / Counter / Fake"]
        H["logger.report_on_crash<br/>per-task crash reporting"]
    end
    A --> B
    B --> C
    B --> D
    B --> H
    D --> G
    E --> D
    F -.->|wrapped inside| E
```

Sources: [libmulticore.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L1-L131), [libcli.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L291-L337), [libtimer.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libtimer.py#L52-L92), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L786-L812)

## The Generic Pool Utilities: `libmulticore`

The workhorse of the utility layer is `pool_function(func, items, method='imap_unordered', ncores=1)`. Its signature encodes two important decisions. First, it is itself a **generator function**: it opens `Pool(ncores)` as a context manager, wraps a `ProgressWatcher` around the input items with the suffix `f'on {ncores} cpus'`, then enters a `while True` loop that yields results one at a time from `imap` and increments the progress bar. Second, the comment in the source explains why a `while` loop is used instead of `for`: it is needed "to allow try/catch options" — the loop body can intercept exceptions per-result without terminating the whole consumption stream.

Sources: [libmulticore.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L55-L94)

The exception-handling matrix inside that loop is a subtle but critical contract for advanced users. An `IndexError` — a known failure mode when picking results out of multiprocessing internals — is logged and *silently ignored*, letting the pool continue. A `ReportOnCrashError` is swallowed with a bare `continue` because the crash-reporting machinery has already recorded it. Any other `IDPConfGenException` is logged with its full traceback via `traceback.format_exc()` at debug level and the error message at error level, then consumption resumes. Only `StopIteration` breaks the loop. This means downstream consumers must treat `pool_function`'s output as **best-effort**: failed items vanish from the result stream rather than raising.

Sources: [libmulticore.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L79-L94)

Two companion utilities handle generator-based workers, which are otherwise incompatible with `multiprocessing` pickling. The source is explicit about the constraint at its only inline comment: *"here can't use closures because those can't be pickled."* `consume_iterable_in_list(func, *args, **kwargs)` wraps a generator function so that each pool task executes it fully and returns a materialized `list`, which *is* picklable. Its counterpart `flat_results_from_chunk(execute, func, *args, **kwargs)` then flattens the nested lists back into a single stream and feeds them to a consumer — the docstring's inline note references `extract_secondary_structure`, indicating these helpers were built for the secondary-structure extraction pipelines (SSCalc-style workloads). Finally, `pool_function_in_chunks(func, items, chunks=5_000, **kwargs)` slices the item list into fixed-size fragments, runs each fragment through `pool_function`, and yields a list per fragment — enabling memory-bounded, checkpoint-friendly batch processing.

> [!TIP]
> If you are porting a new IDPConfGen CLI subcommand and your worker is a generator, do not attempt to `Pool.imap` it directly — wrap it in `consume_iterable_in_list` first, or the pool will fail on pickling. The `chunks=5_000` default in `pool_function_in_chunks` mirrors the `-c/--chunks` CLI convention in `libcli.add_argument_chunks`.

Sources: [libmulticore.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L10-L51), [libmulticore.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L98-L131), [libcli.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcli.py#L325-L337)

## Two Parallelization Topologies

The codebase uses the Pool primitive in structurally different ways, and recognizing the distinction is essential for reasoning about performance and failure modes. The `libmulticore` functions implement **data-parallel mapping**: one function is applied over many small items, and Pool scheduling distributes items across workers. The `build` CLI implements a **worker-replica topology**: the pool is mapped over `range(ncores)` — not over data — so each pool task is an identical, long-running builder process that constructs `conformers_per_core` conformers in an internal loop.

| Dimension | Data-parallel (`pool_function`) | Worker-replica (`cli_build` Pool block) |
|---|---|---|
| Pool input items | The actual workload items | `range(ncores)` — worker indices only |
| Work unit | One item per `func` call | `nconfs // ncores` conformers per worker |
| Result semantics | Generator of per-item results, unordered | Side effects only (files written to disk) |
| State sharing | None — `func` via `partial` | Module globals + `Queue` channels |
| Failure handling | Per-item exception matrix | `report_on_crash` wraps the whole consumer |
| Ordering | `imap_unordered` (unordered) | Deterministic IDs drawn from `CONF_NUMBER` |

Sources: [libmulticore.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L55-L94), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L805-L812)

## The Build Engine's Worker-Replica Orchestration

`cli_build.main()` performs a load-balancing calculation before any pool exists. If `nconfs < ncores`, it degrades gracefully to `ncores = 1` with all conformers in a single batch; otherwise it computes `conformers_per_core = nconfs // ncores` and tracks `remaining_confs = nconfs % ncores` for the indivisible tail. This is followed by the creation of two module-level `Queue` channels — imported at the top of the file alongside `Pool` — that coordinate the replicas:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as main() parent
    participant Q as CONF_NUMBER / RANDOMSEEDS Queues
    participant P as Pool(ncores)
    participant W as Worker process (replica i)
    M->>Q: put seeds random_seed + i (i = 0..ncores)
    M->>Q: put conformer IDs 1..nconfs
    M->>M: partial -> report_on_crash(_build_conformers, ...)
    M->>P: pool.imap(execute, range(ncores))
    P->>W: start replica (inherits globals via fork)
    W->>Q: draw random seed
    loop conformers_per_core times
        W->>Q: draw next conformer ID
        W->>W: build conformer, write PDB
    end
    P-->>M: imap exhausted
    M->>M: execute() remaining_confs serially in parent
```

The queues serve two distinct coordination purposes. `CONF_NUMBER` is pre-filled with the integers `1..nconfs`, and the source comment states it exists so that *"cores can read global variables fast"*-style naming stays conflict-free: workers pull IDs from the shared queue to name output files `conformer_1, conformer_2, ...` without racing. `RANDOMSEEDS` is pre-filled with `random_seed + i` for every core (plus one extra when a remainder batch will run), and the comment notes these derived seeds are *"predictable"* — this is what makes multi-core ensemble generation **reproducible** from a single `--random-seed` flag.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L540-L554), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L641-L649), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L16)

The most consequential design choice in this layer is the **shared-globals strategy**. Roughly twenty module-level variables — the torsion database `ANGLES`, bend angles, bond lengths, the slice dictionary, x-mer probabilities, the `GET_ADJ` sampling closure factory, atom labels/masks/energy functions for both the all-atom and Ala/Gly/Pro-template representations — are declared at module scope. The source comments are explicit about the rationale: globals are used *"to facilitate distributing conformer creation processes across multiple cores.
