In this way cores can read global variables fast and with non-significant overhead,"* and the same strategy is applied for the template masks because *"reading from global variables is performant in Python multiprocessing."* In a fork-based Pool, workers inherit these populated globals at spawn time, avoiding per-task argument pickling of large NumPy arrays. The `are_globals(bgeo_strategy)` guard validates that exactly the right subset is populated for the selected bond-geometry strategy (`sampling`, `exact`/`fixed`, or `int2cart`) before workers launch.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L110-L173), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L180-L220)

Task dispatch itself is a two-stage `partial` composition. The inner consumer (`_build_conformers`, or `_build_long_conformers` when the `--long` mode fragments sequences over ~300 residues) is bound with the output folder, its per-core conformer quota, sidechain parameters, and strategy kwargs. The outer wrapper binds `report_on_crash` with `ROC_exception=Exception`, a `ROC_folder` for crash reports, and the subcommand name as `ROC_prefix`. The pool block then runs `pool.imap(execute, range(ncores))` and drains it, after which the **remainder batch executes serially in the parent process** — `execute(conformers_per_core * ncores, nconfs=remaining_confs)` — a simple tail-balancing tactic that trades a little parallelism for zero coordination overhead. In `--long` mode, an additional global registry `LONG_GLOBALS` (a list of per-fragment dictionaries keyed by `_FRAGMENT_GLOBALS` names) lets each builder iterate over pre-computed fragment state for the extended-IDP workflow.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L785-L812), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L654-L745), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L157-L173)

> [!TIP]
> Because workers inherit globals through the Pool, mutating a global inside a worker has no effect on the parent or sibling workers — the inheritance is one-way at fork time. That is precisely why the mutable coordination state (conformer IDs, seeds) lives in `Queue` objects rather than in globals: queues are the only bidirectional channel in this design.

## Observability: `ProgressWatcher` and `report_on_crash`

`ProgressWatcher` in `libtimer.py` is a factory implemented through `__new__` that returns one of three context-manager backends depending on runtime capability. If the logger's handlers are not `StreamHandler` subclasses, or the terminal size cannot be measured (typical on servers/CI), it returns `ProgressFake` — a silent dummy. If `items` has no `len()` (a generator), it returns `ProgressCounter`, which counts completions without a bar. Only when both a real terminal and a sized iterable exist does it construct a `ProgressBar`, sized to `cols // 2` to fit the display. This polymorphism means the identical `pool_function` code works unchanged on interactive terminals, headless servers, and generator-driven pipelines. `pool_function` integrates it directly, passing `suffix=f'on {ncores} cpus'` and incrementing once per yielded result.

Sources: [libtimer.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libtimer.py#L52-L92), [libmulticore.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L76-L84)

Crash tolerance follows a complementary pattern. Every dispatched build task is wrapped by `report_on_crash(consume, ROC_exception=Exception, ROC_folder=..., ROC_prefix=...)` at the orchestration layer, so an exception inside one replica's consumer is captured, reported, and persisted to disk instead of collapsing the entire pool — which also explains why `pool_function` treats `ReportOnCrashError` as *"nothing to do, report did it already"* and continues. The two layers therefore form a defense-in-depth chain: `report_on_crash` converts worker crashes into durable reports at the replica level, while `pool_function`'s exception matrix converts item-level failures into logged skips at the item level.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L797-L803), [libmulticore.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L87-L94)

## Design Rationale and Known Pitfalls

Four constraints shaped this architecture, and each is verifiable in the source. **Picklability** forbids closures in pool tasks — hence module-level functions, `functools.partial`, and the `consume_iterable_in_list` wrapper. **Inheritance cost** motivates globals: large NumPy torsion databases and mask arrays cross the fork boundary once, not once per task. **Coordination races** on output naming and seeding are eliminated by queue pre-filling, with derived seeds (`random_seed + i`) preserving reproducibility. **Tail imbalance** is handled by the serial remainder execution in the parent. The test suite reflects this hierarchy: `test_consume_in_list` and `test_pool_function` (running over 10,000 items with `ncores=os.cpu_count()`) are active, while the three chunk-composition tests are marked `pytest.mark.skip(reason="something is halting this")` — a candid signal that nested chunked-pool execution has unresolved instability and should not be trusted in production paths.

Sources: [libmulticore.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L15-L16), [tests/test_multicore.py](tests/test_multicore.py#L16-L44), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L641-L649)

## Verification and Extension Points

The reference documentation exposes the entire module via `automodule`, so all five public functions are API-stable surfaces for downstream tooling. When extending the system, follow the established seams: reuse `pool_function` for new data-parallel batch subcommands (respecting its best-effort exception semantics), and replicate the worker-replica recipe — partial-composed consumer, `report_on_crash` wrapper, queue-based ID/seed distribution, `with Pool(ncores)` over `range(ncores)`, serial remainder — for any new long-running generation workload. Note also the `are_globals` pattern: any new strategy adding module-global state should extend that validator rather than relying on ad-hoc `None` checks in workers.

Sources: [docs/reference/libmulticore.rst](docs/reference/libmulticore.rst#L1-L6), [libmulticore.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libmulticore.py#L55-L131), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L180-L220)

## Where to Go Next

The multiprocessing machinery is the transport layer beneath several specialized subsystems covered elsewhere in this catalog. To understand *what* the replicas actually execute — fragment sampling, quaternion-based coordinate placement, energy filtering — continue with [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble), then [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling) for the `GET_ADJ` closure created in `main()`. For the observability primitives referenced here, [Testing Strategy & Fixtures](22-testing-strategy-and-fixtures) covers the test conventions including the skipped multicore cases, while [CLI Subcommand System](17-cli-subcommand-system) details the `libcli` argument conventions (`-n/--ncores`, `-c/--chunks`) that parameterize this architecture.


# Structural File Parsers



IDPConformerGenerator consumes structural data from heterogeneous sources — legacy PDB files, modern mmCIF archives, DSSP secondary-structure assignments, FASTA sequences, and tar/list bundles of thousands of entries. This page documents the parsing stack that makes this possible: how raw bytes are normalized, how format detection dispatches to the right parser, how each parser extracts fields, and how everything converges into a single in-memory representation that the rest of the engine (see [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble)) consumes. All parsers live under `src/idpconfgen/libs/` and `src/idpconfgen/core/`, are implemented with the Python standard library plus `numpy` (no Bio.PDB dependency), and follow the project's convention of raising domain-specific exceptions instead of leaking built-in Python errors.

Sources: [libcif.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcif.py#L1-L47), [libpdb.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libpdb.py#L1-L37), [libstructure.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libstructure.py#L1-L29)

## Architecture: The Layered Parsing Stack

The parsing system is organized as four layers: **normalization** (anything → `str`), **detection** (`str` → parser choice), **format-specific parsing** (PDB / mmCIF / DSSP / FASTA), and a **unified model** (`Structure` backed by a NumPy string array). The `Structure` class is the pivot: it accepts a `Path`, `bytes`, or `str`, normalizes via `get_datastr` (which delegates to the `type2string` dispatcher in `libparse`), detects the format via `detect_structure_type`, and only materializes its data when `.build()` is explicitly called — a deliberately lazy contract guarded by `NotBuiltError`.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph INPUT["Input Sources"]
        PATH["pathlib.Path"]
        BYTES["bytes"]
        STR["str - raw content"]
        LIST[".list file / folder / .tar archive"]
    end

    subgraph L1["Layer 1 - Normalization"]
        T2S["type2string dispatcher - libparse"]
        RPB["read_path_bundle - libio"]
        FIT["FileReaderIterator<br/>FileIterator / TarFileIterator"]
    end

    subgraph L2["Layer 2 - Detection"]
        ISPDB["is_pdb - counts newline ATOM records"]
        ISCIF["is_cif - regex searches loop_"]
        DETECT["detect_structure_type<br/>raises ParserNotFoundError"]
    end

    subgraph L3["Layer 3 - Format Parsers"]
        PPDB["libpdb - fixed-column slicers"]
        PCIF["CIFParser - libcif"]
        DSSP["libdssp - external mkdssp orchestrator"]
    end

    subgraph L4["Layer 4 - Unified Model"]
        ST["Structure - numpy U8 array, n_atoms x 16 cols"]
        FLT["filter chain / custom lambda filters"]
    end

    OUT1["write_PDB"]
    OUT2["save_pairs_to_disk<br/>files or tar"]

    LIST --> RPB --> FIT
    FIT --> T2S
    PATH --> T2S
    BYTES --> T2S
    STR --> T2S
    T2S --> ISPDB --> DETECT
    T2S --> ISCIF --> DETECT
    DETECT --> PPDB
    DETECT --> PCIF
    PPDB --> DSSP
    PPDB --> ST
    PCIF --> ST
    ST --> FLT --> OUT1
    ST --> OUT2
```

The key insight is that **PDB v3 field semantics are the canonical internal format**. The mmCIF parser does not create its own model; its properties are a façade that translates CIF labels into PDB-shaped fields, so every downstream module — conformer builder, clash filter, torsion extractor — operates on identical 16-column rows regardless of origin.

Sources: [libstructure.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libstructure.py#L525-L566), [libparse.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libparse.py#L33-L41)

## Input Normalization and Format Detection

Before any format logic runs, inputs are flattened to strings and format-identified through two lightweight predicates. `get_datastr` looks up the concrete type of the incoming object in the `type2string` registry (`Path` → `read_text()`, `bytes` → `decode('utf_8')`, `str` → identity) and raises `NotImplementedError` for unsupported types, asserting the result is a `str`.

Detection is intentionally cheap and side-effect free: `is_pdb` simply counts occurrences of `'\nATOM '` in the data string, while `is_cif` searches for a case-insensitive `loop_` token via regex. `detect_structure_type` walks a `structure_parsers` dispatcher table of `(predicate, parser)` pairs and returns the first matching parser function; if none matches, it raises `ParserNotFoundError`. This registry pattern means adding a new format requires only appending one condition-parser pair.

> [!TIP]
> The predicate-based dispatcher (`structure_parsers`) plus `ParserNotFoundError` is the extension seam of this stack: a new parser plugs in as one `(is_format, parse_fn)` tuple without touching `Structure` itself.

Sources: [libparse.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libparse.py#L33-L41), [libpdb.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libpdb.py#L216-L220), [libcif.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcif.py#L209-L214), [libstructure.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libstructure.py#L525-L566)

## The PDB Parser: Fixed-Column Slicing

The PDB v3 format is positional, and `libpdb` exploits this with a table of **named `slice` objects** — `atom_record = slice(0, 6)`, `atom_name = slice(12, 16)`, `atom_x = slice(30, 38)`, and so on through `atom_model = slice(78, 80)`. These sixteen slicers are collected in an ordered `atom_slicers` list, which serves two roles: it is the field vocabulary for reading (used by `populate_structure_array_from_pdb`, which strips each sliced substring into a NumPy array cell) and for writing (paired with `atom_line_formatter` and `atom_format_funcs`, which apply `int`/`float` casts per column).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph FILE["Raw PDB lines"]
        L1["ATOM   1234  CA  ALA A  12 ..."]
    end
    subgraph SLICE["atom_slicers - libpdb"]
        S0["atom_record 0:6"] --> S1["atom_serial 6:11"] --> S2["atom_name 12:16"] --> S3["altLoc 16:17"] --> S4["resName 17:20"] --> S5["chainID 21:22"] --> S6["resSeq 22:26"] --> S7["iCode 26:27"] --> S8["x/y/z 30:54"] --> S13["segid 72:76"] --> S14["element 76:78"] --> S15["model 78:80"]
    end
    subgraph ARR["Structure data array"]
        ROW["1 row per atom, 16 str columns, dtype U8"]
    end
    FILE --> SLICE --> ROW
```

Beyond reading, `libpdb` carries format-repair utilities that reflect real-world PDB messiness:

- **`format_atom_name`** re-aligns atom names into PDB columns using `_atom_format_dict`, keyed by *element length × atom-name length*. Notably, it deliberately raises a bare `KeyError` on unformattable input — an inline comment records the project convention that "pure Python exceptions are treated as bugs" and never handled by callers.
- **`format_chainid`** truncates a chain identifier to its first character, explicitly required because mmCIF chain IDs may exceed one letter.
- **`delete_insertions`** (adapted from pdb-tools) strips insertion codes and renumbers residues with an accumulating offset, tracking seen `(chain, resSeq)` pairs to catch both explicit icodes and duplicate numbering without them.
- **`RE_MODEL` / `RE_ENDMDL`** compiled regexes split NMR multi-model files — `Structure` documents that only the first `MODEL` is considered.

Sources: [libpdb.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libpdb.py#L133-L201), [libstructure.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libstructure.py#L492-L522), [libpdb.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libpdb.py#L88-L130), [libpdb.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libpdb.py#L40-L85), [libstructure.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libstructure.py#L32-L45)

## The mmCIF Parser: CIFParser as a PDB Field Façade

`libcif.CIFParser` is scoped tightly: it parses **only the `_atom_site.` loop**, ignoring every other mmCIF category. Construction is a three-step pipeline: `read_cif` splits the data string into lines, `find_cif_atom_site_headers` scans for lines starting with `_atom_site.` and initializes the dictionary with one empty list per label (raising `CIFFileError` if none exist), then `populate_cif_dictionary` streams consecutive data lines until a `#` sentinel or blank line — the blank-line tolerance deliberately handles files missing the trailing `#` at EOF (see the `cif_EOF.cif` test fixture). A field-count mismatch between the line and the registered headers aborts with a `CIFFileError` that reports the offending line repr and both indices.

Storage is **columnar**: `cif_dict` maps each label (`_atom_site.Cartn_x`, …) to a list of per-atom string values, and a cursor property `line` indexes into all columns simultaneously — `get_value(label)` is simply `cif_dict[label][self.line]`.

The parser's most important design decision is its **label-priority resolution**. mmCIF files may contain either `auth_*` or `label_*` namespaces; the constructor's `label_priority='auth'` (or `'label'`) selects the lookup order with graceful fallback via `KeyError` handling:

| PDB field | Primary label | Fallback / normalization |
|---|---|---|
| `record` | `_atom_site.group_PDB` | — |
| `serial` | `_atom_site.Id` | `_atom_site.id` |
| `atname` | `auth_atom_id` | `label_atom_id` |
| `altloc` | `auth_alt_id` | `label_alt_id`; translate void chars, `'1' → 'A'` |
| `resname` | `auth_comp_id` | `label_comp_id` |
| `chainid` | `auth_asym_id` (label) | literal `'?'`/`'.'` falls back to `_atom_site.auth_asym_id` |
| `resseq` | `auth_seq_id` (label) | void-char translation |
| `icode` | `pdbx_PDB_ins_code` | missing label → `' '` |
| `x/y/z` | `Cartn_x/y/z` | — |
| `tempfactor` | `B_iso_or_equiv` | — |
| `element` | `type_symbol` | — |
| `charge` | `pdbx_formal_charge` | void-char translation |

The terminal piece is `get_line_elements_for_PDB`, which emits the sixteen values in exact PDB column order (with `segid` hardcoded to `' '`), making the CIF parser a drop-in producer of PDB-shaped rows.

> [!TIP]
> The chain-ID resolution cascade in `CIFParser.chainid` — label/`auth` namespace choice, then `'?'/'.` sentinel fallback — exists because deposited mmCIF files inconsistently fill `label_asym_id` for author-designated chains. Any new CIF field you expose should follow the same two-tier `try/except KeyError` pattern rather than assuming a namespace.

Sources: [libcif.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcif.py#L8-L47), [libcif.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcif.py#L65-L116), [libcif.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcif.py#L121-L206), [libcif.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcif.py#L217-L319), [libcif.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcif.py#L298-L319)

## DSSP Orchestration: Parsing an External Tool's Output

Unlike PDB/mmCIF, DSSP output is never parsed from user-supplied files — `libdssp` **runs the `mkdssp` binary itself** and defends against its notorious version fragmentation. The module explicitly supports classic-format output from DSSP v2/v3 (cmbi) and v4 (PDB-REDO), and documents three incompatibilities it negotiates: invocation flags (`-i` vs `--output-format dssp`), PDB-read heuristics (v4 requires a leading `HEADER` record), and a libcifpp < 5.1.1 bug where a file lacking a trailing newline makes v4 hang and consume memory until killed.

The version-negotiation pipeline works as follows:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller (libparse/cli)
    participant L as libdssp.run_dssp
    participant V as get_dssp_version
    participant D as mkdssp binary
    C->>L: run_dssp(pdb_file, dssp_cmd)
    L->>V: mkdssp --version
    V-->>L: tuple e.g. (4, 6, 1) or None
    alt is_dssp4(version)
        L->>L: pdb_for_dssp4 context manager
        Note over L: temp copy with blank HEADER 80 cols + trailing newline if missing
        L->>D: mkdssp --output-format dssp tmp.pdb
    else v2/v3 or unknown
        L->>D: mkdssp -i pdb_file
    end
    D-->>L: stdout bytes
    L->>L: check_dssp_output - residue header present?
    Note over L: starts with data_ → mmCIF output error hint
    L-->>C: classic DSSP bytes
```

The parsing contract itself is minimal and positional, mirroring the PDB philosophy: the residue table is anchored by the exact header string `'  #  RESIDUE AA STRUCTURE'` (identical across v2/v3/v4), and secondary-structure codes are read at fixed **column 16** (`DSSP_SS_COLUMN`). Two defensive helpers complete the layer: `check_dssp_output` distinguishes "DSSP wrote mmCIF instead of classic format" (`data_` prefix) from a genuinely missing residue table, and `remove_native_ppii` resets v4's native polyproline-II `'P'` codes to loop so that PPII assignment stays consistent with the DSSP-PPII post-processor regardless of which DSSP major version ran.

Sources: [libdssp.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libdssp.py#L1-L48), [libdssp.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libdssp.py#L50-L138), [libdssp.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libdssp.py#L201-L278), [libdssp.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libdssp.py#L281-L399)

## Identifier Domain: PDBIDFactory → PDBID → PDBList

Structural files are keyed throughout the pipeline by a small value-object hierarchy. `PDBIDFactory` is a `__new__`-based factory that recognizes four identifier grammars — plain `XXXX`, `XXXXC*`, `XXXX_C*`, and `XXXX_C_seg<N>` (plus a catch-all for arbitrary `.pdb`/`.cif` stems) — via ordered regexes, returning existing `PDBID` instances unchanged and raising `PDBIDFactoryError` when no pattern matches. The resulting `PDBID` freezes a `name` (uppercased 4-char code) plus optional `chain`/`segment`, is hashable/equality-comparable on its string form, and sorts by that string.

`PDBList` aggregates these into a `set`, silently skipping `#`-commented lines, and provides `name_chains_dict` (PDB code → list of chains, the shape used by the downloader) and a `write()` method that round-trips identifiers back to `.list` files. This trio is what lets the same user-facing identifier string denote "a PDB entry", "a chain within an entry", or "a chain fragment" everywhere from the fetch CLI (see [CLI Subcommand System](17-cli-subcommand-system)) to the build step.

Sources: [libpdb.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libpdb.py#L223-L300), [libpdb.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libpdb.py#L404-L482), [libpdb.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libpdb.py#L304-L401)

## The I/O Layer: Bundles, Iterators, and Writers

`libio` is the logistics layer that feeds the parsers and carries their products away. On the read side, `read_path_bundle` resolves "path bundles" — a single file, a folder globbed recursively for an extension, or a `.list` file of paths (with `#` comments and blank lines filtered) — while `glob_folder` and `list_files_recursively` provide the underlying traversal primitives.

Iteration is dispatched by `FileReaderIterator`, another condition-keyed `options[True]` factory: origins ending in `.tar` become a `TarFileIterator` (streaming members by extension without extraction), lists become a `FileIterator`. Both yield uniform `(name, bytes)` pairs over a shared `FileIteratorBase` supporting `len()`, slicing, and boolean truthiness — the uniform contract that lets multiprocessing workers consume files from folders or archives identically (see [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture)).

| Component | Trigger | Yields / writes |
|---|---|---|
| `FileReaderIterator` | dispatch on origin type | delegates below |
| `FileIterator` | `list` of paths | `(Path, bytes)` per file |
| `TarFileIterator` | origin endswith `.tar` | `(member name, bytes)` per matching member |
| `read_path_bundle` | str/Path bundle | iterable of Paths (folder / file / `.list`) |
| `paths_from_flist` | `.list` file | Paths, `#` comments removed |
| `save_pairs_to_disk` | destination suffix | dispatches to tar or files |
| `save_pairs_to_tar` | `.tar` destination | appends (`a:`) if tar exists, else creates |
| `save_pairs_to_files` | otherwise | writes each `(name, data)` pair into a folder |

On the write side, `save_pairs_to_disk` dispatches on the destination's suffix to either `save_pairs_to_files` (one file per pair, `write_text` with a `write_bytes` fallback) or `save_pairs_to_tar`, the latter using `save_file_to_tar` with an in-memory `BytesIO` so string or byte payloads stream into archives without touching disk. This pair-of-pairs convention (`(file name, data content)`) is the same shape the iterators produce — reads and writes mirror each other.

Sources: [libio.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libio.py#L290-L349), [libio.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libio.py#L152-L229), [libio.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libio.py#L718-L819), [libio.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libio.py#L622-L715)

## Unified In-Memory Model and Exception Taxonomy

`Structure` ties the layers together. After construction and an explicit `.build()`, all atoms live in a NumPy array of shape `(n_atoms, 16)` with `dtype='<U8'` — allocated via `_empty_data_array`, populated column-by-column from PDB slicers or the CIF façade. Filtering is compositional: `add_filter_chain('A')` registers a predicate, arbitrary lambdas can key on column constants (`col_resSeq`, `cols_coords`), and `filtered_atoms` folds every registered filter over the array with `functools.reduce`. Convenience views include `chain_set`, `coords` (cast to `float32`), and `write_PDB` for re-serializing selections.

| Exception | Raised by | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| `ParserNotFoundError` | `detect_structure_type` | no `(predicate, parser)` matches the data string |
| `NotImplementedError` | `get_datastr` | input is not `Path`/`bytes`/`str` |
| `CIFFileError` | `find_cif_atom_site_headers` / `populate_cif_dictionary` | no `_atom_site.` headers, or line field-count mismatch |
| `PDBIDFactoryError` | `PDBIDFactory` | identifier matches no recognized grammar |
| `DSSPExecutionError` | `_run` / `run_dssp` | `mkdssp` missing, non-zero exit, or killed by signal |
| `DSSPParserError` | `check_dssp_output` | residue table header absent from DSSP output |
| `NotBuiltError` | `Structure.data_array` | property accessed before `.build()` |

Every parser also ships with dedicated test modules — `test_libcif.py`, `test_libpdb.py`, `test_structure.py`, `test_libdssp.py`, `test_libio.py`, `test_libparse.py` — exercising fixtures such as `cif_example_auth.cif`, `cif_no_atom_site.cif`, `wrong.dssp`, and `1BTE_A_dssp4.dssp` that encode each failure mode above (the testing approach is covered in [Testing Strategy & Fixtures](22-testing-strategy-and-fixtures)).

Sources: [libstructure.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libstructure.py#L32-L150), [libstructure.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libstructure.py#L380-L388), [libcif.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libcif.py#L217-L319), [libdssp.py](/src/idpconfgen/libs/libdssp.py#L281-L308)

## Where the Parsers Plug Into the Engine

To close the loop: the `pdbdl`/`fetch` subcommands persist downloads as `(PDBID-chain, bytes)` pairs via `save_pairs_to_disk`, the search/filter stages stream those bundles through `FileReaderIterator` and the DSSP orchestrator, and the conformer builder consumes `Structure` data arrays whose 16 columns match `atom_slicers` exactly. FASTA validation (`is_valid_fasta` on the uppercase one-letter alphabet) and secondary-structure run detection (`group_by` producing `[label, slice]` runs) extend the same parse-normalize-model pattern to non-coordinate formats. For how these arrays drive torsion sampling and assembly, continue with [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble); for the residue/atom dictionaries underpinning the component library that the CIF parser's field façade feeds, see [Component Plugin Pattern](20-component-plugin-pattern) and [Build Definitions Reference](21-build-definitions-reference).


# Component Plugin Pattern



The `idpconfgen.components` package is the library's pluggability layer: a collection of self-contained strategy modules that the building engine selects at runtime through small, declarative registries. Instead of hard-coding algorithm choices into the builder, the codebase isolates each alternative implementation — four bond-geometry strategies, two sidechain-packing algorithms, residue-tolerance policies, fragment-probability profiles — behind a uniform interface of `name` tokens, `init_*` factory functions, and `add_*` CLI argument factories. This page dissects that pattern: the registries that enumerate plugins, the interface contract each plugin must honor, how optional heavy dependencies are quarantined, and how parameters flow from the command line to the selected plugin. For the numerical behavior of the strategies themselves, see [Bond Geometry Strategies](8-bond-geometry-strategies) and [Sidechain Packing Methods](11-sidechain-packing-methods).

Sources: [components/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/__init__.py#L1-L2), [sidechain_packing/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L1-L15)

## Architecture at a Glance

The package follows a two-layer split: **registry modules** (`__init__.py` files that enumerate choices and build CLI arguments) and **plugin modules** (the actual algorithm implementations). The CLI entry point `cli_build.py` never imports plugin internals directly for selection purposes — it imports the registries, derives argument choices from them, and later consults the registry to resolve the user's string choice into an executable object. This keeps the set of valid options defined in exactly one place per plugin family.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph CLI["Consumer Layer — cli_build.py"]
        AP["Argument Parser<br/>add_bgeo_strategy_arg / add_sidechain_method"]
        MAIN["main() dispatcher"]
        GLOB["populate_globals()"]
    end

    subgraph REG["Registry Layer"]
        BGEO["bgeo_strategies/__init__<br/>tuple: (fixed, sampling, exact, int2cart)"]
        SC["sidechain_packing/__init__<br/>dict: {faspr: init_faspr_sidechains,<br/>mcsce: init_mcsce_sidechains}"]
    end

    subgraph PLUG["Plugin Implementations"]
        F["fixed<br/>get_cycle_bend_angles()"]
        S["sampling<br/>bgeo_sampling.tar"]
        E["exact<br/>name token only"]
        I["int2cart<br/>has_int2cart guard"]
        FA["faspr.py<br/>→ idpcpp C++ kernel"]
        MC["mcsce.py<br/>→ external mcsce pkg"]
    end

    AP --> BGEO
    AP --> SC
    MAIN -->|"branch on name"| BGEO
    MAIN -->|"prefix-strip kwargs"| SC
    GLOB -->|"resolve name → object"| BGEO
    BGEO --> F & S & E & I
    SC --> FA & MC
```

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L25-L46), [bgeo_strategies/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py#L8-L28), [sidechain_packing/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L18-L23)

## Two Registry Disciplines

The codebase uses two complementary registry styles, each matched to the shape of the plugin family. **Bond-geometry strategies** are registered as a tuple of string identity tokens — each plugin module defines a module-level `name` attribute, and the registry aggregates them (`bgeo_strategies = (fixed, sampling, exact, int2cart)`) together with a default (`sampling`). Because the values are plain strings, they feed directly into `argparse`'s `choices` parameter. **Sidechain-packing methods** are registered as a dictionary mapping name strings to their `init_*` factory functions (`{'faspr': init_faspr_sidechains, 'mcsce': init_mcsce_sidechains}`), so the registry is not just an enumeration but the dispatch table itself — the selected value *is* the callable.

Sources: [bgeo_strategies/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py#L10-L28), [sidechain_packing/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L18-L27)

| Registry | Data structure | Entries | CLI flag | Default | Dispatch style |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bgeo_strategies` | tuple of `name` tokens | `fixed`, `sampling`, `exact`, `int2cart` | `--bgeo-strategy` | `sampling` | Consumer branches on name (`are_globals`, `main`) |
| `sidechain_packing_methods` | dict: name → `init_*` callable | `faspr`, `mcsce` | `-scm` / `--sidechainmethod` | `faspr` | Direct dict lookup yields the factory |

Sources: [bgeo_strategies/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py#L8-L76), [sidechain_packing/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L18-L36)

## The Sidechain Contract: Uniform Factories with `**ignore`

The `sidechain_packing` package docstring states the contract explicitly: all sidechain-computing functions must output the same types and share a compatible input API, returning an array mask for `all_atom_coords` plus coordinates compatible with that mask. Both plugins satisfy this with an identical factory signature — `init_faspr_sidechains(input_seq, template_masks, all_atom_masks, **ignore)` and `init_mcsce_sidechains(input_seq, template_masks, all_atom_masks, user_parameters=None, **ignore)`. The `**ignore` catch-all is the linchpin of the whole pattern: the caller may pass its full parameter dictionary to any plugin, and each plugin silently discards the keys it does not recognize. This decouples parameter plumbing from plugin selection — adding a plugin never forces changes to the call site.

The factories are **closure builders**: calling `init_*` binds the sequence, masks, and bundled data files into a returned function (`compute_faspr_sidechains(coords)`) that is later invoked inside multiprocessing workers. FASPR additionally defers its `import idpcpp` (the C++ extension) to inside the factory body — a deliberate laziness noted in the source as avoiding problems under `tox`. MCSCE similarly imports the external `mcsce` package inside its factory, and merges user parameters over its `mcsce_defaults` table before constructing the side-chain builder.

Sources: [sidechain_packing/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L1-L15), [faspr.py](src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/faspr.py#L16-L65), [mcsce.py](src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L45-L130)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as main() cli_build
    participant R as sidechain_packing registry
    participant P as init_faspr_sidechains()
    participant W as Worker process

    M->>R: get_sidechain_packing_parameters(kwargs, "faspr")
    R-->>M: prefix-stripped plugin params
    M->>P: init_sidechains(seq, template_masks, all_atom_masks, **params)
    Note over P: binds sequence, masks, dun2010bbdep.bin; lazily imports idpcpp
    P-->>M: closure compute_faspr_sidechains(coords)
    M->>W: closure distributed via multiprocessing globals
    W->>P: closure(bb4_coords)
    P-->>W: (non_Hs_non_OXT mask, packed sidechain coords)
```

Sources: [faspr.py](src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/faspr.py#L35-L64), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L651-L653)

> [!TIP]
> The plugin-specific CLI flags are namespaced by prefix (`--mcsce-mode`, `--mcsce-n_trials`) and `get_sidechain_packing_parameters()` recovers them at runtime by splitting on `_` and stripping the leading mode name. The prefix convention is the contract — a plugin author must keep flag prefixes synchronized with the registry key, since parameter routing depends on it.

## Optional Dependencies: Import-Time Feature Flags

The `int2cart` strategy depends on a heavyweight external stack (`torch`, `yaml`, and the `modelling` package). Rather than making that a hard import, the plugin wraps the imports in a `try/except ImportError` block that sets a boolean capability flag, `has_int2cart`. The consequence is architectural: the *entire* components package imports successfully even when Int2Cart is absent, and the dependency failure is deferred to two controlled surfacing points — the `BGEO_Int2Cart` constructor raises a descriptive `ImportError` if instantiated, and the CLI layer rejects the choice at argument-parsing time (below). No build code path ever reaches an unhandled `ModuleNotFoundError`.

Sources: [bgeo_int2cart.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/int2cart/bgeo_int2cart.py#L8-L24), [bgeo_int2cart.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/int2cart/bgeo_int2cart.py#L30-L41)

## CLI Integration: Registries as Argument Factories

Each component ships its own `add_*` function that attaches its options to a parser, so the consumer's parser-construction code stays a flat list of one-line registrations. The bond-geometry registry goes further: `add_bgeo_strategy_arg` passes a custom `argparse.Action`, `CheckBgeoInstallation`, as the argument's `action`. Because argparse invokes the action during parsing, an `--bgeo-strategy int2cart` selection on a machine without Int2Cart fails immediately with a parser error pointing to the installation docs — validation happens *before* any expensive setup, not deep inside the build. The other components reuse the same idea with their own actions: `EDSS50_indexes` converts matrix column indexes into a substitution dictionary at parse time, and `XmerProbsAction` reads and validates the fragment-probability file, translating each failure mode (`ValueError`, `FileNotFoundError`, `IsADirectoryError`) into a specific parser error.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["--bgeo-strategy int2cart"] --> B{"CheckBgeoInstallation.__call__"}
    B -->|has_int2cart = True| C["namespace.bgeo_strategy = 'int2cart'"]
    B -->|has_int2cart = False| D["parser.error: install Int2Cart first"]
    E["-edss50 5 3 2"] --> F["EDSS50_indexes action"] --> G["namespace.residue_tolerance = subs dict"]
    H["-xp probs.txt"] --> I["XmerProbsAction"] --> J["namespace: XmerProbs namedtuple"]
```

Sources: [bgeo_strategies/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py#L36-L70), [residue_tolerance.py](src/idpconfgen/components/residue_tolerance.py#L37-L60), [residue_tolerance.py](src/idpconfgen/components/residue_tolerance.py#L98-L113), [xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L62-L79)

A second, quieter idiom is the **partial-applied argument factory**: `energy_threshold_type.py` builds `add_et_type_arg` by applying `vartial` (the library's argument-adding variant of `functools.partial`) to `libcli.add_general_arg`, pre-binding flag names, help text, choices, and destination into a reusable callable. The `xmer_probs` module composes the same functional toolkit (`ITEX`, `chainf`, `vartial`) into `prepare_xmer_probs`, a small pipeline that accepts either a parsed `XmerProbs` object or a file path and falls back to logged defaults. These factories mean the `build` CLI's parser block reads as declarative configuration rather than imperative wiring.

Sources: [energy_threshold_type.py](src/idpconfgen/components/energy_threshold_type.py#L21-L32), [xmer_probs.py](src/idpconfgen/components/xmer_probs.py#L82-L135), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L285-L310)

## Dispatch Sites in the Consumer

`cli_build.py` resolves plugin selections at three verified points. First, `main()` accepts the strategy strings (`bgeo_strategy=bgeo_strategies_default`, `sidechain_method=DEFAULT_SDM`) as ordinary keyword parameters, so the library API and the CLI share one entry point. Second, strategy-dependent global-state requirements are expressed as `are_globals(bgeo_strategy)`, which branches on the name token — `sampling` requires the BGEO dictionaries, `int2cart` additionally requires the loaded `INT2CART` object, while `exact` and `fixed` need only the mask/label globals. Third, the sidechain parameters are extracted from the shared `**kwargs` pool via `get_sidechain_packing_parameters(kwargs, sidechain_method)` and passed forward into the multiprocessing partial. Branching on the *exact* strategy (line 619) also selects a different database-alignment mode, since exact-geometry databases carry a different schema.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L439-L464), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L180-L220), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L619-L635), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L651-L653)

| Plugin (bgeo) | `name` token | Bundled asset | Runtime dependency | Distinctive API |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fixed | `"fixed"` | bend angles from `core.build_definitions` | none | `get_cycle_bend_angles()` infinite iterator |
| sampling | `"sampling"` | `bgeo_sampling.tar` | none | `bgeo_sampling_path` constant |
| exact | `"exact"` | none (user-supplied `bgeodb` database) | none | name token only; drives alternate DB schema |
| int2cart | `"int2cart"` | `int2cart.yml`, `model.tar` | `torch`, `yaml`, `modelling` | `BGEO_Int2Cart.get_internal_coords()` |

Sources: [exact/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/exact/__init__.py#L1-L4), [fixed/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/fixed/__init__.py#L1-L22), [sampling/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/sampling/__init__.py#L1-L12), [bgeo_int2cart.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/int2cart/bgeo_int2cart.py#L42-L62)

## Trade-Off Analysis

The pattern optimizes for *swappability and packaging safety* over exhaustive abstraction. Every strategy module is imported eagerly when the registry package loads — the cost is trivial for the three lightweight strategies, and the feature-flag idiom neutralizes the risk for the heavyweight one. String-name registries mean the CLI help text, the defaults, and the dispatch logic all derive from one tuple/dict, at the cost of deferring typo detection to parse-time `choices` checking or the `AssertionError` guard in `are_globals`.

| Design aspect | Benefit | Cost / constraint |
|---|---|---|
| String `name` tokens in a tuple | CLI `choices`, defaults, and errors generated from one source | Strategy-specific behavior requires `if/elif` at consumer dispatch points |
| Dict registry of `init_*` factories | Selection and invocation collapsed into one lookup | Every plugin must keep the uniform factory signature |
| `**ignore` catch-all parameters | Call site is plugin-agnostic; adding plugins needs no caller changes | Wrong parameter names fail silently — flags are absorbed rather than rejected |
| Import-time `has_int2cart` flag | Package imports cleanly without optional dependencies | Two validation layers (flag + custom Action) must be maintained together |
| Prefixed CLI flags (`--mcsce-*`) | Per-plugin options live in the shared parser without collisions | Prefix ↔ registry-key coupling is convention, not enforced |

Sources: [bgeo_strategies/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/__init__.py#L72-L76), [sidechain_packing/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/__init__.py#L38-L58), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L219-L220)

## Adding a New Plugin

Extending a plugin family is a five-step, locally-scoped change — no modification of the building engine's core logic is required for the registry side.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["1. Create plugin module/subpackage<br/>define name token or init_* factory"] --> B["2. Honor the interface contract<br/>uniform signature + **ignore catch-all"]
    B --> C{"Optional heavy dependency?"}
    C -->|Yes| D["Wrap imports in try/except<br/>export has_* flag"]
    C -->|No| E["Import normally at module level"]
    D --> F["3. Register in family __init__<br/>append to tuple / add dict entry"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["4. Add prefixed CLI options<br/>via add_*_subparser if configurable"]
    G --> H["5. Update consumer branching<br/>are_globals() and dispatch sites in cli_build"]
```

For a bond-geometry plugin, the minimal registration is one `name` attribute plus one import-and-append in the registry — as `exact/__init__.py` demonstrates, a plugin can be as small as an identity token that only alters consumer branching. For a sidechain plugin, the plugin author implements `init_<name>_sidechains` with the standard signature, registers it in `sidechain_packing_methods`, and optionally contributes a subparser group with prefixed flags so `get_sidechain_packing_parameters` can route them. The public API documentation pages are generated directly from these modules via Sphinx `automodule` directives, so docstrings on `init_*` functions become the plugin's documentation.

Sources: [exact/__init__.py](src/idpconfgen/components/bgeo_strategies/exact/__init__.py#L1-L4), [mcsce.py](src/idpconfgen/components/sidechain_packing/mcsce.py#L19-L43), [component_sidechain.rst](docs/reference/component_sidechain.rst#L1-L19), [component_res_tol.rst](docs/reference/component_res_tol.rst#L1-L8)

> [!TIP]
> Notice that `residue_tolerance.py` and `xmer_probs.py` are not strategy registries at all — they are **parameter components**: modules that own a domain concept (substitution matrices, fragment-size distributions) together with the CLI machinery to parse it into a runtime object. The `components` package therefore generalizes "plugin" to "any swappable building decision with its parsing logic co-located."

## Where to Go Next

The plugin layer is the seam between user-facing choices and the building engine. To see how the selected strategies execute inside the ensemble loop, continue to [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble); for the mathematics each geometry strategy feeds into, see [Coordinate Geometry & Quaternion Math](7-coordinate-geometry-and-quaternion-math) and [Bond Geometry Strategies](8-bond-geometry-strategies). The sidechain plugins' algorithms are detailed in [Sidechain Packing Methods](11-sidechain-packing-methods), their C++ kernel in [C++ Extension & Numba Kernels](13-c-extension-and-numba-kernels), and the regression tests guarding the contracts live in `tests/test_component_sidechain_packing.py` and `tests/test_component_residue_tolerance.py`, discussed in [Testing Strategy & Fixtures](22-testing-strategy-and-fixtures). For how these component arguments surface as subcommands in the CLI framework, see [CLI Subcommand System](17-cli-subcommand-system).


# Build Definitions Reference



Every conformer IDPConformerGenerator produces is assembled from a fixed set of molecular facts: which atoms belong to each residue, how those atoms are covalently connected, what charges they carry, and what bond lengths and bend angles the backbone should adopt. This page is the canonical reference for **where those facts live and how they flow into the building engine**. It covers the two sibling modules in `src/idpconfgen/core/` — `definitions.py` and `build_definitions.py` — plus the data assets they parse at load time, and the validation contract that keeps them consistent.

The scope boundary matters: this page documents the *definitions themselves* (data structures, schemas, provenance, and extension points). For how these constants drive sampling, see [Bond Geometry Strategies](8-bond-geometry-strategies) and [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling); for how they are consumed during execution, see [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble).

Sources: [definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/definitions.py#L1-L9), [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L1-L16)

## Two Modules, One Contract

The core package splits its responsibilities deliberately. **`definitions.py`** declares itself as *"static definitions that serve the whole program infrastructure"* — it imports nothing beyond the standard library and can be safely imported by any module (including parsers that must avoid circular imports). **`build_definitions.py`** is the heavier sibling: it imports `numpy` and `scipy`, parses an XML force field, and reads residue template PDB files, because everything it defines is *specifically for the building process*. This separation lets lightweight modules (parsers, CLI plumbing, filters) access residue vocabulary without paying the parsing cost.

Sources: [definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/definitions.py#L1-L9), [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L1-L16)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph assets["Raw Assets in core/"]
        XML["data/protein.ff14SB.xml"]
        PDB["sidechain_templates/pdb_names/*.pdb"]
        AMB["sidechain_templates/amber_names/*.pdb"]
        TXT["chem_comp_*.txt<br/>discarded_ids.txt"]
    end

    subgraph static["definitions.py — static vocabulary"]
        AA["aa3to1 / aa1to3"]
        BGEO["bgeo_* lookup keys"]
        DSSP["dssp_ss_keys + trans tables"]
        VDW["vdW radii sets"]
        LIG["pdb_ligand_codes / blocked_ids"]
    end

    subgraph builder["build_definitions.py — builder parameters"]
        NAMES["atom_names_pdb / atom_names_amber"]
        FF["read_ff14SB_params()"]
        TOP["generate_residue_template_topology()"]
        EXP["3-bonds / ≤N-bonds expansions"]
        GEO["bend + distance constants"]
        SCT["sidechain_templates + termini H"]
        REG["forcefields registry<br/>(Amber14SBForceField)"]
    end

    subgraph engine["Build engine"]
        CLI["cli_build.py"]
        COMP["components/* strategies"]
    end

    TXT --> LIG
    XML --> FF
    PDB --> NAMES
    AMB --> NAMES
    PDB --> SCT
    AA --> NAMES
    FF --> REG
    NAMES --> REG
    TOP --> EXP --> REG
    REG --> CLI
    SCT --> CLI
    GEO --> CLI
    CLI --> COMP
```

At runtime, `cli_build.py` imports exactly the pieces it needs: `backbone_atoms`, the terminal bend/length constants (`build_bend_CA_C_O`, `build_bend_H_N_C`, `distance_C_O`, `distance_H_N`), the `forcefields` registry, both N-terminal hydrogen coordinate arrays, and `sidechain_templates` — alongside the DSSP key vocabulary and the pluggable strategy components.

Sources: [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L23-L59)

## The Static Vocabulary: `core/definitions.py`

### Residue Code Maps

The `aa3to1` dictionary holds **25 entries**: the 20 canonical amino acids, three histidine protonation states (`HIP` → `'p'`, `HIE` → `'e'`, `HID` → `'d'`), and two phosphorylated residues (`SEP` → `'s'`, `TPO` → `'t'`). The convention is deliberate: **lowercase 1-letter codes mark modified or protonation variants**, so they can never collide with canonical uppercase codes during sequence handling. `aa1to3` is generated by inverting `aa3to1`, and `aa1set`/`aa3set` expose membership sets for fast validation. The test suite pins the dictionary length at 23 after temporarily removing the phosphorylated pair, with an explicit TODO acknowledging the full count should be 25 given PTM support.

| 3-letter | 1-letter | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `HIS` | `H` | Standard histidine |
| `HID` | `d` | δ-protonated histidine |
| `HIE` | `e` | ε-protonated histidine |
| `HIP` | `p` | Doubly protonated histidine |
| `SEP` | `s` | Phosphorylated serine |
| `TPO` | `t` | Phosphorylated threonine |

Sources: [definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/definitions.py#L26-L57), [test_definitions.py](tests/test_definitions.py#L16-L21)

### Bond Geometry Lookup Keys

Eight string constants define the canonical identifiers under which torsion and bend data are stored in the k-mer libraries: `bgeo_Cm1NCa` (`'Cm1_N_Ca'`), `bgeo_NCaC` (`'N_Ca_C'`), `bgeo_CaCNp1` (`'Ca_C_Np1'`), and `bgeo_CaCO` (`'Ca_C_O'`) for the three backbone bends plus the carbonyl bend, and `bgeo_NCa`, `bgeo_CaC`, `bgeo_CNp1`, `bgeo_CO` for the four backbone bond lengths. The naming convention encodes residue-relative positions — `m1` means the previous residue's C, `p1` means the next residue's N — which is exactly the vocabulary the strategy components match against when sampling.

Sources: [definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/definitions.py#L12-L22), [cli_build.py](src/idpconfgen/cli_build.py#L23-L33)

### Secondary Structure Vocabulary

The `dssp_ss_keys` namespace maps all eight standard DSSP one-character codes (`H`, `G`, `I`, `B`, `E`, `T`, `S`, ` `) plus a custom `P` for polyproline-II. Aggregate tuples (`all_helix`, `all_strand`, `all_loops`, `all`, `valid`) encode deliberate classification decisions documented inline: the 3₁₀ helix (`I`) and PPII (`P`) are treated as **loop-class** states following Balasco et al. 2017 and Mansiaux et al. 2011, and β-bridge (`B`) breaks convention by joining the loops group. Two translation tables — `dssp_trans` for `str` and `dssp_trans_bytes` for `bytes` — collapse the 8-state vocabulary into the 3-state `H`/`E`/`L` scheme the builder actually consumes.

Sources: [definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/definitions.py#L145-L209)

### Physical Radii and Filtering Lists

Three van der Waals radius sets are provided — **Tsai 1999** (the default), **Bondi 1964**, and **CRC82 ionic** (for metals/halogens at coordination number 6) — unified under the `vdW_radii_dict` mapping. Alongside them, `pdb_ligand_codes` is loaded lazily from `chem_comp_parsed.txt` and `chem_comp_added.txt` (comment lines starting with `#` skipped), and `blocked_ids` from `discarded_ids.txt`; these lists feed structure filtering and download sanitation. Two small but critical collections round out the vocabulary: `residue_elements` (the elements legal inside a residue) and `minimal_bb_atoms` (`['N', 'CA', 'C']`, with a comment stressing it is *ordered* — a constraint the internal-coordinate builder depends on).

Sources: [definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/definitions.py#L59-L134), [definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/definitions.py#L212-L235)

## The Builder Layer: `core/build_definitions.py`

### Atom Label Dictionaries

At import time, `_read_labels()` walks each residue template PDB in `sidechain_templates/pdb_names/` and `sidechain_templates/amber_names/`, extracts the atom-name column via `libstructure.Structure`, and registers the resulting tuple **under both the 3-letter and 1-letter code keys** — an intentional duplication to avoid a double dictionary lookup in hot loops. This produces the module-level `atom_names_pdb` and `atom_names_amber` dictionaries. The two vocabularies must stay in lockstep: a dedicated test asserts every residue has the *same number of atoms* in both naming schemes.

Sources: [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L32-L52), [test_build_definitions.py](tests/test_build_definitions.py#L129-L136)

### Amber ff14SB Force-Field Parameters

`read_ff14SB_params()` parses `data/protein.ff14SB.xml` (an OpenMM-format force field bundled in `core/data/`) into a single flat dictionary of **114 top-level keys**. The schema has three shapes, produced by the three XML branches:

| Key pattern | Value schema | XML source tag |
|---|---|---|
| `protein-<TYPE>` (atom types) | `{class, element, epsilon, mass, sigma}` | `AtomTypes` |
| `<RESIDUE>` (e.g., `VAL`) | `{<atom name>: {charge, type}, ...}` | `Residues/Atom` |
| `coulomb14scale`, `lj14scale` | Global scale factors | `NonbondedForce` |

The docstring walks through concrete examples — atom type `'protein-OH'` carries its class/element/Lennard-Jones parameters, while residue `'VAL'` maps each atom name to its partial charge and its force-field type string. Every atom-level `type` value must itself resolve to a `protein-*` key in the same dictionary; a test enforces this closure so no dangling references survive.

Sources: [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L55-L133), [test_build_definitions.py](tests/test_build_definitions.py#L18-L45), [test_build_definitions.py](tests/test_build_definitions.py#L94-L104)

### Residue Template Topology

`generate_residue_template_topology()` builds each residue's covalent connectivity **geometrically**: it computes an all-vs-all `pdist` over template coordinates and marks every pair within **1.6 Å** as bonded, then stores the result symmetrically (if A bonds B, both directions are recorded). Two consequences follow. First, an assertion requires the template's atom-name ordering to match the `atom_names` dictionary exactly — the two data sources are coupled by position. Second, distance-threshold inference is *not* sufficient for sulfur chemistry: the ~1.8 Å C–S bonds fall outside the cutoff, so **CYS and MET connectivity is patched explicitly** after the loop (`CB–SG–HG` and `CG–SD–CE`).

Two helper functions then extend connectivity to cover termini: `add_OXT_to_connectivity()` clones the carbonyl oxygen's neighborhood onto OXT, and `add_Nterm_H_connectivity()` wires `H1`, `H2`, `H3` onto the N-terminal nitrogen — explicitly noted as maintaining "compatibility with XML forcefields obtained from the OpenMM project."

> [!TIP]
> When adding a residue template with any bond longer than 1.6 Å (disulfides, metal coordination, thioethers), the distance-based inference will silently miss it — you must add an explicit patch in `generate_residue_template_topology` following the CYS/MET pattern, or the energy computations built on this topology will under-count bonded exclusions.

Sources: [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L136-L219), [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L222-L243)

### n-Bonds-Apart Expansions

Force-field bookkeeping rarely wants raw bonds; it wants neighborhoods. The module provides three generators for these expanded views:

| Function | Semantics | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| `expand_topology_bonds_apart()` | Atoms **≤ N bonds away** (recursive BFS-style expansion) | build_definitions.py#L293 |
| `topology_3_bonds_apart()` | Atoms **exactly 3 bonds away** — the 1–4 pair set, per the Amber20 manual Figure 14.1 | build_definitions.py#L347 |
| `inter_residue_connectivities` | Static hand-computed tables `{2: bonds_le_2_inter, 3: bonds_le_3_inter}` for the **inter-residue** peptide bond neighborhood | build_definitions.py#L525 |

The inter-residue tables are written out by hand rather than computed — `bonds_equal_3_inter`, for example, states that a previous residue's `C` sees exactly `HA/HA2/HA3/CB/C` of the next residue three bonds away. A source comment notes the authors prioritized "readability and sanity check instead of speed" for this small dataset — the expansion functions carry their own internal assertions instead of micro-optimizing.

Sources: [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L246-L344), [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L347-L436), [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L525-L529)

### The Force-Field Registry and Singleton

`Amber14SBForceField` packages the whole builder layer into one object with `__slots__` (`atom_names`, `bonds_eq3_intra`, `bonds_le2_intra`, `forcefield`, `res_topology`). Its `__new__` implements a **singleton pattern**: the first instantiation eagerly runs `read_ff14SB_params()`, `generate_residue_template_topology()`, and both n-bonds expansions; every subsequent call returns the cached instance. The class is exposed through a registry dictionary — `forcefields = {'Amberff14SB': Amber14SBForceField}` — which is the extension seam `cli_build.py` consumes; a second force field would simply add another entry.

Sources: [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L460-L511)

> [!TIP]
> The singleton is per-*process*, not per-machine. Under the multiprocessing architecture each worker process re-executes the XML parse, template reads, and topology expansion on first build — so import-time cost is paid once per worker, and any mutation of a force-field object mid-run stays local to that worker's cache.

## Backbone Geometry Constants

The builder's fixed geometry comes from a statistical survey of the **Dunbrack PISCES** non-redundant set (`cullpdb_pc90_res1.6_R0.25_d200611_chains8807`), computed **per residue type** rather than as single averages. The historical single-average constants survive only as a commented reference block in `definitions.py`; the live values are the per-residue dictionaries in `build_definitions.py`. A distinctive implementation detail: every value is stored as a **ratio of integers** (e.g., `6579089706805643 / 4503599627370496`), with the decimal equivalent and standard deviation in a trailing comment — this guarantees bit-exact float representation, per the Python documentation on floating-point that the source cites.

The build pipeline needs *pi-corrected* versions of the bends: each measured angle is converted via `(pi − angle) / 2` into the `build_bend_angles_*` dictionaries, because the internal-coordinate placement algorithm positions atoms on cones defined by half-angles (see [Coordinate Geometry & Quaternion Math](7-coordinate-geometry-and-quaternion-math)).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["PISCES cull statistics<br/>(per-residue means)"] --> B["bend_angles_*<br/>measured radians"]
    B -->|"(pi − v) / 2"| C["build_bend_angles_*<br/>pi-corrected half-angles"]
    C --> D["Internal-coordinate placement<br/>(Z-matrix + quaternion)"]
    A --> E["distances_* + mean/stdev<br/>bond lengths in Å"]
    E --> D
```

| Constant group | Meaning | Representative value (± std) |
|---|---|---|
| `bend_angles_N_CA_C` | N–CA–C bend | ≈ 1.94 rad (±0.04) |
| `bend_angles_CA_C_Np1` | CA–C–N(+1) bend | ≈ 2.04 rad (±0.02) |
| `bend_angles_Cm1_N_CA` | C(−1)–N–CA bend | ≈ 2.12 rad (±0.03) |
| `distances_N_CA` (+ `average_`/`std_`) | N–CA bond | ≈ 1.460 Å (±0.012) |
| `distances_CA_C` (+ `average_`/`std_`) | CA–C bond | ≈ 1.524 Å (±0.012) |
| `distances_C_Np1` (+ `average_`/`std_`) | C–N(+1) peptide bond | ≈ 1.331 Å (±0.010) |
| `distance_C_O` / `distance_C_OXT` | Carbonyl / C-terminus OXT | ≈ 1.234 Å / 1.27 Å |
| `distance_H_N`, `build_bend_H_N_C` | Amide H–N | 0.9 Å, bend 114° |

The C-terminal carbonyl entries are scalar constants rather than per-residue dicts: `build_bend_CA_C_OXT = (pi − 2π/3)/2`, `build_bend_CA_C_O = 2.102/2`. The per-residue means and standard deviations for bond lengths are recomputed at import time with `statistics.mean`/`stdev`, so `average_distance_N_CA` always stays consistent with the underlying table.

Sources: [definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/definitions.py#L237-L266), [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L531-L618), [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L620-L706)

## Sidechain Templates and Termini Coordinates

The `sidechain_templates` dictionary maps each residue to a tuple of `(all-atom coordinates, sidechain index array)`, built by filtering each template against the `backbone_atoms` tuple — `('N', 'C', 'CA', 'O', 'OXT', 'H', 'H1', 'H2', 'H3')` — so the builder receives *only* sidechain atoms, pre-extracted and ready for placement. The template PDB files themselves were **pre-rotated 1 radian around the z-axis** (documented in the templates' README, with the transformation script included): the original Head-Gordon templates had N along −x with CA at the origin, which would collide with the builder's own frame of N at origin, CA on the x-axis.

Terminal hydrogens get their own literal coordinate arrays. `n_terminal_h_coords_at_origin` (six atoms, including a CA-position anchor) was generated with Chimera-X given a CA-terminal at `0,0,0`; `n_proline_h_coord_at_origin` (five atoms) handles the special N-terminal proline geometry and was produced from the Amber templates with `pdb4amber --dry --reduce`. Because proline's cyclic imino nitrogen carries only one backbone hydrogen, its template row count differs by exactly one — a detail the builder exploits when dressing chain termini.

Sources: [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L24-L24), [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L709-L748), [README](src/idpconfgen/core/sidechain_templates/README#L1-L3)

## The Validation Contract

`tests/test_build_definitions.py` acts as a machine-checked specification of everything above — a pattern examined further in [Testing Strategy & Fixtures](22-testing-strategy-and-fixtures). The contract's key clauses:

| Test | Invariant enforced |
|---|---|
| `test_ff14SB_params_length` | Exactly 114 top-level force-field keys |
| `test_ff14SB_params_atom_keys` | Atom types carry exactly `{mass, element, class, sigma, epsilon}` |
| `test_ff14SB_coloumb` / `test_ff14SB_lj` | Global `coulomb14scale` / `lj14scale` present |
| `test_ff14SB_has_all_residues` | Every residue in `aa3to1` (minus HIS/SEP/TPO, temporarily) exists in the force field |
| `test_ff14SB_atoms_have_params` | Residue atoms carry exactly `{charge, type}` |
| `test_all_atoms_are_mapped` | Every atom `type` resolves inside the force-field dictionary |
| `test_aa_translate_dict_with_atom_labels` | Both `atom_names_pdb` and `atom_names_amber` contain every 1- and 3-letter code |
| `test_residue_atoms_pdb_amber` | PDB and Amber templates agree on atom counts per residue |
| `test_amber_templates_element` / `test_pdb_templates_element` | Element column matches the atom-name-implied element |
| `test_Nterm_H_connectivity` | H1/H2/H3 wiring mutates only N, leaving other neighbors intact |

Sources: [test_build_definitions.py](tests/test_build_definitions.py#L18-L91), [test_build_definitions.py](tests/test_build_definitions.py#L94-L177)

## Extending the Definitions

Three extension scenarios recur, each with a defined touch-point list. **Adding a residue** requires: a template PDB in *both* `sidechain_templates/pdb_names/` and `amber_names/` (with identical atom ordering), an `aa3to1` entry (use a lowercase 1-letter code if it is a PTM/protonation variant, per the established convention), an explicit bond patch if any covalent distance exceeds 1.6 Å, and passing the atom-label parity tests. **Adding a force field** means creating a `__slots__` singleton class computing its own topology and registering it in the `forcefields` dict — the CLI-side plumbing is already generic (see [Component Plugin Pattern](20-component-plugin-pattern)). **Changing geometry constants** means updating the per-residue ratio tables *and* their comment annotations together, since the comments are the only record of the decimal values and standard deviations.

Any of these edits immediately changes builder output, so run the build-definitions test file first; the contract tests are cheap and fail loudly.

Sources: [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L136-L219), [build_definitions.py](src/idpconfgen/core/build_definitions.py#L509-L511), [test_build_definitions.py](tests/test_build_definitions.py#L78-L91)

## Where to Go Next

This page sits in the Infrastructure section between [Component Plugin Pattern](20-component-plugin-pattern) (how `components/` strategies wrap these constants behind uniform interfaces) and [Testing Strategy & Fixtures](22-testing-strategy-and-fixtures) (the broader test architecture of which this module's contract is a part). To see the definitions in motion, continue to [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble) for end-to-end flow, [Bond Geometry Strategies](8-bond-geometry-strategies) for how `bgeo_*` keys reach sampling data, [Sidechain Packing Methods](11-sidechain-packing-methods) for how `sidechain_templates` are placed, and [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture) for the per-worker singleton economics discussed above.


# Testing Strategy & Fixtures



This page documents how IDPConformerGenerator verifies itself: the tox orchestration layer, the pytest configuration contract, the shared fixture hub in `tests/tcommons.py`, and the curated data fixtures under `tests/data/` and `tests/readfiles/`. The suite follows a strict module-mirroring convention — every `test_lib*.py` file maps to a library module in `src/idpconfgen/libs/`, while `test_cli_*.py` files exercise the CLI subcommands end-to-end. Understanding this architecture matters because the project's CONTRIBUTING policy makes passing the full tox suite a hard prerequisite for any Pull Request, and it requires new tests for all new code.

Sources: [CONTRIBUTING.rst](CONTRIBUTING.rst#L90-L120), [tox.ini](tox.ini#L5-L9)

## Test Architecture at a Glance

The testing stack has three tiers: **orchestration** (tox environments that standardize how tests run everywhere), **execution** (pytest with coverage and hypothesis plugins), and **provisioning** (the `tcommons.py` fixture hub plus on-disk data bundles). Tests are pure pytest — there is no separate unittest framework — and the `tests/` directory is itself a Python package (with `__init__.py`), which enables the idiomatic `from . import tcommons` relative imports seen across the suite.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph ORCH["Orchestration — tox.ini"]
        TESTENV["test env<br/>TOXTESTING=1 · usedevelop<br/>PYTHONPATH=tests"]
        LINTENV["lint env<br/>flake8 · isort"]
        PRENV["pr env<br/>changelog gate"]
        BUILDENV["build env<br/>sdist · wheel · twine"]
    end
    TESTENV --> PYTEST["pytest runner<br/>testpaths = tests"]
    PYTEST --> UNIT["Unit layer<br/>test_lib*.py · test_structure.py"]
    PYTEST --> CLILAYER["CLI layer<br/>test_cli_build · test_cli_pdbdl"]
    PYTEST --> INFRA["Infrastructure<br/>test_multicore · test_logger"]
    UNIT --> TC["Fixture hub — tcommons.py<br/>TmpFolder · TmpFile · path constants"]
    CLILAYER --> TC
    INFRA --> TC
    TC --> DATA["tests/data/<br/>CIF · DSSP · bgeo JSON · tar"]
    TC --> RF["tests/readfiles/<br/>I/O dummy files"]
    TC --> PDBIDS["tests/data/pdbids/<br/>real PDB structures"]
    PYTEST --> TOOLS["pytest-cov + hypothesis<br/>term-missing report"]
```

The `test` tox environment sets `TOXTESTING=1` and `PYTHONPATH={toxinidir}/tests`, installs the package in develop mode, and runs pytest with `--cov-report=term-missing --cov-append --hypothesis-show-statistics`. This environment contract guarantees that every developer and the CI run under identical conditions, with coverage accumulated across runs and hypothesis statistics surfaced for the property-based tests.

Sources: [tox.ini](tox.ini#L16-L35), [tests/\_\_init\_\_.py](tests/__init__.py#L1-L2), [tox.ini](tox.ini#L147-L167)

## The Tox Orchestration Layer

Tox is the single entry point for all quality gates — the project explicitly frames it as a "unified testing platform where all developers are forced to follow the same rules" in a controlled Python environment, matching exactly what GitHub Actions executes. Each concern is isolated in its own environment so you can run only what you need: `tox -e lint`, `tox -e build`, `tox -e docs`, `tox -e test`.

| Environment | Purpose | Key commands / tools |
|---|---|---|
| `test` | Unit + integration tests with coverage | `pytest --cov --cov-report=term-missing`, `hypothesis`, `coverage html/xml` |
| `lint` | Style and import hygiene (no install needed) | `flake8 src tests setup.py docs`, `isort --check-only` |
| `pr` | PR pre-flight: changelog completeness gate | `python devtools/check_changelog.py` |
| `build` | Packaging verification | `setup.py sdist bdist_wheel`, `twine check`, `check-manifest`, `bump2version --dry-run` |
| `radon` | Complexity and maintainability metrics | `radon cc`, `radon mi` over `src tests` |
| `docs` | Sphinx documentation build | `sphinx-build -b html docs dist/docs` |
| `safety` | Dependency vulnerability scan | `safety check` |

Note that the minimum tox version is pinned (`minversion = 4.14.2`) and `pybind11` is declared as a tox requirement — a consequence of the C++ extension backend, since `pyproject.toml` requires `pybind11~=2.6.1` in the build system itself. The `build` environment also wires in `devtools/clean_dist_check.py` as a pre/post step to keep the `dist/` directory clean around packaging checks.

Sources: [tox.ini](tox.ini#L1-L9), [tox.ini](tox.ini#L38-L50), [tox.ini](tox.ini#L52-L55), [tox.ini](tox.ini#L57-L83), [tox.ini](tox.ini#L85-L98), [tox.ini](tox.ini#L101-L104), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L4)

## Pytest Discovery Contract

Pytest configuration lives in the `[tool:pytest]` section of `tox.ini` (pytest stops searching other config files once it finds a section). Discovery is scoped to `testpaths = tests` and recognizes three filename patterns: `test_*.py`, `*_test.py`, and `tests.py`. The `addopts = -p pytest_cov` line force-loads the coverage plugin on every invocation, which is why the tox `commands` can simply append `--cov` flags. Coverage configuration is delegated to a separate `.coveragerc` file referenced by the tox commands.

| Setting | Value | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `testpaths` | `tests` | pytest never scans outside the tests package |
| `python_files` | `test_*.py`, `*_test.py`, `tests.py` | broader-than-default module discovery |
| `addopts` | `-p pytest_cov` | coverage plugin always active |
| flake8 per-file-ignores | `tests/*: D101,D102,D103` | test classes/functions exempt from docstring rules |

The flake8 relaxation for `tests/*` is deliberate: while production code enforces numpy-convention docstrings, test modules are exempted from `D101/D102/D103` (missing docstring in class/method/function), lowering friction for rapid test authoring without abandoning the convention in `src/`.

Sources: [tox.ini](tox.ini#L147-L167), [tox.ini](tox.ini#L108-L123)

## The tcommons.py Fixture Hub

`tests/tcommons.py` is the backbone of fixture provisioning. It is a plain module (not conftest.py), consumed via explicit imports such as `from . import tcommons` or targeted `from .tcommons import cif_example`. It provides three categories of infrastructure: **isolation context managers**, **path constants**, and **expected-value literals**.

The isolation primitives are `TmpFolder` and `TmpFile` — lightweight context managers built on `pathlib` and `shutil` that create directories with `parents=True, exist_ok=True` and silently delete on exit using `contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError)`. These are the suite's workhorse for write-side tests: every test that produces output artifacts (downloads, tar extractions, built conformers) wraps itself in one so that the repository tree stays pristine between runs.

```python
with tcommons.TmpFolder('downloaded_test') as DF:
    main([tcommons.cull], destination=DF, ...)
```

The path constants section anchors every fixture location relative to the test file itself (`Path(__file__).myparents()`, a custom `idpconfgen.Path` method that resolves the parent): `data_folder` → `tests/data/`, `iofiles_folder` → `tests/readfiles/`, and `pdbids_folder` → `tests/data/pdbids/`. Named constants then expose individual fixtures — `cif_example`, `cif_EOF`, `dict1tar`, `file_tar`, `example_dssp`, `EXPL_A`, the four `expl_a_bgeo*` JSONs, and the compressed test database `idp_db_test.tgz` — so tests never hardcode fragile relative paths.

Finally, `cif_example_headers` is a 21-element list of expected `_atom_site.*` column names used as ground truth in CIF parser tests, and `random_type()` returns a random builtin type (int, float, list, dict, None, set...) — the module's own docstring admits via TODO that Hypothesis would be the modern choice, yet it remains useful for cheap type-fuzz assertions.

Sources: [tests/tcommons.py](tests/tcommons.py#L9-L35), [tests/tcommons.py](tests/tcommons.py#L38-L74), [tests/tcommons.py](tests/tcommons.py#L76-L98), [tests/tcommons.py](tests/tcommons.py#L103-L117), [src/idpconfgen/\_\_init\_\_.py](src/idpconfgen/__init__.py#L45-L52)

## Fixture Inventory: tests/data and tests/readfiles

The data fixtures are organized by parser domain, and the naming encodes intent: valid files carry realistic identifiers (`cif_example.cif`, `1BTE_A.dssp`) while negative fixtures are explicitly prefixed `wrong*` or `cif_EOF`/`cif_no_atom_site` to signal malformed-input tests. The `tests/readfiles/` folder is dedicated to file/folder reading functions — it contains numbered dummy files (`file1`, `file2`, `file3`, `file6`–`file8`), a `file.list` with comment lines, and an `other_files/` subfolder, all documented in its README as "dummy files to test the file/folder reading functions."

| Fixture group | Files | Test domain | Example consumers |
|---|---|---|---|
| mmCIF variants | `cif_example`, `cif_example_auth` (auth vs label IDs), `cif_example_noasymid`, `cif_EOF`, `cif_no_atom_site`, `cif_nohash` | `libcif` parsing edge cases | `test_libcif.py` |
| DSSP records | `1ABC_D.dssp`, `1ABC_E.dssp`, `1BTE_A.dssp`, `1BTE_A_dssp4.dssp` (v4 format), `example.dssp`, `wrong.dssp`, `wrong2.dssp` | secondary-structure parsers | `test_libdssp.py` |
| Torsion databases | `EXPL_A_bgeo.json` + `_converted`, `_trimer`, `_res` variants | bond-geometry strategies | `test_build_definitions.py` |
| Container bundles | `files.tar`, `dict1.tar`, `dict1.json` | `libio` tar/JSON round-trips | `test_libio.py` |
| Retrieval lists | `cull.list`, `pdblist.list`, `path_bundle.flist`, `pdbs.fasta`, `fasta1.fasta`, `xmer_prob.col` | CLI pipelines, k-mer probabilities | `test_cli_pdbdl.py`, `test_xmer_probs.py` |
| Real structures | `pdbids/` (PFA1_A, PFA2_A, PFA3_A...), `EXPL_A.pdb`, `EXPL_B.pdb` | structure layer, sidechain packing | `test_structure.py`, `test_component_*` |
| I/O dummies | `tests/readfiles/file*`, `file.list`, `other_files/` | `libio` folder/list readers | `test_libio.py` |

Two fixtures deserve special mention. First, `idpconfgen_test_db.tgz` is a **compressed sampling database** extracted at test time by `libio.extract_from_tar` — this is what lets `test_cli_build.py` run the full conformer-building pipeline offline without downloading anything. Second, `cull.list` is a real RCSB culling list whose five entries (`12E8H`, `16PKA`, `16VPA`, `1A04A`, `6XY7AAA`) double as the network test's download targets, with exact line-count assertions (e.g., 1682 lines for `12E8_H.pdb`) pinning the expected content.

Sources: [tests/readfiles/README](tests/readfiles/README#L1-L2), [tests/tcommons.py](tests/tcommons.py#L47-L74), [tests/test_libio.py](tests/test_libio.py#L17-L28), [tests/test_cli_pdbdl.py](tests/test_cli_pdbdl.py#L18-L43)

## Testing Patterns and Conventions

The suite mixes five distinct verification styles, and recognizing which style a test uses tells you what it can and cannot guarantee. Parametrization is the dominant pattern for parser tables; pytest native fixtures (`tmp_path`, `capsys`) appear where standard tooling suffices; class-based grouping organizes behavioral families; and `pytest.mark.skip` quarantines known-hanging concurrency tests with honest reason strings.

| Pattern | Mechanism | Canonical example | What it verifies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data-table parametrization | `@pytest.mark.parametrize` over fixture/expectation tuples | `test_libcif.py` CIF line regex (3 cases), atom-name formatting (12 cases) | exact string transformations |
| Parametrized fixtures | `@pytest.fixture(params=[...])` | `cif_parsed` over `cif_example` + `cif_example_auth`; `bgeo_strategies` over "fixed"/"sampling" | one test body × many inputs |
| Class-based grouping | `class TestPDBID:`, `TestBuildOptions:` | PDBID equality/ordering suite; build option matrix | coherent behavior families |
| Negative testing | `pytest.raises(EXCPTS.CIFFileError)` | missing `_atom_site` headers, EOF-truncated CIFs | graceful failure paths |
| Property-based | `@given(st.text())` (Hypothesis) | `libpdb._nothing` identity over arbitrary strings | invariants across the input space |
| Cleanup-as-test | Alphabetically-ordered teardown test | `test_remove_folder` after `test_build_option_1` | resource hygiene |

> [!TIP]
> The class-based `TestBuildOptions` suite exploits pytest's **alphabetical method execution within a class**: `test_build_option_1` runs the parametrized builds and `test_remove_folder` — alphabetically after it — deletes the output folder and extracted database even if the build test failed (`shutil.rmtree(..., ignore_errors=True)`). This is deliberate ordering-as-cleanup, not coincidence, and it breaks silently if you rename the tests.

Skipped tests are explicit and documented rather than deleted: `test_multicore.py` marks all three chunked-pool tests with `@pytest.mark.skip(reason="something is halting this")`, preserving the diagnostic assertions for when the concurrency stall is resolved. Output capture is handled by pytest's native `capsys` fixture — `test_libio.py` captures stdout from `save_dictionary(output=None)` and asserts the exact printed representation, with an inline comment cheerfully calling capsys "crazy pytest undeclared variable!"

Sources: [tests/test_libcif.py](tests/test_libcif.py#L22-L42), [tests/test_libcif.py](tests/test_libcif.py#L129-L135), [tests/test_cli_build.py](tests/test_cli_build.py#L54-L86), [tests/test_libpdb.py](tests/test_libpdb.py#L15-L57), [tests/test_multicore.py](tests/test_multicore.py#L33-L45), [tests/test_libio.py](tests/test_libio.py#L184-L191)

## Verification Depth: From Strings to Geometry

The suite's strongest tests assert **physical quantities**, not just file existence. `test_cli_build.py::test_build_long` builds a 108-residue conformer in `--long` fragment mode and then re-parses the output with the `Structure` class to verify: contiguous residue numbering (`range(1, len(seq)+1)`), and at both fragment junctions (residues 49→50 and 99→100) a C–N peptide bond of 1.33 ± 0.05 Å plus CA–C–N, O–C–N, and C–N–CA angles within 10° of ideal values (116.2°, 122.7°, 121.7°).
