This pattern — build, re-parse, recompute geometry — is the project's gold standard for validating the conformer engine itself.

Error-path testing is equally systematic in the parser layer. `test_libcif.py` parametrizes failure injection over fixture *content* (reading `cif_EOF.cif` lines directly into the test), asserting `CIFFileError` for malformed inputs, and verifies positive-path invariants such as "exactly 545 atoms parsed" and "first five `label_atom_id` values are N, CA, C, O, CB" — content-level pinning that catches parser regressions invisible to smoke tests. The logger tests follow the same philosophy for failure reporting: `test_report_on_crash` raises a deliberate `TypeError` inside `report_on_crash`, then asserts that `ReportOnCrashError` propagates **and** that crash-report files (`*.testing_ROC`) were materialized on disk before cleaning them up.

> [!TIP]
> Notice the asymmetry between `test_cli_pdbdl.py` (pure network integration — it downloads five real structures from RCSB and asserts their line counts) and `test_cli_build.py` (fully offline via the packaged `idpconfgen_test_db.tgz`). When adding tests, follow this split: parser/geometry logic should be hermetic, while a small set of thin network tests guards the download pipeline end-to-end. Also note `test_cli_pdbdl` parametrizes over `ncores` in `[1, os.cpu_count() - 1]`, doubling as a multiprocessing regression check.

Sources: [tests/test_cli_build.py](tests/test_cli_build.py#L93-L128), [tests/test_libcif.py](tests/test_libcif.py#L59-L98), [tests/test_logger.py](tests/test_logger.py#L46-L64), [tests/test_cli_pdbdl.py](tests/test_cli_pdbdl.py#L12-L43)

## The PR Gate: Changelog Enforcement

Testing extends beyond code correctness into contribution hygiene. The `pr` tox environment runs `devtools/check_changelog.py`, a 22-line script that reads `CHANGELOG.rst` top-down and raises `ValueError` if it encounters a version heading (`v...`) before the first bullet (`*`) — mechanically enforcing CONTRIBUTING's rule that new additions must be summarized at the top of the changelog, before the most recent version subtitle. Combined with the CONTRIBUTING mandate that "before submitting a Pull Request, verify your development branch passes all tests" and that "if you are developing new code you should also implement new test cases," the gates form a three-point checklist: **tests pass, changelog updated, packaging intact**.

Sources: [devtools/check_changelog.py](devtools/check_changelog.py#L1-L22), [tox.ini](tox.ini#L52-L55), [CONTRIBUTING.rst](CONTRIBUTING.rst#L95-L120)

## Adding Your Own Tests

When extending the suite, mirror the established conventions: place pure-library tests in `test_lib<module>.py`, CLI tests in `test_cli_<command>.py`, register any new fixture paths in `tcommons.py` rather than hardcoding them, wrap filesystem side effects in `TmpFolder`/`TmpFile` or use pytest's `tmp_path`, and prefer parametrized tables over copy-pasted test bodies. Keep the offline/network split intact — hermetic by default, network only for download-pipeline guards.

## Where to Go Next

- To understand the systems these tests exercise, continue with [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture) — the `test_multicore.py` skips are directly relevant there.
- For the fixture formats themselves (CIF, DSSP, PDB fixed-column), see [Structural File Parsers](19-structural-file-parsers).
- To map test files to their production counterparts module-by-module, consult [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview).
- The bgeo JSON fixtures consumed by `test_build_definitions.py` are explained in [Bond Geometry Strategies](8-bond-geometry-strategies).

# Research Examples Library



The `example/` directory is IDPConformerGenerator's curated case-study collection: six self-contained research scenarios, each backed by a README walkthrough, real biological data assets, and — in two cases — working Python scripts that call the library's internals directly. Rather than toy fixtures, these are the workflows used for actual published systems (unfolded drkN SH3, human CNOT7, the D1D2 SNRNP complex, SLC26A9), organized so that each example builds on the database and vocabulary established by the previous one. This page maps the library, decodes each example's target skill, and shows intermediate developers how to reuse the advanced scripting templates for their own systems.

## Library at a Glance

The six examples split into two curriculum tracks plus a preprocessing utility. The **foundation track** (`small_peptide`, `drksh3_example`) produces the torsion-angle database that every downstream example reuses. The **LDRS track** (`cnot7_example`, `complex_example`, `slc26a9_example`) grows disordered regions onto folded PDB templates with increasing structural complexity. `AF_example` sits orthogonally as a preprocessing step for AI-predicted structures feeding either track.

| Example | Biological system | Core skill taught | Key committed assets | Primary subclients exercised |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `small_peptide` | 9-residue test peptide `EGAAGAASS` | Installation smoke test; full build pipeline | `cull100` (100-entry PISCES-format list), `probs8_ex.txt` | `pdbdl`, `sscalc`, `torsions`, `build`, `csssconv` |
| `drksh3_example` | Unfolded drkN SH3 domain (59 aa) | Production database; CSSS sampling; ensemble variation | `drksh3.fasta`, `cull.tar`, `drk_d2D.txt`, `probs8_25501_unfolded.txt`, `customFragments.txt` | `pdbdl`, `sscalc`, `torsions`, `build`, `csssconv`, `makecsss` |
| `cnot7_example` | Human CNOT7 deadenylase | N- and C-terminal IDR growth on a folded domain | `cnot7.fasta` | `ldrs`, `resre`, standalone `mcsce` |
| `complex_example` | D1D2 SNRNP sub-complex (chains A+B) | Multi-chain IDR detection and building | `D1D2.fasta` | `ldrs` |
| `slc26a9_example` | SLC26A9 STAS domain, 86-residue linker | Linker-IDR closure; API-level scripting | `SLC26A9_STAS.fasta`, `SLC26A9_IDR.fasta`, `slc26a9_shortcut.py`, `slc26a9_stitching.py` | `ldrs`, `build`, `resre`, `psurgeon`/`next_seeker` APIs |
| `AF_example` | AlphaFold/ESMFold/RoseTTAFold outputs | Confidence-score filtering of predicted templates | `remove_lowconfidence_residues.py` | `Structure` API script |

Sources: [README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L1-L111), [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L1-L198), [README.rst](example/cnot7_example/README.rst#L1-L107), [README.rst](example/complex_example/README.rst#L1-L52), [README.rst](example/slc26a9_example/README.rst#L1-L213), [README.rst](example/AF_example/README.rst#L1-L27)

The diagram below shows how the examples chain together: solid arrows mark curriculum dependency (later READMEs explicitly instruct you to have completed the earlier database), dashed arrows mark the `AF_example` filtering script feeding cleaned template PDBs into LDRS runs. Green = foundation track, blue = LDRS track, orange = preprocessing.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    SP["example/small_peptide<br/>smoke test · cull100 · EGAAGAASS"]
    DRK["example/drksh3_example<br/>'A Real Case Scenario' · reusable database"]
    C7["example/cnot7_example<br/>N-IDR + C-IDR tails · CNOT7/4GMJ"]
    CX["example/complex_example<br/>multi-chain N/L/C-IDR · D1D2/1B34"]
    SLC["example/slc26a9_example<br/>86-res Linker-IDR · 7CH1 · Python APIs"]
    AF["example/AF_example<br/>pLDDT filtering script"]

    SP -->|"pipeline walkthrough"| DRK
    DRK -->|"reusable database.json"| C7
    C7 -->|"single-chain ldrs"| CX
    CX -->|"multi-chain ldrs"| SLC
    AF -.->|"cleaned template<br/>-fld input"| C7
    AF -.->|"cleaned template"| SLC

    style SP fill:#e8f5e9
    style DRK fill:#e8f5e9
    style C7 fill:#e3f2fd
    style CX fill:#e3f2fd
    style SLC fill:#e3f2fd
    style AF fill:#fff3e0
```

Note on assets: every FASTA, probability file, culled list, and script listed above is committed to the repository, but the folded-domain **template PDBs named in the LDRS walkthroughs** (`4GMJ_CNOT7.pdb`, `1B34.pdb`, `7CH1_SLC26A9.pdb`) are referenced by filename rather than shipped — the `ldrs` runs in those sections expect you to supply the template matching the `-fld` flag.

Sources: [README.rst](example/cnot7_example/README.rst#L8-L14), [README.rst](example/complex_example/README.rst#L8-L14), [README.rst](example/slc26a9_example/README.rst#L8-L18)

## Foundation Track: Small Peptide to Production Database

The `small_peptide` example is deliberately scoped as an installation verification: its database is built from only 100 PDB IDs and the README warns it "will not be used further cases, much less in practice." The value is the complete five-command pipeline it demonstrates against tiny inputs. Input discovery starts from a PISCES-style culled list — only the first column (PDB ID + chain, e.g. `12E8H`) is actually parsed, and no header lines are allowed, a format exactly mirrored by the committed `cull100` file.

Sources: [README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L6-L14), [README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L37-L46), [cull100](example/small_peptide/cull100#L1-L6)

The pipeline itself is a fixed sequence of subclient invocations, each writing an intermediate artifact the next consumes:

| Step | Command | Input → Output |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Download | `idpconfgen pdbdl cull100 -u -n -d pdbs.tar` | culled list → `pdbs.tar` (stripped PDBs: only needed chains/residues retained) |
| 2. Secondary structure | `idpconfgen sscalc pdbs.tar -rd -n` | `pdbs.tar` → `sscalc.json` (seq↔DSSP map) + `sscalc_splitted.tar` (continuous chains) |
| 3. Torsion database | `idpconfgen torsions sscalc_splitted.tar -sc sscalc.json -o idpconfgen_database.json -n` | split PDBs → human-readable JSON torsion database |
| 4. Build | `idpconfgen build -db idpconfgen_database.json -seq EGAAGAASS -nc 10 --dloop-off --dany -n` | database + sequence → 10 conformers |
| 5. CSSS build (optional) | `build ... -csss csss_ex.json --dloop-off -n` | probability-guided conformers |

Sources: [README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L52-L77), [README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L84-L99)

The example also introduces the **CSSS (custom secondary structure sampling) conversion path**: a CheSPI `probs8_*` file is converted into a JSON of per-residue L/H/E probabilities via `idpconfgen csssconv -p8 probs8_ex.txt -o csss_ex.json`. Two grouping subtleties matter for reproducibility — CheSPI/δ2D structure codes (H/G/I/E/space/T/S/B) are collapsed into the three-way L/H/E classification, and this grouping is only consistent if the database itself was built with the `-rd` flag on `sscalc`; opting out requires building without `-rd` and passing `--full` to `csssconv`. All operations accept `-n` for core distribution (bare `-n` uses all threads but one).

Sources: [README.rst](example/small_peptide/README.rst#L84-L99), [probs8_ex.txt](example/small_peptide/probs8_ex.txt#L1-L9)

### drksh3: "A Real Case Scenario"

The `drksh3_example` README is explicitly titled *A Real Case Scenario* and is the example that every LDRS walkthrough points back to for database preparation. Its target is the unfolded state of the drkN SH3 domain, for which processed NMR chemical-shift predictions are committed directly: δ2D output (`drk_d2D.txt`) and CheSPI output (`probs8_25501_unfolded.txt`, BMRB ID 25501). The database step reuses the same `pdbdl → sscalc -rd → torsions` chain but against an extensive culled list shipped as `cull.tar` (the same list used in the project's main publication), unpacked with `tar -xf cull.tar`.

Sources: [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L1-L21), [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L22-L47), [drksh3.fasta](example/drksh3_example/drksh3.fasta#L1-L2)

What makes this example the intermediate developer's main reference is the breadth of `build` variations it documents — each producing a differently biased ensemble from the same database:

| Ensemble recipe | Distinguishing flags | Output folder |
|---|---|---|
| Loops-only, FASPR sidechains | defaults (loop search on, FASPR default) | `drk_L+_nosub_faspr` |
| Loops-only, MCSCE sidechains | `-scm mcsce` | `drk_L+_nosub_mcsce` |
| Backbone-only (pack later) | `-dsd` | `drk_L+_nosub_bb` |
| Helix + strand sampling | `--dstrand --dhelix --dloop-off -et 'pairs'` | `drk_H+E+_nosub` |
| δ2D-guided CSSS | `-csss csss_drk_d2D.json --dloop-off -et 'pairs'` | `drk_CSSSd2D_nosub` |
| Custom fragment sizes | `-xp customFragments.txt` | `drk_fragN_CSSSd2D_nosub` |
| Residue-tolerance substitution | `-urestol '{"R":"RK",...}' --dany` (EDSSMat50 columns 5,3,2) | `drk_ANY_sub532` |

Sources: [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L49-L63), [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L107-L130), [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L169-L198)

Three of these recipes deserve elaboration. **MCSCE integration** appears in two forms: in-process via `-scm mcsce` (with a memory warning recommending reduced `-n` thread counts), or the two-stage fallback where backbones are generated with `-dsd` first and the standalone `mcsce` binary is run afterward. **Custom fragment probabilities** replace the default size distribution — probabilities `(1, 1, 3, 3, 2)` over fragment lengths `(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)` — through a two-column TXT file whose committed example (`customFragments.txt`) maps size 1→1, 2→3, 3→3, 4→2, 5→1. **Residue tolerance** expands torsion sampling beyond strict residue identity by passing a JSON map (e.g., `"F":"FY","F":"FWL"`) derived from the EDSSMat50 substitution matrix.

Sources: [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L65-L105), [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L169-L188), [customFragments.txt](example/drksh3_example/customFragments.txt#L1-L5)

The example also demonstrates the third CSSS input path — building probabilities *from scratch* with `makecsss` when no chemical-shift predictions exist: `idpconfgen makecsss -cp 1-14 L 1.0|15-25 H 1.0|26-59 L 1.0 -o cust_csss_drk.json` hard-codes a helix for residues 15–25 of drkN SH3 and loops elsewhere. Together the three input sources form a complete conversion matrix:

| Probability source | Provided file | Conversion | Consumed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| CheSPI (`probs8_*`) | `probs8_ex.txt`, `probs8_25501_unfolded.txt` | `csssconv -p8 <file> -o <csss.json>` | `build -csss` |
| δ2D | `drk_d2D.txt` | `csssconv -d2D <file> -o <csss.json>` | `build -csss` |
| Manual ranges | none | `makecsss -cp '<ranges> <SS> <prob>|...' -o <csss.json>` | `build -csss` |

Sources: [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L127-L145), [README.rst](example/drksh3_example/README.rst#L147-L157)

## LDRS Track: Constrained Growth on Folded Templates

The three LDRS examples share one subclient (`ldrs`) but escalate the structural problem: terminal tails → simultaneous multi-chain growth → a long internal linker. The underlying taxonomy maps directly onto the `disorder_cases` dictionary in `ldrs_helper.py` (`0: "N-IDR"`, `1: "Linker-IDR"`, `2: "C-IDR"`), and each example exercises a distinct subset:

| IDR case | Definition | Exercised by |
|---|---|---|
| N-IDR | disordered tail before the folded core | `cnot7_example`, `complex_example` (both chains) |
| C-IDR | disordered tail after the folded core | `cnot7_example`, `complex_example` (both chains) |
| Linker-IDR (L-IDR) | disordered segment between two folded regions | `slc26a9_example`, `complex_example` |
| Multi-chain N/L/C combination | IDR cases on ≥2 chains in one run | `complex_example` |

Sources: [ldrs_helper.py](src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L49-L53), [README.rst](example/complex_example/README.rst#L16-L25)

### cnot7 — terminal tails and the MCSCE detour

The CNOT7 walkthrough constructs N- and C-terminal IDR tails on the folded deadenylase domain (template from PDB 4GMJ). The `ldrs` subclient detects tail boundaries automatically by aligning the FASTA (`cnot7.fasta`) against the template's primary sequence and flagging mismatches. The canonical run (`-etbb 100 -etss 250 -nc 100`) took roughly 3 minutes on 50 threads — useful as a calibration point for your own hardware.

Sources: [README.rst](example/cnot7_example/README.rst#L1-L14), [README.rst](example/cnot7_example/README.rst#L30-L55), [cnot7.fasta](example/cnot7_example/cnot7.fasta#L1-L6)

The example's distinctive contribution is its sidechain-quality guidance: FASPR packing may leave sidechain clashes against the folded domain, so two remedies are offered — tighten the clash tolerance with `-tol`, or adopt the backbone-first workflow (`-dsd`, `--dany`) followed by standalone MCSCE packing. The latter path introduces `resre` as a preprocessing utility: because MCSCE requires explicit protonation, histidines are renamed to `HIP` in bulk (`-pt 126:HIP,157:HIP,...`) before packing. Related residue-label substitutions (TPO→THR, SEP→SER for phosphorylated residues) are flagged in the README's opening note, with `resre` again suggested as the tool.

Sources: [README.rst](example/cnot7_example/README.rst#L16-L27), [README.rst](example/cnot7_example/README.rst#L57-L100)

### complex — multi-chain detection

The D1D2 example (crystal structure of the human SNRNP core sub-complex, PDB 1B34) is the shortest README in the library because the complexity is absorbed by automation: one `ldrs` command builds N-IDR, L-IDR, and C-IDR cases on **both** chains A and B simultaneously (~1 hour on 10 threads). The critical input contract is that `D1D2.fasta` must contain sequences for *all* chains — including any you do not want IDR-processed — because chain-to-sequence assignment is inferred from multi-chain detection in the FASTA. The committed FASTA demonstrates the exact header format (`>1B34_1|Chain A|...`).

Sources: [README.rst](example/complex_example/README.rst#L9-L14), [README.rst](example/complex_example/README.rst#L16-L42), [D1D2.fasta](example/complex_example/D1D2.fasta#L1-L4)

For the algorithms that make single-command multi-chain building possible, see [Multi-chain Complex Modeling](16-multi-chain-complex-modeling); the `ldrs` subcommand's full parameter surface is covered in [LDRS Workflow Overview](14-ldrs-workflow-overview).

### slc26a9 — the long-linker problem

The SLC26A9 example models an 86-residue IDR (residues 568–652) connecting two folded parts of the STAS domain (template from PDB 7CH1), and its README is the longest in the library because it documents both the built-in and script-assisted solutions to the same problem. The built-in path offers two loop-closure strategies: the default `--loop-closure ccd`, which attempts to close every backbone onto both folded ends using a clash-aware damped least-squares method, and `--loop-closure next_seeker`, which builds halves from each side independently and joins matching pairs. The README's rules of thumb are explicit: `next_seeker` demands very large libraries beyond ~40-residue linkers; past ~100 residues, `ccd` is the only practical choice. A defining property of the closure is that sampled bond lengths, bond angles, and ω angles never change, and φ/ψ only shift within bounded amounts — closed loops retain IDPConformerGenerator's torsion sampling rather than being fitted to the gap. Failure reasons (`final_endpoint`, `omega`, `energy`, `folded_clash`, `folded_overlap`) are logged per round, and `--membrane` extends the clash environment to bilayer atoms.

Sources: [README.rst](example/slc26a9_example/README.rst#L60-L112), [README.rst](example/slc26a9_example/README.rst#L113-L133)

For the closure mathematics behind these two modes, see [Loop Closure Algorithms](15-loop-closure-algorithms).

## Advanced Scripting Templates: slc26a9's Python Entry Points

The most architecturally significant content in the library is not the walkthroughs but the two committed scripts — they are working examples of *programmatic* IDPConformerGenerator use, importing internal machinery rather than shelling out to the CLI. Both scripts are parameterized by **editing variables at the top of the file**, not by command-line arguments, and are intended to run inside the `idpconfgen` environment.

| API element | Imported from | Role in the scripts |
|---|---|---|
| `Structure`, `parse_pdb_to_array`, `structure_to_pdb`, `write_PDB`, column constants | `idpconfgen.libs.libstructure` | PDB parsing, atom-column access, output writing |
| `pool_function` | `idpconfgen.libs.libmulticore` | Worker-pool parallelization of per-conformer jobs |
| `align_coords`, `count_clashes` | `idpconfgen.ldrs_helper` | Rigid-body alignment of IDR halves onto folded anchors; clash counting with explicit `max_clash`/`tolerance` |
| `next_seeker` | `idpconfgen.ldrs_helper` | Pairwise matching of N-half and C-half conformer libraries |
| `psurgeon` | `idpconfgen.ldrs_helper` | Surgical stitching of all-atom IDR models onto the template |

Sources: [slc26a9_shortcut.py](example/slc26a9_example/slc26a9_shortcut.py#L1-L27), [slc26a9_stitching.py](example/slc26a9_example/slc26a9_stitching.py#L1-L23), [ldrs_helper.py](src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L1-L46)

The six-step advanced workflow decouples sampling from stitching so the expensive steps parallelize independently: (1) generate 10,000 backbone-only IDR conformers with `build -dsd` (the README notes more is better for sampling diversity); (2) create the working folders (`slc26a9_cterm`, `slc26a9_nterm`, `slc26a9_matches`, `slc26a9_results`, `slc26a9_sidechains`); (3) run `slc26a9_shortcut.py`, which uses `pool_function` to align every backbone against the C-terminal anchor, then the N-terminal anchor, then executes `next_seeker` across the two half-libraries; (4) run `slc26a9_stitching.py`, whose `psurgeon` call attaches each matched IDR to the folded domain; (5) `resre` renames post-stitch histidines to `HIP`; (6) standalone `mcsce` packs sidechains. The README's performance notes reward reading: splitting conformer folders across cluster jobs parallelizes both `next_seeker` and `mcsce`, and the shortcut path needs only ~8 GB RAM for a 221-residue IDR in one to two days.

Sources: [README.rst](example/slc26a9_example/README.rst#L135-L194), [slc26a9_shortcut.py](example/slc26a9_example/slc26a9_shortcut.py#L107-L159), [README.rst](example/slc26a9_example/README.rst#L195-L213)

> [!TIP]
> The shortcut script hard-codes its parallelism — line 112 reads `ncores = 32  # MUST BE CHANGED to number of actual CPUs for multiprocessing` — and likewise expects all folder paths to be edited in-file before execution. Treating these scripts as copy-and-run utilities is the most common integration mistake; they are templates meant to be adapted per system (the README even names the editable `case`, `lower`, `upper` variables in `slc26a9_stitching.py`).

A second subtlety lives in the FASTA convention for internal IDRs: the LDRS growth logic assumes an N-IDR-like geometry at the C-terminal side of the first folded domain and a C-IDR-like geometry at the N-terminal side of the second, so the dedicated `SLC26A9_IDR.fasta` carries **two overlapping residues at each junction** ("QK" and "LA" — visible as the leading `QK` and trailing `LA` of the committed sequence) relative to the full `SLC26A9_STAS.fasta`.

Sources: [slc26a9_shortcut.py](example/slc26a9_example/slc26a9_shortcut.py#L107-L121), [README.rst](example/slc26a9_example/README.rst#L135-L156), [SLC26A9_IDR.fasta](example/slc26a9_example/SLC26A9_IDR.fasta#L1-L3), [SLC26A9_STAS.fasta](example/slc26a9_example/SLC26A9_STAS.fasta#L1-L3)

These scripts double as the most concrete illustration of the library's extension surface; for the underlying design pattern, see [Component Plugin Pattern](20-component-plugin-pattern), and for the worker-pool mechanics invoked via `pool_function`, see [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture).

## Preprocessing AI-Predicted Structures: AF_example

Despite the name similarity, `AF_example` is **not** the AlphaFlex database (covered in [AlphaFlex Proteome Ensembles](24-alphaflex-proteome-ensembles)); it is a preprocessing utility for using AlphaFold/ESMFold/RoseTTAFold predictions as `ldrs` folded templates. Since `ldrs` accepts any PDB/mmCIF template, the problem is that predicted structures carry disordered low-confidence regions that must be removed first — which is exactly what `remove_lowconfidence_residues.py` automates by thresholding the B-factor column (where pLDDT scores are stored) and rewriting the PDB with corrected serial numbers.

| Predictor | Score stored in B-factor column | Recommended threshold | Comparison direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| AlphaFold | pLDDT (0–100 scale) | `70` | keep `s > threshold` |
| ESMFold | pLDDT (0–1 scale) | `0.7` | keep `s > threshold` |
| RoseTTAFold full-model | distance in Ångströms | `5.0` | **flip to `s < threshold`** |

Sources: [README.rst](example/AF_example/README.rst#L1-L14), [remove_lowconfidence_residues.py](example/AF_example/remove_lowconfidence_residues.py#L1-L43)

> [!TIP]
> The threshold comparison is not parameterized: the script's loop keeps rows where `s > threshold` (line 33), so RoseTTAFold — whose B-factor column holds distances rather than confidences — requires manually flipping the operator to `<` at the comment marked "Change the comparison operator here" (lines 30–31). The thresholds themselves are plain variables at the bottom of the file, alongside `input_file`/`output_file`, all of which must be edited before running.

The README closes with a qualitative warning that the script cannot catch: short *confident* segments sandwiched between large unconfident stretches (e.g., 2 confident residues among 10 unconfident ones) survive filtering but should be removed manually in a molecular viewer such as PyMOL for optimal `ldrs` performance. A template-formatting note from the SLC26A9 README applies here too — predicted template PDBs must carry the element symbol in the second-to-last atom column, which PyMOL's *Export Molecule* adds automatically.

Sources: [README.rst](example/AF_example/README.rst#L16-L27), [remove_lowconfidence_residues.py](example/AF_example/remove_lowconfidence_residues.py#L29-L55), [README.rst](example/slc26a9_example/README.rst#L135-L145)

## Choosing Your Entry Point

For a developer arriving fresh, the library encodes a deliberate reading order, and the cross-references inside the READMEs make it explicit: `cnot7_example`, `complex_example`, and `slc26a9_example` all defer database construction to the drksh3 "Real Case Scenario", while drksh3 itself positions `small_peptide` as the introduction. The recommended progression through this documentation catalog follows the same spine:

1. **[Tutorial: First Conformer Ensemble](4-tutorial-first-conformer-ensemble)** — guided first run before touching the examples.
2. **`small_peptide`** — verify your installation reproduces the five-command pipeline end to end.
3. **`drksh3_example`** — build your reusable production database and learn every `build` variation.
4. **[LDRS Workflow Overview](14-ldrs-workflow-overview)** → `cnot7_example` → **[Multi-chain Complex Modeling](16-multi-chain-complex-modeling)** → `complex_example` → **[Loop Closure Algorithms](15-loop-closure-algorithms)** → `slc26a9_example`.
5. **`AF_example`** — if your folded templates come from structure prediction rather than experiment.
6. **`slc26a9_shortcut.py` / `slc26a9_stitching.py`** — when CLI throughput caps out, adopt the scripting templates for cluster-scale runs.

Each example's README also links to reference output archives (hosted externally for the LDRS tutorials) so you can validate your runs against expected results before adapting the workflows to your own protein systems.

# AlphaFlex Proteome Ensembles



This page documents the **AlphaFlex (AFX-IDPCG) proteome-scale ensemble methodology** as distributed inside IDPConformerGenerator: the `alphaflex/` data bundle describing predicted disorder across the human proteome, the preprocessing tools that convert AlphaFold-family predictions into usable templates, and the `ldrs` subclient that rebuilds disordered regions as all-atom ensembles. Unlike the sequence-first pipeline documented in [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble), the AlphaFlex route starts from a full-length predicted structure and regenerates only the disordered segments — a strategy that scales to thousands of proteins.

## The `alphaflex/` Data Bundle

The repository ships AlphaFlex as a **data-plus-protocols bundle** rather than integrated Python modules: the three JSON databases are versioned with the package, while the executable protocol scripts are intentionally *archived inside a `.zip` file* to prevent them from interfering with the main IDPConformerGenerator package. The canonical, complete archive lives in the companion Zenodo repository referenced by the bundle README.

| File | Role | Structure |
|---|---|---|
| `AlphaFlex_database_July2024_v2.json` | Proteome-wide disorder annotation | JSON dictionary: key = UniProt ID; values = IDR boundaries (`idrs`), mean PAEs between folded (F) and disordered (D) regions (`mean_pae`), and folded–folded domain `interactions` where mean PAE < 15 Å |
| `AF2_9606_HUMAN_v4_num_residues.json` | Protein length index | UniProt ID → total residue count, one entry per protein in the AlphaFold2 Human v4 (taxid 9606) database |
| `AF2_9606_HUMAN_v4_sequences.json` | Sequence companion | Full-length protein sequences paired with the length index (the README refers to this companion as a FASTA-style sequence source) |
| Archived `.zip` (per README) | AFX-IDPCG protocol scripts | Building, analysis, benchmarking, and scoring scripts, including a `transmembrane` subfolder |

The length index is verifiably a flat map — its opening records (`"A1A580": 65`, `"Q5VUM1": 108`, ...) confirm the UniProt-keyed integer schema, and the file contains roughly 20,506 entries, matching the coverage of the AF2 Human v4 proteome.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph bundle["alphaflex/ bundle (versioned in repo)"]
        DB["AlphaFlex_database_July2024_v2.json<br/>UniProt → idrs, mean_pae, interactions"]
        NR["..._num_residues.json<br/>UniProt → length (~20,506 proteins)"]
        SEQ["..._sequences.json<br/>full-length sequences"]
        ZIP["archived .zip<br/>AFX-IDPCG protocol scripts"]
    end
    DB --> PS["proteome selection &amp; annotation<br/>(protocol scripts)"]
    NR --> PS
    SEQ --> PS
    AF2["AlphaFlex / AF2 predicted structure<br/>pLDDT in B-factor column"] --> FF["confidence filtering"] --> LDRS["idpconfgen ldrs"] --> ENS["per-protein IDP ensembles"]
    PS --> LDRS
    ZIP -. canonical archive .-> ZEN[("Zenodo<br/>records/17684897")]
```

Note the split of responsibilities: the JSON databases feed *proteome-level selection and annotation* (which proteins, where are their IDRs, which folded domains interact), while `ldrs` consumes *per-protein inputs* (a filtered template, a FASTA, a torsion database). The bundle never replaces the torsion-database machinery documented in [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling).

Sources: [alphaflex/README.rst](/alphaflex/README.rst#L1-L22), [AF2_9606_HUMAN_v4_num_residues.json](/alphaflex/AF2_9606_HUMAN_v4_num_residues.json#L1-L5), [AF2_9606_HUMAN_v4_sequences.json](/alphaflex)

## Why the Entry Point Changes

In the canonical pipeline, IDPConformerGenerator builds an entire conformer from sequence alone. The AlphaFlex route instead exploits a **structure-first invariant**: the folded domains of a predicted structure are trustworthy enough to keep, while disordered regions — exactly the parts AlphaFold-family models represent poorly — are *re-sampled* from experimental torsion statistics. The `ldrs` subclient implements this as "filling in the tails of folded proteins with IDRs", building from the same torsion/secondary-structure database produced by `idpconfgen torsions`.

| Dimension | Canonical `build` route | AlphaFlex `ldrs` route |
|---|---|---|
| Input | FASTA sequence only | Predicted full-length PDB/mmCIF (`-fld`) + FASTA (`-seq`) + torsion DB (`-db`) |
| Folded domains | Not modeled (fully disordered input) | Fixed template; disorder rebuilt around them |
| Disordered regions | Entire chain sampled | N-IDRs, Linker-IDRs, C-IDRs detected and rebuilt per case |
| Proteome scaling | Per-protein, de novo | Proteome database (`idrs`, PAE) drives candidate selection |
| Multi-chain | Via complex examples | Native `MULTICHAIN` handling in `ldrs` |

The disorder detection is explicit in the engine: `ldrs_helper.py` enumerates three topology cases — `0: "N-IDR"`, `1: "Linker-IDR"`, `2: "C-IDR"` — and junction finding splices folded rows against these regions. The full mechanics of junction discovery and splicing are covered in [LDRS Workflow Overview](14-ldrs-workflow-overview); here we focus on the proteome-facing contract.

Sources: [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1-L15), [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L1-L5), [ldrs_helper.py](/src/idpconfgen/ldrs_helper.py#L25-L30)

## Preprocessing Predictions: Confidence Filtering

AlphaFlex and AlphaFold2 predictions ship with **per-residue confidence in the B-factor column** (`col_temp` in IDPConformerGenerator's `Structure` API). Before such a file can serve as an `ldrs` template, low-confidence residues must be removed so the remaining folded segments are rigid anchors. The bundled example automates this: it loads the structure into the column-oriented `data_array`, filters rows whose B-factor fails the threshold, renumbers atom serials, and re-serializes with `structure_to_pdb`.

The thresholds are **predictor-specific** because each method encodes confidence differently:

| Predictor | Confidence metric | Recommended threshold | Operator |
|---|---|---|---|
| AlphaFold / AlphaFlex | pLDDT (0–100 scale) | `70` | `>` (keep) |
| ESMFold | pLDDT (0–1 scale) | `0.7` | `>` (keep) |
| RoseTTAFold (full-model) | FAPE in Å | `5.0` | `<` (keep) — requires flipping the comparison |

> [!TIP]
> These thresholds are hard-coded at the bottom of `remove_lowconfidence_residues.py` (`input_file`, `output_file`, `threshold`) — you edit the script in place before running it, rather than passing command-line arguments. Also note the operator change for RoseTTAFold flagged in the script comments: its metric is a distance error where *low* is good.

The project documentation itself warns that automated filtering can leave **orphan confident segments** — two confident residues stranded between ten unconfident ones — and recommends manual cleanup in PyMOL when the confidence landscape is fragmented. This example is not just bundled; it is wired into the official usage documentation via an RST `include` directive, making it the sanctioned entry step of the AlphaFlex workflow.

Sources: [example/AF_example/README.rst](/example/AF_example/README.rst#L4-L27), [remove_lowconfidence_residues.py](/example/AF_example/remove_lowconfidence_residues.py#L16-L50), [usage.rst](/docs/usage.rst#L118-L123)

## Driving `ldrs` with AlphaFlex Templates

The `ldrs` subclient is registered in the CLI dispatcher alongside the core database-creation routines (`pdbdl`, `sscalc`, `torsions`, `build`), and its `main()` exposes the full parameter surface below. For proteome-scale AlphaFlex runs, three behavioral groups matter most: **loop closure strategy** for Linker-IDRs, **fragmenting** of long terminal IDRs, and **template-aware flags** (`--membrane`, `--stitching-off`) that adapt to predicted-structure quirks.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["AlphaFlex/AF2 prediction<br/>pLDDT in B-factor"] --> B["remove_lowconfidence_residues.py<br/>threshold 70 (pLDDT)"]
    B --> C["filtered template → -fld"]
    S["target FASTA → -seq"] --> D["idpconfgen ldrs"]
    T["torsions.json → -db"] --> D
    C --> D
    D --> E{"IDR topology"}
    E -->|"N-IDR / C-IDR"| F["fragmented build<br/>≤150 residues per fragment"]
    E -->|"Linker-IDR"| G["--loop-closure<br/>ccd (default) | next_seeker"]
    F --> H["stitching, clash &amp; energy filter<br/>sidechain packing"]
    G --> H
    H --> I["all-atom conformer ensemble<br/>(-nc per protein)"]
```

| Flag | Purpose | Default / Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `-fld / --folded-structure` | Predicted folded template (PDB) | Required; skip chains in multi-chain templates by supplying identical `-seq` FASTA |
| `--loop-closure` | Linker-IDR closure method: `ccd` (torsion-space, clash-aware damped least squares) or `next_seeker` (grow from both ends, join at meeting) | `ccd`; recommended even for long L-IDRs (~17× faster than `next_seeker`) |
| `--ccd-max-trials` | Backbone conformer trials per core per Linker-IDR conformer, per round | `100`; rounds stall after 5 without new distinct loops |
| `--membrane` | Template carries a PPM v3 / CHARMM-GUI bilayer | Off; required for membrane-protein predictions |
| `--stitching-off` | Skips stitching; IDRs only aligned + clash-checked, enables temporary retention | Off |
| Long-IDR fragmenting | N-IDRs, C-IDRs, and long `next_seeker` halves built in fragments ≤150 residues, chained | Automatic per docstring |
| `-tol / --clash-tolerance` | Spherical clash allowance (0.0–1.0; 0.5 ⇒ max 40 clashes, 0.4 Å tolerance) | `0.5` |
| `-nc / --nconfs`, `-nc`-style scaling with `--ncores` | Ensemble size and parallelism | 1 conformer, 1 core |

> [!TIP]
> The `ccd` loop-closure default exists precisely because proteome-scale runs hit long Linker-IDRs: the changelog explicitly recommends `ccd` for L-IDRs longer than 40 residues as ~17× faster with more diversity (verified on the D1D2 complex example). `next_seeker` remains valuable when you can afford very large libraries — its halves are now compared backbone-first via a single KD-tree pass, with sidechains packed only after closure.

Sources: [cli.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli.py#L35-L76), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L260-L460), [cli_ldrs.py](/src/idpconfgen/cli_ldrs.py#L1-L15), [CHANGELOG.rst](/CHANGELOG.rst#L12-L25)

## Proteome-Scale Environment and Protocols

Running the AFX-IDPCG protocol scripts requires the standard `idpconfgen` conda environment **plus a set of extra dependencies** that never enter the core package's requirements. This isolation is deliberate: proteome tooling churns faster than the validated building engine.

| Package | Purpose in the AlphaFlex protocol |
|---|---|
| `pdbfixer` (conda-forge) | Structure repair during ensemble building |
| `pdb-tools` | PDB file manipulation |
| `chardet==5.2.0`, `tqdm==4.67.1`, `biopython==1.85`, `mdtraj==1.11.0` | Parsing, progress, and trajectory/structure handling |
| `freesasa==2.2.1` | Surface chemistry profiling (scoring stage) |
| TMbed v1.0.2 (separate environment) | Transmembrane-region annotation (`tm02_1` step only) |
| UCBShiftv2 (Docker container) | NMR chemical-shift benchmarking |
| Pepsi-SAXS v3.0 | SAXS-curve benchmarking (bundled in the scripts `.zip`) |

**Transmembrane proteins** follow the same building logic but need an annotation pre-step: the `transmembrane` folder in the protocol archive implements a five-step pipeline (`tm01`, `tm02_1`, `tm02_2`, `tm02_3`, `tm03`). Only the TMbed annotation step needs the external environment — and its output (`step2_tmbed_uniprot_full_boundaries.json`) is pre-computed in the Zenodo repository, so you can skip TMbed entirely if you accept the published boundaries.

**Benchmarking and scoring** close the loop against experiment: ensemble SAXS curves via Pepsi-SAXS, chemical shifts via the UCBShiftv2 container, and solvent-accessible surface chemistry via FreeSASA. Canonical resources are the AlphaFlex preprint (`doi.org/10.1101/2025.11.24.690279`) and the Zenodo archive (`zenodo.org/records/17684897`) — treat Zenodo as the source of truth for the protocol scripts, since the repository copy is intentionally frozen.

Sources: [alphaflex/README.rst](/alphaflex/README.rst#L6-L30), [alphaflex/README.rst](/alphaflex/README.rst#L32-L43)

## Version Lineage of the AlphaFlex Integration

The changelog dates the integration precisely and shows the engine evolving to serve proteome-scale loads:

- **v0.8.0 (2025-11-26)** — introduced AlphaFlex methodologies and citation; the `alphaflex/` folder first appears.
- **v0.8.2 (2026-06-22)** — updated AlphaFlex methodologies, again pointing to the `alphaflex/` folder.
- **v0.10.0 / v0.10.1 (2026-10-28)** — added the `libccd` torsion-space loop solver and ported the fragment-by-fragment `build --long` logic into `ldrs` for IDRs longer than 150 residues; optimized `next_seeker` half comparison.

This trajectory confirms the architectural pattern: AlphaFlex *methodology* ships as data and archived protocols, while its *computational demands* flow back into the core `ldrs` engine (CCD closure, fragmentation, KD-tree comparisons). The algorithmic internals of those engine changes belong to [Loop Closure Algorithms](15-loop-closure-algorithms) and [Multi-chain Complex Modeling](16-multi-chain-complex-modeling).

Sources: [CHANGELOG.rst](/CHANGELOG.rst#L42-L45), [CHANGELOG.rst](/CHANGELOG.rst#L32-L35), [CHANGELOG.rst](/CHANGELOG.rst#L12-L23)

## Recommended Reading Path

To go deeper from here, follow the catalog in this order:

1. [LDRS Workflow Overview](14-ldrs-workflow-overview) — the engine mechanics behind every AlphaFlex ensemble.
2. [Loop Closure Algorithms](15-loop-closure-algorithms) — how `ccd` closes Linker-IDRs in torsion space.
3. [Multi-chain Complex Modeling](16-multi-chain-complex-modeling) — applying `ldrs` to multi-domain and multi-chain predictions.
4. [Research Examples Library](23-research-examples-library) — worked cases including the AF confidence-filtering example.
5. [UML Design Diagrams](25-uml-design-diagrams) — structural overview of the modules referenced above.

For the complementary sequence-first perspective that AlphaFlex bypasses, see [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble) and the torsion statistics it relies on in [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling).


# UML Design Diagrams



The `docs/UMLs/` folder is the design-time documentation layer of IDPConformerGenerator: a set of PlantUML sources (`.pu`) paired with pre-rendered SVG images that describe, in visual form, how the tool's command-line subcommands process structural data and how the internal parsing libraries relate to each other. This page walks you through each diagram, explains how to read the two diagram families used here (activity diagrams and class diagrams), shows how the diagrams map onto the actual code, and how to edit or regenerate them. No prior UML experience is assumed.

## The Diagram Inventory: Two Families, One Directory

Everything in `docs/UMLs/` follows a simple naming convention: `idpconfgen_<subject>.pu` is the editable PlantUML source, and `idpconfgen_<subject>.svg` is its rendered image. There are exactly eight SVGs and seven `.pu` sources — the eighth SVG, `idpconfgen_pipeline.svg`, is a special case discussed below. The diagrams split into two families that serve different readers: **activity diagrams** (flowcharts of what a subcommand does, step by step) and one **class diagram** (the architecture of the structural parsing libraries).

| Diagram pair (`.pu` / `.svg`) | Diagram type | Subject | What it documents |
|---|---|---|---|
| `idpconfgen.pu` | Class diagram | `libstructure`, `libpdb`, `libcif` | The `Structure` API and its parser dependencies |
| `idpconfgen_fetch.pu` | Activity diagram | `fetch` subcommand | Raw PDB/mmCIF download flow |
| `idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu` | Activity diagram | `pdbdl` subcommand | Download + cleaning + chain selection |
| `idpconfgen_sscalc.pu` | Activity diagram | `sscalc` subcommand | DSSP secondary-structure assignment |
| `idpconfgen_bbsplit.pu` | Activity diagram | `bbsplit` subcommand | Backbone splitting into continuous fragments |
| `idpconfgen_secextract.pu` | Activity diagram | `secextract` subcommand | Extracting segments by structure type |
| `idpconfgen_filter.pu` | Activity diagram | Database filtering | Two-layer fragment query design with timings |
| `idpconfgen_pipeline.svg` only | Activity diagram | Download stage (legacy) | An earlier revision of the download flow |

Sources: [idpconfgen.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen.pu#L1-L106), [idpconfgen_fetch.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_fetch.pu#L1-L57), [idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu#L1-L117), [idpconfgen_sscalc.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_sscalc.pu#L1-L129), [idpconfgen_bbsplit.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_bbsplit.pu#L1-L46), [idpconfgen_secextract.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_secextract.pu#L1-L26), [idpconfgen_filter.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_filter.pu#L1-L55), [idpconfgen_pipeline.svg](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pipeline.svg#L1-L64)

> [!TIP]
> `idpconfgen_pipeline.svg` is a legacy artifact, not a current pipeline map. Its embedded PlantUML source (lines 1–62 of the SVG) describes an early revision of the download flow — rendered with PlantUML 1.2020.05 — rather than the complete end-to-end pipeline. For accurate per-step documentation, rely on the per-subcommand `.pu`/`.svg` pairs.

## Reading the Activity Diagrams: The Data-Preparation Workflow

Six of the diagrams are **activity diagrams** — annotated flowcharts that trace a subcommand from `start` to `stop`. They use PlantUML conventions worth knowing before you read them: rounded boxes are processing steps, diamond-shaped nodes are decisions, `fork`/`end fork` blocks mark work that happens **in parallel** (in practice, across CPU cores), and `repeat`/`backward` loops mark the **chunked batch processing** used throughout the tool. These diagrams double as executable documentation because every one embeds real, copy-pasteable CLI examples in a light-grey "Examples" partition — for instance, `pdbdl`'s examples show the difference between downloading into a folder (`-d folder`) versus a tar archive (`-d pdbs.tar`) ([idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu#L7-L18)).

The six activity diagrams collectively cover the data-preparation pipeline that produces the torsion-angle database consumed by `build`. The diagram below shows where each UML artifact fits in that workflow:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph UMLs["docs/UMLs/ activity diagrams"]
        FETCH["idpconfgen_fetch.pu<br/>raw download"]
        PDBDL["idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu<br/>download + clean"]
        SSCALC["idpconfgen_sscalc.pu<br/>DSSP assignment"]
        BBSPLIT["idpconfgen_bbsplit.pu<br/>fragment splitting"]
        SECEXT["idpconfgen_secextract.pu<br/>segment extraction"]
        FILTER["idpconfgen_filter.pu<br/>query design notes"]
    end
    IN["PDB / mmCIF entries"] --> PDBDL
    PDBDL --> CLEAN["cleaned single-chain PDBs"]
    CLEAN --> SSCALC
    SSCALC --> DSSP["DSSP info JSON"]
    CLEAN --> BBSPLIT
    DSSP --> BBSPLIT
    BBSPLIT --> DB["idpconfgen_database.json<br/>built via the torsions step<br/>(no UML artifact)"]
    DB --> BUILD["build subcommand"]
    FETCH -.simpler alternative to.-> PDBDL
    SECEXT -.optional.-> CLEAN
    FILTER -.informs query layers of.-> BUILD
```

The most instructive of the six is the `pdbdl` diagram, because it documents the cleaning rules that define the whole database's quality. After tokenizing input into PDB IDs and chains, it filters out a hard-coded list of conflictive chains, then for each entry downloads PDB-format first (falling back to mmCIF), converts everything to one internal format, keeps only MODEL 1 and altLoc `None`/`A`/`1`, drops non-backbone atoms, non-ribonucleotides, and large ligands, and probes case variants of chain IDs before renumbering atoms and stripping insertion codes ([idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu#L20-L31), [idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu#L36-L62), [idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu#L64-L89)). The rendered diagram is worth studying directly:

![pdbdl subcommand activity diagram](https://github.com/julie-forman-kay-lab/IDPConformerGenerator/blob/main/docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pdbdl.svg?raw=true)

Two recurring design ideas appear in these flowcharts and are worth anchoring in your mental model. First, **multiprocessing is diagrammed as a `fork`**: the note beside `pdbdl`'s fork block states that in multiprocessing mode each core picks one PDB code, runs the entire block, and then picks another — a work-queue pattern reused verbatim in `sscalc` ([idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu#L93-L99), [idpconfgen_sscalc.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_sscalc.pu#L90-L93)). Second, **outputs accumulate per chunk**: both `pdbdl` and `sscalc` save results after each chunk completes, and `sscalc` additionally supports resumable runs via a `--complete` flag that merges entries from a previous run's JSON ([idpconfgen_sscalc.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_sscalc.pu#L31-L51)). For deeper background on these two mechanisms, see [Multiprocessing Architecture](18-multiprocessing-architecture) and [CLI Subcommand System](17-cli-subcommand-system).

Sources: [idpconfgen_fetch.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_fetch.pu#L5-L57), [idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu#L7-L117), [idpconfgen_sscalc.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_sscalc.pu#L1-L129)

The remaining three activity diagrams each capture a distinct stage with unique detail. The `bbsplit` diagram documents how PDBs are split at backbone gaps — detected via discontinuous residue numbering or discontinuous N, CA, C atoms — and notably reads `.pdb` files directly inside a tar archive *without unpacking it* ([idpconfgen_bbsplit.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_bbsplit.pu#L13-L32)). The `sscalc` diagram explains that the pipeline shells out to `mkdssp` via subprocess, and that this choice is swappable: the opening note states the pipeline "can be configured to others by dispatching different functions without altering the main pipeline" ([idpconfgen_sscalc.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_sscalc.pu#L4-L6)). Finally, `filter.pu` is a design-notes diagram for the `build` fragment query engine: it sketches the torsion-angle database schema (PHI, PSI, OMEGA, residue name, DSSP tag) and records measured query timings for its two layers — unique secondary-structure queries (~0.5–0.8 s) through length-range and motif combinations (~104 s) in the first layer, and FASTA sequence/pattern matching in the second ([idpconfgen_filter.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_filter.pu#L3-L17), [idpconfgen_filter.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_filter.pu#L19-L42)). The sampling engine that consumes this database is covered in [K-mer Torsion Probability Sampling](9-k-mer-torsion-probability-sampling).

Sources: [idpconfgen_bbsplit.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_bbsplit.pu#L13-L32), [idpconfgen_sscalc.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_sscalc.pu#L4-L6), [idpconfgen_filter.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_filter.pu#L3-L42)

> [!TIP]
> Two `.pu` files carry titles that have drifted from the subcommands they actually document: `idpconfgen_secextract.pu` opens with `:idpconfgen //pdbdl//;` and `idpconfgen_filter.pu` opens with `:idpconfgen //build//;`. These are design-time notes rather than rendered help text, so always confirm a diagram's true subject against its filename and the corresponding `cli_*.py` module before citing it.

## The Class Diagram: How the Parsing Libraries Fit Together

The seventh `.pu` file, `idpconfgen.pu`, is the only **class diagram** in the collection, and it documents the architecture that [Structural File Parsers](19-structural-file-parsers) describes in prose. It organizes three library packages and the dependencies between them. In UML class notation, `+` marks public members and `-` marks private ones; plain `object` boxes are module-level functions. The diagram places the `Structure` class — with its public API of `add_filter()`, `add_filter_chain()`, `add_filter_record_name()`, `build()`, `clear_filters()`, `pop_last_filter()`, `write_PDB()` — at the center of the `libstructure` package ([idpconfgen.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen.pu#L45-L59)), surrounded by module functions that implement PDB/mmCIF parsing and PDB writing ([idpconfgen.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen.pu#L61-L72)).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph LIBSTRUCTURE["package libstructure"]
        S["class Structure<br/>add_filter / add_filter_chain / build / write_PDB"]
        SP["structure_parsers dispatch"]
        PDB2A["parse_pdb_to_array"]
        CIF2A["parse_cif_to_array"]
        S2PDB["structure_to_pdb"]
    end
    subgraph LIBCIF["package libcif"]
        CP["class CIFParser"]
        ISCIF["is_cif"]
        CHAIN["find_cif_atom_site_headers → parse_cif_line → populate_cif_dictionary"]
    end
    subgraph LIBPDB["package libpdb"]
        ISPDB["is_pdb"]
        FMT["atom_format_funcs / format_atom_name / format_chainid"]
        SLICE["atom_slicers"]
    end
    SP --> ISPDB
    SP --> ISCIF
    CIF2A --> CP
    S2PDB --> FMT
    PDB2A --> SLICE
    S --> SP
```

The central architectural message of this diagram is that **PDB and mmCIF converge on one internal representation**. The `structure_parsers` dispatch checks input format via `is_pdb` and `is_cif`; CIF input flows through the `CIFParser` class into `parse_cif_to_array`; PDB input flows through `populate_structure_array_from_pdb`; and both produce the same data array that `Structure.build()` fills. Writing reverses the path: `structure_to_pdb` depends on the atom formatting helpers in `libpdb` ([idpconfgen.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen.pu#L88-L95)). This design is verified directly in the source: `libstructure.py` imports `CIFParser` and `is_cif` from `libcif` ([libstructure.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libstructure.py#L26-L29)), defines the `Structure` class whose docstring demonstrates exactly the `build → add_filter_chain → write_PDB` sequence shown in the diagram ([libstructure.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libstructure.py#L49-L62)), and `libcif.py` defines `CIFParser` as an mmCIF parser restricted to structural atom-site fields ([libcif.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcif.py#L8-L18)). The two final hidden arrows in the `.pu` source (`libstructure -right[hidden]-> libpdb`, `-left[hidden]-> libcif`) are purely cosmetic layout hints, not dependencies ([idpconfgen.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen.pu#L101-L102)).

Here is the rendered class diagram:

![Structural parser class diagram](https://github.com/julie-forman-kay-lab/IDPConformerGenerator/blob/main/docs/UMLs/idpconfgen.svg?raw=true)

Sources: [idpconfgen.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen.pu#L4-L106), [libstructure.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libstructure.py#L26-L70), [libcif.py](src/idpconfgen/libs/libcif.py#L8-L18)

## Choosing the Right Diagram for Your Task

Because the two families answer different questions, the fastest way in is to match your task to the diagram type:

| Question you are asking | Diagram family to consult | Notation to know |
|---|---|---|
| "What does subcommand X do, step by step?" | Activity diagrams (`fetch`, `pdbdl`, `sscalc`, `bbsplit`, `secextract`) | `fork` = parallelism, `repeat` = chunk loop, grey partitions = CLI examples |
| "Which part of the code do I need to modify?" | Class diagram (`idpconfgen.pu`) | `+` public / `-` private members, arrows = function-level dependencies |
| "What cleaning rules define database quality?" | `pdbdl` diagram, "filtering in"/"filter out" partitions | Color-coded partitions: green keeps, red drops |
| "How fast are database queries, and how are they layered?" | `filter.pu`, the two request layers | Embedded performance annotations in seconds |

Sources: [idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu#L42-L62), [idpconfgen_filter.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_filter.pu#L19-L42)

## Editing and Regenerating the Diagrams

The `.pu` files are plain text, so contributing a diagram change is a two-step workflow: edit the PlantUML source, then re-render the SVG locally and commit both files together. PlantUML is a Java-based tool that converts its text syntax into images — `plantuml idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu` produces the matching `.svg` next to it. An interesting property of these SVGs is that **the source is embedded inside them**: `idpconfgen_pipeline.svg` contains its full PlantUML source between the XML header and a trailing metadata block that records the rendering environment (PlantUML 1.2020.05, OpenJDK 11, Linux) ([idpconfgen_pipeline.svg](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pipeline.svg#L1-L64)). This means you can always recover a diagram's source even from a rendered file alone.

| Task | Action | Notes for beginners |
|---|---|---|
| Understand a subcommand | Read the matching `.svg` | Start with the grey "Examples" partition for runnable commands |
| Propose a workflow change | Edit the `.pu` source | Keep CLI examples in sync with actual flags in `cli_*.py` |
| Re-render after editing | Run PlantUML on the `.pu` file | Commit both `.pu` and regenerated `.svg` |
| Recover source from a rendered image | Open the `.svg` as text | Source is embedded; metadata footer shows the PlantUML version used |

Sources: [idpconfgen_pipeline.svg](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pipeline.svg#L1-L64), [idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu](docs/UMLs/idpconfgen_pdbdl.pu#L7-L18)

And to follow the database these diagrams describe into conformer generation itself, proceed to [Building Pipeline: Database to Ensemble](6-building-pipeline-database-to-ensemble).
